SUMMARY:
<summary>
This OECD report (2017) examines the intergenerational mobility of natives with immigrant parents across EU and OECD countries, comparing their educational and labour market outcomes with those of natives with native-born parents. Key findings include:

**Demographics:** Native-born persons with two foreign-born parents are a growing group, accounting for 9% of youth aged 15-34 in the EU and 11% of children under 15.

**Educational Outcomes:** There is a convergence in educational attainment across generations. Natives with immigrant parents have on average 1.3 years more schooling than their parents (vs. 0.7 years for natives with native-born parents). The educational gap between groups has almost halved within one generation. However, in many European countries, natives with low-educated immigrant parents have a lower probability of completing medium-level or higher education compared to peers with equally low-educated native-born parents. Natives with immigrant parents are also less likely to enrol in academic tertiary education.

**Labour Market Outcomes:** In Europe, the employment gap between natives with non-EU immigrant parents and those with native-born parents decreases with higher educational attainment. Higher parental education translates less into better labour market chances for children of immigrants. Natives with non-EU parents experience less occupational upward mobility—only 1 in 5 moves up the occupational ladder compared to about 1 in 3 for other groups. A remarkable 15% of natives with non-EU parents have a mother with no formal education (five times the rate of other groups).

**Key Drivers:** Language skills, parental education, early childhood education, school quality, and neighbourhood characteristics all affect intergenerational mobility. Educational aspirations are high among migrant families but insufficient without support structures. Immigrant mothers' labour market participation has a particularly strong impact on children's outcomes.

**Policy Implications:** Helping immigrant parents integrate is crucial for their children's success. Integration should be seen as a long-term investment. About a dozen OECD countries have policies to promote employment of children of immigrants in the public sector.

Using (anonymized) tax records, Chetty's research has transformed understanding of U.S. social mobility. The article presents 14 charts highlighting major findings:

1. The chances of moving from the bottom to top income quintile are lower in the U.S. than in other nations like Canada.
2. There is a strong relationship between parents' incomes and their children's adult incomes—inequality is strongly inherited.
3. Relative intergenerational mobility rates in the U.S. have been flat for decades.
4. Absolute mobility (how a person does compared to their parents) has sharply declined—most Americans born in 1940 ended up better off than their parents, but only half of those born in 1980 did.
5. Place matters significantly for mobility, with cities in the Deep South and Midwest having more sluggish mobility.

7. Housing vouchers that help families move to higher-opportunity areas significantly boost children's later earnings if moves occur before age 13.
8. There is a gender gap—boys growing up in low-opportunity places feel effects more strongly than girls.
9. Childhood poverty damages outcomes for boys more than girls.
10. Experienced kindergarten teachers boost earnings by $1,104 on average.
11. College education acts as a leveler, reducing the correlation between parents' income and children's adult incomes.
12. However, college attendance is strongly related to household income, making higher education a "great stratifier" in practice.
13. Inventors (as measured by patent acquisition by age 30) are much more likely to have been raised in affluent families.
14. Poverty is linked to life expectancy—poverty takes nearly 10 years off men's lifespan from age 40.

args.summary:
This report by the Georgetown University Center on Education and the Workforce (CEW), authored by Anthony P. Carnevale, Tamara Jayasundera, and Ban Cheah, analyzes how the Great Recession (which began in December 2007) affected workers of different education levels and demonstrates the clear "college advantage" during economic downturns. It is based on Current Population Survey (CPS) data from 2007-2012 and is accessible at cew.georgetown.edu/collegeadvantage.

KEY FINDINGS:
• The unemployment rate for all four-year college graduates was 4.5 percent (May 2012), while recent college graduates (ages 21-25) faced a rate of 6.8 percent—over 50 percent higher. Recent high school graduates faced unemployment near 24 percent.
• College graduate unemployment peaked at 6.3 percent during the recession, compared to 13.4 percent for high school graduates (peak in February 2010). New college graduate unemployment peaked at 11.1 percent in July 2011, while new high school graduate unemployment peaked at 30 percent in January 2010.
• Workers with high school diplomas or less lost about 5.6 million jobs during the recession and an additional 230,000 jobs in recovery (net -5,841,000). Workers with Associate's degrees or some college lost 1.75 million jobs but regained 1.6 million. Workers with Bachelor's degrees or better gained 187,000 jobs during the recession and 2,012,000 more during recovery—a net gain of 2,199,000 jobs.
• Nearly four out of every five jobs destroyed by the recession were held by workers with a high school diploma or less.
• The underemployment rate for four-year college graduates was 8.4 percent, versus 17.3 percent for high school graduates. One out of seven new college graduates was underemployed in May 2012, compared to nearly half of new high school graduates.
• College graduates still earn nearly twice as much as high school graduates, with the college earnings premium at 97 percent.

INDUSTRY IMPACTS:
• Even in blue-collar industries, better-educated workers fared better. In manufacturing, employment dropped 19 percent for those with a high school diploma or less but only 9 percent for those with Bachelor's degrees or better. In construction, employment dropped 24 percent for high school diploma holders versus 4 percent for college graduates.
• Manufacturing and construction accounted for nearly 5.2 million of the 7.2 million jobs lost; wholesale and retail trade added another 1 million in losses. Industries with high concentrations of college-educated workers (public administration, education, healthcare) held up relatively well, adding 1.5 million jobs.

GENDER IMPACTS:
• Men with Bachelor's degrees lost nearly 200,000 jobs in the recession, but gains by college-educated women more than offset those losses. Women with a high school diploma or less lost 2 million jobs, while men with high school diplomas or less lost 3.6 million.
• Two out of every three jobs lost by men were in construction and manufacturing. The recession prompted men to enroll in postsecondary education at faster rates than women, and men moved into fields traditionally dominated by women (such as nursing and healthcare) that are more "recession proof."
• Postsecondary enrollment grew by 7 percent in 2009 (after 1 percent growth in 2005) as workers sought shelter from the weak labor market, though growth slowed to 3 percent in 2010.

LONG-TERM TRENDS:
• Since 1989, employment growth has been driven entirely by workers with education beyond high school. The number of workers with a high school diploma as their highest attainment dropped by 14 percent from 1989 to 2012, while workers with some college or an Associate's degree increased 40 percent and workers with Bachelor's degrees or better nearly doubled.
• The shift toward more-educated workers stems from labor-saving technology (especially computing), automation of routine tasks, and globalization/offshoring of low-skilled jobs. Manufacturing shed 5.5 million jobs from 1980 to 2007 while healthcare and education added 11.6 million jobs.
• The report concludes that the recession "laid bare" the shortcomings of the American workforce, especially the lack of postsecondary education, leaving an urgent need to train workers for more skilled jobs.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243)Abstract

Job loss is an involuntary disruptive life event with a far-reaching impact on workers’ life trajectories. Its incidence among growing segments of the workforce, alongside the recent era of severe economic upheaval, has increased attention to the effects of job loss and unemployment. As a relatively exogenous labor market shock, the study of displacement enables robust estimates of associations between socioeconomic circumstances and life outcomes. Research suggests that displacement is associated with subsequent unemployment, long-term earnings losses, and lower job quality; declines in psychological and physical well-being; loss of psychosocial assets; social withdrawal; family disruption; and lower levels of children’s attainment and well-being. While reemployment mitigates some of the negative effects of job loss, it does not eliminate them. Contexts of widespread unemployment, although associated with larger economic losses, lessen the social-psychological impact of job loss. Future research should attend more fully to how the economic and social-psychological effects of displacement intersect and extend beyond displaced workers themselves.

**Keywords:**job loss, worker displacement, unemployment, socioeconomic mobility, psychological and physical well-being, social withdrawal

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243)Trends in and Risk Factors Associated with Job Loss

Widespread job insecurity, waves of job loss, and associated periods of unemployment and income loss have characterized the last several decades in the U.S. ([Farber 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R35); [Farley 1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R36); [Kalleberg 2000](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R56), [2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R57); [Kletzer 1998](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R63); [Wetzel 1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R90)). Most Americans believe that employment stability has declined ([Hollister 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R45)), and job displacement is now considered a common feature of the U.S. labor market. The macroeconomic trends commonly associated with worker displacement include: technological change; foreign trade and the shift to production offshore to take advantage of low-wage foreign workers; immigration; firms’ greater use of outside suppliers, subcontractors, and partners, and the paring down of the activities of the firm; the shift in U.S. consumption from manufactured goods to services; poor firm management; weakened labor unions; and regional and national economic downturn.

High levels of workers displacement marked the last four recessions in the U.S. The early 1980s recession convinced firms to utilize effective new equipment, shift production to modern plants, and lay off thousands of workers ([Farley 1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R36)). [Wetzel (1995)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R90) wrote: “Industrial firms that had prided themselves on lifetime paternalistic commitments to their production workers – largely men with average or below-average educational attainment – slashed employment … The abrupt contraction struck at the heart of the middle class by drastically impacting mature family men with strong labor force attachment, good work histories, and long job tenure” (p. 101). The economic recovery of the 1980s was marked by large employment gains; nevertheless, unemployment persisted at a relatively high rate and newly created jobs were in general of a lower quality than jobs from which workers had lost. The early 1990s recession was marked by the creation of flat organization and elimination of middle management positions. High levels, particularly during economic recessions, of job loss and unemployment characterize the U.S. labor market since 1990. In the 1990s through early 2000s, worker layoffs, once regarded as organizational failure, were increasingly utilized as a labor allocative process available to firms in order to preserve shareholder value. Ensuing waves of downsizing, reorganization, mergers and takeovers rewarded some individuals with great prosperity while others were threatened with displacement, unemployment, and downward mobility ([Baumol et al. 2003](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R3)). The recessionary period from the end of 2007 to mid-2009, the “Great Recession,” was deeper and more extensive than any other since the Great Depression of the 1930s ([Hout, Levanon, and Cumberworth 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R46)). The U.S. unemployment rate hovered around 9 to 10 percent in 2009–2011, the highest rate since the early 1980s recession and roughly twice the pre-crisis rate. The proportion of families with an unemployed member was roughly 12 percent in 2009, up from about 6 percent in 2007. The large increase in long-term unemployment in this most recent recession is suggestive of longer-term structural labor market changes ([Katz 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R58)).

While macroeconomic and firm-level factors influence the incidence of job loss and unemployment, a number of individual-level characteristics also govern the risk of displacement. Men and blacks and Hispanics had a higher probability of being displaced than women and whites in the 1980s; family background disadvantage, blue-collar and manufacturing work, low occupational status, low job tenure, and low levels of education likewise heightened the risk of job loss over this period (Brand 2005; [Farber 2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R34)). Job loss rates increased for women and for whites in the 1990s, as well as for college-educated and high tenure workers (Couch 1998; [Farber 1993b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R31), [1997b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R32), [2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R34)). While educated workers maintain a lower risk of displacement, the increased rates have nevertheless aroused public concern that the structure of job loss qualitatively changed over recent decades, increasing vulnerability to job loss across the population ([Fallick 1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R29); [Farber 1993a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R30), [1993b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R31), [2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R35)).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243)Estimating Effects of Job Loss

Abrupt changes in socioeconomic conditions provide a sort of “natural experiment” offering a stronger basis for inference than the usual practice of examining the covariation of outcomes with socioeconomic status that may arise from a variety of sources over an indeterminate period of time. The study of job displacement, thus, provides a unique opportunity to assess within individual changes in socioeconomic conditions that are relatively exogenous to individual characteristics. Indeed, scholars often explicitly describe the study of displacement as a purer way to estimate the effects of socioeconomic shocks ([Stevens 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R83)). Nevertheless, the study of displacement does not fully mitigate selection issues, as job loss is clearly conditioned by factors that are also associated with levels of subsequent outcomes. A primary concern in attempting to identify effects of job loss is the potential presence of unobservable characteristics that affect both worker displacement and subsequent outcomes. That is, we are left with the fundamental question of whether workers who were displaced from jobs have outcomes that are different than they otherwise would have been had they not been displaced. If employers make targeted decisions regarding whom to displace, there is a possibility that it is relatively less productive workers (e.g. lower levels of motivation, commitment, and ability), workers with physical or mental health issues, and socially inept workers who both are more likely to lose jobs and have worse economic and social outcomes. Scholars, however, have found few differences across several leading estimators of causal effects (including regression, matching, difference-in-difference and fixed effects models), suggesting a degree of robustness regarding the nature of the observed associations between displacement and life outcomes in the face of various technical assumptions and model specifications ([Brand 2006](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R5); [Coelli 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R20); Stevens and Schaller 2009).

Yet another strategy to deal with possible selection bias is to adopt a quasi-experimental strategy that tracks the well-being of workers following a plant closure. When an entire organization closes, it is unlikely that a workers’ specific characteristics are responsible for the displacement. Thus if the results for plant closings and more individualized lay-offs are similar, we have a firmer basis for claiming the validity of the effect estimates for the full population of displaced workers. Likewise, job losses occurring during recessionary periods, in which large numbers of individuals lose jobs, may provide better causal estimates of job loss ([Stevens 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R83)). A few caveats as to inferences we can make from mass layoff studies are nevertheless in order. While such studies make strong claims for having eliminated the influence of selection, plant closure studies are typically limited to specific populations (often blue-collar workers) in specific geographic areas, restricting generalizability to the U.S. workforce as a whole. That is, studies of plant closures ostensibly sacrifice external for internal validity. Some closure studies are also lacking a control group of non-displaced workers. Additionally, plant closure studies may still be subject to selection bias, as more qualified and adaptive employees may leave the plant upon word of the impending closure. The same can be said for studies of workers displaced during recessions.

Job losses due to layoffs and those due to plant closings, and job loss occurring in different economic contexts, may also produce different effects because they are potentially different treatment conditions. In the case of layoffs and job loss during economic expansions, the greater likelihood for discretionary dismissal of employees can call into question competency and character and act as a signal of below-average productivity, to the displaced workers, as well as to their families and communities, and in the labor market. If potential employers interpret layoffs as indications of ineptitude, hiring will be discouraged. The resulting difficulty of laid-off workers to secure suitable reemployment may result in greater long-term economic losses. Economic distress, alongside attribution of job loss to one’s own shortcomings, and the stigma of a layoff and resulting strained relations with colleagues, friends, and/or family members, can in turn lead laid off workers to lower self-esteem, anxiety, and depressive symptoms (Leana and Feldman 1992; [Miller and Hoppe 1994](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R70)). Individually laid of workers may also lack similarly strained workers to offer a network of support ([Miller and Hoppe 1994](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R70); [Brand, Levy, and Gallo 2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R7)). These circumstances contrast with that of job loss due to plant closings and loss occurring in economic recessions, in which clearly external influences, including the health of the macro-economy and firms’ decisions to restructure or relocate business units, provokes separation. Because such factors are clearly beyond the control of individual employees, plant closings do not involve a negative signal that raises transaction costs for displaced workers. Indeed workers displaced due to business closings are victims of an event that could befall anyone, and seldom perceive themselves as responsible for the job loss. Thus, such workers may endure lower economic and social-psychological burdens.[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#FN2)

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243)Economic Effects of Job Loss

Increasing job insecurity and displacement has motivated a large body of research on effects, beginning with economic losses. The average displaced worker experiences a long period of unemployment ([Brand 2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R4); Chan and Stevens 1999; [Fallick 1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R29); Farber 2003, [2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R34); [Kletzer 1998](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R63); [Podgursky and Swaim 1987](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R77); [Ruhm 1991](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R81)), but the duration has a high degree of worker variance ([Seitchik 1991](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R82)). Unemployment among displaced workers generally lasts longer during recessions than expansions ([Farber 1993a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R30); [Kletzer 1991](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R62), [1998](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R63)). The impact of job loss on careers is considerable even when workers do not experience long-term unemployment. Displaced workers suffer substantial earnings losses, which are generally more persistent than unemployment effects ([Brand 2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R4); [Cha and Morgan 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R14); Chan and Stevens 1999, [2001](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R15); Couch 1998; [Couch, Jolly, and Placzek 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R21); [Couch and Placzek 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R22); [Davis and von Wachter 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R24); [Fallick 1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R29); Farber 2003, [2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R34); [Jacobson, LaLonde, and Sullivan 1993](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R47); [Kletzer 1998](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R63); [Podgursky and Swaim 1987](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R77); [Ruhm 1991](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R81); [Seitchik 1991](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R82); [Stevens 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R83); [von Wachter 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R88)). [Couch and Placzek (2010)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R22) report an immediate 33 percent earnings loss and as much as a 15 percent loss six years following job separation. The cumulative lifetime earning loss is estimated to be roughly 20 percent, with wage scarring observed as long as 20 years post-displacement ([Brand and von Wachter 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R9); [Davis and von Wachter 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R24); [von Wachter 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R88); von Wachter, Song, and Manchester 2009). Reemployed displaced workers are more likely than their non-displaced counterparts to be employed part-time, and this likelihood has increased over time, particularly during recessions ([Farber 1993b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R31), 2003, [2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R34)). Displaced workers may also find, when reemployed, that their jobs are of lower quality in terms of job authority, autonomy, and employer-offered benefits in comparison to both the jobs they lost and those held by their non-displaced counterparts ([Brand 2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R4), [2006](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R5); [Podgursky and Swaim 1987](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R77)). Workers also withstand greater job instability for at least a decade following a displacement event ([von Wachter 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R88)).

While economic losses occur for displaced workers across demographic categories, across industries and throughout the skill distribution ([von Wachter 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R88)), there is nevertheless effect variation by worker characteristics. Displaced workers’ losses reflect both industry-specific decline and the loss of firm- and industry-specific skills ([Kalleberg 2000](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R56)). Older workers with higher pre-displacement tenure, those who change industries, and those who experience multiple job losses thus experience greater earnings losses ([Carrington and Zaman 1994](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R12); Couch, Jolly, and Placzek 2009; [Fallick 1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R29); [Jacobson, LaLonde, & Sullivan 1993](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R47); Stevens 1997; [von Wachter 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R88)). As greater skill transferability is expected for educated workers, employment, earnings, and job quality reductions are typically more pronounced for less-educated workers ([Farber 1997](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R32), 2003, [2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R34); [Kletzer 1991](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R62), [1998](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R63); [Podgursky and Swaim 1987](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R77); [Seitchik 1991](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R82)). Still, as the incidence of displacement for more educated workers has increased, the transition difficulties for such workers have increased as well.

While displaced workers’ economic costs are substantial during both economic recessions and expansions, losses are cyclical ([Couch, Jolly, and Placzek 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R21); [Davis and von Wachter 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R24); [Fallick 1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R29); [Farber 1993a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R30), [1997a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R32), [2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R34); [Jacobson, LaLonde, and Sullivan 1993](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R47); [Kletzer 1998](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R63); [von Wachter 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R88)). As few firms hire during economic contractions, displaced workers seeking reemployment are in a poorer negotiating position than during economic expansions. [Davis and von Wachter (2012)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R24) find that men lose an average of 1.4 years of pre-displacement earnings if displaced in mass-layoff events that occur when the national unemployment rate is below 6 percent, and lose 2.8 years of pre-displacement earnings if displaced when the unemployment rate exceeds 8 percent. Similarly, [Couch, Jolly, and Placzek (2011)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R21) find that long-term earnings losses for displaced workers during a recessionary period are about 2 to 4 times larger than for those observed during a period of economic expansion.

There is some debate over variation in economic losses by the specific form of job loss. Recent work (Kashinsky 2002; Stevens 1997; [von Wachter 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R88)) has questioned the findings of an influential study by [Gibbons and Katz (1991)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R43) that suggested that layoffs are associated with greater economic losses than are plant closings. [Gibbons and Katz (1991)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R43) argued that in the case of a layoff, the discretionary dismissal of employees acts as a signal of below average productivity, stigmatizing laid-off workers, resulting in large employment and earnings losses. On the contrary, a plant closing, in which all workers are terminated without discretion, does not carry a comparable performance signal, rendering earnings penalties less severe. Extending this argument to differences in earnings losses by economic context, we might expect countercyclical earnings losses, as the stigma associated with displacement during an economic contraction should be less than that during an economic expansion. However, as I note above, such losses are cyclical. In support of the evidence for cyclicality, we should expect larger earnings losses from job loss due to plant closings as such closures may indicate weak local or macro economic conditions. [Krashinsky (2002)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R64) argues that the [Gibbons and Katz (1991)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R43) result is driven by the fact that small plants are more likely to close, and that layoffs that occur from larger, higher-wage employment establishments result in larger earnings losses.[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#FN3)

Several mechanisms help explicate the large economic losses of displaced workers. Earnings and job quality declines are likely to increase with unemployment duration. Yet it is unclear whether this association is the result of length of unemployment itself, and possible stigma effects, or because those workers facing the greatest challenges in the labor market take longer to find a new job ([von Wachter 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R88)). Workers are also disadvantaged in the market if industries in which they were previously employed shift their operations elsewhere or permanently reduce their employment levels. Relatedly, lower job quality upon reemployment is a function of the loss of a high quality match between the worker and the job ([Fallick 1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R29)). While a worker generally only leaves a job voluntarily when he or she believes there are relative gains in career attainment to be made, displaced workers likely feel an urgency to find a new job and are in a poor position to perform a quality job screening ([Newman 1988](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R72)).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243)Non-Economic Effects of Job Loss

Job loss is a negative, often unpredictable event that entails a sequence of stressful experiences, from job loss notification, anticipation, dismissal, and often unemployment, to (in most cases) job search, re-training and eventual reemployment, often at jobs with lower wages and job quality. Yet the impact of job loss and unemployment is not limited to economic decline; it is also associated with considerable, long-term non-economic consequences for displaced workers, as well as for their families and communities. Displaced workers face psychological and physical distress, personal reassessment in relation to individual values and societal pressures, and new patterns of interaction with family and peers. Much of the work on the non-economic consequences of job loss is consistent with a large literature demonstrating a strong correlation between indicators of socioeconomic status and individual life chances and well-being. However, as displacement is a relatively exogenous labor market shock, its study enables a stronger causal link between socioeconomic circumstances and life outcomes. In this section, I begin reviewing individual worker effects on psychological and physical well-being, and then consider the consequences for families and communities.

### Job Loss and Psychological Well-Being

A large literature on mental health has focused on the impact of stressful life events, such as unemployment and job loss. Job loss disrupts more than just income flow; it disrupts individuals’ status, time structure, demonstration of competence and skill, and structure of relations. It carries societal stigma, creating a sense of anxiety, insecurity, and shame ([Newman 1988](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R72)). The loss of a job presents a source of acute stress associated with the immediate disruption to a major social role, as well as chronic stress resulting from continuing economic and social and psychological strain (House 1987; [Pearlin et al. 1981](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R76)). Research suggests that displaced workers report higher levels of depressive symptoms, somatization, and anxiety and the loss of psychosocial assets including self-acceptance, self-confidence, self-esteem, morale, life satisfaction, goal and meaning in life, social support, and sense of control ([Brand, Levy, and Gallo 2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R6); [Burgard, Brand and House 2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R10); [Catalano et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R13); [Dooley, Fielding and Levi 1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R25); [Darity and Goldsmith 1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R23); [Dooley, Prause, and Ham-Rowbottom 2000](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R26)): [Gallo et al. 2000](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R38); [Gallo et al. 2006a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R40); [Hamilton et al. 1990](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R44); [Jahoda 1981](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R48), [1982](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R49); [Jahoda, Lazarsfeld, and Zeisel 1933[1971]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R50); Kasl and Jones 2000; [Kessler, Turner, and House 1988](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R60), [1989](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R61); [Leana and Feldman 1992](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R65); [McKee-Ryan et al. 2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R67); [Miller and Hoppe 1994](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R70); [Paul and Moser 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R75); [Pearlin et al. 1981](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R76); [Turner 1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R87); [Warr and Jackson 1985](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R89)).[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#FN4) The increase in reported symptoms of depression and anxiety among displaced workers compared to non-displaced workers is roughly 15 to 30 percent ([Burgard, Brand, and House 2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R10); [Catalano et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R13); [Paul and Moser 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R75)). Leading explanations for why job loss and unemployment negatively impact well-being include lowered self-esteem, sense of purpose, and control; heightened apathy, idleness, isolation, and the breakdown of social personality structure; and a loss of the positive derivatives of participating in a work environment, such as skill use, time structure, economic security, interpersonal socialization, and valued societal position ([Darity and Goldsmith 1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R23); [Jahoda 1982](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R49); [Jahoda, Lazarsfeld, and Zeisel 1933[1971]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R50); [McKee-Ryan et al. 2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R67)).[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#FN5)

Although displacement is more of an exogenous shock than other types of job mobility, the possibility of omitted variable bias nevertheless threatens the validity of results associating job loss to subsequent outcomes. Of particular concern in the study of psychological well-being, workers with psychological distress and lacking self-confidence and morale may be those workers most likely to be displaced from jobs. Studies have used various approaches to address this selection problem, most often attempting to control for a range of factors that impact the likelihood of job loss and subsequent well-being. Studies continue to find an association, although often reduced in magnitude. For example, [Burgard, Brand, and House (2007)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R10) adjust for numerous social background characteristics, including baseline psychological health, and find a significant effect of job loss on depressive symptoms. Moreover, using meta-analytic techniques drawing on over 100 empirical studies, [McKee-Ryan et al. (2005)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R67) find consistency in results across multiple kinds of studies and hundred of data points suggesting a relationship between job loss and worker well-being. Studies based on plant closures, thought to be less prone to issues of selection, continue to find an increased risk of mental distress among the displaced ([Hamilton et al. 1990](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R44)).[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#FN6)

As is true with the economic consequences of job loss, the effects of job loss on psychological well-being vary by a range of factors, including demographic characteristics, socio-emotional skills and social support, and the economic context. While more disadvantaged workers may be more vulnerable to financial shocks ([Hamilton et al. 1990](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R44)), such economic adversity is a comparatively normative experience; by contrast, job displacement and socioeconomic decline may instigate an acute sense of deprivation among more advantaged families whose peers tend to be likewise advantaged and for whom displacement is a considerable shock ([Brand and Simon Thomas 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R8)). That is, judgments of disruptive events depend on the experience of similar situations in the past, and higher levels of past adversity may lessen the impact of current adversity ([Clark, Georgellis, and Sanfey 2001](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R19); [Dooley, Prause, and Ham-Rowbottom 2000](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R26)). If the difficulties posed by job loss and unemployment are primarily financial, then reemployment has the potential to remove much of the stress, particularly if the income is comparable to what the worker had been earning. If job loss profoundly alters one’s self-concept and place in society, however, the extent to which reemployment will reverse these effects is unclear. While significant effects of reemployment have been documented among blue-collar workers ([Kessler, Turner, and House 1989](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R61); [Warr and Jackson 1985](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R89)), professionals and upper-level, white-collar workers do not seem to recover as readily. In contrast to the literature on the economic effects, attention has also been paid to variation in the effects of job loss by socio-emotional skills and social support. For example, worker response to displacement varies by individual work-role centrality, or employment commitment, where workers who place more importance on the work role to their sense of self suffer more from job loss. Individuals also vary in their coping resources, i.e. the personal, financial, and social resources they draw on to cope with job loss, and social support, such as social integration, availability of friends, relatives, and co-workers, and marital status and spousal support ([Darity and Goldsmith 1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R23); [Leana and Feldman 1988](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R59); [Pearlin et al. 1981](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R76)).

The experience of job loss and unemployment may also vary by the economic context. Displacement that occurs during recessions, in which many workers are laid off, is associated with greater economic losses than displacement that occurs during economic expansions ([Couch, Jolly, and Placzek 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R21); Davis and von Wachter 2011; [Fallick 1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R29); [von Wachter 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R88)). However, contexts of widespread unemployment lessen the internalization of blame and social stigma associated with job loss ([Brand, Levy, and Gallo 2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R7); [Charles and Stephens 2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R16); [Clark 2003](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R17), [2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R18); [Miller and Hoppe 1994](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R70)). That is, displaced workers may benefit from a “social norm effect”: as aggregate unemployment increases, one’s own unemployment represents a smaller deviation from the social norm ([Clark 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R18)), and thus displacement effects on social-psychological well-being may be less in contexts of mass layoffs. [Turner (1995)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R87) shows a three-way interaction, indicating that unemployment effects on psychological well-being are strongest in low unemployment areas, particularly among individuals with a college-level education. While economic burden is greater among workers with lower socioeconomic status and those displaced in higher unemployment contexts, personal attribution is greater among higher status victims of job loss and those displaced in low unemployment contexts ([Kessler, Turner, and House 1988](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R60); [Pearlin et al. 1981](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R76); [Turner 1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R87)). These interactions highlight that results are sensitive to the population, geographic location, and time period under study.

Scholars have proposed a number of mechanisms to explain the relationship between job loss and psychological well-being. First, economic deprivation and downward socioeconomic mobility provide leading explanations for the relationship between job loss and psychological distress, as indicated by unemployment duration ([Clark, Georgellis, and Sanfey 2001](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R19); [McKee-Ryan et al. 2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R67)) and income loss ([Gallo et al. 2006a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R40); Kasl and Jones 2000; [Kessler, Turner, and House 1988](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R60); [Warr and Jackson 1985](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R89)). Second, job loss and unemployment can dampen self-esteem, aspirations, and time structure; incite resignation, apathy, uncertainty, and stigmatization; and frustrate one’s social identity by replacing a socially approved role with one of markedly lower prestige ([Jahoda 1982](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R48); [Jahoda, Lazarsfeld, and Zeisel 1933[1971]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R50)). Scholars either include these measures within the set of dependent variables of interest, or treat the psychosocial indicators as mediators linking job loss to depressive symptoms. Third, family and social strain help to explain the relationship ([Darity and Goldsmith 1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R23)). Fourth, additional stressful life events that occur subsequent to job loss, such as additional job losses, divorce, health shocks, and migration explain some of the effects. Although scholars routinely implicate these mechanisms, few studies rigorously empirically test these mediating influences ([Catalano et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R13)).

### Job Loss and Physical Well-Being

Job loss has been linked to both short and long-term declines in physical health, including worse self-reported health, physical disability, cardiovascular disease, a greater number of reported medical conditions, increase in hospitalization, higher use of medical services, higher use of disability benefits, an increase in self-destructive behaviors and suicide, and mortality ([Burgard, Brand, and House 2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R10); [Catalano et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R13); [Dooley, Fielding, and Levi 1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R25); [Ferrie et al. 1998](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R37); [Gallo et al. 2000](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R38); [Gallo et al. 2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R39); [Gallo et al. 2006b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R41); [Gallo et al. 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R42); Kasl and Jones 2000; [Kessler, Turner, and House 1988](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R60); [McKee-Ryan et al. 2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R67); [Strully 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R85); [Turner 1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R87)). For example, [Gallo et al. (2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R39), [2006b)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R41) found that job loss doubled the risk of subsequent myocardial infarction and stroke among older workers. [Sullivan and von Wachter (2009)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R86) and [von Wachter (2010)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R88) found a 50 to 100 percent increase in mortality the year following displacement and a 10 to 15 percent increase in mortality rates for the next 20 years.

Despite a large literature suggesting an association between job loss and ill health, the causal relationship remains contested due to concerns over selection bias. The fundamental concern is whether job loss leads to ill health, or whether at least some or all of the observed association occurs because those individuals who have poor health are more likely to lose jobs. Even with a rich set of pre-displacement covariates, the question remains as to whether models fully adjust for pre-displacement health, personality and psychosocial characteristics, lifestyle, and labor market experiences that may lead to both job loss and ill health. [Burgard, Brand, and House (2007)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R10) continue to find a significant association between involuntary job loss and overall self-rated health even after adjustment for social background characteristics and baseline health. More nuanced analyses of specific reasons for job loss and the timing of job loss relative to health shocks reveal that those who lose their jobs for health-related reasons have, not surprisingly, the most precipitous declines in health. Effects of job losses for non-health reasons on self-rated poor health are relatively small ([Burgard, Brand, and House 2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R10)). Studies of plant closures also show that workers’ health declines following job loss (Arnetz et al. 1991; Beal and Nethercott 1987; Gore 1978; Iversen, Sabroe, and Damsgaard 1989; Kasl and Cobb 1970; Kessler, House, and Turner 1987; [Strully 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R85)).

Variation in displacement effects and the mechanisms linking job loss to physical health are similar to psychological effects, including economic loss ([Sullivan and von Wachter 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R86); [von Wachter 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R88)) and erosion of psychosocial assets and social support ([Eliason and Storrie 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R28)) and subsequent adverse life events. Yet a few comments specific to the mediating effects on physical health are merited. The effect of job loss and unemployment on depressive symptoms may manifest itself in physiological outcomes, thus the impact of job loss on psychological well-being can help explain the effect on physical health. In addition, health behaviors, such as greater alcohol and drug use, unhealthy food consumption and less exercise, and sleep quality, may partially mediate the association. On the other hand, for some individuals, the increase in discretionary time due to unemployment may be used to pursue health-promoting behaviors, such as physical activity, that might precipitate weight loss or encourage alcohol temperance ([Catalano et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R13)). Another clear mechanism is the loss of employer-offered health insurance and reduced access to medical care.

### Job Loss and Families

As job displacement has significant, long-term effects on workers’ socioeconomic status and psychological and physical well-being, we reasonably expect these consequences to impact the families of displaced workers. The displaced have an increased risk of family tension, and of family disruption ([Attewell 1999](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R2); [Charles and Stephens 2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R16); [Jahoda, Lazarsfeld, and Zeisel 1933 [1971]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R50)). [Charles and Stephens (2004)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R16) considered differences in the mode of displacement on subsequent risk for divorce, reporting increased likelihood of divorce following a layoff but not a plant closing. The authors attributed the higher risk for marital dissolution to the spouse’s negative inference about the worker’s personal role in the layoff, i.e. the discretionary nature of the termination conveys to the spouse certain qualities of the displaced worker which may suggest a lack of marital fitness.

A literature is also emerging which suggests deleterious effects of parental displacement on children, including lower self-esteem and higher likelihood of grade repetition, dropout, and suspension or expulsion from school ([Johnson, Kalil, and Dunifon 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R51); [Kalil and Ziol-Guest 2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R54), [2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R55); [Stevens and Schaller 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R84)), educational attainment ([Kalil and Wightman 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R53)), and lower income of children in adulthood ([Page, Stevens, and Lindo 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R74)). These studies largely emphasize the deleterious effects of fathers’ loss of financial standing in the family among married couple households. Studies examining differences between paternal and maternal displacement effects among married couples find significant effects of paternal but not maternal displacement ([Kalil and Ziol-Guest 2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R55); [Rege, Telle, and Votruba 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R79)). They hypothesize that maternal displacement is not as detrimental to children’s outcomes as paternal due to greater psychological consequences associated with economic loss among fathers who are largely expected to maintain the role of primary provider. [Brand and Simon Thomas (2014)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243#R8), however, focus on displacement among single mothers, and find significant negative effects on children’s educational attainment and social-psychological well-being in young adulthood. Overall, the evidence suggests a significant impact of parental displacement on children’s life outcomes.

args.key_excerpts: "Job loss is an involuntary disruptive life event with a far-reaching impact on workers' life trajectories... Research suggests that displacement is associated with subsequent unemployment, long-term earnings losses, and lower job quality; declines in psychological and physical well-being; loss of psychosocial assets; social withdrawal; family disruption; and lower levels of children's attainment and well-being."
args.summary:
This is a peer-reviewed academic article by Jennie E. Brand, published in the Annual Review of Sociology (February 11, 2015), titled "The Far-Reaching Impact of Job Loss and Unemployment." The article synthesizes research on the consequences of involuntary job displacement on workers' life trajectories.

**Key Topics and Findings:**

1. **Trends and Risk Factors**: Job displacement has become a common feature of the U.S. labor market, driven by technological change, offshoring, immigration, outsourcing, weakened labor unions, and economic downturns. High displacement levels marked the last four U.S. recessions, with the "Great Recession" (2007-2009) being the deepest since the Great Depression. Unemployment reached 9-10% in 2009-2011, roughly twice the pre-crisis rate. Risk factors include being male, black/Hispanic, less educated, blue-collar/manufacturing workers, and those with low job tenure, though risks increased for women, whites, and college-educated workers in the 1990s.

2. **Methodology**: The study of displacement is treated as a "natural experiment" because job loss is a relatively exogenous labor market shock, enabling stronger causal inference. However, selection bias remains a concern. Scholars found few differences across various causal estimators (regression, matching, difference-in-difference, fixed effects). Plant closure studies offer stronger internal validity but limited generalizability.

3. **Economic Effects**: Displaced workers face long-term earnings losses—an immediate 33% earnings loss and up to 15% loss six years after separation (Couch and Placzek 2010). Cumulative lifetime earnings loss is roughly 20%, with "wage scarring" lasting up to 20 years post-displacement. Reemployed workers more often find part-time work with lower job quality. Losses are cyclical: men displaced in mass layoffs when unemployment is below 6% lose 1.4 years of pre-displacement earnings, versus 2.8 years when unemployment exceeds 8% (Davis and von Wachter 2012). Older workers, those with high tenure, industry-changers, and the less-educated suffer greater losses. There is debate over whether layoffs (stigmatizing) versus plant closings produce different economic outcomes (Gibbons and Katz 1991 vs. Krashinsky 2002).

4. **Psychological Effects**: Displaced workers report 15-30% higher rates of depressive symptoms and anxiety compared to non-displaced workers, plus loss of psychosocial assets (self-esteem, life satisfaction, sense of control). Effects vary by demographic characteristics, work-role centrality, coping resources, and economic context. Reemployment mitigates but does not eliminate these effects, particularly for professionals/white-collar workers. A "social norm effect" means contexts of widespread unemployment lessen the social-psychological impact, though economic losses are larger during recessions.

5. **Physical Effects**: Job loss is linked to worse self-rated health, cardiovascular disease, increased hospitalization, higher use of disability benefits, increased suicide, and mortality. Gallo et al. found job loss doubled the risk of myocardial infarction and stroke among older workers. Sullivan and von Wachter (2009) found a 50-100% increase in mortality the year following displacement and a 10-15% increase over the next 20 years. Causal inferences remain contested due to selection bias, though plant closure studies corroborate findings.

6. **Family Effects**: Displaced workers face increased risk of family tension and disruption. Layoffs (but not plant closings) increase divorce risk (Charles and Stephens 2004). Parental displacement negatively affects children's self-esteem, educational attainment, grade repetition, dropout, and adult income. Paternal displacement has stronger effects on children than maternal among married couples, but displacement among single mothers also significantly harms children's outcomes.

**Conclusions**: While reemployment mitigates some negative effects of job loss, it does not eliminate them. Future research should attend more fully to how economic and social-psychological effects intersect and extend beyond displaced workers themselves.

*   [Discussion](https://www.clevelandfed.org/publications/economic-commentary/2025/ec-202514-are-young-college-graduates-losing-their-edge-in-the-job-market#discussion)

High school graduates in their twenties have consistently experienced a higher unemployment rate than college graduates in the same age range. However, the unemployment gap between the two education groups has recently narrowed, reaching its lowest level since the late 1970s. This _Economic Commentary_ shows that this narrowing coincides with a decades-long decline, one that began around 2000, in the job-finding rate among young college graduates.

*   ![Image 9: Headshot of Alexander Cline](https://www.clevelandfed.org/-/media/project/clevelandfedtenant/clevelandfedsite/people/profiles/c/cline-alexander-web.png?h=360&iar=0&w=280&extension=webp&hash=2A24D990F79917C10D0CE78BAF25A014)[Alexander Cline](https://www.clevelandfed.org/people/profiles/c/cline-alexander "Cline Alexander")Research Analyst 
*   ![Image 10:  Barış Kaymak](https://www.clevelandfed.org/-/media/project/clevelandfedtenant/clevelandfedsite/people/profiles/k/kaymak_baris_220927.png?h=360&iar=0&w=280&extension=webp&hash=9BAFE65D09A021B706693E54DB7BCC82)[Barış Kaymak](https://www.clevelandfed.org/people/profiles/k/kaymak-baris "Kaymak Barış")Economic and Policy Advisor

[Labor economics](https://www.clevelandfed.org/search?q=Labor+economics)

11.24.2025 ISSN 2163-3738 EC 2025-14 DOI [10.26509/frbc-ec-202514](https://doi.org/10.26509/frbc-ec-202514 "Article Detail")

_The views authors express in_ Economic Commentary _are theirs and not necessarily those of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland or the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. The series editor is Tasia Hane. This paper and its data are subject to revision; please visit [clevelandfed.org](https://www.clevelandfed.org/)for updates._

For decades, college graduates have typically faced lower unemployment rates, found jobs faster, and experienced more stable employment than high school graduates without college experience. Combined with higher expected wages, these advantages reinforced higher education as a pathway to economic security. However, some of the long-standing job market advantages offered by having a college degree may be eroding.

The postpandemic labor market shows signs of diminished prospects for young college graduates. Relative to the broader population, young graduates are experiencing higher-than-average unemployment rates (Lahart and Chen, 2025; Tasci, 2025) alongside widespread anecdotes of difficulties in finding employment (Horsley, 2025; Pettypiece, 2025) and stories of tech industry contractions (Ellis and Bindley, 2025). Concerns about AI automation of entry-level positions traditionally filled by college graduates have compounded these worries (Brynjolfsson, Chandar, and Chen, 2025; Murray et al., 2025), especially since poor job market outcomes early in life can translate into persistent earnings shortfalls over the course of a career (Kahn, 2010; Oreopoulos, von Wachter, and Heisz, 2012).

In this _Economic Commentary_, we examine unemployment trends for high school and college graduates aged 22–27.[1](https://www.clevelandfed.org/publications/economic-commentary/2025/ec-202514-are-young-college-graduates-losing-their-edge-in-the-job-market#cf-fn-1)The unemployment gap between these groups has declined continually since the 2008 financial crisis, recently reaching its lowest level since the late 1970s. Comparing trends in transition rates among unemployment, employment, and economic inactivity (not in the labor force), we document that the shrinking unemployment gap has been accompanied by a secular decline in the job-finding rate—the fraction of the unemployed who find a job on a monthly basis—for young college graduates beginning around 2000. Recently, the job-finding rate for young college-educated workers has declined to be roughly in line with the rate for young high-school-educated workers, indicating that a long period of relatively easier job-finding prospects for college grads has ended. Trends in other transitions to and from unemployment, such as the job separation rate or entries from outside of the labor force, have moved in tandem for both schooling groups in the long run, despite diverging temporarily over business cycles in some cases. In particular, the entry rate into unemployment for young high-school-educated workers remains above that for young college-educated workers. As a result, despite convergence in job-finding rates, young college graduates maintain advantages in job stability and compensation once hired.

## The Employment Situation for Young High School and College Graduates

[](https://www.clevelandfed.org/ "Copy link")
We use panel data from the Current Population Survey (CPS) spanning 1976–2025 (IPUMS, Flood et al., 2024). The CPS is a monthly survey sponsored jointly by the US Census Bureau and the US Bureau of Labor Statistics that tracks the socioeconomic characteristics of respondents over time, thus enabling the detection of changes in labor force status. Our sample includes respondents aged 22–27, split into college-educated (four-year degree or higher) and high school-educated groups.

Figure 1a shows the evolution of the unemployment rates for young high school and college workers since 1976. Dashed lines show raw data with seasonal noise; solid lines show smoothed series using locally weighted running-mean estimation (Cleveland, 1979). High school workers have historically had a higher and more procyclical unemployment rate (meaning it rose more during economic expansions and fell more during recessions) than that of college workers. But this gap has narrowed recently. Figure 1b illustrates this convergence. The unemployment gap oscillated around 5 percentage points for decades before climbing steeply after the 2008 financial crisis as high school workers particularly struggled with re-employment. Since then, the gap has steadily narrowed except for a brief pandemic-related spike. The current (July 2025) 12-month moving average of the gap—2.5 percentage points—sits near its March 2024 all-time low of 2.4 percentage points, with the last 20 months comprising the series’ lowest string of realizations on record.[2](https://www.clevelandfed.org/publications/economic-commentary/2025/ec-202514-are-young-college-graduates-losing-their-edge-in-the-job-market#cf-fn-2)

![Image 11: ec 202514 college graduates img1](https://www.clevelandfed.org/-/media/project/clevelandfedtenant/clevelandfedsite/publications/economic-commentary/2025/ec-202514-are-young-college-graduates-losing-their-edge-in-the-job-market/ec-202514-college-graduates-img1.png?h=563&iar=0&w=1151&extension=webp&hash=90642931F18AF7BA2E9A01ADE894A4B3)

This narrowing reflects a tale of two job markets. Young high school workers are riding the wave of the historically tight postpandemic labor market with well-below-average unemployment compared to that of past high school graduates, while young college workers are experiencing unemployment rates rarely observed among past college cohorts barring during recessions. To understand this convergence, we turn to the underlying job market dynamics.

## Movements In and Out of Unemployment

[](https://www.clevelandfed.org/ "Copy link")
Unemployment is a temporary status that many experience at various points in their careers. Figure 2 displays the different channels through which people enter and exit unemployment. People may enter unemployment by losing their jobs (separation) or (re)joining the labor force to search for jobs (engagement). People can exit unemployment by finding jobs or leaving the labor force (discouragement). The relative size of these entry and exit “flows” determines the unemployment rate: higher entry rates raise it, while higher exit rates lower it. Distinguishing between entry and exit flows, therefore, can shed light on the converging unemployment trends of the two education groups. We decompose these flows using two common methods.

![Image 12: ec 202514 college graduates img2](https://www.clevelandfed.org/-/media/project/clevelandfedtenant/clevelandfedsite/publications/economic-commentary/2025/ec-202514-are-young-college-graduates-losing-their-edge-in-the-job-market/ec-202514-college-graduates-img2.png?h=450&iar=0&w=1151&extension=webp&hash=34850833248BD992E31410E9AFB24D5E)

First, we track monthly employment-status changes using the panel structure of the CPS. We measure exit rates as unemployed respondents’ becoming employed or leaving the labor force in subsequent monthly interviews and entry rates as newly unemployed divided by employed workers.

Second, following Shimer (2005), we use cross-sectional unemployment duration data to address time aggregation concerns that arise from monthly data’s missing short unemployment spells that fall between consecutive interviews. Shimer (2005) defines monthly exit rates as one minus the ratio of workers unemployed for at least a month to the total number of unemployed workers in the preceding month, then solves for entry rates accounting for monthly changes in total unemployment given the exit rate.[3](https://www.clevelandfed.org/publications/economic-commentary/2025/ec-202514-are-young-college-graduates-losing-their-edge-in-the-job-market#cf-fn-3) This approach better captures short unemployment spells but lacks detail on reasons for exit (job-finding versus discouragement) and requires data available only after 1994.

Figure 3 shows unemployment exit rates for young high school and college graduates using both methods. Dashed lines are smoothed to capture short-run movements primarily from business cycle fluctuations; both groups show strongly procyclical exit rates with comparable amplitudes, meaning that economic cycles do not affect the exit rates of the two groups differentially. Solid lines reveal longer-term trends: High school exit rates remained stable until 2008, dropped during the jobless recovery from the 2008 recession, and now sit near long-run averages.[4](https://www.clevelandfed.org/publications/economic-commentary/2025/ec-202514-are-young-college-graduates-losing-their-edge-in-the-job-market#cf-fn-4) College exit rates trended upward from 1976 to 2000 and then declined sharply. The gap between the exit rates for high-school-educated and college-educated workers narrowed after 2000, closing entirely around 2019.

![Image 13: ec 202514 college graduates img3](https://www.clevelandfed.org/-/media/project/clevelandfedtenant/clevelandfedsite/publications/economic-commentary/2025/ec-202514-are-young-college-graduates-losing-their-edge-in-the-job-market/ec-202514-college-graduates-img3.png?h=593&iar=0&w=1151&extension=webp&hash=3AAEBED54B986801F99E4EBE3274D3FA)

Both methods show exit rates among college graduates to be declining relative to that of high school graduates. High school graduates now exit unemployment faster than college graduates. These changing dynamics entail shorter unemployment spells for high school graduates, a circumstance which acts to bring the unemployment rates of the two education groups closer to each other.

Figure 4 shows unemployment entry rates. High school graduates have had higher entry rates historically, a situation which, in combination with lower exit rates prior to 2019, explains their higher average unemployment. Entry rates are countercyclical, with college graduates showing lower amplitude over business cycles, indicating better job stability. Long-run trends show broad stability for both groups, though duration-based measures show declining entry rates over time. Importantly, the gap between groups remains stable, so trends in entry rates cannot be key to understanding the convergence in unemployment rates.

![Image 14: ec 202514 college graduates img4](https://www.clevelandfed.org/-/media/project/clevelandfedtenant/clevelandfedsite/publications/economic-commentary/2025/ec-202514-are-young-college-graduates-losing-their-edge-in-the-job-market/ec-202514-college-graduates-img4.png?h=563&iar=0&w=1151&extension=webp&hash=716445DB459FCBF2B9471DFA42F20B9D)

Table 1 contrasts the average entry and exit rates of young high school and college graduates from 1976 to 2000 with their corresponding rates during the 12-month period ending in June 2025.[5](https://www.clevelandfed.org/publications/economic-commentary/2025/ec-202514-are-young-college-graduates-losing-their-edge-in-the-job-market#cf-fn-5) Prior to 2001, young high school graduates had lower exit rates from unemployment (41.2 percent versus 47.0 percent) and higher entry rates (3.9 percent versus 1.8 percent), consistent with a significantly higher unemployment rate among high school graduates than college graduates. There has, however, been a reversal of exit rates in recent years. While high school graduates historically exited unemployment more slowly, they now exit faster than college graduates (41.5 percent versus 37.1 percent), with a nearly 10 percentage point decline in the exit rate for college graduates. In contrast, entry rates currently stand near their historical averages for both education groups (3.9 percent versus 1.9 percent). This suggests that the reversal of exit rates is the key factor behind the narrowing of the unemployment rate gap.

![Image 15: ec 202514 college graduates img5](https://www.clevelandfed.org/-/media/project/clevelandfedtenant/clevelandfedsite/publications/economic-commentary/2025/ec-202514-are-young-college-graduates-losing-their-edge-in-the-job-market/ec-202514-college-graduates-img5.png?h=413&iar=0&w=1151&extension=webp&hash=FD59064E3047D8AC6457B74855065604)

## Unemployment Departures: Finding Jobs or Leaving the Labor Force?

[](https://www.clevelandfed.org/ "Copy link")
What explains the reversal in exit rates? Recall that exit occurs through job-finding or labor force departure (discouragement); thus, differences in trends in either how quickly each group finds a job or how often each group gets discouraged from job searching could both explain this pattern. It is essential to distinguish between these two explanations because they imply opposite interpretations of comparative job prospects. Are high school graduates getting discouraged more easily or finding jobs more quickly relative to college graduates?

Figure 5 separates the two components of exit from unemployment: the job-finding rate (left) and the discouragement rate (right). Historically, college graduates have found jobs faster. Both groups experienced cyclical fluctuations, but long-term trends moved together between 1976 and 2000, consistent with parallel exit rates during this period. Patterns diverged after 2000: high school job-finding rates remained stable despite a prolonged downturn after the 2008 recession, while college rates have declined consistently since 2000. The series converged around 2019, with recent data showing similar job-finding rates.

![Image 16: ec 202514 college graduates img6](https://www.clevelandfed.org/-/media/project/clevelandfedtenant/clevelandfedsite/publications/economic-commentary/2025/ec-202514-are-young-college-graduates-losing-their-edge-in-the-job-market/ec-202514-college-graduates-img6.png?h=600&iar=0&w=1151&extension=webp&hash=77F59F406671694A7A0422CE445A0036)

args.summary:
This Economic Commentary from the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (EC 2025-14, published November 24, 2025) by Alexander Cline (Research Analyst) and Barış Kaymak (Economic and Policy Advisor) examines whether young college graduates are losing their job market edge. Using Current Population Survey (CPS) panel data spanning 1976–2025 for respondents aged 22–27, the authors find that the unemployment gap between young high school and college graduates has narrowed to its lowest level since the late 1970s—currently 2.5 percentage points (as of July 2025, near the March 2024 all-time low of 2.4 percentage points).

Key findings:
- The narrowing gap reflects two contrasting developments: young high school workers benefit from the historically tight postpandemic labor market, while young college workers face unemployment rates rarely seen outside recessions.
- The primary driver is a secular decline in the job-finding rate among young college graduates that began around 2000. College graduate job-finding rates trended upward from 1976 to 2000, then declined sharply.
- By around 2019, the job-finding rates of the two education groups converged, ending a long period of relatively easier job-finding prospects for college graduates.
- Historically (1976–2000), high school graduates had lower unemployment exit rates (41.2% vs. 47.0%) and higher entry rates (3.9% vs. 1.8%). This has reversed: high school graduates now exit unemployment faster than college graduates (41.5% vs. 37.1%), with nearly a 10 percentage point decline in college graduates' exit rate.
- Discouragement rates (leaving the labor force) show no differential trends between the groups, indicating the exit rate reversal is driven by job-finding, not discouragement.
- Entry rates into unemployment remain stable, with high school graduates' entry rates still above college graduates' rates, meaning college graduates retain advantages in job stability and compensation once hired.

The authors use two methods for decomposition: monthly employment-status transitions from CPS panel data, and Shimer's (2005) duration-based approach. The commentary contextualizes findings against concerns about AI automation of entry-level positions and persistent earnings effects of poor early-career outcomes (citing Kahn 2010; Oreopoulos, von Wachter, and Heisz 2012).

This webpage from the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) provides employment statistics for students who earned a bachelor's degree in 2015–16, based on data from the Baccalaureate and Beyond (B&B:16/20) survey. The data reflects employment characteristics measured 4 years after degree completion (as of 2020).

Key findings:
- Employment status: 74.3% of graduates worked full time, 7.5% worked part time, 14.3% were out of the labor force, and 4.0% were unemployed.
- Income distribution (annualized, in most recent job): 24.0% in the lowest income quarter (under $31,186), 24.7% in the lower middle quarter ($31,186–$46,990), 24.3% in the higher middle quarter ($46,991–$65,989), and 24.3% in the highest quarter ($65,990 or more). 2.6% had no job within 4 years of completion.
- Occupations of most recent job: Business/management (19.7%), other white-collar (12.8%), other occupations (11.5%), business support/administrative assistance (9.6%), math/computer/physical science (8.0%), other health care (7.2%), nurses (6.0%), PreK-12 educators (5.8%), sales (5.8%), social services (5.0%), engineers (4.6%), and life science (1.3%).
- Military status as of 2020: 4.0% were veterans, 1.5% were on active duty/Reserves/National Guard, and 94.4% had no military service.

Notable notes: Approximately half of the B&B:16/20 sample's 4-years-after-graduation period included the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic. The table includes all 2015–16 bachelor's degree earners, including the 8.7% for whom this was not their first bachelor's degree. The source is NCES publication NCES 2022-241.

## Data on display Education pays, 2020

Elka Torpey | June 2021

**Note: These data have been updated. Find the most recent chart in the [education level](https://www.bls.gov/careeroutlook/subject/education_level.htm "Education level") archives.**

Even in the best of economic times, data show that workers who have higher levels of education typically earn more and have lower rates of unemployment compared with workers who have less education. In the challenging economy created by the COVID-19 pandemic, the data tell a similar story.

The chart highlights differences in 2020 earnings and unemployment rates by education, using data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Current Population Survey. For example, workers with a bachelor’s degree had median weekly earnings of $1,305 in 2020, compared with $781 for workers with a high school diploma. And the unemployment rate for bachelor’s-level workers was 5.5 percent, compared with 9.0 percent for those whose highest level of education was a high school diploma.

| Educational attainment | Median usual weekly earnings | Unemployment rate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Doctoral degree | $1,885 | 2.5% |
| Professional degree | 1,893 | 3.1 |
| Master's degree | 1,545 | 4.1 |
| Bachelor's degree | 1,305 | 5.5 |
| Associate degree | 938 | 7.1 |
| Some college, no degree | 877 | 8.3 |
| High school diploma, no college | 781 | 9.0 |
| Less than a high school diploma | 619 | 11.7 |
|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Note: Data are for persons age 25 and over. Earnings are for full-time wage and salary workers.  Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Population Survey. | | |

Unemployment rates were higher in 2020 than in 2019 at all education levels, as the pandemic caused many workers to lose jobs. Weekly earnings also rose at all levels, but the increases may have been due, in part, to the large number of jobs lost by lower paid workers in 2020—which in turn put upward pressure on the 2020 earnings estimates.
