# Regular Research Article

The American dream revisited: intergenerational education mobility in immigrant households

Author links open overlay panel Yiping Wu a, Jinghong Zhou b, [Julan Du c](https://www.sciencedirect.com/author/8850784100/julan-du)

Show more

Add to Mendeley

Share

Cite

[https://doi.org/10.1016/j.worlddev.2026.107353](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.worlddev.2026.107353 "Persistent link using digital object identifier")[Get rights and content](https://s100.copyright.com/AppDispatchServlet?publisherName=ELS&contentID=S0305750X26000422&orderBeanReset=true)

## Highlights

*   •We find that immigrant children show upward educational rank mobility within their cohort. 
*   •We isolate pecuniary effects, i.e. economic factors have limited impact on educational mobility in immigrant families. 
*   •Educational mobility positively correlates with labor income mobility, but translation into broader economic mobility remains incomplete. 
*   •Intergenerational mobility varies by parental origin (developed vs. developing countries) and race, notably in families with Black fathers. 

## Abstract

This study uses American Community Survey microdata from 2005 to 2019 to investigate the interactive effect of parents’ education and immigrant status on their children’s economic and education outcomes. We find a significant positive correlation between the education achievements of parents and those of their children, which diminishes for immigrant parents. However, the low transmissibility likely reflects the upward mobility of immigrant children, who may surpass their parents’ and native children’s education levels, despite starting from similar or lower educational baselines. The influence of immigrant parents’ education on their children’s outcomes is complex, involving parental nurturing, pecuniary constraints, socioeconomic disparities, foreign credential non‑recognition, language barriers and cultural hurdles. Our findings present a nuanced picture. While the translation of educational mobility into broader economic mobility remains incomplete, there is a positive association between educational mobility and labor income mobility. Importantly, the analysis reveals substantial heterogeneity across immigrant subgroups. Distinct patterns emerge between immigrants from developed and developing countries, and intergenerational mobility outcomes also vary by parental race—particularly in families with Black fathers. These findings shed light on the challenges and implications of immigrant parents’ education for their children’s outcomes and emphasize the need to address these unique obstacles to secure the success of future generations.

## Introduction

In the context of immigrant households, it is imperative to address a fundamental question in academic discourse: to what extent does parents’ education exert an impact on the human capital development of their children through intergenerational transmission, particularly in light of the challenges posed by language, culture, and income disparities? The scholarly literature underscores the central importance of intergenerational education transmission for intergenerational income mobility (Gong et al., 2012, Zhou et al., 2018, Abramitzky et al., 2021). These studies collectively report that when other conditions are held constant, a higher level of parents’ education is positively associated with their children’s education achievement (Ermisch and Francesconi, 2001, Behrman and Rosenzweig, 2002, Rege et al., 2007). Moreover, the division of household labor can play a role in shaping this dynamic, as demonstrated by the finding of Rege et al. (2007) that unemployed mothers may allocate more time to their children’s education, thereby exerting a positive influence on their education outcomes. Research drawing on microdata from the United Kingdom, Germany, and Spain has identified a reinforcement phenomenon in long-term intergenerational education persistence (Blanden and Machin, 2004, Guell, et al., 2007, Heineck and Riphahn, 2007).

However, when examining the intergenerational mobility of immigrant households, divergent conclusions have emerged from analyses of nearly identical data sources. For instance, Abramitzky et al. (2021) found heightened long-term intergenerational income mobility among immigrant families, primarily owing to their propensity to select areas with improved education opportunities. Conversely, the study of Akee et al. (2020), which investigated the intergenerational income dynamics of immigrant families from a labor supply perspective using American Community Survey microdata from 2005 to 2014 supplemented by W-2 (Personal Income Tax Wage Income Return) data from the Internal Revenue Service, revealed that the long-term Gini coefficient for both historical and recent immigrants from Asia consistently remains below the Lorenz curve, indicating unequal income distribution. The main objective of this study is to examine the intergenerational transmission versus the mobility of educational attainment within immigrant families, and to assess whether such educational mobility translates into broader socioeconomic advancement.

Based on the literature, we can expect that intergenerational education mobility plays a crucial role in understanding intergenerational income mobility among immigrant families. However, there is a notable gap in research examining the influence of intergenerational education mobility within immigrant households. Many empirical studies on intergenerational educational mobility estimate the correlation between one additional year of schooling for immigrant parents and their children’s years of schooling, with some focusing on immigrant samples (Aydemir et al., 2013). Nevertheless, few explore the gap in intergenerational educational transmission between immigrant and native children while holding the father’s educational rank constant. While Lam and Liu (2019) examine the interaction between Hong Kong immigrant status and parents’ education on their children’s educational outcomes, their sample may be less diverse than that of the U.S. immigrant population. Additionally, although some studies use rank models to analyze intergenerational educational mobility and class reproduction in immigrant families, Feliciano and Lanuza (2017) use National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health), spanning from 1994 to 2009, and capture a time period during which the composition of immigrant populations in the U.S. has shifted. This study adds on the existing literature by isolating economic factors that influence the educational mobility of immigrant families. Given the ongoing upward trend in global mobility, it is important to investigate the mechanisms that underpin the intergenerational education mobility effect within immigrant households. As economic globalization is further solidified, the swift cross-border mobility of human resources presents an exceptional opportunity to explore the dynamics of intergenerational education mobility within immigrant households. While socioeconomic and cultural factors dominate the literature on immigrant mobility, emerging behavioral genetics research suggests an additional layer: inherited genetic endowments that predispose individuals to educational success. These endowments, often proxied by polygenic scores (PGS) from genome-wide association studies, may explain part of the “immigrant paradox”—where children outperform parental baselines despite transmission gaps—through positive selection in migration (Lee et al., 2018, Barth et al., 2020). Building on this, we hypothesize that a significant positive correlation between the education achievements of parents and those of their children, which diminishes for immigrant parents.

In addition to the environmental mechanisms outlined above, genetic endowments represent a promising channel for understanding diminished transmissibility in immigrant families. PGS derived from large-scale genome-wide association studies aggregate thousands of genetic variants associated with educational attainment, predicting approximately 0.5 to 1 additional years of schooling per standard deviation increase while capturing traits like cognitive ability (e.g., IQ proxies), noncognitive skills (e.g., grit and conscientiousness), and behavioral predispositions (e.g., delayed gratification), which collectively explain approximately 10–15% of variance in human capital outcomes (Lee et al., 2018, Barth et al., 2020). For immigrants, positive selection during migration—where distance and risks filter for high-endowment individuals (Borjas, 1987)—concentrates these advantages, amplified by assortative mating in origin countries, where educational rank proxies for underlying genetic fitness (Mare and Schwartz, 2006, Domingue et al., 2014).1 Although our empirical design does not directly measure PGS, this mechanism motivates our focus on heterogeneity and immigrant status-parental education attainment interactions.

This paper takes advantage of American Community Survey data to examine intergenerational education mobility, for two reasons. First, the United States is renowned for its significantly large immigrant population, with a substantial portion of U.S. residents either having immigrant origins or tracing their ancestral roots back to immigrants. Currently, one in four individuals residing in the United States can trace their heritage to first- or second-generation immigrants. As of 2017, immigrants constituted 13.7% of the U.S. population; however, it is worth noting that the rate of immigration to the United States has experienced a gradual decline over the past decade (see Fig. 2). Second, immigrants, particularly those with high skill levels or advanced education attainment, have had a profound impact on the economic trajectory of the United States. According to a study by the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP),2 immigrants or the children of immigrants have founded over half (55%) of America’s startup companies valued at $1 billion or more. Moreover, immigrants and their descendants have been instrumental in establishing nearly two-thirds (64%) of U.S. billion-dollar companies, with almost 80% of America’s unicorn companies having immigrant founders or immigrants holding key leadership positions. A report by the American Immigration Council 3 further highlights immigrants’ economic importance by revealing that in 2023, 44.8% of Fortune 500 companies, equivalent to 224 firms, were founded by immigrants or their children. These companies collectively generated $8.1 trillion in revenue in fiscal year 2022 and employed over 14.8 million people, underscoring their vital role in job creation and economic prosperity. Data from the IPUMS-USA 4 also highlights immigrants’ outsized presence in key sectors, with immigrants representing 33% of the engineering workforce, 27% of mathematicians, statisticians, and computer scientists, and 24% of physical scientists, while only 16% of the resident population hold a bachelor’s degree or higher.

In this paper, we use the immigrant household data provided by the IPUMS-USA database to build an intergenerational dataset that includes parent–child relationships.5 This comprehensive dataset forms the basis for our investigation of the mechanisms behind the impact of immigrant parents’ education achievements on their children’s outcomes. This paper employs a rank-to-rank model to examine the intergenerational transmission versus the mobility of educational attainment for immigrant families compared with native households, and to assess whether such educational mobility translates into broader socioeconomic advancement. Our findings indicate that immigrant children exhibit a more pronounced pattern of upward mobility in their cohort’s educational rank than do their native-born peers. In exploring the channels for this upward mobility for immigrant households, we isolate the impact of economic factors on educational mobility among immigrant families. We demonstrate that pecuniary effects have limited influences on intergenerational mobility, likely due to the financial constraints these immigrant families face. On the contrary, children from immigrant families typically overcome various obstacles to their educational success, wherein aspirations to enhance their socioeconomic status through education and the nurturing effects play an important role. Moreover, although intergenerational educational mobility does not fully translate into proportional socioeconomic mobility in terms of investment income and socioeconomic status, we do find some evidence on the transmission of educational mobility to labor income mobility.

This paper makes a substantial contribution to two strands of the literature. First, this study extends the body of knowledge on the socioeconomic implications of transnational migration (Boubtane et al., 2016, Clemens and Pritchett, 2019, Burchardi et al., 2020) on intergenerational educational mobility by incorporating the effects of genetic endowments, financial resources, parental nurturing, and cultural educational aspirations. Our findings highlight parental nurturing as a key mechanism in addressing the immigrant paradox, shedding light on the factors that facilitate educational attainment among immigrant families despite economic constraints. Second, this study advances the literature on intergenerational educational mobility (Ermisch and Francesconi, 2001, Rege et al., 2007, Aydemir et al., 2013, Feliciano and Lanuza, 2017, Lam and Liu, 2019) by examining the educational attainment of immigrants in their countries of origin, providing insights into whether they belong to the educational elite. Immigrant families with relatively higher educational standing in their local contexts tend to be more knowledgeable about education, place greater emphasis on academic achievement, and may exhibit cognitive or genetic advantages that contribute to their children's educational success. Additionally, this study integrates analyses of the impact of contextual educational attainment on earnings, the role of educational investment, and the distinct challenges faced by immigrant families from developing countries. By doing so, it offers a comprehensive perspective on the determinants of intergenerational educational mobility among immigrant populations. Thirdly, this study contributes to the expanding literature on educational disparities between immigrant and native-born populations by utilizing the Kitagawa-Oaxaca-Blinder (KOB) decomposition to examine the evolution of the educational attainment rank gap between immigrant children and U.S.-born children with native-born parents over a 15-year period (2005–2019). By disentangling the relative contributions of endowments and coefficients, this study provides new insights into the underlying mechanisms driving this gap and its changes over time. Additionally, by adopting a longitudinal and visual decomposition approach, this research advances the understanding of dynamic educational disparities and their broader implications for intergenerational mobility.

In summary, this study provides a theoretical framework to comprehensively understand education mobility within the context of transnational migration and offers practical insights for attracting global talent and fostering high-quality economic development. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 gives a brief overview of the evolution of U.S. immigration and develops the hypotheses. Section 3 describes the data and lays out the empirical strategy. Section 4 reveals the primary findings and decomposition analyses. Section 5 delves into the prospective framework for intergenerational education mobility in immigrant households. Section 6 sheds light on the broader social and economic implications of the profound influence of the education levels of immigrant parents on their children’s education achievements. Section 7 succinctly summarizes the research conclusions and the policy implications drawn from the study. The Appendix presents the results from two-stage least squares (2SLS) estimations, along with additional robustness tests.

This webpage presents a regular research article from World Development (Volume 203, July 2026, Article 107353) titled "The American dream revisited: intergenerational education mobility in immigrant households" by Yiping Wu, Jinghong Zhou, and Julan Du.

**Study Purpose & Methodology:**
The study uses American Community Survey (ACS) microdata from 2005 to 2019, obtained via the IPUMS-USA database, to investigate how parents' education and immigrant status interactively affect children's economic and educational outcomes. It employs a rank-to-rank model comparing immigrant and native households, focusing on families with US-born children.

**Key Findings:**
- A significant positive correlation exists between parents' and children's education achievement, but this correlation is diminished for immigrant parents
- The low transmissibility reflects upward mobility of immigrant children, who can surpass their parents' and native children's education levels despite starting from similar or lower baselines
- Immigrant children show upward educational rank mobility within their cohort
- Pecuniary (economic) factors have limited impact on educational mobility in immigrant families
- Educational mobility positively correlates with labor income mobility, but translation into broader economic mobility remains incomplete
- Intergenerational mobility varies by parental origin (developed vs. developing countries) and race, particularly in families with Black fathers

**Context & Significance:**
- One in four US residents can trace heritage to first- or second-generation immigrants; immigrants constituted 13.7% of the US population as of 2017
- Immigrants or their children founded over 55% of America's startup companies valued at $1 billion or more, and nearly two-thirds (64%) of US billion-dollar companies
- In 2023, 44.8% of Fortune 500 companies (224 firms) were founded by immigrants or their children, generating $8.1 trillion in revenue and employing over 14.8 million people
- Immigrants represent 33% of the engineering workforce, 27% of mathematicians/statisticians/computer scientists, and 24% of physical scientists

**Mechanisms Explored:**
The study isolates economic factors and examines multiple channels including parental nurturing, pecuniary constraints, socioeconomic disparities, foreign credential non-recognition, language barriers, cultural hurdles, and potential genetic endowments (polygenic scores) as a possible explanation for the "immigrant paradox."

**Methodological Contributions:**
1. Extends knowledge on socioeconomic implications of transnational migration, highlighting parental nurturing as a key mechanism
2. Examines immigrant educational attainment in countries of origin to assess educational elite status
3. Uses Kitagawa-Oaxaca-Blinder (KOB) decomposition to examine educational attainment rank gap evolution between immigrant and native children over 2005-2019

The paper's structure includes sections on immigration trends and hypotheses, data and empirical strategy, primary findings and decomposition analyses, a unified framework for intergenerational educational mobility, social/economic outcomes, and conclusions with policy implications. * The Long-Term Effects of Divorce on Children

## Divorce Can Negatively Affect Children, Even Into Adulthood

Written by:

Travis Shoemaker

Nearly one-third of Americans born between 1988 and 1993 experienced their parents’ divorce before reaching adulthood, a watershed event for a child that can negatively impact them throughout their life.

A U.S. Census Bureau [working paper](/library/working-papers/2025/adrm/CES-WP-25-28.html) linked parental divorce to lower income, reduced likelihood of living away from home while attending college, and higher rates of teen pregnancy, incarceration and mortality.

Before 1950, less than 2% of children lived with a single parent who was divorced, separated or never married. By 2000, nearly 25% did.

Researchers Maggie R. Jones (U.S. Census Bureau), Andrew C. Johnston (University of California Merced) and Nolan G. Pope (University of Maryland) analyzed Census Bureau data, federal tax records and Social Security Administration information to determine the long-term impact of divorce on children.

They traced parental marital histories and connected them to household and child outcome data.

### Divorce Outcomes

The effects of divorce often last into adulthood.

For example, the working paper found that divorce in early childhood reduced children’s income in their mid- to late 20s by 9% to 13%.

Teen birth rates among children of divorce jumped 63% following the split, compared to pre-divorce levels.

The risk of early death (before age 25) increased by 35% to 55% at the time of divorce and remained elevated for at least a decade — an impact comparable to lacking health insurance.

The sample group’s incarceration rate of 0.46% in 2010 was three times higher than for children of always-married parents. Divorce when children were between ages 5 and 20 increased incarceration risk by 0.15 to 0.28 percentage points.

Additionally, experiencing the divorce of their parents before the child is age 18 lowered the likelihood of living away from home while attending college by about 4 percentage points.

### The Younger They Are

Outcomes were worse for children whose parents divorced in early childhood (ages 0-5). Compared to siblings who experienced a parental divorce in adulthood, early-childhood divorce:

* Increased teen births by roughly 60%.
* Increased the likelihood of incarceration by 40%.
* Increased mortality risk at age 25 by 45%.
* Reduced income at age 25 by 9%, and by age 27, by 13%.
* Lowered the likelihood the child lives on a college campus in their late teens and early 20s.

These estimates capture the average effect among children of divorce.

Notably, divorce did not significantly impact the likelihood of marriage or employment among sampled children in their mid-twenties.

### Change of Circumstances

According to the research, divorce disrupts key aspects of parenting: financial investments (education, nutrition, health care and shelter) and what researchers call “direct transmission” (modeling behavior to teach values).

Divorce can impact parental activities by altering family resources and parent-child interaction. When one household splits into two, household income drops, potentially lowering each parent’s ability to provide the pre-divorce levels of monetary investment and personal attention.

Divorced households fell from the 57th to the 36th percentile of income and recovered only about half of that lost income over the next decade.

Post-divorce, both parents may work more due to increased financial strain: mothers worked 8% more hours and fathers 16% more, possibly reducing parent-child contact.

The probability of moving nearly tripled after a divorce. Sampled families relocated to neighborhoods with 7% lower incomes and fewer economic opportunities.

The researchers also found that divorce increased the average distance between children and their nonresident parent by 100 miles on average, a gap that widened to over 200 miles after 10 years.

“These changes in family life reveal that, rather than an isolated legal shock, divorce represents a bundle of treatments — including income loss, neighborhood changes and family restructuring — each of which might affect children’s outcomes," Pope said.

The working paper’s authors caution that these same outcomes may occur in similar families that remain intact. Divorce is simply a marker for family disruption observable in the data.

### Divorce Across the U.S. Population

The impact and prevalence of divorce are not spread evenly across the U.S. population.

Divorce rates declined sharply as income rose: children in the bottom fifth of parent income were over 30 percentage points more likely to experience divorce than those in the top fifth (Figure 1a).

Parental divorce rates experienced by children also varied substantially by racial/ethnic group (Figure 1b):

* Asian children: 17%.
* White children: slightly under 30%.
* Hispanic children: slightly over 30%.
* Black children: 45%.

[![Figure 1. Divorce Rates of U.S. Married Parents of Children Born Between 1988 and 1993 by Income and Race/Ethnicity](/library/stories/2026/01/divorce-affects-children/_jcr_content/root/responsivegrid/responsivegrid_1971482390/imagecore.coreimg.jpeg/1768417231674/figure-1-divorce-affects-children.jpeg "Figure 1. Divorce Rates of U.S. Married Parents of Children Born Between 1988 and 1993 by Income and Race/Ethnicity")](/content/dam/Census/library/stories/2026/01/divorce-affects-children/figure-1-divorce-affects-children.jpg)

### Trends Across Time

The structure of American families has changed dramatically over the past century.

Before 1950, less than 2% of children lived with a single parent who was divorced, separated or never married. By 2000, nearly 25% did.

This increase was driven by three distinct trends (Figure 2):

1. Separation rates increased after World War II, before which divorce was still difficult to obtain.
2. Divorce rates climbed significantly between 1960 and 1980 as laws changed from fault-based to no-fault.
3. “Never-married” rates rose from only 1% in 1965 to 13% by 2000.

[![Figure 2. Share of U.S. Children Living in Single-Parent Households: 1880-2018](/library/stories/2026/01/divorce-affects-children/_jcr_content/root/responsivegrid/responsivegrid_19714/imagecore.coreimg.jpeg/1767826122542/figure-2-divorce-affects-children.jpeg "Figure 2. Share of U.S. Children Living in Single-Parent Households: 1880-2018")](/content/dam/Census/library/stories/2026/01/divorce-affects-children/figure-2-divorce-affects-children.jpg)

These changes have affected families unevenly, hitting the impoverished and less educated the hardest.

### Key Takeaways

“First, we show that divorce significantly alters children’s resources and living arrangements,” Pope said. “Second, divorce represents a turning point, with child outcomes changing meaningfully at divorce.”

In addition, the research shows that effects persist into adulthood, contributing to lower income, reduced college residency, and higher incarceration, teen birth and mortality rates.

“Lastly, given that divorce has negative effects on children’s outcomes and is more prevalent among low-income families,” Pope said, “addressing its impacts may be important for reducing the intergenerational transmission of disadvantage.”

***Travis Shoemaker is a writer/editor at the Census Bureau.***

args.summary:
This U.S. Census Bureau America Counts story (written by Travis Shoemaker) summarizes a Census Bureau working paper examining the long-term effects of parental divorce on children, based on research by Maggie R. Jones (Census Bureau), Andrew C. Johnston (UC Merced), and Nolan G. Pope (University of Maryland). Nearly one-third of Americans born between 1988 and 1993 experienced parental divorce before adulthood.

KEY FINDINGS ON DIVORCE OUTCOMES:
- Divorce in early childhood reduced children's income in their mid-to-late 20s by 9% to 13%.
- Teen birth rates among children of divorce jumped 63% following the split.
- Risk of early death (before age 25) increased by 35% to 55% at the time of divorce and remained elevated for at least a decade.
- The sample group's incarceration rate of 0.46% in 2010 was three times higher than for children of always-married parents; divorce between ages 5 and 20 increased incarceration risk by 0.15 to 0.28 percentage points.
- Parental divorce before age 18 lowered likelihood of living away from home while attending college by about 4 percentage points.
- Divorce did not significantly impact likelihood of marriage or employment in mid-twenties.

EARLY-CHILDHOOD DIVORCE (AGES 0-5) WAS WORSE: Increased teen births by ~60%, incarceration likelihood by 40%, mortality risk at age 25 by 45%, reduced income at age 25 by 9% and age 27 by 13%, and lowered likelihood of living on a college campus.

CHANGES IN CIRCUMSTANCES: Divorced households fell from the 57th to 36th percentile of income, recovering only half of lost income over the next decade. Mothers worked 8% more hours and fathers 16% more post-divorce. Probability of moving nearly tripled; families relocated to neighborhoods with 7% lower incomes. Divorce increased distance between children and nonresident parent by 100 miles on average, widening to over 200 miles after 10 years. The authors caution the same outcomes may occur in similar intact families; divorce is a marker for observable family disruption.

DEMOGRAPHICS: Divorce rates declined sharply with rising income—children in the bottom fifth of parent income were over 30 percentage points more likely to experience divorce than the top fifth. By race/ethnicity, divorce rates among children born 1988-1993 were: Asian 17%, White slightly under 30%, Hispanic slightly over 30%, Black 45%.

HISTORICAL TRENDS: Before 1950, less than 2% of children lived with a single parent (divorced, separated, or never married); by 2000, nearly 25% did. This increase was driven by: separation rates rising after WWII, divorce rates climbing between 1960 and 1980 (fault-based to no-fault laws), and "never-married" rates rising from 1% in 1965 to 13% by 2000.

The research concludes divorce effects persist into adulthood, and because divorce is more prevalent among low-income families, addressing its impacts may be important for reducing intergenerational transmission of disadvantage.

The Program on Children and Families uses economic tools to study the factors that inform the wellbeing of children and families. She has been an NBER affiliate since 1991.

<webpage_content>
Numbers, Facts and Trends Shaping Your World

#### [Republican Gains in 2022 Midterms Driven Mostly by Turnout Advantage](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/07/12/republican-gains-in-2022-midterms-driven-mostly-by-turnout-advantage/)

# 1. Voter turnout, 2018-2022

**American Trends Panel:** Pew Research Center’s [online probability survey panel](https://www.pewresearch.org/our-methods/u-s-surveys/the-american-trends-panel/), which consists of more than 12,000 adults who take two to three surveys each month. Some panelists have been participating in surveys since 2014.

**Defectors/Defection:** People who either switch their vote to a different party’s candidate from one election to the next, or those who in a given election do not support the candidate of the party they usually support. Also referred to as **“vote switching.”**

**Drop off/Drop-off voters:** People who vote in a given election but not in a subsequent election. The term commonly refers to people who vote in a presidential election but not in the next midterm. It can also apply to any set of elections.

**Midterm elections:** General elections held in all states and the District of Columbia in the even-numbered years between presidential elections. All U.S. House seats are up for election every two years, as are a third of U.S. Senate seats (senators serve six-year terms).

**Mobilize:** Efforts by candidates, political campaigns and other organizations to encourage or facilitate eligible citizens to turn out to vote.

**Nonvoter:** Citizens who didn’t have a record of voting in any voter file or told us they didn’t vote.

**Panel survey:** A type of survey that relies on a group of people who have agreed to participate in multiple surveys over a time period. Panel surveys make it possible to observe how individuals change over time because the answers they give to questions in a current survey can be compared with their answers from a previous survey.

**Party affiliation/Party identification:** Psychological attachment to a particular political party, either thinking of oneself as a member of the party or expressing greater closeness to one party than another. Our study categorizes adults as Democrats or Republicans using their self-reported party identification in a survey.

**Split-ticket voting/Straight-ticket voting:** Voters typically cast ballots for more than one office in a general election. People who vote only for candidates of the same party are “straight-ticket” voters, while those who vote for candidates of different parties are “split-ticket” voters.

**Turnout:** Refers to “turning out” to vote, or simply “voting.” Also used to refer to the share of eligible adults who voted in a given election (e.g., “The turnout in 2020 among the voting eligible population in the U.S. was 67%”).

**Validated voters/Verified voter:** Citizens who told us in a post-election survey that they voted in the 2022 general elections *and* have a record for voting in a commercial voter file. (The two terms are interchangeable).

**Voter file:** A list of adults that includes information such as whether a person is registered to vote, which elections they have voted in, whether they voted in person or by mail, and additional data. Voter files do not say who a voter cast a ballot for. Federal law requires states to maintain electronic voter files, and businesses assemble these files to create a nationwide list of adults along with their voter information.

The elections of 2018, 2020 and 2022 were three of [the highest-turnout U.S. elections](https://www.electproject.org/election-data/voter-turnout-data) of their respective types in decades. About two-thirds (66%) of the voting-eligible population turned out for the 2020 presidential election – the highest rate for any national election since 1900. The 2018 election (49% turnout) had the highest rate for a midterm since 1914. Even the 2022 election’s turnout, with a slightly lower rate of 46%, exceeded that of all midterm elections since 1970.

![Chart shows most Americans are not consistent voters](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2023/07/PP_2023.07.12_validated-voters_1-01.png?w=420)

While sizable shares of the public vote either consistently or not at all, many people vote intermittently. Given how closely divided the U.S. is politically, these intermittent voters often determine the outcome of elections and how the balance of support for the two major political parties swings between elections.

Overall, 70% of U.S. adult citizens who were eligible to participate in all three elections between 2018 and 2022 voted in at least one of them, with about half that share (37%) voting in all three.

Adults who voted in at least one election during the period divide evenly between Democrats and independents who lean toward the Democratic Party or Republicans and Republican-leaning independents in their current party affiliation (48% each). The subset who voted in all three elections are similarly divided (49% Democrats, 50% Republicans). Citizens who did not vote in any of the three tilt Republican by 46% to 41%.

Democrats outnumbered Republicans among the 8% of adult citizens who voted in 2018 and 2020 but not 2022 (55% Democratic, 40% Republican). A similar-sized group (8%) voted in 2020 and 2022 but not 2018, and this group’s composition tilts Republican (57%, vs. 40% Democratic). The 12% who voted in 2020 and opted out of both the 2018 and 2022 midterms were roughly evenly divided among Democrats (46%) and Republicans (43%).

Given the sizable number of intermittent voters and chronic nonvoters, as well as the fact that this group, collectively, is fairly evenly divided in partisan affiliation, both parties have plenty of *potential* supporters on the sidelines in any given election.

### Political preferences differ a lot by race and ethnicity … and so does voter turnout

![Chart shows the racial and ethnic divide in 2022 vote choice for U.S. House](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2023/07/PP_2023.07.12_validated-voters_1-02.png?w=310)

Race and ethnicity are fundamental dividing lines in American politics, with political preferences and electoral participation varying greatly by race and ethnicity.

In the current partisan alignment, Black, Hispanic and Asian voters are all majority Democratic groups, to different degrees, though Republican candidates have gained some ground in the past four years among Hispanic voters.

Black voters remain Democratic stalwarts, voting 93% to 5% for the party’s candidates for U.S. House in 2022. Hispanic and Asian voters clearly favored Democratic candidates as well, but by narrower margins: 60% to 39% for Hispanic voters, and 68% to 32% for Asian voters.

![Chart shows White adults voted more consistently than those of other racial or ethnic backgrounds from 2018 through 2022](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2023/07/PP_2023.07.12_validated-voters_1-03.png?w=310)

But White Americans are much more consistent voters than Black, Hispanic or Asian Americans. Compared with the national average of 37% who voted in 2018, 2020 and 2022, 43% of White citizens who were age eligible to vote in all three elections did so; just 24% did not vote in any of these.

Black, Hispanic and Asian adults lagged far behind, with 27% of Black, 19% of Hispanic and 21% of Asian age-eligible citizens voting in all three elections. Hispanic citizens were most likely to have not voted in any of the most recent three general elections (47%, compared with 36% for Black and 31% for Asian citizens ages 22 and older in 2022).

#### Differences by education

Over the past few election cycles, Republicans have gained ground among White adults who do not have a college degree, who make up 41% of eligible voters. This group is about average in its consistency of voter turnout, with 35% of those ages 22 and over in 2022 voting in 2018, 2020 and 2022, and 31% voting in none of these three elections. White voters without a college degree favored Republican House candidates 66% to 32% in 2022.

By contrast, White adults with college degrees vote at very high rates: 56% of those eligible turned out in all three elections and just 13% participated in none of them. College-educated White adults make up 24% of the eligible electorate but about a third of voters in 2022 (34%). White voters with college degrees had tilted Republican for several decades, but in the past four elections have favored Democratic candidates (52% to 47% in 2022).

![Chart shows White adults without a college degree
strongly prefer GOP candidates, vote at
lower rates than those with degrees](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2023/07/PP_2023.07.12_validated-voters_1-04.png?w=310)

The education gap in White voters’ preferences in 2022 was not apparent among either Black or Hispanic voters (the sample size of Asian voters without a college degree was too small to produce a reliable estimate). College-educated Black and Hispanic adults also voted at higher rates than Black and Hispanic adults without a college degree in each of the three elections.

A small education gap appeared in 2020 presidential preference among Hispanic voters: College-educated Hispanic voters preferred Biden by a margin of 69% to 29%, while Hispanic voters without a college degree preferred Biden by a somewhat narrower margin (58% to 39%). But no significant education gap in candidate preference was observed for Black or Hispanic voters in 2018 or 2022, nor for Black voters in 2020.

The upshot of racial differences in candidate preference and turnout patterns is that Republican candidates benefited from both the relatively large size of the White adult population without a college degree and their somewhat higher turnout rates compared with Black, Hispanic and Asian adults.

Growth in support for Democratic candidates among White voters with a college degree, along with the high turnout levels among this group, offset some of the growth in support for the Republican Party among White voters without a college degree. But college-educated White adults remain a smaller share of all eligible voters than White adults without a college degree.

### Voters and nonvoters

![Chart shows wide disparities by age, race and education in who is a voter, nonvoter](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2023/07/PP_2023.07.12_validated-voters_1-05.png?w=420)

The two most recent midterms – 2022 and 2018 – both featured unusually high turnout compared with nearly every other recent midterm election year. But the differences between those who turned out to vote in 2022 versus 2018 – and between those who did *not* vote – accounted for much of the difference in outcomes between the two elections.

The stark demographic differences between voters and nonvoters in 2022 are similar to those seen in previous U.S. elections.

Voters were much older, on average, than nonvoters. Adults under 50 made up 36% of voters, but 64% of nonvoters. This is very similar to the pattern seen in 2018 – although those under 50 made up a somewhat larger share of voters in 2018 (40%).

Turnout also differed by race and ethnicity.

Three-quarters of voters (75%) were White, non-Hispanic adults. But this group accounted for a smaller share (55%) of nonvoters. Hispanic adults and Black, non-Hispanic adults each made up 9% of voters, but slightly larger shares of nonvoters (18% and 15%, respectively). Asian Americans made up 3% of voters, and a slightly higher share (5%) of nonvoters. These differences are nearly identical to the patterns seen in 2018.

There are also large educational and income differences between voters and nonvoters. Adults with a college degree made up 43% of voters in 2022, but only 25% of nonvoters. Those without a college degree made up 56% of voters, but 74% of nonvoters.

### Voting methods in the 2022 election

![Chart shows smaller shares voted by absentee or mail-in ballot in 2022 than in 2020](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2023/07/PP_2023.07.12_validated-voters_1-06.png?w=420)

As concerns over [the COVID-19 pandemic](https://www.pewresearch.org/topic/coronavirus-disease-covid-19/) declined, fewer voters reported having voted absentee or by mail in 2022 than in 2020.

In 2022, 43% of voters said they cast their ballot in person on Election Day. A somewhat smaller share (36%) said they cast an absentee or mail-in ballot, and 21% said they voted in person *before* Election Day.

In the 2020 election, held during the first year of the coronavirus pandemic, 45% of voters said they cast their ballots by absentee or mail-in ballot, while identical shares (27%) said they voted in person either on Election Day or beforehand.

As was the case in 2020, voters who supported Republican candidates were more likely to report having voted in person on Election Day than by other methods. About half (51%) of those who supported Republicans said they voted this way, while smaller shares said they voted by mail or absentee ballot (27%) or voted in person before Election Day (22%). In 2020, 38% said they voted in person on Election Day, while somewhat smaller shares said they voted by mail or absentee (32%) or voted in person before Election Day (30%).

![Chart shows large divides in candidate support by vote method](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2023/07/PP_2023.07.12_validated-voters_1-07.png?w=310)

Voters who supported Democratic candidates were more likely to say they cast absentee or mail-in ballots (45%). About one-third (34%) said they voted in person on Election Day and two-in-ten said they voted in person before Election Day. In 2020, a 58% majority said they voted by mail or absentee ballot, while just 17% said they voted in person on Election Day.

Reflecting these patterns, Republicans won a majority of votes among those who said they voted in person on Election Day, 60% to 38%. Democrats won – by an identical margin – voters who said they voted by mail or absentee ballot. Those who said they voted in person before Election Day were divided: 53% supported Republican candidates, while 46% voted for Democratic candidates.

args.summary:
This Pew Research Center report examines U.S. voter turnout patterns from 2018-2022, based on the American Trends Panel survey. Key findings include:

**Turnout Overview:**
- The 2020 presidential election (66% turnout) had the highest rate for any national election since 1900
- The 2018 midterm (49% turnout) was the highest since 1914
- The 2022 midterm (46% turnout) exceeded all midterms since 1970
- 70% of age-eligible citizens voted in at least one of the three elections (2018, 2020, 2022), while 37% voted in all three
- Adults who voted in at least one election divided evenly between Democrats/leaners (48%) and Republicans/leaners (48%)

**Racial and Ethnic Differences:**
- White Americans (43%) were much more consistent voters than Black (27%), Hispanic (19%), or Asian (21%) citizens across all three elections
- 47% of Hispanic citizens did not vote in any of the three elections
- Black voters supported Democratic House candidates 93% to 5% in 2022; Hispanic voters 60-39%; Asian voters 68-32%

**Education Differences:**
- White adults with college degrees (56%) voted in all three elections vs. White adults without degrees (35%)
- White voters without college degrees favored Republican House candidates 66% to 32% in 2022
- College-educated White voters tilted Democratic (52% to 47% in 2022)
- White adults without college degrees make up 41% of eligible voters; college-educated White adults make up 24% but 34% of 2022 voters

**Voters vs. Nonvoters (2022):**
- Adults under 50 made up 36% of voters but 64% of nonvoters
- White adults made up 75% of voters but only 55% of nonvoters; Hispanic and Black adults were underrepresented among voters
- College degree holders made up 43% of voters but only 25% of nonvoters

**Voting Methods:**
- In 2022: 43% voted in person on Election Day, 36% by mail/absentee, 21% in person before Election Day (down from mail voting in 2020)
- Republican supporters (51%) were more likely to vote in person on Election Day; Democratic supporters (45%) more likely to vote by mail/absentee
- Republicans won in-person Election Day voters 60-38%; Democrats won mail voters by the same margin

**Key Definitions Provided:** The report defines defectors, drop-off voters, midterm elections, mobilize, nonvoters, panel surveys, party affiliation, split-ticket voting, turnout, validated voters, and voter files.

#### [For Most Trump Voters, ‘Very Warm’ Feelings for Him Endured](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2018/08/09/for-most-trump-voters-very-warm-feelings-for-him-endured/)

# An examination of the 2016 electorate, based on validated voters

One of the biggest challenges facing those who seek to understand U.S. elections is establishing an accurate portrait of the American electorate and the choices made by different kinds of voters. Obtaining accurate data on how people voted is difficult for a number of reasons.

Surveys conducted before an election can overstate – or understate – the likelihood of some voters to vote. Depending on when a survey is conducted, voters might change their preferences before Election Day. Surveys conducted after an election can be affected by errors stemming from respondents’ recall, either for whom they voted for or whether they voted at all. Even the special surveys conducted by major news organizations on Election Day – the “exit polls” – face challenges from refusals to participate and from the fact that a sizable minority of voters actually vote prior to Election Day and must be interviewed using conventional surveys beforehand.

This report introduces a new approach for looking at the electorate in the 2016 general election: matching members of Pew Research Center’s nationally representative American Trends Panel to voter files to create a dataset of verified voters.

**See also**: [A Demographic Profile of 2018 Midterm Voters](https://www.pewresearch.org/methods/2020/09/08/democrats-made-gains-from-multiple-sources-in-2018-midterm-victories/)

The analysis in this report uses post-election survey reports of 2016 vote preferences (conducted Nov. 29-Dec. 12, 2016) among those who were identified as having voted using official voting records. These voter file records become available in the months after the election. (For more details, see “[Methodology](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2018/08/09/methodology-94/).”) Among these verified voters, the overall vote preference mirrors the election results very closely: 48% reported voting for Hillary Clinton and 45% for Donald Trump; by comparison, the official national vote tally was 48% for Clinton, 46% for Trump.

This data source allows researchers to take a detailed look at the voting preferences of Americans across a range of demographic traits and characteristics. It joins resources already available – including the National Election Pool exit polls, the American National Election Studies and the Current Population Survey’s Voting and Registration Supplement – in hopes of helping researchers continue to refine their understanding of the 2016 election and electorate, and address complex questions such as the role of race and education in 2016 candidate preferences.

It reaffirms many of the key findings about how different groups voted – and the composition of the electorate – that emerged from post-election analyses based on other surveys. Consistent with other analyses and past elections, race was strongly correlated with voting preference in 2016. But there are some differences as well. For instance, the wide educational divisions among white voters seen in other surveys are even more striking in these data.

![](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2018/08/2-12.png?w=309)

Overall, whites with a four-year college degree or more education made up 30% of all validated voters. Among these voters, far more (55%) said they voted for Clinton than for Trump (38%). Among the much larger group of white voters who had not completed college (44% of all voters), Trump won by more than two-to-one (64% to 28%).

There also were large differences in voter preferences by gender, age and marital status. Women were 13 percentage points more likely than men to have voted for Clinton (54% among women, 41% among men). The gender gap was particularly large among validated voters younger than 50. In this group, 63% of women said they voted for Clinton, compared with just 43% of men. Among voters ages 50 and older, the gender gap in support for Clinton was much narrower (48% vs. 40%).

About half (52%) of validated voters were married; among them, Trump had a 55% to 39% majority. Among unmarried voters, Clinton led by a similar margin (58% to 34%).

Just 13% of validated voters in 2016 were younger than 30. Voters in this age group reported voting for Clinton over Trump by a margin of 58% to 28%, with 14% supporting one of the third-party candidates. Among voters ages 30 to 49, 51% supported Clinton and 40% favored Trump. Trump had an advantage among 50- to 64-year-old voters (51% to 45%) and those 65 and older (53% to 44%).

*For a detailed breakdown of the composition of the 2016 electorate and voting preferences among a wide range of subgroups of voters, see Appendix. For the survey methodology and details on how survey respondents were matched to voter records, see “[Methodology](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2018/08/09/methodology-94/).”*

### 2016 vote by party and ideology

![2016 electorate was deeply divided along ideological lines](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2018/08/2-2.png?w=309)

Voter choice and party affiliation were nearly synonymous. Republican validated voters reported choosing Trump by a margin of 92% to 4%, while Democrats supported Clinton by 94% to 5%. The roughly one-third (34%) of the electorate who identified as independent or with another party divided their votes about evenly (43% Trump, 42% Clinton).

Similarly, voting was strongly correlated with ideological consistency, based on a scale composed of 10 political values – including opinions on race, homosexuality, the environment, foreign policy and the social safety net. Respondents are placed into five categories ranging from “consistently conservative” to “consistently liberal.” (For more, see “[The Partisan Divide on Political Values Grows Even Wider](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2017/10/05/1-partisan-divides-over-political-values-widen/).”)

Virtually all validated voters with consistently liberal values voted for Clinton over Trump (95% to 2%), while nearly all those with consistently conservative values went for Trump (98% to less than 1% for Clinton). Those who held conservative views on most political values (“mostly conservative”) favored Trump by 87% to 7%, while Clinton received the support of somewhat fewer among those who were “mostly liberal” (78%-13%). Among the nearly one-third of voters whose ideological profile was mixed, the vote was divided (48% Trump, 42% Clinton).

### Religious affiliation and attendance

![Wide divisions by religious affiliation, attendance by 2016 validated voters](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2018/08/2-3.png?w=309)

As in previous elections, voters in 2016 were sharply divided along religious lines. Protestants constituted about half of the electorate and reported voting for Trump over Clinton by a 56% to 39% margin. Catholics were more evenly divided; 52% reported voting for Trump, while 44% said they backed Clinton. Conversely, a solid majority of the religiously unaffiliated – atheists, agnostics and those who said their religion was “nothing in particular” – said they voted for Clinton (65%) over Trump (24%).

Within the Protestant tradition, voters were divided by race and evangelicalism. White evangelical Protestants, who constituted one out of every five voters, consistently have been among the strongest supporters of Republican candidates and supported Trump by a 77% to 16% margin.

This is nearly identical to the 78% to 16% advantage that Mitt Romney held over Barack Obama among white evangelicals in Pew Research Center polling on the eve of the 2012 presidential election.

Among white mainline Protestants (15% of voters overall) 57% said they voted for Trump and 37% reported voting for Clinton. Clinton won overwhelmingly among black Protestants (96% vs. 3% for Trump).

White non-Hispanic Catholics supported Trump by a ratio of about two-to-one (64% to 31%), while Hispanic Catholics favored Clinton by an even larger 78% to 19% margin.

Among all voters, those who reported attending services at least weekly favored Trump by a margin of 58% to 36%; the margin was similar among those who said they attended once or twice a month (60% to 38%). Those who reported attending services a few times a year or seldom were divided; 51% supported Clinton and 42% supported Trump. Among the nearly one-quarter of voters (23%) who said they never attend religious services, Clinton led Trump by 61% to 3o%.

### Demographic and political profiles of Clinton and Trump voters

As the pattern of the votes implies, the coalitions that supported the two major party nominees were very different demographically. These differences mirror the broad changes in the compositions of the two parties: [The Republican and Democratic coalitions](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2018/03/20/wide-gender-gap-growing-educational-divide-in-voters-party-identification/) are more dissimilar demographically than at any point in the past two decades.

In 2016, a 61% majority of those who said they voted for Clinton were women, while Trump voters were more evenly divided between men and women. Whites constituted nearly nine-in-ten (88%) of Trump’s supporters, compared with a smaller majority (60%) who voted for Clinton. Clinton’s voters also were younger than Trump’s on average (48% were younger than 50, compared with 35% for Trump).

![](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2018/08/2-4.png?w=614)

Among Clinton voters, 43% were college graduates, compared with 29% of Trump voters. And while non-college whites made up a majority of Trump’s voters (63%), they constituted only about a quarter of Clinton’s (26%).

About a third of Clinton voters (32%) lived in urban areas, versus just 12% among Trump voters. By contrast, 35% of Trump voters said they were from a rural area; among Clinton voters, 19% lived in a rural community.

The religious profile of the two candidates’ voters also differed considerably. About a third of Clinton voters (35%) were religiously unaffiliated, as were just 14% of Trump voters. White evangelical voters made up a much greater share of Trump’s voters (34%) than Clinton’s (7%). One-in-five Trump voters (20%) were white non-Hispanic Catholics, compared with just 9% of Clinton voters. And black Protestants were 14% of Clintons supporters, while almost no black Protestants in the survey reported voting for Trump.

### How did 2016 voters and nonvoters compare?

The data also provide a profile of voting-eligible nonvoters. Four-in-ten Americans who were eligible to vote [did not do so in 2016](http://www.electproject.org/2016g). There are striking demographic differences between voters and nonvoters, and significant political differences as well. Compared with validated voters, nonvoters were more likely to be younger, less educated, less affluent and nonwhite. And nonvoters were much more Democratic.

![Profiles of validated voters and nonvoters in 2016; nonwhites made up nearly half of nonvoters, but only a quarter of voters](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2018/08/2-5.png?w=614)

Among members of the panel who were categorized as nonvoters, 37% expressed a preference for Hillary Clinton, 30% for Donald Trump and 9% for Gary Johnson or Jill Stein; 14% preferred another candidate or declined to express a preference. Party affiliation among nonvoters skewed even more Democratic than did candidate preferences. Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents made up a 55% majority of nonvoters; about four-in-ten (41%) nonvoters were Republicans and Republican leaners. Voters were split almost evenly between Democrats and Democratic leaners (51%) and Republicans and Republican leaners (48%).

While nonvoters were less likely than voters to align with the GOP, the picture was less clear with respect to ideology. Owing in part to the tendency of nonvoters to be politically disengaged more generally, there are far more nonvoters than voters who fall into the “mixed” category on the ideological consistency scale. Among nonvoters who hold a set of political values with a distinct ideological orientation, those with generally liberal values (30% of all nonvoters) considerably outnumbered those with generally conservative values (18%).

Voters were much more highly educated than nonvoters. Just 16% of nonvoters were college graduates, compared with 37% of voters. Adults with only a high school education constituted half (51%) of nonvoters, compared with 30% among voters. Whites without a college degree made up 43% of nonvoters, about the same as among voters (44%). But nonwhites without a college degree were far more numerous among nonvoters (at 42%) than they were among voters (19%).

There also were wide income differences between voters and nonvoters. More than half (56%) of nonvoters reported annual family incomes under $30,000. Among voters, just 28% fell into this income category.

*CORRECTION (October 3, 2019): The text of the report has been edited to correct an error in the reported vote choice of non-Hispanic white mainline Protestants, 57% of whom voted for Donald Trump vs. 37% for Hillary Clinton. The graphics and tables were unaffected by this error.*

*CORRECTION: (August 9, 2018): In the chart “Among validated voters in 2016, wide gap among whites by education,” the “share of electorate” column has been edited to reflect updated percentages for gender by race to correct for a data tabulation error. Changes did not affect the report’s substantive findings. The associated detailed tables have also been updated accordingly.*

args.summary:
This report from Pew Research Center (published August 9, 2018) presents an examination of the 2016 U.S. electorate using a new methodology: matching Pew's American Trends Panel to official voter files to create a dataset of "verified voters." The analysis is based on post-election survey reports (Nov. 29-Dec. 12, 2016) among those identified as having voted using official records. Among verified voters, 48% reported voting for Hillary Clinton and 45% for Donald Trump, closely mirroring official results (48% Clinton, 46% Trump).

KEY FINDINGS:
- Education gaps among whites were striking: Whites with a college degree (30% of voters) supported Clinton 55% to 38%, while whites without a college degree (44% of voters) backed Trump 64% to 28%.
- Gender: Women were 13 points more likely than men to vote for Clinton (54% vs. 41%). Among voters under 50, the gap was larger (63% of women vs. 43% of men backed Clinton).
- Marital status: Married voters (52% of electorate) favored Trump 55% to 39%; unmarried voters favored Clinton 58% to 34%.
- Age: Just 13% of voters were under 30; this group backed Clinton 58% to 28%. Trump led among voters 50-64 (51%-45%) and 65+ (53%-44%).
- Party: Republicans voted Trump 92% to 4%; Democrats voted Clinton 94% to 5%; independents (34% of electorate) split nearly evenly (43% Trump, 42% Clinton).
- Ideology: Consistently liberal voters backed Clinton 95% to 2%; consistently conservative voters backed Trump 98% to <1%. Those with mixed ideological views split 48% Trump, 42% Clinton.
- Religion: Protestants backed Trump 56% to 39%; Catholics split more evenly (52% Trump, 44% Clinton). White evangelicals (1 in 5 voters) supported Trump 77% to 16% (nearly matching Romney's 78%-16% margin in 2012). White mainline Protestants favored Trump 57% to 37%; black Protestants backed Clinton 96% to 3%. White non-Hispanic Catholics favored Trump 64% to 31%, while Hispanic Catholics favored Clinton 78% to 19%. Those attending services at least weekly favored Trump 58% to 36%; the 23% who never attend favored Clinton 61% to 30%.

DEMOGRAPHIC PROFILES OF CANDIDATES' VOTERS:
- 61% of Clinton voters were women; Trump voters were more evenly split by gender.
- Whites made up 88% of Trump's voters vs. 60% of Clinton's.
- 48% of Clinton voters were under 50 vs. 35% of Trump's.
- 43% of Clinton voters were college graduates vs. 29% of Trump's. Non-college whites were 63% of Trump voters vs. 26% of Clinton's.
- 32% of Clinton voters lived in urban areas vs. 12% of Trump voters; 35% of Trump voters were rural vs. 19% of Clinton voters.
- 35% of Clinton voters were religiously unaffiliated vs. 14% of Trump voters; white evangelicals were 34% of Trump voters vs. 7% of Clinton voters.

VOTERS VS. NONVOTERS:
- Four-in-ten eligible Americans did not vote in 2016. Nonvoters were younger, less educated, less affluent, and more nonwhite than voters.
- Nonvoters were much more Democratic: 55% were Democrats/Democratic-leaning vs. 41% Republicans. Among nonvoters, 37% preferred Clinton, 30% Trump.
- Only 16% of nonvoters were college graduates vs. 37% of voters. Nonwhites without college degrees were 42% of nonvoters vs. 19% of voters.
- 56% of nonvoters had annual family incomes under $30,000 vs. 28% of voters.

The report notes that this method "reaffirms many of the key findings" from other surveys while revealing "wide educational divisions among white voters" that are "even more striking" in these validated data. Two corrections were issued (Aug 2018 regarding a chart data error; Oct 2019 correcting the white mainline Protestant vote: 57% Trump vs. 37% Clinton).

We also wanted to compare how turnout and vote choices differed from previous elections in 2020 and 2016. Measuring turnout among different groups in the electorate is challenging; it is particularly difficult to assess changes in turnout from election to election. Panel-based survey data provides us a unique opportunity to study elections. By surveying the same people over time and measuring their choice among the candidates (for both voters and nonvoters), we can more clearly see how differences in who stays home – and who turns out to vote – affect each election. We can also measure how adults’ partisan voting preferences change (or do not change) between elections. For this study, we surveyed U.S. adults on our nationally representative American Trends Panel (ATP). We verified their turnout using commercial voter files that aggregate publicly available official state turnout records. The first analysis of validated voters was completed after the 2016 election. Turnout was validated for subsequent elections in 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024. Each state and the District of Columbia compiles these publicly available turnout records as part of their routine election administration. To validate 2024 election turnout, we attempted to match adult citizens who are part of the ATP to a turnout record in at least one of three commercial voter files: one that serves conservative and Republican organizations and campaigns, one that serves progressive and Democratic organizations and campaigns, and one that is nonpartisan. A member of the ATP is considered a validated voter for a given election if they: ▪ Told us they voted, and ▪ Were recorded as having voted in at least one of the three commercial voter files. Those who said they did not vote in an election are considered nonvoters. Nonvoters also include anyone – regardless of their self-reported vote – for whom we could not locate a voting record in any of the three commercial voter files. Those who could not be matched were also considered nonvoters. Overall, 94% of panelists who we attempted to match were successfully matched to at least one of the three voter files. 4 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org The survey is weighted to be representative of the U.S. adult population by gender, race, ethnicity, partisan affiliation, education and other factors. For benchmarks of partisan affiliation within racial and ethnic categories, we used estimates produced by the Center’s 2023-24 Religious Landscape Study of more than 36,000 adults. Additional information about the voter file matching and verification process, as well as sample sizes for all elections reflected in the validated voter variables, can be found in the methodology section of this report. 5 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org Terminology Validated voters: Adult citizens who told us in a postelection survey that they voted in a given general election and have a record of voting in a commercial voter file. Voting-eligible: In this report, any U.S. adult citizen in the American Trends Panel is considered “eligible” to vote. In some states, criminal records disqualify adult citizens from voting in elections. This study does not attempt to identify such individuals if they are in the panel. In addition, eligible voters living abroad are not included in the panel. New and returning voters: Validated voters who turned out in the 2024 election, but not in the 2020 election. This includes both those who were old enough to vote in 2020, but did not, and voters who were too young to vote in 2020, but were 18 years of age or older in 2024 and cast a ballot. Differential partisan turnout: Refers to the difference in turnout between supporters of different parties (e.g., “More 2020 Trump voters than 2020 Biden voters turned out in 2024”). args.summary:
Pew Research Center analysis of the 2024 presidential election, based on validated voters from their American Trends Panel survey conducted Nov. 12-17, 2024, with turnout verified through three commercial voter files. Donald Trump defeated Kamala Harris by 1.5 percentage points, winning 312 Electoral College votes and the national popular vote for the first time. Trump's victory was built on a more racially and ethnically diverse coalition than in 2020 or 2016, driven primarily by differential partisan turnout rather than large-scale vote switching.

Key shifts: Among Hispanic voters, Trump nearly reached parity (51% Harris, 48% Trump) after losing 61%-36% to Biden in 2020. Trump won 15% of Black voters (up from 8% in 2020), and 40% of Asian voters (up from 30%). Trump's 2020 voters turned out at higher rates than Biden's (89% vs. 85%), and Trump won new/returning voters (those eligible but who did not vote in 2020) by 54%-42%. Unlike past elections where nonvoters favored Democrats, 2024 nonvoters were closely divided (44% Trump, 40% Harris), meaning universal turnout would not have significantly changed the popular vote margin.

Demographic patterns: The educational divide widened, with Trump winning noncollege voters by 14 points (double his 2016 margin) and Harris winning college graduates 57%-41%. The urban-rural gap grew, with Trump winning rural voters by 40 points (69%-29%) and Harris winning urban voters 65%-33%. Men under 50 shifted from favoring Biden by 10 points in 2020 to splitting evenly (49% Trump, 48% Harris). Trump won frequent religious service attenders 64%-34%. Trump made gains among naturalized citizens (who split nearly evenly, 51% Harris, 47% Trump, after favoring Biden 59%-38% in 2020), Catholics (55% Trump vs. 43% Harris after splitting evenly in 2020), and Protestants (26-point margin, up from 19 points).

Turnout was 64% in 2024 (second highest since 1960, behind 2020's 66%). Only 41% of eligible citizens voted in all three recent national elections (2020, 2022, 2024), while 26% voted in none. Regular voters skew White (75%), older (63% of 65+ voted in all three), and more educated (54% of college grads). In-person early voting grew to 32% of 2024 voters (up from 27% in 2020). Voters who only voted in 2024 (12% of voters) were Trump's strongest group, backing him 55%-41%.
