# Behind Biden’s 2020 Victory

## An examination of the 2020 electorate, based on validated voters

![](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/06/PM_21.06.24_validatedVoters_featured-1-1.jpg?w=640)

*Note (July 2023): A [new report about the 2022 validated voters](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/07/12/republican-gains-in-2022-midterms-driven-mostly-by-turnout-advantage/) used slightly revised 2020 estimates. There was nothing inaccurate about the 2020 results, but we chose to use a slightly different survey weighting approach that increases the precision of our estimates. None of the substantive findings from the 2020 report have been impacted. See the [2022 methodology](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/07/12/validated-voters-2022-methodology/) for more detail.*

Pew Research Center conducted this study to understand how Americans voted in 2020 and how their turnout and vote choices differed from 2016 and 2018. For this analysis, we surveyed U.S. adults online and verified their turnout in the three general elections using commercial voter files that aggregate official state turnout records. Panelists for whom a record of voting was located are considered validated voters; all others are presumed not to have voted.

We surveyed 11,818 U.S. adults online in November 2020, 10,640 adults in November 2018 and 4,183 adults in November and December 2016. The surveys were supplemented with measures taken from annual recruitment and profile surveys conducted in 2018 and 2020. Everyone who took part is a member of Pew Research Center’s American Trends Panel (ATP), an online survey panel recruited through national, random sampling of telephone numbers or, since 2018, residential addresses. This way nearly all U.S. adults have a chance of selection. The surveys are weighted to be representative of the U.S. adult population by gender, race, ethnicity, partisan affiliation, education, turnout and vote choice in the three elections, and many other characteristics. Read more about the [ATP’s methodology](https://www.pewresearch.org/our-methods/u-s-surveys/the-american-trends-panel/).

Here are the [questions used](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2021/06/PP-2021.06.30_validated-voters_TOPLINE.pdf) for this report and its [methodology](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2021/06/30/validated-voters-methodology/).

The 2020 presidential election was historic in many ways. Amid a [global pandemic](https://www.pewresearch.org/topics/coronavirus-disease-2019-covid-19/), with unprecedented [changes in how Americans voted,](https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/2020/elections/early-voting-numbers-so-far/) voter turnout rose 7 percentage points over 2016, resulting in a total of [66% of U.S. adult citizens](http://www.electproject.org/2020g) casting a ballot in the 2020 election. Joe Biden defeated Donald Trump 306-232 in the Electoral College and had a 4-point margin in the popular vote. While Biden’s popular vote differential was an improvement over Hillary Clinton’s 2016 2-point advantage, it was not as resounding as congressional Democrats’ 9-point advantage over Republicans in votes cast in the 2018 elections for the U.S. House of Representatives.

#### Validated voters, defined

Members of Pew Research Center’s nationally representative American Trends Panel were matched to public voting records from three national commercial voter files in an attempt to find a record for voting in the 2020 election. **Validated voters** are citizens who told us in a post-election survey that they voted in the 2020 general election *and* have a record for voting in a commercial voter file. Nonvoters are citizens who were not found to have a record of voting in any of the voter files or told us they did not vote.

A new analysis of validated 2020 voters from Pew Research Center’s American Trends Panel examines change and continuity in the electorate, both of which contributed to Biden’s victory. It looks at how new voters and voters who turned out in one or both previous elections voted in the 2020 presidential election and offers a detailed portrait of the demographic composition and vote choices of the 2020 electorate. It also provides a comparison with findings from our previous studies of the [2016](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2018/08/09/an-examination-of-the-2016-electorate-based-on-validated-voters/) and [2018 electorates](https://www.pewresearch.org/methods/2020/09/08/democrats-made-gains-from-multiple-sources-in-2018-midterm-victories/).

A number of factors determined the composition of the 2020 electorate and explain how it delivered Biden a victory. Among those who voted for Clinton and Trump in 2016, similar shares of each – about nine-in-ten – also turned out in 2020, and the vast majority remained loyal to the same party in the 2020 presidential contest. These voters formed substantial bases of support for both Biden and Trump. Overall, there were shifts in presidential candidate support among some key groups between 2016 and 2020, notably suburban voters and independents. On balance, these shifts helped Biden a little more than Trump.

![Chart shows voters who voted in 2018 but not 2016 favored Biden in 2020](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/06/PP_2021.06.30_validated-voters_00-01.png?w=420)

Overall, one-in-four 2020 voters (25%) had not voted in 2016. About a quarter of these (6% of all 2020 voters) showed up two years later – in 2018 – to cast ballots in the [highest-turnout midterm election in decades](https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2019/04/behind-2018-united-states-midterm-election-turnout.html). Those who voted in 2018 but not in 2016 backed Biden over Trump in the 2020 election by about two-to-one (62% to 36%).

Both Trump and Biden were able to bring new voters into the political process in 2020. The 19% of 2020 voters who did not vote in 2016 or 2018 split roughly evenly between the two candidates (49% Biden vs. 47% Trump). However, as with voters overall, there was a substantial age divide within this group. Among those under age 30 who voted in 2020 but not in either of the two previous elections, Biden led 59% to 33%, while Trump won among new or irregular voters ages 30 and older by 55% to 42%. Younger voters also made up an outsize share of these voters: Those under age 30 made up 38% of new or irregular 2020 voters, though they represented just 15% of *all* 2020 voters.

One somewhat unusual aspect of the 2016 election was the relatively high share of voters (nearly 6%) who voted for one of the third-party candidates (mostly the Libertarian and Green Party nominees), a fact many observers attributed to the [relative unpopularity](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2016/07/07/2016-campaign-strong-interest-widespread-dissatisfaction/) of both major party candidates. By comparison, just 2% of voters chose a third-party candidate in 2020. Overall, third-party 2016 voters who turned out in 2020 voted 53%-36% for Biden over Trump, with 10% opting for a third-party candidate. Among the 5% of Republicans who voted third-party in 2016 and voted in 2020, a majority (70%) supported Trump in 2020, but 18% backed Biden. Among the 5% of Democrats who voted third-party in 2016 and voted in 2020, just 8% supported Trump in 2020 while 85% voted for Biden.

Here are some of the other key findings from the analysis:

This analysis is based on a survey of 11,818 members of Pew Research Center’s American Trends Panel conducted Nov. 12-17, 2020, shortly after the general election. It also draws on surveys conducted among 10,640 panelists from Nov. 7-16, 2018, after the midterm election that year and 4,183 panelists from Nov. 29 to Dec. 12, 2016, after the general election. Researchers attempted to match the panelists to three different [commercial voter files](https://www.pewresearch.org/methods/2018/02/15/commercial-voter-files-and-the-study-of-u-s-politics/)that contain official records of voter registration and turnout for 2016, 2018 and 2020. (For more details, see [Methodology](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2021/06/30/validated-voters-methodology/).)

This study marries official turnout records with a post-election survey among a large, ongoing survey panel, with the goal of improving the accuracy of the results compared with relying on self-reported turnout alone. The survey panel also makes it possible to examine change in turnout and vote preference over time among many of the same individuals. This analysis joins a growing body of research seeking to achieve a more accurate assessment of the 2020 election, each based on somewhat different sources of data.[2](#fn-47028-2) Different methods and data sources have unique strengths and weaknesses, meaning that specific estimates are likely to vary among the studies and no single resource can be considered definitive.

#### Voting patterns in the 2020 election

The 2020 election featured continuity in the voting patterns of major demographic and political groups in the population, but there were a few important shifts. The gender gap in the 2020 election was narrower than it had been in 2016 as Democrats made gains among men and Republicans made gains among women. In the 2016 election, Donald Trump won men by 11 percentage points (52% to 41%) while Hillary Clinton won women by 15 points (54% to 39%). In the 2018 election, Democrats substantially narrowed the gap with men (50% of men voted for Democratic candidates, 48% for Republican candidates) while maintaining an 18-point lead among women. In the 2020 election, men again divided nearly evenly (50% Trump, 48% Biden), while Biden’s advantage narrowed to 11 points among women (55% to 44%).

![Chart shows the gender gap narrowed among White voters](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/06/PP_2021.06.30_validated-voters_00-02.png?w=640)

Similarly, as Biden increased his level of support among White men in the 2020 election relative to Clinton’s in 2016, Trump gained among White women, which had the effect of further narrowing the gender gap among White voters. In 2016, Trump won White men by 30 points (62% to 32%). That gap narrowed to a 17-point margin for Trump in 2020 (57% to 40%). White women, a group sometimes categorized as swing voters and who broke nearly evenly in 2016 (47% for Trump to 45% for Clinton), favored him in 2020 (53% to 46%).

Biden received the support of 92% of Black voters, nearly the same as Clinton received in 2016 and Democratic candidates for the U.S. House received in 2018.

While Biden took a 59% majority of the Hispanic vote, Trump (with 38%) gained significantly over the level of support Republican candidates for the House received in 2018 (25%). To be sure, [Hispanic voters](https://www.pewresearch.org/topic/race-ethnicity/racial-ethnic-groups/hispanics-latinos/hispanic-latino-voters/) are not a monolith; there is [substantial diversity](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2020/10/02/most-cuban-american-voters-identify-as-republican-in-2020/) within the Hispanic electorate.

![Chart shows as in 2016 and 2018, wide educational differences among 2020 voters](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/06/PP_2021.06.30_validated-voters_00-03.png?w=640)

One noteworthy feature of the 2020 election was the wide education gap among Hispanic voters. In 2020, Biden won college-educated Hispanic voters 69% to 30%. At the same time, Biden’s advantage over Trump among Hispanic voters who did not have a college degree was far narrower (55% to 41%).

One of the most pivotal groups in the 2016 election was White voters without a four-year college degree, who were critical to Trump’s electoral college victory that year (nationally, he won them by a wide 36-point margin in 2016, 64% to 28%). Prior to 2016, differences in candidate preferences by education were typically [much smaller](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2016/09/15/educational-divide-in-vote-preferences-on-track-to-be-wider-than-in-recent-elections/) than they were that year. In 2020, Trump won 65% of White non-college voters – nearly identical to his 2016 share – even as Biden outperformed Clinton among this group (33% of White non-college voters backed Biden, up from the 28% of this group Clinton won in 2016). At the same time, White voters with a college degree or higher supported Biden by roughly the same margin they had backed Clinton in 2016.

Trump’s stronghold among White men without a four-year college degree loosened somewhat in 2020. While he still won this group by a little more than two-to one (66% to Biden’s 31%), that 35 percentage point gap is notably smaller than the 50-point gap in the 2016 election, when 73% of White men without a college degree supported Trump, compared with 23% who supported Clinton. Meanwhile, White men with a four-year college degree have become increasingly supportive of Democratic candidates, breaking close to evenly in 2016 (47% for Clinton, 44% for Trump) but supporting Biden by a 10-point margin in 2020.

At the same time, Trump’s vote share among White women without a college degree grew slightly between the 2016 and 2020 presidential elections. In 2016, White, non-college women supported Trump by a margin of 56% to 33%. By 2020, Trump’s vote share rose to 64% among this group compared with 35% supporting Biden. Among white women with a college degree, support for Biden was on par with support for Clinton in 2016 (59%-40% in 2020).

#### Party and ideology

Biden and Trump benefited from similar levels of party loyalty in 2020, with Trump receiving 92% support among Republicans and Republican-leaning independents and Biden getting 94% among Democrats and Democratic leaners. Comparable levels of support for each candidate were seen among Democrats (95% for Biden) and Republicans (94% for Trump), not including leaners. Among independents and those who affiliated with other parties, Biden led Trump by 52%-43%.

![Chart shows Biden substantially increased Democratic support among independents from 2016](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/06/PP_2021.06.30_validated-voters_00-04.png?w=640)

Ideological divisions within the parties were also apparent in the vote, with both Trump and Biden doing better among the ideological core of their parties. Trump received the votes of 97% of conservative Republicans and leaners but a smaller majority (79%) of Republicans who describe themselves as moderate or liberal. Biden took 98% of the vote among liberal Democrats and leaners and 91% among those who are moderate or conservative.

#### Age and generation

A yawning age gap in voter support – a pattern that [emerged in the 2004 presidential election](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2012/11/26/young-voters-supported-obama-less-but-may-have-mattered-more/) for the first time since 1972 – continues to be evident, with voters under 30 favoring Joe Biden by 24 percentage points (Biden 59%, Trump 35%).

Perhaps reflecting the enduring impact of this long-term age gap, voters ages 30 to 49 were also solidly in the Democratic candidate’s camp in 2020, favoring Biden by 12 points (55%-43%), similar to Clinton’s share among this age group. By contrast, older age groups divided fairly evenly between Biden and Trump, a result not too different from 2016.

![Chart shows young voters were a strong group for the Democrats, but less so than in 2018](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/06/PP_2021.06.30_validated-voters_00-05.png?w=640)

These patterns also are apparent when the lens is shifted to birth cohorts, or [generations](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2019/01/17/where-millennials-end-and-generation-z-begins/) – groups of voters who share birth years and perhaps formative political experiences in common, such as the popularity of the president at the time they were first eligible to vote. Voters in the youngest adult generations today – Generation Z (those ages 18 to 23 in 2020) and the Millennial generation (ages 24 to 39 in 2020) – favored Biden over Trump by a margin of 20 percentage points, though Trump gained 8 points among Millennials compared with his 2016 performance. Generation Xers, those ages 40 to 55 in 2020, divided relatively evenly (51% to 48%), as did Baby Boomers. Only among members of the Silent Generation, ages 75 to 92 in 2020, was Trump clearly favored (by 58%-42%). Notably, Boomers and Silents (and the very small number of voters from the Greatest Generation) made up less than half of the electorate in 2020 (44%), compared with just over half in both 2016 and 2018.

#### Geography

The political split between America’s rural areas and its suburban and urban locales remained substantial in 2020. Biden did considerably better among suburban voters in 2020 than Clinton did in 2016 (54% for Biden, 45% for Clinton). By contrast, Trump garnered the support of 65% of rural voters, including 71% of White rural voters; the latter represented an increase over the 62% he received among this group in 2016. Biden received a solid majority of votes among urban residents (66% overall), but Trump gained among urbanites relative to his performance in 2016 (33% in 2020, 24% in 2016).

![Chart shows Democrats gained among suburban voters in 2018 and 2020](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/06/PP_2021.06.30_validated-voters_00-06.png?w=640)

#### Religion

Voters in 2020 sorted along religious lines in ways consistent with recent elections. Protestants constituted nearly half of all voters (46%), as they did in 2016. Within the Protestant tradition, White evangelicals accounted for 19% of all voters, but a much higher share of Trump’s voters (34%). Without such broad support for Trump among White evangelicals, Biden would have beaten him by more than 20 points.

White non-evangelical Protestants voted for Trump over Biden by a 14-point margin (57%-43%), while Black Protestants were an overwhelmingly Democratic group (91% voted for Biden).

![Chart shows stable voting patterns among most religious groups](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/06/PP_2021.06.30_validated-voters_00-07.png?w=640)

Biden, by contrast, drew strong support from religiously unaffiliated voters – atheists, agnostics, and those who say their religion is “nothing in particular.” Together, these voters made up 25% of voters, which is a slightly larger share of the total electorate than White evangelicals (19%). But support for Biden among the unaffiliated was not quite as lopsided as Trump’s support among White evangelicals (a 45-point margin for Biden among the unaffiliated vs. a 69-point margin for Trump among White evangelicals). Without the religiously unaffiliated, Trump would have had a 9-point popular vote margin over Biden.

White non-Hispanic Catholics were more supportive of Biden (at 42%) than they had been of Clinton in 2016 (31%), but Trump still captured a solid majority of their votes (57%). White Catholics made up 14% of all voters.

#### Demographic profiles of Trump and Biden voters

![Chart shows Biden’s voters more racially and ethnically diverse than Trump’s, but GOP voters slightly less likely to be White in 2020 than in 2016](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/06/PP_2021.06.30_validated-voters_00-08.png?w=420)

As was the case in the 2016 and 2018 elections, the Democratic voting coalition in 2020 looked quite different from the Republican coalition in several respects. Overall, Biden voters were younger, more racially and ethnically diverse, and less likely to live in rural areas than Trump voters.

In 2020, 85% of voters who cast a ballot for Trump were White non-Hispanic; this compares with just 61% of Biden voters. These differences are roughly consistent with the share of White voters in each party’s coalition in 2016.

Nearly two-in-ten voters who cast a ballot for Biden in the 2020 election (19%) were Black, identical to the share of Clinton voters in 2016 who were Black. That is significantly higher than the share of Trump voters who were Black (2%).

![Chart shows higher share of Biden’s voters were from suburban areas compared with Clinton](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/06/PP_2021.06.30_validated-voters_00-09.png?w=420)

The community profiles of Trump and Biden voters are similar in some fundamental ways to the previous two elections – but more voters who cast ballots for Biden in 2020 say they live in a suburban area compared with Clinton’s 2016 voters.

Overall, urban voters continue to constitute a larger share of the Democratic coalition compared with the Republican coalition. And rural voters remain a significantly larger portion of the Republican electorate.

However, when comparing Clinton’s voters with Biden’s, there are some significant shifts. In 2016, about half of Clinton’s voters described their communities as suburban (48%), while 32% said they were from an urban area and 19% were from a rural area.

![Chart shows differences in educational attainment of Trump, Biden coalitions](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/06/PP_2021.06.30_validated-voters_00-010.png?w=420)

In 2020, suburban voters made up a majority of Biden’s coalition (55%); 28% of his voters said they lived in urban areas and 17% were from rural areas.

In 2020, 31% of Trump voters had at least a four-year college degree – similar to the share of Trump voters who had a college degree in 2016. Far more Trump voters (roughly 70% in each presidential election) did not have a four-year college degree.

The Democratic electorate is more evenly divided when it comes to education. In 2020, 46% of Biden voters had at least a college degree; 53% did not have a degree.

As was the case in 2016, White voters without a four-year college degree made up a considerably larger share of GOP voters (58%) than Democratic voters (27%). At the same time, White voters with a college degree made up a larger share of Biden voters (34%) than Trump voters (27%).

![Chart shows nearly half of Biden’s voters were younger than 50](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/06/PP_2021.06.30_validated-voters_00-011.png?w=420)

In 2020, the age profiles of Democratic and Republican voters looked largely similar to 2016. Younger adults continue to make up a larger share of Democratic voters compared with Republican voters. For example, in 2020, nearly half of Biden voters (49%) were younger than 50; that compares with 39% of Trump voters in 2020.

Protestants made up a majority of those voting Republican in 2020, just as they did in 2016. Overall, 58% of Trump voters were Protestant, compared with just 35% of Biden voters. White evangelical Protestants, in particular, remained a critical part of the Republican voting coalition, making up 34% of Trump’s voters but just 6% of Biden’s.

![Chart shows Catholics were about one-fifth of both candidates’ voters in 2020](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/06/PP_2021.06.30_validated-voters_00-012.png?w=420)

Catholics made up similar shares of Biden and Trump voters (19% and 22%, respectively); in 2016, Catholics made up a slightly higher share of Trump voters compared with Clinton voters (23% vs. 18%). Voters who were unaffiliated with any religious tradition (atheists, agnostics and those who describe themselves as “nothing in particular”) made up 35% of Biden voters but just 14% of Trump voters in 2020.

![Chart shows White evangelical Protestants constituted roughly a third of voters for Republican candidates in the past three elections](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/06/PP_2021.06.30_validated-voters_00-013.png?w=640)

#### Voting methods in the 2020 presidential election

![Chart shows large share of voters cast a ballot by absentee or mail in the 2020 election](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/06/PP_2021.06.30_validated-voters_00-014.png?w=420)

The 2020 election brought a huge change in howAmericans cast their ballots. As some states looked to adapt to challenges in administering elections amid the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://www.pewresearch.org/topic/coronavirus-disease-covid-19/), large numbers of voters [were offered expanded access](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2020/06/24/as-states-move-to-expand-the-practice-relatively-few-americans-have-voted-by-mail/) to absentee and vote-by-mail options in the 2020 election. As a result, a record number of voters said they cast their ballots this way (46%). And smaller shares of voters said they either voted in person on Election Day (27%) or in person *before* Election Day (27%).

A majority of absentee voters said they had previously voted this way before the 2020 election (56%). Still, a sizable share (43%) said the November election was the first time they had cast an absentee or mail ballot.

![Chart shows Black voters were more likely than others to cast ballots in person before Election Day in 2020](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/06/PP_2021.06.30_validated-voters_00-015.png?w=420)

Sizable shares of voters across racial and ethnic subgroups cast absentee or mail-in ballots in the 2020 election – though there are some differences in voting methods when comparing across groups. White voters were most likely to say they voted in person on Election Day (30%). Comparably smaller shares of Black (20%) and Hispanic voters (18%) said the same.

Black voters were more likely than White or Hispanic voters to say they cast their ballot in person *before* Election Day (42% of Black voters, vs. 27% of Hispanic voters and 25% of White voters).

Voters ages 65 and older stand out in their voting behavior: 55% say they voted absentee or by mail in the 2020 election – 13 percentage points higher than the share of adults under 65 who cast a ballot by mail.

Urban and suburban voters were considerably more likely than rural voters to say they cast their ballot by mail (50% of urban and suburban vs. 35% of rural voters). In contrast, rural voters were more likely to report voting in person on Election Day.

![Chart shows sizable divides in candidate support by vote method](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/06/PP_2021.06.30_validated-voters_00-016.png?w=420)

A majority of Biden voters said they voted absentee or by mail in the 2020 election (58%). By contrast, about a third of Trump voters (32%) voted by mail. Roughly two-thirds of Trump voters (68%) said they voted in person, either on (38%) or before (30%) Election Day.  Reflecting these differences, Trump performed much better among voters who cast their ballots in person on Election Day (65% for Trump vs. 33% for Biden). These shares were reversed among absentee and mail-in voters: 65% of absentee voters said they voted for Biden, compared with 33% who voted for Trump.

Preferences were more evenly divided among those who cast their ballots in person ahead of Election Day: 52% voted for Trump while 47% voted for Biden.

#### Voters and nonvoters

The 2020 general election featured the [highest rate of voter turnout](https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2021/04/record-high-turnout-in-2020-general-election.html) in more than a century, with 66% of eligible adults casting a ballot for president.

All members of the American Trends Panel who took the 2020 post-election survey – whether they voted or not – were asked which candidate they preferred in the race for president. Nonvoters – citizens for whom no record of turnout could be located or who told us they did not vote – preferred Joe Biden over Donald Trump by 15 percentage points, 50% to 35%, compared with Biden’s 4-point overall advantage among voters.

Voters were nearly evenly divided on party affiliation, with 50% identifying or leaning Democratic and 48% identifying or leaning Republican, similar to the 51%-48% split in 2016. Nonvoters in 2020 were more closely divided on partisanship than they were in 2016. Among nonvoters in 2020, 46% were Democrats or leaned Democratic, while 41% were Republicans or leaned Republican. A majority of nonvoters in 2016 (55%) were Democrats or Democratic leaners, compared with about four-in-ten (41%) who were Republicans or leaned toward the Republican Party.

Despite notable changes in the demographics of the two candidates’ coalitions, the demographic composition of the electorate as a whole in 2020 did not differ much from that of 2016.

Although turnout was strong, stark demographic differences between voters and nonvoters similar to those seen in past U.S. elections were present in 2020, a pattern familiar to political observers.

Voters as a group were considerably older than nonvoters. Adults younger than 50 made up 45% of all voters but 68% of nonvoters – nearly identical to the pattern seen in 2016.

But generational change in the electorate was quite apparent. Very few members of Gen Z (born 1997 and later) were eligible to vote in the 2016 electorate, and they made up just 1% of all voters that year. In 2020, they were 8% of the total, though their lower rate of turnout compared with older age cohorts is reflected in the fact that they were 15% of eligible nonvoters. At the other end of the generational spectrum, members of the Silent and Greatest generations (born 1945 and earlier) fell from 16% of all voters in 2016 to just 8% in 2020, but their turnout rates remained among the highest of all generations.

![Chart shows despite higher turnout, wide disparities by age and race in voting persist](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/06/PP_2021.06.30_validated-voters_00-017.png?w=640)
![Chart shows as in 2016, voters in 2020 had higher incomes and more formal education than nonvoters](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/06/PP_2021.06.30_validated-voters_00-018.png?w=420)

Turnout differences by race and ethnicity persisted as well. White non-Hispanic adults were 72% of voters in 2020 but just 55% of nonvoting citizens. Black Americans made up 11% of voters, but a slightly larger share (14%) of nonvoting citizens, and Hispanic adults were 10% of voters but 20% of nonvoting citizens. Asian Americans (a relatively small but [fast-growing](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2021/04/09/asian-americans-are-the-fastest-growing-racial-or-ethnic-group-in-the-u-s/) group in the U.S.) made up 4% of voters and an identical share of nonvoting citizens (*note: nonvoters in this analysis do not include noncitizens)*.

Some of the largest differences between voters and nonvoters are seen on education and income. College graduates made up 39% of all voters in 2020 (about the same as in 2016) but only 17% of nonvoters. Adults with a high school education or less were 29% of all voters but half of nonvoters.

args.summary:
**Pew Research Center Report: "Behind Biden's 2020 Victory" (June 2021)**

This report examines the 2020 U.S. presidential election electorate based on validated voters, analyzing how turnout and vote choices differed from 2016 and 2018. The study surveyed 11,818 U.S. adults online in November 2020 (plus 10,640 in 2018 and 4,183 in 2016) through Pew Research Center's American Trends Panel, and verified turnout using commercial voter files aggregating official state records. "Validated voters" are citizens who reported voting AND have a matching record in a commercial voter file.

**Election Overview:**
- Voter turnout rose 7 points over 2016, reaching 66% of U.S. adult citizens - the highest rate in over a century.
- Joe Biden defeated Donald Trump 306-232 in the Electoral College with a 4-point popular vote margin (vs. Clinton's 2-point margin in 2016 and Democrats' 9-point House margin in 2018).

**New and Returning Voters:**
- 25% of 2020 voters had not voted in 2016. Those who voted in 2018 but not 2016 backed Biden 62%-36%.
- The 19% who voted in 2020 but neither prior election split nearly evenly (Biden 49%, Trump 47%), but under-30 new voters heavily favored Biden (59%-33%), while those 30+ favored Trump (55%-42%). Under-30 voters made up 38% of new/irregular voters but only 15% of all voters.
- Third-party 2016 voters who turned out in 2020 voted 53%-36% for Biden over Trump.

**Key Demographic Findings:**
- Gender gap narrowed: In 2016 Trump won men by 11 points and Clinton won women by 15 points; in 2020 men split nearly evenly (Trump 50%, Biden 48%) while Biden's women's advantage narrowed to 11 points (55%-44%).
- Biden won 92% of Black voters; took 59% of Hispanic vote (Trump gained significantly among Hispanics vs. 2018 House races).
- Trump won 65% of White non-college voters (nearly identical to 2016's 64%); Biden took 33% of this group (up from Clinton's 28%).
- Wide educational divide among Hispanics: Biden won college-educated Hispanics 69%-30% but only 55%-41% among non-college Hispanics.
- Trump won White men without degrees 66%-31% (a 35-point gap, down from 50 points in 2016).

**Party and Ideology:**
- Party loyalty was comparable: Trump got 92% from Republicans/leaners, Biden got 94% from Democrats/leaners.
- Among independents, Biden led 52%-43%.
- Ideological core voting was strong: Trump won 97% of conservative Republicans; Biden won 98% of liberal Democrats.

**Age and Generation:**
- Voters under 30 favored Biden by 24 points (59%-35%); ages 30-49 favored Biden by 12 points (55%-43%).
- Gen Z (ages 18-23) and Millennials (ages 24-39) favored Biden by 20 points overall.
- Silent Generation (75-92) was the only age group clearly favoring Trump (58%-42%).
- Boomers and Silents fell to 44% of the electorate in 2020 (from just over 50% in 2016/2018).

**Geography:**
- Biden improved among suburban voters (54% in 2020 vs. 45% for Clinton in 2016).
- Trump won 65% of rural voters, including 71% of White rural voters (up from 62% in 2016).
- Biden won 66% of urban voters, but Trump gained among urbanites (33% in 2020 vs. 24% in 2016).

**Religion:**
- White evangelicals were 19% of voters but 34% of Trump's voters; without them, Biden would have won by more than 20 points.
- Religious unaffiliated made up 25% of voters (larger than White evangelicals share); Biden won them by 45 points. Without them, Trump would have had a 9-point popular vote margin.
- White non-evangelical Protestants favored Trump 57%-43%; Black Protestants voted 91% for Biden.
- White Catholics supported Trump 57%-42%, though Biden improved among them vs. Clinton (42% vs. 31%).

**Candidate Coalitions:**
- Trump voters were 85% White non-Hispanic vs. 61% for Biden; 19% of Biden voters were Black vs. 2% for Trump.
- Suburban voters made up 55% of Biden's coalition (up from 48% for Clinton); 31% of Trump voters had college degrees vs. 46% of Biden voters.
- 49% of Biden voters were under 50 vs. 39% of Trump voters.
- White evangelicals made up 34% of Trump voters but just 6% of Biden voters; unaffiliated made up 35% of Biden voters vs. 14% for Trump.

**Voting Methods:**
- Record 46% voted absentee or by mail; 27% voted in person on Election Day; 27% voted in person early.
- 58% of Biden voters voted by mail vs. 32% of Trump voters; Trump won Election Day in-person voters 65%-33%, while Biden won absentee/mail voters 65%-33%.
- Black voters were most likely to vote in person early (42%); seniors 65+ voted by mail most (55%).

**Voters vs. Nonvoters:**
- Nonvoters preferred Biden by 15 points (50%-35%), vs. his 4-point margin among voters.
- Voters were older: under-50 adults were 45% of voters but 68% of nonvoters. Gen Z was 8% of voters (up from 1% in 2016) but 15% of eligible nonvoters.
- White adults were 72% of voters but 55% of nonvoters; Hispanics were 10% of voters but 20% of nonvoters.
- College graduates were 39% of voters but only 17% of nonvoters; those with high school education or less were 29% of voters but half of nonvoters.

*Note (July 2023): A new report on 2022 validated voters used slightly revised 2020 estimates with a different survey weighting approach; none of the 2020 substantive findings were impacted.*

#### [Republican Gains in 2022 Midterms Driven Mostly by Turnout Advantage](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/07/12/republican-gains-in-2022-midterms-driven-mostly-by-turnout-advantage/)

# 3. Demographic profiles of Republican and Democratic voters

**American Trends Panel:** Pew Research Center’s [online probability survey panel](https://www.pewresearch.org/our-methods/u-s-surveys/the-american-trends-panel/), which consists of more than 12,000 adults who take two to three surveys each month. Some panelists have been participating in surveys since 2014.

**Defectors/Defection:** People who either switch their vote to a different party’s candidate from one election to the next, or those who in a given election do not support the candidate of the party they usually support. Also referred to as **“vote switching.”**

**Drop off/Drop-off voters:** People who vote in a given election but not in a subsequent election. The term commonly refers to people who vote in a presidential election but not in the next midterm. It can also apply to any set of elections.

**Midterm elections:** General elections held in all states and the District of Columbia in the even-numbered years between presidential elections. All U.S. House seats are up for election every two years, as are a third of U.S. Senate seats (senators serve six-year terms).

**Mobilize:** Efforts by candidates, political campaigns and other organizations to encourage or facilitate eligible citizens to turn out to vote.

**Nonvoter:** Citizens who didn’t have a record of voting in any voter file or told us they didn’t vote.

**Panel survey:** A type of survey that relies on a group of people who have agreed to participate in multiple surveys over a time period. Panel surveys make it possible to observe how individuals change over time because the answers they give to questions in a current survey can be compared with their answers from a previous survey.

**Party affiliation/Party identification:** Psychological attachment to a particular political party, either thinking of oneself as a member of the party or expressing greater closeness to one party than another. Our study categorizes adults as Democrats or Republicans using their self-reported party identification in a survey.

**Split-ticket voting/Straight-ticket voting:** Voters typically cast ballots for more than one office in a general election. People who vote only for candidates of the same party are “straight-ticket” voters, while those who vote for candidates of different parties are “split-ticket” voters.

**Turnout:** Refers to “turning out” to vote, or simply “voting.” Also used to refer to the share of eligible adults who voted in a given election (e.g., “The turnout in 2020 among the voting eligible population in the U.S. was 67%”).

**Validated voters/Verified voter:** Citizens who told us in a post-election survey that they voted in the 2022 general elections *and* have a record for voting in a commercial voter file. (The two terms are interchangeable).

**Voter file:** A list of adults that includes information such as whether a person is registered to vote, which elections they have voted in, whether they voted in person or by mail, and additional data. Voter files do not say who a voter cast a ballot for. Federal law requires states to maintain electronic voter files, and businesses assemble these files to create a nationwide list of adults along with their voter information.

Many of the prominent demographic differences that have defined the two parties’ voting coalitions in recent years persisted in the 2022 elections. Democratic voters were once again, on average, younger, more racially and ethnically diverse, and more likely to possess college degrees than Republican voters. Those who voted for a Democratic candidate for the U.S. House were also less likely to live in a rural area and more likely to be religiously unaffiliated than Republican voters.

### Racial and ethnic composition of 2022 voters

![Chart shows Racial and ethnic composition of the 2022 electorate was quite similar to previous midterms in 2018](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2023/07/PP_2023.07.12_validated-voters_3-01.png?w=420)

More than eight-in-ten Republican voters in 2022 (85%) were White, non-Hispanic, down slightly (from 88%) compared with the 2018 midterms. Nearly identical shares of Democratic voters in 2022 (64%) and 2018 (65%) were White.

Black, non-Hispanic voters represented 17% of Democratic voters in 2022, while Hispanic and Asian voters accounted for 11% and 4%, respectively, of the Democratic Party’s support at the polls. Hispanic voters made up 7% of Republican voters, while 2% of GOP voters were Asian and 1% were Black.

### Rural, suburban and urban composition of 2022 voters

Even as the Democratic voting coalition has remained more urban and the Republican coalition more rural overall, the share of suburban voters among Democratic voters has been rising since 2016.

![Chart shows Suburban voters have grown as a share of Democratic voters since 2016](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2023/07/PP_2023.07.12_validated-voters_3-02.png?w=420)

In Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential victory, suburban voters made up nearly half of Democratic voters (48%). By the 2022 midterm elections, they comprised 57% of the Democratic voting coalition. Among the electorate as a whole, the share of suburban voters was 55% in 2022, up 5 percentage points from 2016.

The share of Democratic voters who describe their communities as urban declined by 5 points since 2016 (from 32% to 27%).

Among Republican voters, shifts have been much more modest in recent years. Roughly half of Republican voters in 2022 (53%) reported living in suburban communities, while 36% reported living in rural communities and 11% in urban areas. These shares were nearly identical to the shares of Republican voters living in suburban (53%), rural (35%) and urban (12%) communities in 2016.

### Educational composition of 2022 voters

![Chart shows White voters without college degrees were a smaller
share of Republican voters than in 2020, 2018, 2016](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2023/07/PP_2023.07.12_validated-voters_3-03.png?w=420)

A somewhat larger share of the electorate has held college degrees in each of the past two midterm elections (43% each) than in the past two presidential elections (39% in 2020, 37% in 2016).

As was the case in the 2018 midterms, voters with and without college degrees each accounted for roughly half of the Democratic Party’s voters in 2022 (51% held college degrees while 49% did not).

By contrast, a majority of Republican voters in 2022 had no college degree (63%); a smaller share had a college degree or more (37%). This is similar to the shares of Republican voters with and without a college degree in 2018.

White voters without college degrees made up a majority (54%) of Republican voters in 2022, compared with 27% of Democratic voters. Yet the share of Republican voters who are members of this group was down 4 points compared with the 2020 presidential election.

### Age composition of 2022 voters

The electorate was somewhat older in 2022, on average, than in other recent elections, with 64% of validated voters ages 50 and older. And while the Democratic voting coalition was once again younger than the Republican coalition, both parties relied slightly more on the ballots of older voters than they have in other recent elections.

![Chart shows a third of the electorate was 65 or older in 2022](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2023/07/PP_2023.07.12_validated-voters_3-04.png?w=420)

A majority of Democratic voters (57%) were ages 50 and older in the 2022 midterms, compared with 51% of Joe Biden’s voters in 2020 and 53% of voters who supported a Democratic House candidate in 2018. Just 14% of Democratic voters were under the age of 30 in 2022 — similar to the 15% of Democratic voters who were in this age group in 2018, but less than their share of Democratic voters in 2020 (17%).

Seven-in-ten Republican voters were 50 and older in the most recent election, compared with 62% of Republican voters in 2020 and 68% in 2018.

### Religious composition of 2022 voters

![Chart shows Protestants accounted for nearly six-in-ten Republican voters, compared with a third of Democratic voters](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2023/07/PP_2023.07.12_validated-voters_3-05.png?w=420)

Protestants once again accounted for a majority of Republican voters (59%), with their share of the party’s voters essentially unchanged across the past four elections. Protestants constituted a third of Democratic voters in 2022; a larger share of Democratic voters (39%) described themselves as religiously unaffiliated (including atheists, agnostics and those who describe themselves as “nothing in particular”).

White evangelical Protestant voters made up about a third of the Republican voting coalition in 2022, while accounting for just 5% of Democratic voters. And while Black Protestants continue to represent a more substantial share of Democratic voters than Republican voters (12% vs. 1%), the share of Republican voters who are Protestant and have a racial or ethnic background other than Black or White grew slightly in 2022 (to 8%, up from 5% in the previous three election cycles).

![Chart shows roughly a third of Republican voters have been White evangelical Protestants in each of the past four national elections](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2023/07/PP_2023.07.12_validated-voters_3-06.png?w=640)

--- SOURCE 3: Education and Lifetime Earnings in the United States ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4534330

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This research article, published in Demography (2015), examines differences in lifetime earnings by educational attainment in the United States. Using data from the Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP) matched to longitudinal tax earnings records from the Social Security Administration (SSA), the authors estimate 50-year work career effects of education on lifetime earnings for both men and women.

**Key findings:**

- **Gross lifetime earnings:** Men with a high school diploma earn approximately $1.54 million over a lifetime; those with a bachelor's degree earn $2.43 million; and those with a graduate degree earn $3.05 million. For women, the figures are $811,000, $1.44 million, and $1.87 million respectively.

- **Net lifetime earnings (after controlling for covariates):** The gap between high school graduates and bachelor's degree holders decreases from $896,000 to $655,000 for men and from $630,000 to $445,000 for women. Accounting for key covariates reduces the estimated lifetime earnings return to college by approximately 30%.

- **Net present value at age 20 (4% discount rate):** The value of a bachelor's degree compared to high school drops to about $259,000 for men and $180,000 for women.

**Methodology:** The study uses a semi-synthetic cohort approach, combining four birth cohorts (1932-1939, 1942-1949, 1952-1959, 1962-1969) to estimate 50-year earnings from ages 20 to 69. The authors employ quantile regression at the median, controlling for race/ethnicity, marital status, number of children (for women), region of birth, and high school academic preparation.

**Key comparisons:** The study finds that purely synthetic cohort methods (using cross-sectional data) overstate the earnings gains associated with a bachelor's degree by 23% for men and 42% for women compared to the longitudinal administrative data approach. The authors conclude that while higher education has persistent positive effects on earnings, the net effects on lifetime earnings are notably smaller than previously reported estimates.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis explores the stagnation of the college wage premium over the past two decades. The college wage premium (the gap in average wages between college-educated and high school–educated workers) rose dramatically from 39% in 1980 to 79% by 2000, but has remained flat since then, even declining slightly after the Great Recession. In 2023, it was slightly lower than its 2000 value.

The article highlights a key problem: while the wage premium has stagnated, the cost of a four-year degree has risen 40% between 2000-2001 and 2022-2023, reducing the financial return on college education.

Research by economists Leila Bengali and Robert Valletta (San Francisco Fed) examines potential causes. They find that both supply and demand factors are at play, but the key explanation is increased substitutability between college-educated and high school–educated workers. Since 2000, firms have become more willing to substitute high school–educated workers for college graduates, reducing demand for the latter. This shift reflects technological changes that no longer advantage college-educated workers as strongly as before. The authors note this trend predates recent AI tools.

The share of college graduates in the workforce grew from 31% in 2000 to 45% in 2025. Online job postings requiring a college degree declined from 1.2 per non-degree posting in 2010 to 0.6 per non-degree posting in 2020.

Despite the stagnation, experts note the college wage premium remains high (still ~76% higher wages for college graduates). Lifetime earnings for bachelor's degree holders average $2.8 million versus $1.6 million for high school graduates. The article cautions that these are averages and individual outcomes vary based on factors like major and personal characteristics.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Liberty Street Economics blog post (Federal Reserve Bank of New York), published April 16, 2025, by Jaison R. Abel and Richard Deitz, examines whether a college degree is still a worthwhile investment. Using internal rate of return methodology with quantile regression to estimate the return for the *median* (rather than average) graduate, the authors estimate the return to college at 12.5% in 2024—well above the threshold for a sound investment and comparing favorably to long-term stock market returns (~8%) and bonds (~4%). This return has held between 12-13% for the past three decades.

Key findings on costs: Direct out-of-pocket costs of college have actually fallen in recent years after inflation adjustment—average published tuition was ~$21,000/year in 2024, but after grant aid the average net price over four years was ~$30,000. However, opportunity costs (forgone wages, estimated at ~$150,000 in 2024 using median wages of high school graduates) have risen, pushing the average total cost of a degree from ~$140,000 in the late 1990s to $180,000 in 2024.

Key findings on benefits: The median college graduate with a bachelor's degree earns about $80,000/year compared to $47,000 for the median high school graduate—a premium of over $32,000 (about 68%), near its all-time high. The wage premium tends to grow over one's career.

Caveats: The estimates apply only to graduates (not dropouts); those who start but don't complete college incur costs with fewer benefits. Factoring dropout risk would reduce the return by roughly 1.5 percentage points. Calculations assume average costs over four years and median college wages. The post is part one of a two-part series; part two ("When College Might Not Be Worth It") examines whether college is worth it for at least a quarter of graduates.

URL: https://docs.iza.org/dp13182.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This IZA Discussion Paper (DP No. 13182, April 2020) by Barbara A. Butrica (Urban Institute) and Nadia S. Karamcheva (Congressional Budget Office) examines how rising household debt among older Americans affects retirement decisions. Using Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) data from 1989-2016 for adults aged 55-70, the study finds that more indebted older adults are more likely to work, less likely to be retired, and expect to work longer than those with less debt.

Key findings include:
- Household debt among older Americans has risen dramatically; the share of debt held by adults age 60-69 increased 61% and 90% for those age 70+ between 2003-2018.
- Between 1989 and 2016, the share of households age 55-70 with debt increased from 64% to 75% (peaking at 77% during the 2007 recession).
- Mean debt value more than doubled (from $48,800 to $125,300) and median debt more than quadrupled (from $14,500 to $61,000) between 1989-2016.
- Mortgages remain the predominant debt type (69% of total debt in 2016), but student loans increased most rapidly — the share of households with student debt more than tripled from 3% to 10%, with median amounts rising from $5,400 to $18,000.
- The average debt-to-asset ratio increased from 12% to 26% between 1989-2016; average debt-to-income ratio rose from 45% to 107%.

Regression results show:
- Those with debt are 11.2 percentage points more likely to work and 10.3 percentage points less likely to be retired.
- Doubling per person debt increases work likelihood by 1.1 percentage points and reduces retirement likelihood by 1.0 percentage point.
- Having mortgage debt raises work probability by 5.8 percentage points; credit card debt effects are stronger per dollar — a $10,000 credit card debt increase raises work likelihood by 9.4 percentage points vs. only 0.3 points for mortgages.
- Student loan debt has no statistically significant effect on retirement behavior on average, but reduces benefit receipt and retirement among the lowest-wealth older adults.
- Having credit card debt (uniquely) increases likelihood of receiving Social Security benefits by 4.5 percentage points.

The study uses inverse hyperbolic sine transformations, controls for Social Security program rules (EEA, FRA, RET), and addresses endogeneity concerns through instrumental variables based on SCF survey questions about attitudes toward debt. The authors conclude that while working longer can improve retirement security, people working longer to pay debts instead of saving may only marginally improve their retirement prospects.
</summary>

On AI concerns, Abel and Deitz were skeptical that AI is having widespread effects on recent graduates' employment, pointing instead to the tech sector weakness beginning in 2022 and general cooling of labor demand.

Cost analysis: Despite perceptions, direct out-of-pocket costs have fallen in recent years. While average published tuition at four-year colleges was about $21,000/year in 2024, most students receive nearly $15,000 in grants and aid. The average net price over four years was about $30,000. The biggest cost is the opportunity cost of foregone wages, not tuition.

Returns vary by major and time to graduation: Taking five years drops the median return to about 9%, and six years to 7%. For about a quarter of graduates, college doesn't pay off much financially.

The article concludes that while stock market investments offer potential for spectacular returns, those outcomes are not guaranteed and require timing; higher education remains a surer investment and a powerful engine of economic mobility.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"College is still worth it, at least, for most people. Even though some recent graduates may be having difficulty finding a good job right now, they are in a much better position than similarly aged workers without a college degree, who tend to have higher unemployment and lower wages." — Jaison R. Abel and Richard Deitz
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 18: Returns to Different Postsecondary Investments: Institution ... ---
URL: https://edworkingpapers.com/sites/default/files/Differential%20Returns%20Chapter%20-%20Final_0.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This chapter (Lovenheim and Smith, September 2022) is a comprehensive literature review on the returns to different postsecondary investments in the U.S. and internationally. It moves beyond the traditional treatment of college as a monolith, examining how returns vary by institution type (two-year vs. four-year, public vs. private not-for-profit vs. private for-profit), college quality/selectivity, credential type (associates, bachelor's, certificates, graduate degrees), field of study, vocational programs, and remedial education.

The authors begin by describing the structure of higher education. In the U.S., there were 3,757 degree-granting institutions in 2019-20, with 66% being four-year and 34% two-year institutions. Two-year colleges serve more disadvantaged populations (59.4% Pell Grant recipients vs. 46.8% at four-year colleges). Private for-profit institutions have the highest rates of Pell Grant and underrepresented minority enrollment and differ substantially in tuition and expenditures. More selective institutions serve fewer economically disadvantaged students, have higher expenditures per student, and higher graduation rates (75.4% for more selective vs. 40.3% for inclusive institutions).

The chapter highlights key methodological challenges, particularly the issue of students not randomly selecting into educational environments (selection bias and two-sided college-student matching). The authors adapt a model from Altonji and Zhong (2021) to clarify the assumptions underlying different estimation strategies.

Key findings from the literature include: (1) more-selective and higher-resource institutions yield higher returns; (2) there are wide variations in returns across programs, majors, and credentials; and (3) lower-SES students in the U.S. disproportionately sort into colleges and programs with lower returns, potentially reducing intergenerational economic mobility. The chapter reviews five policy interventions designed to support postsecondary success among disadvantaged students: recruiting and information simplification, lowering college entrance exam costs, coaching/mentoring high school students, promise programs, and comprehensive multi-barrier supports.

The authors note important limitations: they focus on gross rather than net returns, distinguish between enrollment and completion effects, and limit their analysis to educational and labor market outcomes, excluding health, family formation, civic engagement, and other potential returns. International contexts (such as centralized application systems in Chile, Norway, Colombia, and Croatia) provide unique identification opportunities for researchers.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"There is clear evidence that more-selective and higher-resource educational environments lead to higher returns.", "The wide variation in the returns to different postsecondary investments that we document leads to the question of how students from different backgrounds sort into these different institutions and programs.", "lower-SES students tend to invest in less-selective and lower-resource colleges. These differences, combined with the evidence on returns, suggest that features of the U.S. postsecondary system may actually reduce intergenerational economic mobility.", "In the 2019-20 academic year, there were 3,757 degree-granting institutions in the U.S. Of these, 2,476 (66 percent) are four-year institutions... and 1,269 (34 percent) are two-year institutions.", "46.8 percent of four-year college enrollees receive a Pell Grant, a measure of financial need, compared to 59.4 percent at two-year colleges."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 19: Should you compare your returns to a market index? | Leelyn Smith ---
URL: https://www.leelynsmith.com/insights/article/should-you-compare-your-returns-to-a-market-index

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Leelyn Smith (a financial advisory firm) addresses why investors should not compare their personal portfolio returns directly to market indexes like the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, or Nasdaq. The article outlines five key reasons why personal returns diverge from index performance:

1. **Different holdings**: Portfolios rarely match index composition. For example, a 75% stock/25% bond portfolio can't be compared to all-stock indexes; the Dow contains only 30 large-cap companies, and the S&P 500 only covers U.S. large-caps. Following the 2016 election of Donald Trump, the Dow gained over 1,000 points, with just three companies (Caterpillar, UnitedHealth Group, and Goldman Sachs) responsible for about 50% of those gains.

2. **Systematic investing prevents accurate comparisons**: Index returns assume a one-time lump sum investment on January 1, while most investors add or withdraw funds throughout the year at varying price points.

3. **Volatility distorts returns**: The S&P 500's average annual return was about 9.6% from 1992-2011, but yearly returns ranged from +37.58% (1995) to −37.00% (2008). The compounded annualized return was actually about 7.8%. A simplified example shows that a 10% loss followed by a 10% gain leaves you with $99, not $100, illustrating how volatility creates gaps between average and compounded returns.

4. **Trades and expenses affect results**: Indexes don't reflect trading activity, buying/selling costs, fees, or expenses that impact actual portfolio performance.

The article advises investors to set their own benchmarks based on the rate of return needed to achieve their personal goals (like retirement), rather than trying to match market indexes. The purpose of a portfolio isn't to beat the market, but to achieve financial goals while managing risk and time horizon.

The article also includes an "index of indexes" overview describing major market benchmarks: Dow Jones Industrial Average (30 blue chip companies), S&P 500 (500 large U.S. companies), Nasdaq Composite (approximately 4,500 over-the-counter stocks, heavily influenced by technology sector), Wilshire 5000 (broadest U.S. index, capitalization-weighted), Russell 2000 (about 2,000 smallest U.S. companies, used for small-cap benchmarking), MSCI All Country World Index (stocks from 46 countries, half developed/half emerging markets), and Bloomberg Barclays U.S. Aggregate Bond Index (most widely quoted bond index).

The content includes disclaimers noting that indexes are unmanaged, cannot be directly invested in, past performance doesn't guarantee future results, and investment decisions should be based on individual goals, time horizon, and risk tolerance.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Quite simply, your investment portfolio's performance won't match that of an index because the holdings in your portfolio are not identical to the securities that make up the index."; "An index's performance is stated in annual returns, which means that the numbers assume a one-time lump sum investment at the beginning of the year."; "The average annual return of the S&P 500 (including dividends) was about 9.6% from 1992 – 2011, but during this time period, the yearly returns ranged from a high of +37.58% in 1995 to low of –37.00% in 2008... the compounded annualized return... was about 7.8%."; "Keep in mind that the purpose of building a portfolio isn't to beat, or even match, the market. Rather, the objective is a build a portfolio that allows you to achieve your goals for retirement and other financial goals."; "Just three companies – Caterpillar, UnitedHealth Group and Goldman Sachs – were responsible for about 50% of the Dow's gains during this period."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 20: Stay the course: Investing for college through volatile markets | J.P. Morgan Asset Management ---
URL: https://am.jpmorgan.com/us/en/asset-management/adv/investment-strategies/529-college-savings-plan/staying-invested

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from J.P. Morgan Asset Management is an article titled "Stay the course: Investing for college through volatile markets," authored by Tricia Scarlata (Head of Education Savings) and Douglas Polak, CFA, CAIA (Investment Specialist). The article advises families to stay invested in 529 college savings plans during market volatility rather than overreacting to downturns.

The article presents three key principles for staying invested longer for college:
1. **Put time on your side** - Risk of loss historically decreases as time horizons increase; longer investing allows funds to ride out short-term volatility.
2. **Diversify your portfolio** - Combining stocks and bonds helps reduce risk since different investments rise and fall at different times.
3. **Focus on your goals, not the market** - Avoid major changes when stocks drop; doing nothing is usually best if goals and timelines haven't changed.

The article also explains how 529 plans help navigate market volatility through:
- **Tax benefits** - Money grows tax-free when used for qualified education expenses; only 1.9% of participants take early withdrawals before a child turns 18.
- **Broad investment menu** - Options range from conservative to aggressive, including "age-based" portfolios that automatically reduce risk as college approaches.
- **Professional investment management** - Managers like J.P. Morgan's Multi-Asset Solutions team actively monitor and adjust portfolios during volatile markets.
- **Automatic investing** - Regular scheduled contributions remove guesswork and emotion from decisions.

Key data points include: average annual S&P 500 return of 10.6% from 1980-2024 (data as of June 30, 2025), and intra-year market drop statistics. Since 529 plans have no mandatory withdrawal ages, investors aren't forced to sell at a loss, and can alternatively transfer 529 assets to a tax-free Roth IRA for the beneficiary's retirement (subject to requirements and limitations).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"During volatile times, remember that down markets don't last, but over-reacting to them can have lasting consequences on a child's education. The key to success isn't avoiding normal market ups and downs, it's staying invested through them with a long-term perspective and 529 plan."
</key_excerpts>

The webpage from EducationData.org provides comprehensive statistics on the average cost of college in the United States for the 2022-23 academic year. The average total cost of college (including tuition, fees, books, supplies, and living expenses) is $38,270 per student per year. The average cost of college has more than doubled in the 21st century, with a compound annual growth rate of 4.04% for tuition.

Key cost breakdowns: In-state students at public 4-year institutions living on campus spent $27,146 annually (tuition: $9,750). Out-of-state tuition at public 4-year institutions averages $28,386. The median weekly income for high school graduates is $899 ($46,748/year), representing lost income potential while studying. Student borrowers pay an average of $2,636 in interest each year and spend roughly 20 years paying off loans.

Historically, in 1963 the annual tuition at a 4-year public college was $243 (equivalent to $2,489 in 2024 dollars). From 1963 to 2022, tuition increased at a CAGR of 2.34% after adjusting for inflation. Between 2012-13 and 2022-23, tuition increased 25.6% at all 4-year colleges.

The most expensive states for public university tuition are Vermont ($17,600), New Hampshire ($17,019), and Pennsylvania ($16,217). The least expensive states are Florida ($4,540), Wyoming ($5,100), and the District of Columbia ($6,152). The page also includes lists of the most expensive and most affordable private nonprofit universities, along with detailed breakdowns of room and board costs, books and supplies, and additional expenses.

--- SOURCE 5: Cost of College Every Year Since the 1960s | BestColleges ---
URL: https://www.bestcolleges.com/research/college-costs-over-time

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from BestColleges.com examines how the cost of college education in the United States has changed over roughly the past 60 years, based on data from the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES). The report uses 2022-2023 constant dollars to account for inflation.

KEY DATA POINTS:
- One year's college tuition and fees cost just over $4,939 in 1963, rising to roughly $14,690 by 2022 — tuition has more than tripled, or increased by over 125% (about 2.3 times), between 1963 and 2022.
- The average total cost of a year of college (including room and board, books, and supplies) rose from about $12,130 in 1963 to just under $28,000 in 2022 — more than doubled, an increase of 128%.
- Between 2000 and 2022, average tuition and fees rose by 60%, from $9,204 to $14,688 per year. In just the 12 years between 2010 and 2022, tuition rose by 13%, from $12,979 to $14,688.
- Room and board almost doubled between 1963 and 2022, increasing 81% from $7,187 to $12,986. In the 20 years between 2000 and 2022, room and board rose about 39% while tuition rose 60%.
- Tuition spikes are the primary driver of rising overall college costs.

HISTORICAL TRENDS:
- The period 1973-1980 was one of the only periods when average tuition and fees fluctuated and decreased.
- Tuition rose again by the 1981-1982 academic year and continued rising nearly every year since.
- The only other exception was between 2020 and 2022, when tuition and fees dropped by about 6%.

BY SCHOOL TYPE:
- Four-year private nonprofit colleges have the highest average tuition; two-year public colleges have the lowest.
- Between 2000 and 2022, tuition increased most at private nonprofit two-year institutions, rising 68%.
- Private for-profit institutions saw the smallest changes; two-year for-profit tuition actually decreased by about 3%.
- Four-year public colleges saw the steepest price hikes from 2000-2022, jumping from roughly $13,000 to just over $20,000 annually (39% increase). Two-year public colleges cost roughly 30% more in 2022 than in 2002.
- Between 1963 and 2022, average cost of attendance increased most at private institutions (180%, or 2.79 times); four-year institutions increased ~147%, two-year institutions increased 63%, and public institutions rose 130%.
- From 2012-2022, average total cost rose 5%, from $26,209 to $27,673. Public school costs rose from $19,458 to $20,401 (~5%); private college costs rose from $44,668 to $49,320 (~10%).

OTHER NOTES:
- College tuition became more expensive than room and board for the first time in 1999 (room and board previously cost more than tuition).
- Over the last decade, total cost of attendance increased 8% at four-year schools for students living on campus versus 2% for students living off campus.
- As of July 2023, for-profit schools can no longer count students' GI Bill benefits as part of mandatory non-federal revenue, a change advocates hope will curb aggressive veteran recruiting.
- Rising costs have discouraged many students from attending college, contributing to declines in enrollment.
</summary>

One year's college tuition and fees in 1963 cost just over $4,939, when adjusting for inflation. By 2022, it cost roughly $14,690.

--- SOURCE 6: Average Debt for Class of 2020 Varies Widely by State and College; Private Student Loans Drive Up Debt Loads in High-Debt States - The Institute for College Access & Success ---
URL: https://ticas.org/affordability-2/average-debt-for-class-of-2020-varies-widely-by-state-and-college-private-student-loans-drive-up-debt-loads-in-high-debt-states

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This press release from The Institute for College Access & Success (TICAS), dated November 17, 2021, announces the release of "Student Debt and the Class of 2020," TICAS's sixteenth annual report on debt for bachelor's degree graduates of public and nonprofit colleges. The report finds vast variation in debt levels across states and colleges. Average student debt at graduation in 2020 ranged from $18,350 in Utah to $39,950 in New Hampshire, while the likelihood of having debt ranged from 39 percent in Utah to 73 percent in South Dakota. In nineteen states, average debt exceeded $30,000, and it was over $35,000 in six states.

Key findings include:
- Many high-debt states also had higher average private debt; eight states ranked in the top 10 for both private and overall debt. States with more private borrowing were concentrated in the Northeast, while states with less private debt were in the West.
- The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted students' lives in 2020, and early enrollment trends signal that the crisis has exacerbated existing inequities in access to quality, affordable higher education. While federal emergency aid helped mitigate disruptions, basic needs insecurity remained a major obstacle.
- Private loans are among the riskiest ways to pay for college—they typically cost more and lack federal consumer protections. The percentage of 2020 graduates with private loans ranged from 3 percent in Utah to 27 percent in North Dakota. Graduates of nonprofit colleges were more likely to graduate with private debt and with higher amounts than public college attendees: 39% of nonprofit institutions had over 15% of graduates with private debt, compared to 22% of public institutions.

Policy recommendations include the Education Department making a robust plan to protect borrowers as COVID-19 emergency federal benefits transition; Congress funding public colleges sustainably and equitably; strengthening protections for private student loan borrowers; and protecting access to federal loans. The report does not include national figures due to unavailable NPSAS data. TICAS is a trusted source of research, design, and advocacy for student-centered public policies promoting affordability, accountability, and equity in higher education.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Despite flattening levels of student loan debt in recent years, the debt of graduating classes has remained near an all-time high, and the debt borrowers hold continues to make their lives financially perilous," noted Sameer Gadkaree, TICAS president. "Given pre-existing economic disparities and vast racial disparities in wealth accumulation in our country, the students who suffer most from these disruptions tend to be BIPOC, first-generation, and those from low-income backgrounds.", "While historic levels of public investment in both federal safety nets and emergency aid for students and colleges helped to lessen the blunt of the economic impact of the pandemic for many, financial supports have not addressed long-term downward trend in funding for public higher education, as well as persistent inequities that predated the crisis," said Oliver Schak, TICAS research director and report co-author.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: classof2020.pdf ---
URL: https://ticas.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/classof2020.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This report from The Institute for College Access & Success (TICAS) is the 16th annual report on student loan debt among recent graduates from four-year colleges, documenting changes and variation in student debt across states and colleges for the Class of 2020. The report covers public and private nonprofit colleges only, as virtually no for-profit colleges report debt data.

**Key Findings:**
- State averages for debt at graduation in 2020 ranged from $18,350 (Utah) to $39,950 (New Hampshire)
- New graduates' likelihood of having debt varied from 39% (Utah) to 73% (South Dakota)
- In 19 states, average debt exceeded $30,000; six states had averages over $35,000
- High-debt states remain concentrated in the Northeast; low-debt states are mainly in the West
- The private student loan market grew from $92.6 billion in 2014 to $136.3 billion in 2021 (~47% increase), now comprising about 8% of all undergraduate and graduate debt
- More than half (53%) of undergraduates who took out private loans did not exhaust their federal loan eligibility; 30% took no federal loans at all

**COVID-19 Impacts:**
- Fall 2020 enrollment declined 3% overall, with community colleges dropping 13% (declines concentrated among Black -16%, Latina/o -15%, and Indigenous -15% students)
- Recent high school graduate enrollments fell 6.9%, concentrated among low-income students
- Fall 2020 saw the lowest persistence rates among first-year students since 2012
- Over a million students newly defaulted on federal loans in the 12 months preceding the pandemic
- Emergency forbearance on federal loans ended January 31, 2022
- In California, borrowers were nearly 4x more likely than non-borrowers to lose housing (22% vs 6%), 3x more likely to have difficulty paying for dependent care (30% vs 10%), and 2x as likely to miss a mortgage/rent/utility payment (41% vs 19%)

**Debt by School Type:**
- Public colleges: 75% of institutions reported over 50% of graduates with debt; only 12% reported average debt over $35,000
- Private nonprofits: 31% reported average debt over $35,000, with debt ranging widely based on need-based aid and student demographics
- For-profit colleges: Students default at much higher rates (30% within 12 years vs 4% at public and 5% at nonprofit colleges)

**Private Debt by State:**
- Percentage of graduates with private loans ranged from 3% (Utah) to 27% (North Dakota)
- Average private debt ranged from $13,600 (New Mexico) to $51,750 (District of Columbia)
- Nonprofit college graduates are more likely to graduate with private debt than public college graduates

**Undocumented Students/DACA:**
- An estimated 427,000 undocumented students were enrolled in higher education in 2019 (including 181,000 DACA recipients/eligible)
- Undocumented students cannot access federal financial aid and often must rely on costlier private loans
- 16 states and DC provide in-state tuition and some aid; 5 states bar access; 3 states prohibit enrollment of undocumented students
