[![my529](https://my529.org/wp-content/themes/my529-savings-plan/assets/img/color-logo-tagline.svg)](https://my529.org "my529")



# High school graduates have many educational opportunities and some pay more than ever

Market factors like artificial intelligence are reconfiguring the workforce, leading many recent high school graduates to consider apprenticeships, trade schools, technical colleges and additional cost-saving methods for achieving degrees. Gen Z wants to be certain that their investments of time and money will pay off. Between constantly evolving technology, the cost of education, and the truly countless paths available to students today, there are many paths for success.

Future outcomes are forged between the ages 14-24, a time known as the “decisive decade.” During this period students navigate from one growth opportunity to another and experience brain development around decision making and risk-taking to help shape their futures.[1](#_edn1) The conventional tradition is “you graduate from high school and go to a four-year university.” That wisdom doesn’t reflect current data or career outcomes, as seen in the following research on ROI across various paths to higher education.

##### **Specialized trades are offering solid skills and high starting salaries**

The promises of trade school are working. The National Student Clearinghouse Research Center found student enrollment in vocational-focused (rather than transfer-focused) community colleges jumped by 17.6% from 2023 to 2024, on top of a 4% increase the prior year.[2](#_edn2) Additionally, people who complete a [registered apprenticeship](https://www.apprenticeship.gov/sites/default/files/DOLIndFSCareerSeeker-043024-508.pdf) earn an average starting salary of $80,000 and have a lifetime earning average of $300k over peers who don’t.[3](#_edn3)

Trade positions work well for individuals who are entrepreneurial and capable of promoting their services through social media and local marketing. If you have recently hired anyone for a renovation, you know that quality work generates enough positive word of mouth to book out months in advance, allowing tradespeople to control their calendars and benefit directly from their overtime efforts. Plus, students can earn money while attending apprenticeship programs, creating a longer runway for saving goals like retirement and their children’s 529 plans.

##### **Technical colleges deliver strong ROI**

Gen Z prioritizes staying ahead of the AI learning curve to ensure their educational investments keep up with — and survive — technology improvements. Technical colleges help students learn entry-level skills, while also achieving higher average wages. The Foundation for Research on Equal Opportunity found “median ROI for the technical trades is $313,000, compared to just $160,000 for the median bachelor’s degree. Two-year degrees in nursing and other health professions also boast a strong median ROI of $224,000.”[4](#_edn4)

The Utah Foundation examined long term value of higher education programs over 40 years and Neumont College of Computer Science surpassed all other Utah schools.[5](#_edn5) Attending a technical college allows students to skip general education classes and jump straight to building on marketable skills, empowering them to take on paying projects or internships simultaneous to completing their coursework, all while still enjoying the social and extracurricular opportunities a school campus offers.

##### **Not all four-year degrees break even, but some majors offer dependable returns**

Four-year universities are seeing their enrollment numbers drop and are concerned about continuing to attract new students, but they aren’t dead yet! With careful consideration, students can choose an undergraduate major that will reliably pay off.

A recent Salt Lake Tribune study of 656 occupations across 22 industries tracked earnings over an individual’s career and the range is significant. Over a 20-year career, these numbers accumulate to a range of $577,408 to $1,962,883. In addition to illustrating the benefits of a bachelor’s degree, the Tribune study also reinforced that not every well-paying job requires a bachelor’s degree. “An associate’s degree can also be lucrative in the health care field — like magnetic resonance imaging technologists, who make a median annual wage of $78,000.”[6](#_edn6)

Not all degrees are equal, but regardless of degree choice, starting at a community college can help boost returns by keeping costs low. Not only do students have the opportunity to experience greater variety during their education, but the final diploma will be no different — and cost less. Attending summer school at community college or earning college credit during high school can shave off semesters or help a student narrow their academic focus.

When it comes to ROI on coursework, we want your time and money to result in credits you can use toward your certification or diploma. Classes that aren’t completed or don’t apply to your ultimate degree may be the costliest.

##### **How long until you can expect to break even?**

Higher education is an expensive endeavor, but the rewards exceed purely financial gains to include intellectual, social and societal benefits. Those qualitative factors are important to consider and thanks to some insightful tools, you can compare some of the quantitative variables.

The Foundation for Research on Equal Opportunity did extensive reporting on the rate of return across various certificates and degrees, and you may find their interactive graphs helpful. You can utilize the drop downs to isolate the majors you are considering and see the dispersion of earnings, including what percentage of those degree owners never achieve a positive ROI.[7](#_edn7) If you wish to explore these resources, they can be found in the endnotes.

Students can also explore average outcomes across specific majors at various schools with Georgetown University’s ROI calculator.[8](#_edn8) Paired with the my529 [College Savings Estimator](https://my529.org/learn/college-savings-estimator/?utm_source=FA&utm_medium=Newsletter&utm_campaign=SummerFAN&utm_content=CollegeEstimator) tool, students can use these resources to capture a clear picture of anticipated total costs against the predicted future earnings of individual programs. This will help ensure that their investments of time and money are well spent, as almost one third of higher education students are enrolled in programs that are unlikely to pay off.

--- SOURCE 1: Center on Society and Health ---
URL: https://societyhealth.vcu.edu/work/the-projects/education-it-matters-more-to-health-than-ever-before.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage, published February 13, 2015, by the Center on Society and Health at Virginia Commonwealth University, presents the first installment of the "Education and Health Initiative." It argues that the link between education and health has never been stronger, with Americans who have fewer years of education experiencing poorer health and shorter lives. Since the 1990s, life expectancy has actually decreased for people without a high school education, especially white women.

**Key Findings:**

- **Saving Lives:** Policies that support children's educational success are smart strategies for reducing chronic diseases like diabetes and heart disease. More education leads to higher earnings, which provide access to healthy food, safer homes, and better healthcare.
- **Saving Dollars:** Investments in education, jobs, and economic growth may be the best way to curb rising healthcare costs. Cutting "non-health" programs can ultimately cost more by creating a sicker population.

**The Widening Health Disadvantage:**

- **Shorter Lives:** Between 1990 and 2008, the life expectancy gap between the most and least educated Americans grew from 13 to 14 years for males and from 8 to 10 years for females.
- **Worse Health:** By 2011, diabetes prevalence reached 15% for adults without a high school education, compared to 7% for college graduates.
- **More Risk Factors:** Smoking rates in 2011 were 27% for those without a high school diploma vs. 8% for those with a Bachelor's degree. Obesity rates among girls in households headed by someone without a high school diploma increased from 11.3% to 22.3% (1988-2010), compared to 5.4% to 7.1% in college-educated households.
- **Greater Disability:** The ratio of disability levels between those with grade school education and those with some college increased between 1970 and 1990.

**Americans Without a High School Diploma Are at Greatest Risk:**

- Death rates among adults with less than 12 years of education increased between 1993 and 2001 (by 0.5% among blacks, 1.3% among white males, and 3.2% among white females).
- Among whites with less than 12 years of education, life expectancy at age 25 fell by more than three years for men and by more than five years for women between 1990 and 2008.

**Compared to College Graduates, Those with Less Education:**

- Die 9 years sooner at age 25.
- Are more likely to have diabetes, heart disease, and diminished health status.
- Generate higher medical care costs, are less productive at work, and experience more psychological distress.
- Are more likely to smoke, be physically inactive, and be obese.

**Race and Education:** Differences in life expectancy by education are now greater among whites than among people of color. Blacks with more education live longer than whites with less than a high school education. Even a few additional years of education make a difference for health across all racial and ethnic groups.

**Why Education Matters More Now:** In today's knowledge economy, education paves the way to good jobs, better health insurance, and healthier lifestyles. Additionally, "upstream" factors like early childhood living conditions and neighborhood stress can disturb education and cause lasting biological harms, shaping health trajectories for a lifetime.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A study published January 23, 2025, in The Lancet Public Health by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) at the University of Washington found that US college graduates live an average of 11 years longer than those who never finished high school. The gap widened from 8 years in 2000 to nearly 11 years in 2019. College graduates increased their lifespans by 2.5 years to 84.2 years (ranking 4th globally if a country), while those without a high school diploma saw no improvement, remaining at 73.5 years (ranking 137th globally). High school graduates increased to 77.3 years, and those with some college reached 82.1 years. Across 3,110 US counties, life expectancy for the least educated ranged from 57.9 to 90.1 years, while college graduates ranged from 75.2 to 93.9 years. Geographic disparities were largest in the Southeast, Appalachia, and parts of South Dakota. Females generally lived longer than males, and the education gap was larger for males. The study was the first to examine educational disparities in life expectancy by sex at age 25 across all US counties from 2000 to 2019 across four educational levels.
</summary>

"In the US, more formal education often translates to better employment opportunities, including higher-paying jobs that have fewer health risks," said the study's senior author and IHME Associate Professor Laura Dwyer-Lindgren. In contrast, those with less than a high school degree would have ranked 137th.,The variation across counties was largest for those who didn't finish high school at 57.9 to 90.1 years, a difference of 32.2 years. The range across counties was smallest for college graduates at 75.2 to 93.9 years, a difference of 18.7 years.,Those who did not finish high school in California had large increases in LE while many other counties had declines. This may be related to the state's large immigrant population. --- SOURCE 3: Education levels may affect mortality trends | National Institutes of Health (NIH) ---
URL: https://www.nih.gov/news-events/nih-research-matters/education-levels-may-affect-mortality-trends

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A study published in JAMA Health Forum on June 13, 2025, led by Dr. Andrew Stokes at Boston University School of Public Health, examined U.S. mortality rates by educational attainment before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Using CDC and Census Bureau data on over 47 million deaths, researchers compared actual mortality rates from 2011-2023 against expected rates based on 2006-2010 trends among adults aged 35+.

Key findings: In 2023, there were 525,505 excess deaths total. Among those without a bachelor's degree, there were more than 480,000 excess deaths (26% higher than anticipated). Among those with a bachelor's degree, there were about 44,000 excess deaths (8% higher than anticipated). While COVID-19 was a leading cause of excess deaths between 2020-2023, much of the increase was associated with circulatory diseases and diabetes. Drug poisoning deaths also increased, especially among men without a college degree.

The study noted limitations: more adults graduated from college in 2023 than in 2006, making the non-college group relatively more disadvantaged. The research was funded by NIH's NICHD and the W.K. Kellogg Foundation.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic article from PMC examines the relationship between educational attainment and adult mortality in the United States. The article, authored by Robert A. Hummer and Elaine M. Hernandez, analyzes how higher levels of education correlate with lower mortality rates and longer life expectancy.

Key findings include:

1. **Education-Mortality Gradient**: Highly educated adults have significantly lower mortality rates than less-educated individuals across every age, gender, and racial/ethnic subgroup. 2. **Methodological Issues**: Education level is often inaccurately reported on death certificates, and using only 3-4 educational categories may underestimate the true mortality differences. Survey-based data with self-reported education and more granular categories reveals wider gaps.

3. **Demographic Variations**: Educational differences in mortality are wider among younger adults (25-44) compared to older adults (65+), wider among men than women, and wider among whites than among Black or Hispanic adults.

4. **Historical Trends**: Educational differences in mortality have widened significantly over the past 50 years. The gap is likely the widest in U.S. history. 5. **Causality**: The majority of U.S. evidence suggests the education-mortality association is predominantly causal, though a Danish twin study casts some doubt. Even after accounting for childhood socioeconomic status and intelligence, a strong association remains.

6. **Mechanisms**: Four key mechanisms link education to lower mortality: socioeconomic attainment (income/occupation, 30-40% of the difference), health behaviors (another ~30%, especially smoking), social ties (10-15%), and cognitive functioning.

7. **Policy Implications**: The article argues that educational investments should be considered "upstream" health policy. Targeting high school completion rates could significantly reduce mortality, as obtaining a high school degree shows a steep reduction in mortality odds. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This research article, published in *Research in Higher Education*, examines how college attendance increases voting and for whom these effects are strongest. The authors—Ahearn, Brand, and Zhou—use a nonparametric causal mediation analysis with data from the 1979 and 1997 National Longitudinal Surveys of Youth (NLSY) cohorts.

**Key findings:**
- College attendance increases self-reported voting by about 12 percentage points overall.
- The effect operates primarily through a **direct pathway** (socialization, civic literacy, social networks), accounting for nearly two-thirds of the total effect (7.5 percentage points).
- **Indirect pathways** via bachelor's degree completion, family formation, and socioeconomic attainment account for the remaining 4.5 percentage points.
- **Heterogeneity is significant**: The largest impact of college on voting is for individuals least likely to attend college (about 17 percentage points), decreasing to about 6 percentage points for those most likely to attend. - The authors find little heterogeneity in the indirect effects via degree completion, family, or SES.

**Methodology:** The study uses boosted regression trees for estimation, a causal mediation framework that accounts for causally dependent mediators (college completion → family characteristics → SES → voting), and propensity score-based heterogeneity analysis. The authors address potential biases from self-reported voting data and survey attrition through sensitivity analyses.

**Conclusion:** Civic returns to college are not contingent upon degree completion or socioeconomic returns. The findings suggest that expanding higher education to disadvantaged youth has broader societal benefits beyond economic returns, particularly in boosting political participation among those least likely to attend college.

--- SOURCE 9: Public Opinion Polling Basics ---
URL: https://www.pewresearch.org/course/public-opinion-polling-basics

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive educational course from Pew Research Center titled "Public Opinion Polling Basics," authored by Senior Survey Advisor Scott Keeter. The course is structured into six lessons:

**Lesson 1: Why do we have opinion polls?** Polls provide an equal voice to everyone in the population regardless of wealth, age, education, or race. Unlike elections (which are blunt and exclude non-voters), polls use random sampling to give everyone a known chance of being included. Without polls, we'd rely on unreliable "man on the street" interviews.

**Lesson 2: How does polling work?** A poll requires three things: a mode of interview (phone, mail, web, in-person), a sample (ideally random), and a questionnaire. Random sampling gives everyone an equal chance of being included. Weighting adjusts for differences between those who participate and those who don't. Opt-in sampling (where people volunteer) is less accurate than random sampling and vulnerable to bogus respondents. The course highlights a cautionary example where an opt-in poll found 20% of adults under 30 agreed "the Holocaust is a myth," while Pew's probability-based panel found only 3%.

**Lesson 3: Different kinds of polls** - Includes the decennial census, government surveys, issue polling (e.g., abortion views post-Dobbs), market research, and election polls. Also discusses non-survey methods like focus groups and social media analysis.

**Lesson 4: Election polls** - These polls need to determine who will actually vote, which is challenging. In 2020, national polls overstated Joe Biden's margin over Trump by 3.9 percentage points on average (largest error since 1980). However, accuracy improved in 2022.

**Lesson 5: Is accurate polling becoming harder?** Response rates have declined dramatically (illustrated by Pew's telephone survey response rates over 25 years). People with higher education and income are more likely to participate. However, for issue polling (non-election topics), errors in candidate support make little difference.

**Lesson 6: What to look for in a poll** - Consumers should look for transparency: methodology statements, question wording (toplines), who conducted the poll, sample size, mode of interview, dates conducted, and margin of error. Reputable organizations like Pew Research Center, Gallup, CNN, Fox News, and various university research centers have track records to protect.
</summary>

Educational aspirations are high among migrant families but insufficient without support structures. Immigrant mothers' labour market participation has a particularly strong impact on children's outcomes.

1. **Philosophical Distinctions:** Life satisfaction is rooted in subjectivist theories of well-being (allowing individuals to evaluate their lives by their own criteria), while PA and NA are grounded in hedonistic theories (defining well-being by affective experience). 2. **Subjective vs. Objective:** The author argues that hedonism is actually an objective theory of well-being because it imposes a fixed criterion (pleasure/pain balance) on all individuals. Only life satisfaction is truly "subjective" in the normative sense—letting people define happiness for themselves.

3. **Competing Models:** The article reviews and compares the Affective Component Model (where PA and NA directly influence LS judgments) versus the Underlying Sense of Well-Being (USWB) model (where a latent factor drives all three components). Statistical analyses using Busseri & Erb's meta-analytic data show both models are consistent with the data, and neither can be definitively confirmed.

4. **Psychometric Critique:** The USWB model faces problems when PA and NA are only weakly correlated (as with PANAS scales), leading to implausible factor loadings. The author emphasizes that latent variables require theoretical justification, not just statistical convenience.

5. **Conclusion:** SWB is not a well-defined unitary construct. Life satisfaction should be treated as a distinct subjective social indicator that captures people's own evaluations of their lives, not merely a component of hedonic well-being or a proxy for affective experience. The article recommends studying PA, NA, and LS separately rather than collapsing them into a composite score.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Life satisfaction is a subjective indicator in the normative sense—it allows individuals to evaluate their lives based on their own criteria. In contrast, PA and NA are rooted in hedonistic theories, where well-being is defined by affective experience.", "The key conclusion is that variance in life satisfaction judgments that is not shared with hedonic indicators should not be dismissed as measurement error. Instead, it may contain valid information about how people personally assess their lives.", "I have argued that SWB is not a well-defined theoretical construct. The label simply groups two theories of happiness—hedonistic and subjectivist—under a broad umbrella, but this does not mean they form a unified concept.", "Life satisfaction is a valid indicator of happiness only under the assumption that happiness cannot be objectively defined and that people can generate meaningful, personal theories of well-being.", "This makes life satisfaction a unique and important social indicator. It is not merely a component of SWB, but an independent construct that captures people's own evaluations of their lives—evaluations that may or may not align with affective states."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Marriage and divorce: patterns by gender, race, and educational ... ---
URL: https://www.bls.gov/opub/mlr/2013/article/marriage-and-divorce-patterns-by-gender-race-and-educational-attainment.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Monthly Labor Review article (by Alison Aughinbaugh, Omar Robles, and Hugette Sun) examines marriage and divorce patterns using the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 (NLSY79), a nationally representative cohort born 1957–1964. The study tracks 7,357 men and women (with 8,112 marriages) from ages 15 to 46, using data through 2010.

KEY FINDINGS:
• About 85% of the NLSY79 cohort married by age 46 (86.8% overall); among those who married, almost 30% married more than once.
• Approximately 42-44% of first marriages ending in divorce by age 46.
• Marriage rates declined across cohorts: 93.1% of the 1940-1945 cohort married vs. 89.5% of 1950-1955 cohort vs. 86.8% of NLSY79 cohort.
• Average age at first marriage rose to 25.6 for men and 23.4 for women (up from 24.7 and 22.6 in the 1950-1955 cohort).
• Marriages beginning at younger ages were more likely to end in divorce; women married younger than men and were more likely to marry, remarry, and divorce.

DIFFERENCES BY RACE/ETHNICITY:
• Three out of ten Black non-Hispanics did not marry by age 46 (68.3% ever married, down from 77.6% in the 1950-1955 cohort), while ~90% of Whites married.
• Conditional on marriage, Blacks had higher divorce rates. Blacks were less likely to remarry.
• Hispanics married at younger ages and their first marriages lasted longer.

DIFFERENCES BY EDUCATION (the starkest finding):
• The "divorce gap" between college graduates and less-educated groups grew larger than in earlier cohorts.
• Over half of marriages of those who did not complete high school ended in divorce vs. approximately 30% for college graduates.
• College-educated men and women married at older ages (26.5 average at first marriage for those with bachelor's+ vs. 22.7 for those with less than high school).
• Among the NLSY79 cohort, divorce among college graduates fell to 29.7% from 34.8% in earlier cohorts, while overall divorce rose to 44.8% from 40.8%.
• Men with bachelor's degrees were about 11 percentage points more likely to marry by 46 than men without high school diplomas; the gap for women was only ~4 percentage points.
• For men, college graduates' probability of divorce was ~25 percentage points lower than high school-only graduates; the difference was roughly half as large for women.
• College-educated men remained in second marriages at much higher rates (85%) vs. college-educated women (65.8%).
• Women's probability of divorce declined with education, but less steeply than men's; about a quarter of college-educated men divorced vs. 35% of college-educated women.

METHODOLOGY: The study is descriptive (no causal claims). NLSY79 respondents were interviewed annually until 1994, then biennially. Marital separations were ignored; divorce and widowhood were classified as marriage termination. Sample required participation at age 45+, valid marriage date reports, and education reported in round 9 (1988) or later. The study compares findings to Betsey Stevenson and Justin Wolfers' 2007 study using SIPP data for 1940-1945 and 1950-1955 birth cohorts, finding the trends of declining marriage and increasing divorce continued, with the NLSY79 showing even starker education-based differences. The article includes detailed tables (Tables 1-5) showing marriage outcomes by gender, race/ethnicity, and educational attainment, as well as marital history at ages 15, 25, 35, and 45. Historical context notes that the women's liberation movement, sexual revolution, increased female labor force participation, reduced stigma of divorce, and no-fault divorce laws all contributed to changing marriage and divorce rates.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"About 85 percent of the NLSY79 cohort married by age 46, and among those who married, a sizeable fraction, almost 30 percent, married more than once."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: [PDF] TRENDS IN MARRIAGE, DIVORCE AND FERTILITY Adam Isen Betsey ... ---
URL: https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w15725/w15725.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This NBER working paper (No. 15725, February 2010) by Adam Isen and Betsey Stevenson examines how marital and fertility patterns have changed along racial and educational lines for men and women. 

The paper argues that the benefits of marriage have shifted from production efficiencies (household specialization as theorized by Gary Becker) to consumption complementarities, driven by home production technology, women's increased labor force participation, fertility control, and changing divorce laws. 

Key findings include:
- Historically, college-educated women were the least likely to marry, but this marriage gap has eroded as returns to marriage changed.
- Marriage and remarriage rates have risen for college-educated women relative to those with less education; college-educated women are now about as likely to marry as those without a degree.
- There are large racial differences: white college-educated women remain less likely to marry than less-educated white women, while college-educated black women are now the most likely to marry among blacks.
- The age of first marriage has risen for all, but especially for college-educated women. Among white women with a college degree, ever-married rates at age 25 fell from 74% in 1970 to 36% in 2007.
- Among whites, the education gap in marriage has closed; among blacks, marriage declined more steeply, especially for the less educated, opening a racial marriage gap.
- Divorce rates rose through the 1970s then fell more sharply among college graduates; those with "some college" have the highest divorce rates.
- Among college graduates marrying in the 1970s, 37% of female and 34% of male marriages ended in divorce within 20 years; rates for the 1980s cohort fell back to 1960s levels.
- Remarriage rates have fallen for all groups; college-educated white women remain the least likely to remarry, and the education gap in remarriage has not closed.
- Fertility declines with education; the delay in fertility is concentrated almost exclusively among college-educated women, whose median age of having an infant at home rose by 4 years, while there was no change for less-educated women.
- Marriage patterns for men show fewer differences by education, though recent years show college-educated men slightly more likely to marry.
- Out-of-wedlock birth increases reflect changes in marriage (not fertility), especially among less-educated black women.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Historically, women with more education have been the least likely to marry and have children, but this marriage gap has eroded as the returns to marriage have changed." "College educated women marry later, have fewer children, are less likely to view marriage as 'financial security', are happier in their marriages and with their family life, and are not only the least likely to divorce, but have had the biggest decrease in divorce since the 1970s compared to women without a college degree." "In 1970, 74% of 25 year old college graduates had ever-married; this compares to 53%, 43%, and 36% in 1980, 1990, and 2007 respectively. In contrast, the percent of 25 year old high school graduates who had ever-married was 90%, 83%, 73%, and 52% in 1970, 1980, 1990, and 2007 respectively." "While the ever-married rates of 40 year old white female college graduates fell only 4 percentage points between 1980 and 2007, the fall among black female college graduates was 19 percentage points." "In sum, both men and women with a college degree have been consistently less likely to divorce and have also experienced a larger decline in divorce probabilities in the last few decades."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: The growth of education differentials in marital dissolution in the United ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8980992

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed research article by Kim McErlean (University of Texas at Austin), published in Demographic Research (2021, Vol. 45, Article 26, doi: 10.4054/demres.2021.45.26), examining educational differentials in marital dissolution in the United States.

**Background & Objective:** While overall US divorce rates have been declining since the 1980s, prior research (through marriages formed by 2004) showed declines were not equal across educational groups. This study examines whether education differentials in marital dissolution and divorce have continued to grow in the new millennium, using marriages formed between 2000 and 2014.

**Data & Methods:** The study uses the 2006–2019 National Survey of Family Growth (NSFG) female dataset, focusing on first marriages of 6,356 women. Analyses use life tables and discrete-time event-history analysis (28,356 person-years), examining dissolution by the 5th and 10th anniversaries. Key variables include five-year marital cohorts (2000–2004, 2005–2009, 2010–2014) and four education categories (less than high school, high school, some college, college degree or more). Controls included age at marriage, premarital cohabitation, premarital fertility, region, and race/ethnicity.

**Key Results:**
- Overall marital dissolution and divorce rates are declining over time, but this downward trend is driven entirely by those with higher education.
- Those with the least education are seeing RISING marital dissolution rates, even after controlling for correlated risk factors.
- The 5-year marital dissolution rate gap between the most and least educated grew from 12% (2000–2004 cohort) to 23% (2010–2014 cohort); 10-year risk diverged even more.
- The divorce rate gap (11%) is much smaller than the dissolution gap (23%), showing the least educated are more likely to informally separate rather than formally divorce.
- By the 2010–2014 cohort, college-educated women had a 70% lower dissolution risk than those without a high school degree, based on average marginal effects.
- Event-history analysis showed this widening gap could not be explained by the measured risk factors; controls eliminated education differentials for the 2000–2004 cohort but not for later cohorts.

**Contribution & Significance:** The study demonstrates that overall dissolution trends hide important and growing differentials by educational attainment. Declines in dissolution are not equally distributed across social classes. Those women with the least education—who are most vulnerable to the negative financial consequences of divorce and least likely to formalize (and thus recover from) their dissolution—face the highest and increasing risk, suggesting one way gender and class inequality is reproduced via family structure. Limitations include the use of education as a proxy for SES, lack of relationship quality measures, and sample restrictions (respondents up to age 44/49, marriages within 10 years of interview, and under age 35).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Overall marital dissolution and divorce rates are declining over time. However, this downward trend is driven by those with higher education; those with the least education are seeing rising marital dissolution rates, even when controlling for correlated risk factors."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Divorce Rate by Education Level: Understanding The Relationship ... ---
URL: https://divorce-education.com/divorce-rate-by-education-level

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from The Center for Divorce Education examines the correlation between education level and divorce rates in the United States, presenting data from the U.S. Census Bureau (2019) and research from the National Center for Family & Marriage Research at Bowling Green State University.

Key statistics on divorce rates by education level (2019 U.S. Census Bureau data):
- Bachelor's degree or higher: 25.9%
- Associate's degree: 30.1%
- Some college: 36.3%
- High school diploma: 38.8%
- Less than high school diploma: 45.3%

The data consistently shows that higher education levels are associated with lower divorce rates. Nearly 78 percent of college-educated women married for the first time between 2006 and 2010 can expect their marriages to last at least two decades, and marriages of college-educated couples last longer than they did 30 years ago.

The page identifies three main factors influencing the education-divorce relationship: (1) Economic stability — higher education is associated with better job opportunities and income, contributing to financial security; (2) Access to support — higher education provides greater access to resources and support networks for navigating marital challenges; (3) Cognitive skills — education improves communication, decision-making, and conflict-resolution abilities essential for healthy relationships.

The page notes the relationship is complex, and education level alone cannot determine divorce rates—other factors such as age, income, cultural norms, and personal beliefs also play a role. The remainder of the page promotes The Center for Divorce Education's online court-approved parenting courses (Children In Between and High Conflict Solutions), located in Ashland, Oregon.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Recent studies have shown that there is a significant correlation between higher education and divorce rates."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: The link between a college education and a lasting marriage | Pew Research Center ---
URL: https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2015/12/04/education-and-marriage

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Pew Research Center article examines the link between a college education and lasting marriages in the U.S., based on government estimates from the National Center for Health Statistics and the National Survey of Family Growth (2006-2010 data). Key findings include:

- About half of first marriages in the U.S. are likely to survive at least 20 years.
- College-educated women have a 78% chance of a first marriage lasting at least 20 years, compared to only 40% for women with a high school education or less.
- College-educated adults are more likely to be married overall: 65% of those with a bachelor's degree or more were married (2014, ages 25+), versus 53% of less-educated adults.
- College-educated men also stand out: 65% of men with bachelor's degrees could expect their first marriage to last 20+ years, versus 50% of men with a high school diploma or less.
- Possible reasons cited: college-educated adults marry later in life and are more financially secure.

Patterns by race/ethnicity:
- Asian women have the highest chance of long-term marriage (nearly 70%), followed by about half of Hispanic and white women, and 37% for black women.
- Among men, Hispanics have the highest likelihood (62%), compared with 54% of white men and 53% of black men.

Cohabitation findings:
- Women who did not live with their spouse before marrying had a 57% chance of a 20-year marriage, versus 46% for those who lived together beforehand.
- For men, engagement status mattered: men who lived with a partner without being engaged had a 49% chance, those engaged first had 57%, and men who didn't cohabit had 60%.

Methodology notes: findings refer only to opposite-sex marriages (same-sex sample too small), marriages ending in death were excluded, the survey did not include adults over 44, and adults with advanced degrees were not separately analyzed due to small sample size. The article was authored by Wendy Wang, a former senior researcher at Pew Research Center.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
College-educated women have an almost eight-in-ten chance of still being married after two decades.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Is a College Degree Worth It in 2024? ---
URL: https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2024/05/23/is-college-worth-it-2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
**Pew Research Center Study: "Is College Worth It?" (May 2024)**

This Pew Research Center study examines public views on the value of a four-year college degree alongside economic outcome trends for young adults (ages 25-34) with and without degrees.

**Methodology & Data Sources:**
- Three data sources: U.S. Census Bureau's Current Population Survey (labor force, earnings, income, poverty), Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances (net worth), and a Pew Research Center survey of 5,203 U.S. adults conducted Nov. 27 to Dec. 3, 2023 via the American Trends Panel (ATP).
- Survey weighted to represent the U.S. adult population by gender, race, ethnicity, partisan affiliation, education, and other categories.

**Key Findings:**
- **Economic improvements:** After decades of falling wages, young workers (25-34) without a bachelor's degree have seen earnings increase over the past 10 years, wealth has risen, and fewer live in poverty. However, outcomes also improved for college graduates, so the earnings gap between the two groups has NOT narrowed.
- **A narrow majority (54% in 2023) of workers ages 25-34 do not have a four-year college degree.**
- **Cost concerns:** Only 22% of U.S. adults say the cost of college is worth it even if someone has to take out loans. Even among four-year college graduates, only about a third (32%) agree — though they are more likely than non-graduates to say this.
- **Skills/job utility:** 58% of four-year college graduates (vs. only 26% of those without a degree) say their education was extremely or very useful in providing skills/knowledge for a well-paying job (excluding 9% who said the question didn't apply).
- **Partisan divide:** Republicans and Republican-leaning independents are more likely than Democrats and Democratic leaners to question the importance of college for getting a well-paying job. About 4 in 10 Americans say a college degree is not too or not at all important to get a well-paying job.

**Demographic trends:**
- Economic outcomes have been especially poor historically for young men without degrees, who saw falling labor force participation and sagging earnings starting in the early 1970s — but the last decade has been a turning point.
- The analysis separates young men and women due to their different labor force experiences.

**Key Definitions Used:** Noncollege adults include those with some college or high school only (excluding the ~6% without a high school diploma); "some college" includes associate degree holders.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
At a time when many Americans are questioning the value of a four-year college degree, economic outcomes for young adults without a degree are improving, Fewer are living in poverty today, Only 22% of U.S. adults say the cost of college is worth it even if someone has to take out loans, Even among four-year college graduates, only about a third (32%) say college is worth the cost even if someone has to take out loans, Four-year college graduates (58%) are much more likely than those without a college degree (26%) to say their education was extremely or very useful in giving them the skills and knowledge they needed to get a well-paying job
</key_excerpts>



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


--- SOURCE 8: The Fed - Higher Education and Student Loans ---
URL: https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2024-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2023-higher-education-student-loans.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a section from the Federal Reserve Board's "Report on the Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2023" (published May 2024), specifically the chapter on "Higher Education and Student Loans." The report uses data from the Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking (SHED).

KEY FINDINGS ON EDUCATIONAL ATTAINMENT:
- 70% of adults ever enrolled in education after high school; just over half received at least a certificate/technical degree, and 37% received at least a bachelor's degree.
- Educational attainment varies by demographics: Asian adults (90% enrolled, 67% bachelor's) vs. Hispanic adults (58% enrolled, 21% bachelor's). Adults with college-graduate parents were far more likely to earn a bachelor's degree (66% vs. 25%).

VALUE OF HIGHER EDUCATION:
- More than half of adults who ever enrolled beyond high school said lifetime financial benefits exceeded costs; one in five said costs were higher.
- Those who completed at least an associate degree were far more likely to see net benefits (68% of bachelor's holders vs. 43% with associate degree vs. 28% without degree completion).
- Perceptions of value increased with age and were lower among those with student loans (44% saw net benefits) vs. those who paid off or never had debt (68%).
- Value varied by institution type: 64% public, 66% private not-for-profit, but only 38% for-profit attendees saw net benefits.

EDUCATION DECISION RETROSPECTIVE:
- 45% of attendees would complete more education in hindsight; only 10% would complete less or not attend.
- 39% of those with for-profit bachelor's degrees would attend a different school (vs. 25% not-for-profit, 19% public).
- Engineering, computer science, and health fields had the lowest rates of desire to change fields.

STUDENT LOAN DEBT:
- 30% of all adults took out student loans (18% still owe, 24% repaid fully).
- Median outstanding education debt was between $20,000 and $24,999; 28% of borrowers owed less than $10,000.
- Borrowers ages 30-44 were most likely to have borrowed.
- Debt incidence by institution: 40% public, 57% private not-for-profit, 63% private for-profit attendees had debt.
- 5% of all adults had loans for a child's or grandchild's education (median $15,000-$19,999).
- Black borrowers were more likely than White or Hispanic borrowers to carry higher debt balances.

PAYMENT STATUS (following the $2023 restart):
- Federal student loan payment pause ended September 1, 2023; payments required as of October 2023.
- 65% of borrowers were required to make payments as of October 2023 (up from 37% in 2022, returning to pre-pandemic levels of 66% in 2019).
- 16% of borrowers were behind or in collections (slightly up from 15% in 2022, below 17% in 2019).
- Borrowers with less education or lower income were more likely to be behind: 22% of associate degree holders vs. 7% of bachelor's holders; 24% of those earning under $25,000 vs. 7% earning $100,000+. Hispanic (27%) and Black (23%) borrowers had higher rates of being behind than White (10%) and Asian (13%) borrowers.
- 27% of for-profit institution borrowers were behind vs. 13% public and 11% private not-for-profit.
- Among those who EVER borrowed: 57% had completely paid off loans (up 7 percentage points), 36% had outstanding debt and were current, and 7% were behind.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"With the restart of federal student loan payments, the share of student loan borrowers making payments returned to pre-pandemic levels. As of October 2023, 65 percent of borrowers with student loans for their own education reported that they were currently required to make monthly payments on their student loans... similar to the 66 percent of borrowers who reported owing monthly payments in 2019."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 9: U.S. Confidence in Higher Education Now Closely Divided ---
URL: https://news.gallup.com/poll/646880/confidence-higher-education-closely-divided.aspx

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Gallup news article (published July 8, 2024) reports that U.S. confidence in higher education is now closely divided. Americans are split into roughly equal thirds: 36% have "a great deal or quite a lot" of confidence, 32% have "some" confidence, and 32% have "little or no" confidence in higher education. This reflects a sharp decline from 2015, when 57% had high confidence and only 10% had little or none. The findings are based on a Gallup telephone survey (June 3-23, 2024, with 1,005 adults, ±4 percentage points margin of error) and a contemporaneous web survey of more than 2,000 Gallup Panel members, conducted in partnership with the Lumina Foundation.

Key findings include:
- **Party divisions:** Republicans' confidence has changed most dramatically—in 2015, 56% of Republicans had high confidence and 11% had little/none; today, 20% are confident and 50% have little or none. Independents fell from 48% to 35% confidence, and Democrats from 68% to 56%.
- **Reasons for confidence:** Those who are confident value education and training (27% cite importance of education for individuals/society, 24% cite career opportunities, 19% cite training like critical thinking).
- **Reasons for lack of confidence:** 41% of those lacking confidence cite colleges pushing political agendas/"too liberal"/indoctrination; 37% say colleges don't teach relevant skills or degrees don't lead to jobs; 28% cite cost concerns and student debt. A majority of Republicans lacking confidence (53%) cite political agendas, while Democrats primarily cite cost.
- **Outlook:** 68% say higher education is headed in the wrong direction (31% right direction). Even 81% of those with "some" confidence and 30% of those with high confidence say it's headed the wrong way. Democrats (52%) and liberals (49%) are most optimistic.
- **Implications:** The article notes confidence has dropped among all key subgroups but more so among Republicans. Concern extends beyond politics to workforce relevance and cost, which could lead to drops in college applications and enrollment.
- **Methodology notes:** A related article reports Americans are significantly more confident in two-year colleges than four-year colleges. Those retaining trust often regard the U.S. higher education system as "the best in the world."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"As a result, Americans are now nearly equally divided among those who have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence (36%), some confidence (32%), or little or no confidence (32%) in higher education. When Gallup first measured confidence in higher education in 2015, 57% had a great deal or quite a lot of confidence and 10% had little or none."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 10: The Student Loan Default Divide: Racial Inequities Play a Role  | The Pew Charitable Trusts ---
URL: https://www.pew.org/en/research-and-analysis/reports/2024/12/the-student-loan-default-divide-racial-inequities-play-a-role

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This report from The Pew Charitable Trusts examines racial inequities in federal student loan repayment, focusing on default and redefault rates among Black and Hispanic or Latino borrowers. Based on a representative survey of borrowers who first received undergraduate loans between 1998 and 2018, alongside a review of academic literature, the research finds that half (50%) of Black and 40% of Hispanic or Latino borrowers have had a loan default compared with less than a third (29%) of White borrowers. Redefault rates are also higher: about three-quarters of Black (74%) and Hispanic or Latino (75%) borrowers who have ever defaulted reported doing so more than once, compared with 56% of White borrowers.

The report identifies several underlying factors. Black borrowers face significant financial barriers: 70% reported annual household income under $50,000 in 2019, 51% reported being in debt when considering net worth, and they are more likely to hold high-interest debts including credit card debt (52%), medical debt (37%), municipal debt (12%), and payday loans (10%). Black borrowers also disproportionately experience employment gaps and difficulty securing employment upon leaving school. Academically, 83% of Black borrowers were first-generation students and 45% did not complete the degree for which they borrowed. Hispanic or Latino borrowers also face challenges, with 49% earning under $50,000, 78% being first-generation students, and 43% living in states with higher-than-average cost of living (primarily California). Hispanic or Latino borrowers were also more likely to attend school part time, online, or at for-profit institutions.

The report details the severe consequences of default, including Treasury offsets (tax refund and Social Security seizure), wage garnishment (up to 15% of income), collection fees (up to ~24% of principal and interest), credit notation for seven years, ineligibility for financial aid and repayment plans, and potential loss of professional licenses. Exit options from default—rehabilitation, consolidation, and full payment—are of limited value for redefaulters, as rehabilitation and consolidation can each only be used once. The top three reasons borrowers cited for both default and redefault were having other higher-priority debts (72%), feeling overwhelmed (71-74%), and having unaffordable payments (68-67%).

The report contextualizes these findings within structural inequities, including discriminatory housing policies like redlining (contributing to homeownership gaps: 45% Black and 49% Hispanic or Latino homeownership vs. 74% White), labor market discrimination (Black and Hispanic or Latino earners making 76 cents and 73 cents on the dollar compared to White earners), and educational segregation. The report recommends targeted changes to student loan default rules and requirements to help address racial disparities, while acknowledging these measures won't fully address historical discrimination. The findings are particularly timely given that collections of defaulted loans resumed in October 2023 after a pandemic-era pause, with new defaults expected to begin occurring as early as summer 2025.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Half (50%) of Black and 40% of Hispanic or Latino borrowers have had a loan default compared with less than a third (29%) of White borrowers." "Of borrowers who have ever had a defaulted loan, around three-quarters of Black (74%) and Hispanic or Latino (75%) borrowers reported doing so more than once. These redefault rates are significantly higher than among White borrowers (56%)." "7 out of 10 Black borrowers (70%) said their 2019 annual household income was less than $50,000." "Default, which occurs after 270 days of nonpayment, often triggers severe economic consequences for borrowers, such as seizure of tax refunds, wage garnishments, high fees, and a decline in creditworthiness." "The top three reasons given for experiencing initial default and redefault by borrowers from all demographic groups were the same: 1) having other, higher-priority debts (72% for default/72% for redefault); 2) feeling overwhelmed (71%/74%); and 3) having unaffordable student loan payments (68%/67%)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 14: How Unnecessary College Degree Requirements Hurt The Working Class - FREOPP ---
URL: https://freopp.org/whitepapers/how-unnecessary-college-degree-requirements-hurt-the-working-class

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This report from FREOPP (Foundation for Research on Equal Opportunity) examines the phenomenon of "degree inflation" — the trend of employers demanding bachelor's degrees for jobs that previously only required a high school diploma. This threatens to close off millions of middle-class job opportunities for the 62 percent of American adults without a four-year degree, exacerbates labor shortages, and reduces the financial return of a college education.

**Key statistics:**
- Degree requirements increased by 60% since 2007, even after controlling for changes in job types (Blair & Deming study)
- In 1990, just 9% of secretaries had college degrees; the proportion has nearly quadrupled to 33% today
- Workers without bachelor's degrees face a "paper ceiling" — employment penalties at every career stage (Blair, Debroy, and Heck NBER study)
- Four in ten recent college graduates are underemployed, earning just $37,330/year vs. $47,470 for graduates in appropriate jobs
- Bachelor's degree holders among middle-class workers (earning $40,000-$60,000) rose from 26% in 1980 to 38% today
- The share of Americans 25+ with a four-year degree rose from 21% in 1990 to 38% by 2022

**Historical context:** The Harvard Business School 2017 report "Dismissed by Degrees" (Fuller & Raman) brought the phenomenon to light, finding 67% of production supervisor job postings requested degrees though only 16% of current workers had one. The Great Recession of 2007-09 had a double impact: it increased college enrollment and allowed employers to become choosier. A study found 40% of jobs experienced "persistent upskilling" after the recession. A 2022 Burning Glass Institute report found some progress ("degree reset"), with degree requirements disappearing from millions of job postings by 2020.

**Top occupations driving degree inflation** (measured by the report's "excess degrees" metric, which combines education-level increases with occupation size): managers and administrators (over 1 million excess degrees), registered nurses (738,754 excess degrees), computer software developers, salespersons, and secretaries.

**Detailed case studies:**
- *Secretaries/administrative professionals*: Salary rose only 23% since 1990 (in line with the 24% average), yet education requirements quadrupled — little justification for degree requirements. Alternative certifications exist, like the PACE credential ($475, associated with $10,000 salary increase).
- *Managers/administrators*: Promotion to management is significantly harder without a degree (during the Great Recession, degree-holders were more than twice as likely to be promoted). The "upcredentialing" of HR professionals may create hiring bias. Companies like AT&T, IBM, Liberty Mutual, and Accenture have made progress hiring without degrees; Accenture's apprenticeship program fills 20% of entry-level roles.
- *Registered nurses*: The strongest case for degree requirements. BSN share rose from 46% (1990) to 73% today, and salaries rose 43% (an above-average increase). Studies link BSN-educated nurses to better patient outcomes, though most are associational. New York passed a 2017 law requiring RNs to obtain a bachelor's degree within 10 years of licensure; North Dakota repealed a similar mandate in 2003 after facing a nursing shortage.

**Policy recommendations:**
1. Employers should lead the fight by removing degree requirements, fixing automated recruiting systems, and using alternative credentials
2. State/local governments should remove degree requirements from public-sector jobs — ten states (Alaska, Colorado, Maryland, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Utah, Virginia) have announced skills-based hiring efforts; Maryland saw a 34% increase in applications from non-degree holders
3. Repeal laws/regulations that mandate unnecessary degree requirements (e.g., New York's "BSN in 10" law, DC's child care worker mandates)
4. Federal government should allow alternative educational pathways to access the same funding streams as traditional colleges
5. Treat college-degree requirements similarly to other employment practices under nondiscrimination law

The report concludes that while some progress has been made (a 64% increase in registered apprenticeships 2012-2021, growing coding bootcamp enrollment), education levels rose in every major occupational category between 2019 and 2021, indicating degree inflation persists.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 18: Health Insurance and Mortality in US Adults - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2775760

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific study published in the American Journal of Public Health titled "Health Insurance and Mortality in US Adults" by Wilper, Woolhandler, Lasser, McCormick, Bor, and Himmelstein (accepted March 16, 2009).

OBJECTIVE: To analyze the relationship between lack of health insurance and mortality using more recent data than the 1993 study (Franks et al.) that found a 25% higher risk of death among uninsured adults.

METHODS: The researchers conducted a survival analysis using data from the Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES III, conducted 1988-1994) with mortality follow-up through 2000. They analyzed participants aged 17-64 years (final sample: 9,005 individuals with complete data, contributing 80,657 person-years of follow-up). The analysis excluded Medicare recipients, Medicaid, and VA/CHAMPUS-covered persons. Cox proportional hazards survival analysis was used, replicating Franks' methodology. Sensitivity analyses included propensity score modeling, inclusion of Medicaid-covered participants, and exclusion of potentially endogenous covariates (employment and self/physician-rated health).

KEY RESULTS:
- Among all participants, 3.1% (95% CI = 2.5%, 3.7%) died by end of follow-up in 2000.
- 16.2% (95% CI = 14.1%, 18.2%) of the sample were uninsured at the time of interview.
- The hazard ratio for mortality among uninsured vs. insured, adjusted only for age and gender, was 1.80 (95% CI = 1.44, 2.26).
- After full adjustment (race/ethnicity, income, education, self- and physician-rated health, BMI, exercise, smoking, alcohol use), uninsured individuals were still significantly more likely to die: HR = 1.40 (95% CI = 1.06, 1.84).
- This HR of 1.40 is similar to the 1.25 found in the 1993 Franks study.
- The uninsured hazard ratio of 1.40 translates to an estimated 27,424 deaths among Americans aged 25-64 in 2000; applying to 2005 census data for ages 18-64 yields 35,327 deaths annually; using the Urban Institute (non-age-stratified) approach yields approximately 44,789 deaths annually (more than deaths from kidney disease, n=42,868).

NOTABLE FINDINGS: Uninsurance was associated with younger age, minority race/ethnicity, unemployment, smoking, lower exercise, lower education/income, and worse self-rated health. Other notable mortality predictors included current smoking (HR 2.02), poorer physician-rated health (HR 3.22 for fair/poor), male gender (HR 1.37), and older age.

DISCUSSION/CONCLUSIONS: Uninsurance is associated with mortality at a magnitude similar to the 1993 study despite changes in therapeutics and demographics. The mechanisms by which insurance improves health (per the IOM) include getting care when needed, having a regular source of care, and continuity of coverage. The authors conclude the increased risk of death attributable to uninsurance suggests community health centers do not provide the same protection as private health insurance, and advocate for universal coverage given health reform is again on the political agenda.

LIMITATIONS: Health insurance was assessed at a single point in time; NHANES III did not validate self-reported insurance status (7-11% misclassification possible, which would dilute the true effect); 29.5% of the sample excluded for missing data (these individuals were more likely to be uninsured and to die, potentially biasing toward null); no data on insurance duration or cost-sharing; unmeasured characteristics could offer alternative explanations, though the analysis controlled for tobacco, alcohol, obesity, and exercise.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 24: Community Service: Mandatory or Voluntary? | AASA ---
URL: https://www.aasa.org/resources/resource/community-service-mandatory-or-voluntary

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This AASA article (from August 1, 2000) examines the debate over mandatory vs. voluntary community service for high school graduation, contrasting the outcomes in Chicago and Jefferson Parish, Louisiana. Chicago successfully implemented a 40-hour service requirement (class of 2001 was first), with over 500,000 hours completed in the first semester of 1999-2000, while Jefferson Parish (which required 60 hours) revoked its policy after only 35% of juniors completed their hours by March 2000. 

Key statistics: High school students performing service increased nearly seven-fold from 1984 to 1997 (6.1 million students); 96% of districts offered community service by 1997 (up from 27% in 1984); 16-18% of districts required service for graduation.

Success factors identified include: building community support before implementation, letting students choose activities, training teachers (with coaching stipends, as in Chicago), recognizing student projects, and requiring student reflection. Programs lacking administrative or community support, or perceived as detracting from academics, tend to fail.

The article features perspectives from multiple superintendents and experts: Cozette Buckney (Chicago's Chief Education Officer), Randy Collins (Waterford, Conn.), James Holster (Passaic, N.J.), Dixie Binford (Corpus Christi, Texas), Janet Delaney (San Diego), Luke Frazier (Maryland Student Service Alliance), and consultant Marilyn Swierk.

Notable state/local programs: Maryland is the only state requiring all students to complete 75 hours; Washington, D.C. requires 100 hours; Corpus Christi integrates service into 1st-8th grade social studies but not high school (which rejected mandating it); San Diego uses a voluntary recognition citation program.

Examples of real-life learning: D.C. geometry students analyzing liquor store locations near schools; San Diego students as literacy tutors; Corpus Christi students raising money to preserve the city's oldest house. Passaic reported improved attendance (90.1% to 93.4%), lower dropout rate (12.2% to 10.6%), and fewer suspensions (down nearly 1,100) partly attributed to service programs.

Safety concerns (with pre-screened partner agencies in Chicago and San Diego via United Way) and tracking/evaluation systems are also addressed. Experts recommend starting small with non-required programs, using study groups for stakeholder buy-in, and recognizing that service quality varies widely even in mandatory states like Maryland.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"No matter how bad off you think you are, someone's worse. ... Well, maybe I can't buy $100 Michael Jordan shoes, but I can have a coat drive for children in the neighborhood." — Chicago's Chief Education Officer Cozette Buckney; "This is not something you can jump into." — Buckney, advising careful preparation; "Although I'm a huge proponent of service learning--where we use service to the community as a teaching strategy--I would not advocate every school system mandate it. In some systems, that would be more destructive than helpful." — Waterford Superintendent Randy Collins; "We have to have students and young people feel that they are stakeholders in their community... We have to promote our young people as not part of the problem in a community, but they are part of the solution in the community." — Janet Delaney, San Diego City Schools; "All genuine education comes through experience." — John Dewey, quoted by Passaic Superintendent Robert H. Holster
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 30: Low-Income, First-Generation College Students | American Sociological Association ---
URL: https://www.asanet.org/footnotes-article/low-income-first-generation-college-students

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from ASA Footnotes (Volume 50, Issue 2, published in ASA's publication) contains an article titled "Low-Income, First-Generation College Students" authored by Kristen A. Renn, Professor in the Department of Educational Administration at Michigan State University. The article examines the dual role of higher education as both an engine of social mobility and a machine of social reproduction for low-income, first-generation (LIFG) college students.

KEY DATA POINTS:
- As of 2015–2016, 56 percent of all undergraduates were first-generation (neither parent held a bachelor's degree)
- About half of first-generation students are also from low-income families
- Women of color are overrepresented among LIFG students who attend college
- Only 11 percent of LIFG students earned a bachelor's degree within six years, compared to 55 percent of continuing-generation students
- Median adjusted household income: $99,600 for first-generation degree holders vs. $135,800 for second-generation degree holders
- 35 percent of first-generation graduates (ages 22-59) hold advanced degrees vs. 43 percent of peers
- Median household wealth: $152,000 for first-generation vs. $244,500 for continuing-generation households
- 66 percent of first-generation graduates incurred education debt vs. 56 percent of peers

MAIN SECTIONS:
1. Social Mobility: Economist Raj Chetty's "mobility report cards" (using data from 30 million students, 1999-2013) show highest mobility rates at less selective public institutions with many low-income students and good graduate outcomes. First-generation students more often pursue majors like education, engineering, health, and social work with clear career pathways.

2. Social Reproduction: A college degree cannot overcome systemic racism and sexism — Black women with degrees earn less than Black men or white women; Hispanic women earn even less. Campus jobs, Greek life, and legacy admissions concentrate wealth advantage.

3. Campus Climate: Most institutions were not designed for LIFG students. LIFG students navigate opaque bureaucracies (financial aid verification, etc.) without "college knowledge." Pay-to-play campus activities, unpaid internships, and study abroad create marginalization. Scholars Elizabeth Aries and Maynard Seider, Elizabeth Armstrong and Laura Hamilton, and Anthony Jack have raised awareness; the #RealCollege movement (led by Sara Goldrick-Rab) emphasizes most LIFG students attend community colleges and public comprehensives.

4. Improving LIFG Experiences: Recommendations include visibility campaigns ("I'm First"), first-generation resource centers (at UCLA, University of Pennsylvania, Reynolds Community College), eliminating legacy admissions, auditing curricular/cocurricular activities for money-based prerequisites, and addressing deficit mindsets of instructors.

The article concludes that higher education has served as both mobility engine and reproduction machine, and institutions must transform to retain LIFG students to graduation and improve outcomes. A disclaimer states opinions expressed are the author's, not the ASA's.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: The Uninsured Population and Health Coverage ---
URL: https://www.kff.org/uninsured/health-policy-101-the-uninsured-population-and-health-coverage

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This KFF Health Policy 101 article (published October 8, 2025, by authors Jennifer Tolbert, Clea Bell, Sammy Cervantes, and Rakesh Singh) examines the uninsured population and health coverage in the United States.

**Coverage Landscape (2023):** About 8% of the U.S. population is uninsured. Most residents had private insurance (nearly half via employer-based plans), about 1 in 5 had Medicaid, roughly 15% had Medicare, about 6% had private non-group insurance (ACA Marketplace or off-market), and just over 1% had military TRICARE/VA coverage. The total-population uninsured rate was 7.9%.

**Trends:** In 2023, there were 25.3 million uninsured residents ages 0-64, with a record-low uninsured rate of 9.5%. Pre-ACA, over 40 million people were uninsured, but the number dropped to 27 million by 2016 after ACA implementation (which expanded Medicaid to adults up to 138% FPL and created subsidized Marketplaces). The uninsured count rose again from 2017-2019 due to Trump-era policies. COVID-era policies (Medicaid continuous enrollment, enhanced ACA Marketplace subsidies from ARPA and the Inflation Reduction Act) drove declines from 2019-2023. As of early 2025, 40 states and D.C. had adopted Medicaid expansion.

**Who is Uninsured:** Mostly adults under 65 in working low-income families, people of color, and those in the South/West. Key 2023 figures: 73.7% had at least one full-time worker in the family; 80.9% were in families below 400% FPL; people of color comprised 62.9% of the uninsured though only 46% of the population; 74.2% were U.S. citizens. Children's uninsured rate (5.3%) was less than half the adult rate (11.1%). AIAN (18.7%) and Hispanic (17.9%) people had the highest uninsured rates, nearly triple the White rate (6.5%). Nearly one-third of noncitizen immigrants were uninsured.

**Why People are Uninsured:** Cost is the primary barrier (63.2% cited unaffordable coverage in 2023); other reasons include ineligibility (27.0%), not needing coverage (26.6%), and difficulty signing up (23.9%). Ten states have not adopted Medicaid expansion, leaving a coverage gap for 1.4 million people. Undocumented immigrants are ineligible for federally-funded coverage, and lawfully-present immigrants face a five-year Medicaid waiting period. In 2023, 14.5 million uninsured were eligible for financial assistance, while 10.9 million were outside ACA reach.

**Consequences:** Uninsured adults are nearly five times more likely to lack a usual source of care, nearly three times more likely to report not getting medical care due to cost versus publicly insured adults, and four times more likely than privately insured. When hospitalized, they receive fewer services and have higher mortality. Nearly half report difficulty paying for healthcare, and 84% worry about healthcare debt.

**Future Outlook:** Pandemic-era policies drove historic coverage lows, but the 2025 Federal Budget Reconciliation Bill ("One Big Beautiful Bill Act"), signed July 4, 2025, makes significant cuts to Medicaid, Medicare, and Marketplace subsidies. The CBO estimates it will increase the uninsured by 10 million. Combined with the December 2025 expiration of enhanced Marketplace subsidies, the CBO projects over 14 million more uninsured by 2034. The 2027 immigration eligibility restrictions and heightened immigration enforcement are also expected to increase uninsurance. Despite the ACA remaining favorable to the public by a 2-to-1 margin, these policy changes threaten to reverse recent coverage gains.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 9: The Stubborn Unresponsiveness of Youth Voter Turnout to Civic Education: Quasi-experimental Evidence from State-Mandated Civics Tests - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11654633

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed academic article published in PMC (PubMed Central) titled "The Stubborn Unresponsiveness of Youth Voter Turnout to Civic Education: Quasi-experimental Evidence from State-Mandated Civics Tests" by Jilli Jung and Maithreyi Gopalan (Pennsylvania State University), issue date December 2024.

**Research Question & Background:** The study addresses the persistently low youth voter turnout in the US, which has the largest age gap in voting among advanced democracies. In the 2020 presidential election, turnout among 18-24 year olds was approximately 25 percentage points lower than those aged 65-74, reaching only 48%. The authors evaluate the causal effect of the Civics Education Initiative (CEI)—a state-mandated civics test policy requiring high school students to take and/or pass a civics test for graduation—on youth voter turnout.

**Policy Context:** CEI was an advocacy campaign led by the Joe Foss Institute (September 2015-2017) that lobbied states to adopt mandatory civics tests using 100 questions from the USCIS naturalization test. Arizona adopted it in 2015, followed by 18 states between 2015-2018. Treatment states were classified into "strong" civics test requirements (graduation conditional on passing) and "weak" requirements (not conditional). The analytical sample included 15 treatment states and 34 comparison states.

**Data & Methodology:** Using nationally-representative data from the 1996-2020 Current Population Survey (CPS) Voting and Registration Supplement, the authors analyzed self-reported voting of US citizens aged 18-22 across seven presidential election waves (1996, 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020). They employed Difference-in-Differences (DD) and event study analyses, with two-way fixed effects models, state and year fixed effects, individual and state-level time-varying covariates, and state-specific linear trend controls. The final analytic sample was 36,627 respondent-wave observations (32,452 for strong treatment, 31,897 for weak treatment), with standard errors clustered at the state level and CPS weights applied.

**Key Findings:**
1. CEI has NO statistically significant effect on youth voter turnout across all model specifications (omnibus DD coefficients ranged from 0.004 to -0.012, none significant at p<.05).
2. Results were consistent regardless of whether states had strong or weak civics test requirements.
3. A concerning, marginal negative effect was found for Black youth voter turnout (b=-0.097, p<.10), interpreted with caution due to low sample size.
4. Event study results showed parallel pre-treatment trends (supporting the identification strategy) but null effects post-treatment.
5. Heterogeneity analyses by age, sex, race/ethnicity, and immigrant status yielded statistically insignificant null results overall.

**Robustness Checks:** The null results were robust to placebo group checks (28-32 year olds), triple-difference (DDD) analysis, alternative comparison groups, and additional state-level time-varying covariates (including a cost of voting index).

**Conclusions:** The study provides evidence regarding the lack of efficacy of civic test policies for improving youth voter participation. The authors suggest that more direct interventions—such as voting information interventions, preregistration, same-day registration, and online registration—might be far more effective. They also suggest broader curricula targeting non-cognitive skills (grit, perseverance, psychosocial skills) may show more promise than narrowing civic education to rote memorization of political knowledge. The authors note the policy failed to move the needle during a period of historic uncertainty (pandemic, structural racism, political polarization).
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article, published January 14, 2026 in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (doi: 10.3390/ijerph23010108), examines how parental legal status operates as a fundamental social determinant of health and educational equity. Author Igor Ryabov (University of Texas-Rio Grande Valley) investigated long-term outcomes among U.S.-born and foreign-born children of immigrants using data from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health), a nationally representative cohort (N=20,738) followed from 1994-1995 into adulthood across five waves.

Parents were categorized into three groups: native-born, documented immigrant, and undocumented immigrant. Outcomes included high school graduation, college enrollment, depression (CES-D), psychological distress, self-rated health, and chronic conditions. The measure was validated against Pew Research Center and DHS benchmarks, with Monte Carlo simulations and sensitivity checks. Missing data were handled via Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE).

KEY FINDINGS: Children of undocumented parents exhibited the most adverse outcomes across all domains. Descriptively, they had the lowest high school graduation (63.8%) and college enrollment rates (39.9%) versus 86.9% and 65.5% for children of native-born parents. The sample of children with undocumented parents was predominantly Latino (77.2%), with the lowest mean parental education (10.2 years) and median household income ($27,600). In models controlling for socioeconomic factors, parental undocumented status independently predicted 26% lower odds of high school graduation (OR=0.74, p<0.001) and 39% lower odds of college enrollment (OR=0.61, p<0.001). The study notably found that children of documented immigrants showed only modest differences from native-born peers.

CONCLUSIONS: The findings challenge the generalized "immigrant paradox" and support segmented assimilation theory and the "legal violence" framework, indicating legal precarity is a powerful, independent driver of intergenerational disadvantage. Limitations include proxy-based inference of legal status and the dataset's age relative to the contemporary immigration policy landscape.
