- Jobless rate for bachelor's degree holders is less than 3%; poverty incidence is **3.5 times lower** than for high school graduates [4].
- **Over the past decade, all net job growth has gone to workers with bachelor's or graduate degrees** [4].
- Bachelor's degree holders are **47% more likely to have employer-provided health insurance**, with employers contributing 74% more toward coverage [4].
- Studies suggest those who attended some college live **seven years longer** than peers with no postsecondary education [4].
- Two-thirds of bachelor's degrees in the U.S. are awarded by public universities [4].

#### E. Utah System of Higher Education (January 10, 2017; based on College Board "Education Pays 2016")

#### F. UNC Charlotte (2026, citing BLS and UNC System data)
- Workers with a bachelor's degree earn about **$1,533 per week** on average, compared with **$946 per week** for workers with only a high school diploma (BLS) [17].

- "The biggest financial risk in college isn't always picking the wrong major. **It's not finishing the degree at all**" [17].

#### G. AEFP Live Handbook (Webber & Carruthers, updated July 2026)
- The median college graduate in 2023 can expect to earn **$1.3 million more than the median high-school graduate** over a lifetime. After accounting for taxes, costs, and discounting, the net benefit is roughly **$243,000** [18].

For those with "some college" but no degree, the median lifetime premium is only **$260,000** (vs. $1.3M for graduates); after taxes and discounting it's just **$17,000**. Only 48% of "some college" individuals earn more than the median high-school graduate [18].

- The average total cost of college (including tuition, fees, books, supplies, and living expenses) is **$38,270 per student per year** [6].

- In-state students at public four-year institutions pay an average of **$11,610 in tuition and fees** (total budget $29,910) [7].

### III. STUDENT DEBT STATISTICS

#### A. Aggregate debt totals (Education Data Initiative, updated July 16, 2026; NY Fed; SoFi)

- **42.6 million federal borrowers** [11].
- Average federal balance: **$40,467**; total average balance (including private): **$43,521** [11].
- SoFi reports average debt of **$39,547** per borrower; student loan debt is the **third-largest category of U.S. household debt** (behind mortgages and auto loans) [27].

- Trends: After declining in 2023-24 (first YoY declines in over a decade), debt resumed growth in 2025. In 2026 Q1, total debt increased $57.2 billion YoY. Federal debt grew $31.3 billion in H1 2026. Quarterly YoY growth averaged 3.63% in H1 2026. Private loan debt totaled $166.4 billion in 2026 Q1 [11].

- **Total student loan borrowers: 43.1 million** as of 2024Q4, down from a peak of ~44.5 million in 2017-2018 [14].
- **Total outstanding balances: $1.612 trillion** in 2024Q4, up from $1.507 trillion in 2019Q4 [14].

- By degree type (SoFi, NPSAS-based): associate $23,854; bachelor's **$29,490 (public)** / **$33,689 (private nonprofit)**; master's $81,870 average / $95,381 private nonprofit; MBA $76,996; doctoral $77,331; professional degrees: medical school $235,788, law $167,399, professional-doctorate (private nonprofit) $281,817 [27].

#### D. Borrower demographics
- 20% of U.S. adults with undergraduate degrees carry student debt; 24% of postgraduate degree holders do [11].
- Women borrow more than men (female bachelor's holders borrow 3.63% more); **Black students are most likely to borrow (82.9% of Black bachelor's degree holders)** [11].

- **Women hold 60.3% of all student loan debt (~$929 billion)** [27].
- Twelve years after graduation, white men have paid off up to **44%** of debt vs. 28% for white women; Black graduates owe average **$25,000 more** than white graduates (average $53,340); four years after graduation, Black borrowers carry balances **88.3% higher** than white borrowers [27].

#### E. Default and delinquency — post-pandemic resurgence

**NY Fed Liberty Street Economics (May 13, 2025) — "Student Loan Delinquencies Are Back":**
- Student loan delinquency rate surged from below 1% to nearly **8%** after the on-ramp preventing negative credit reporting expired in October 2024 [15].
- **13.7% of student loan borrowers (nearly 6 million) were 90+ days past due or in default** in Q1 2025, comparable to the 14.4% rate in Q1 2020 [15].

Lowest: Illinois (13.7%), Massachusetts (14.0%), Connecticut (14.5%), Vermont (14.7%), New Hampshire (14.8%) [15].
- Older borrowers are more affected: over 25% of those aged 40+ with a payment due are delinquent; average age of a delinquent borrower rose from 38.6 to 40.4 [15].
- 56.6% of newly delinquent borrowers already had subprime credit scores (<620). However, **2.4 million newly delinquent borrowers had scores above 620** and will face steep borrowing cost increases or credit denial. Over 2.2 million saw their credit scores drop more than 100 points; over 1 million saw drops of at least 150 points [15].
- The U.S. Department of Education, with the Treasury, began collection efforts in May 2025, including **wage garnishment and tax refund/Social Security payment seizure** [15].

**NY Fed Liberty Street Economics (May 12, 2026) — "Federal Student Loan Defaults Return":**
- Student loan payments were paused from March 2020 to September 2023, with a 12-month "on-ramp" (through October 2024). First delinquencies appeared on credit reports in 2025:Q1 [13].
- Approximately **1 million federal student loan borrowers defaulted in 2025:Q4**, and an additional **2.6 million defaulted in 2026:Q1** — totaling 3.6 million borrowers [13].
- **Over 17% of student loan borrowers have fallen at least 90 days past due at least once** [13].
- The average borrower entering default is nearly 40 years old (38.9 years, up from 36.4 pre-pandemic), with a notable shift toward older borrowers (50+). Most defaulters were NOT past due before the pandemic: nearly 30% were current, ~50% had no payment due, and only about 20% were past due [13].
- Defaults are concentrated in Southern states (Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, South Carolina) [13].
- Defaulted borrowers saw credit scores drop an **average of 91 points (from 567 to 476)** [13].
- Newly defaulted borrowers also tend to be behind on other debts: nearly 40% past due on auto loans, 56% on credit cards, and 20% on mortgages [13].
- The authors believe the largest wave of defaults has passed, though a second wave may emerge from the **7 million borrowers in the defunct SAVE repayment plan** who are yet to re-enter repayment [13].
- Spillover to broader credit markets is likely limited: defaulted/delinquent borrowers represent only 2% of the credit population and hold small shares of total debt balances (2.7% of auto loans, 2% of credit cards, 1% of mortgages) [13].

**SoFi (July 28, 2026):**
- ~9 million borrowers with $220 billion in loans in default (March 2026), more than 13% of federally managed portfolio [27].
- 15.9% of borrowers at least 60 days past due (returning to pre-pandemic levels; was 16.7% in August 2019, dropped to 2.3% during payment pause); 90+ day delinquency rate: 10.3% in Q1 2026 [27].
- ~20% of borrowers in active repayment (~3.5 million) at least 30 days delinquent [27].
- Federal loans enter default after **270 days** of missed payments; default can trigger wage garnishment, seizure of tax refunds, loss of federal aid eligibility [27].
- Highest delinquency in the South: Louisiana (22.6%), Mississippi (22.3%), Georgia (21.1%) [27].
- ~13 million borrowers on income-driven repayment (IDR) plans (~44% of those in repayment); 6.5+ million borrowers remained in SAVE plan forbearance at end of 2025 amid litigation; 44.6% on standard 10-year fixed payment plan; average borrower takes **~20 years to pay off loans** [27].
- New repayment assistance plan (RAP) launched **July 1, 2026**, replacing existing income-driven plans; borrowers with pre-date loans have until July 1, 2028 to choose between RAP, tiered standard plan, or IBR. Under RAP, remaining balance forgiven after 360 payments over at least 30 years (longer than previous 20-25 year timelines) [27].
- Forgiveness: $87.6 billion discharged across ~1.18 million borrowers through PSLF and related programs (avg ~$78,200 per PSLF borrower, through September 2025). Early in the program (2018-2020), **99.7% of PSLF applications were rejected**. Teacher Loan Forgiveness: $3.87 billion across 469,867 teachers (avg $8,497). Federal forgiveness applications have an 11.2% acceptance rate. Final PSLF rule taking effect July 1, 2026 narrows qualifying employers [27].
- Education Data Initiative: Only 3.3% of PSLF applications have been approved since inception, though $46.8 billion has been forgiven through PSLF; $197.3 million through Teacher Loan Forgiveness [11].
- COVID-19 impact: Federal loan interest was 0% from March 2020 to September 2023; 66% of federal debt remained in forbearance until September 2023; as of the report, 44% of federal borrowers are in repayment, 21% in forbearance [11].
- Loan servicer issues: 70% of complaints relate to mismanagement/deception; Navient was sued by CFPB in 2017 and is no longer contracted to service federal loans as of 2022; "Operation Game of Loans" pursued 36 enforcement actions against student debt relief companies, securing judgments worth over $131 million [11].

#### F. Federal Reserve Board SHED 2024 (published May 2025)
- 71% of adults have enrolled in postsecondary education; 37% hold a bachelor's degree or higher [12].
- Educational attainment varies significantly by parental education (**66%** of those with a college-educated parent earn a bachelor's vs. **25%** otherwise) and by race/ethnicity (Asian 67%, White 41%, Black 28%, Hispanic 21%) [12].
- 30% of all adults have taken out student loans for their own education; 17% still owe money (borrowers), 24% have fully repaid [12].
- The **median outstanding education debt is between $20,000-$24,999**; 28% of borrowers owe less than $10,000 [12].
- Borrowers who attended for-profit institutions are more likely to have debt and to be behind on payments (**65% with debt, 35% behind**) compared to public (38% with debt, 16% behind) and private non-profit (54% with debt, 15% behind) [12].
- As of October 2024, **57% of borrowers were required to make monthly payments** (up from 37% in 2022). **20% of borrowers were behind on payments or in collections** (up from 16% in 2023) [12].
- Borrowers with less education and lower incomes are more likely to be behind: 30% behind for those with some college/associate degree; 27% behind for those earning under $25,000 [12].
- Among all who ever borrowed: **59% have fully repaid their loans, 33% are current on payments, and 8% are behind** [12].

#### G. Impact on major life decisions

**Homeownership (EducationData.org, 2026):**
- **Homeownership among recent college graduates declines 1.8% for every $1,000 of student loan debt** [26].
- Average monthly mortgage payments rose from $1,318 in 2016 to **$2,005 in 2025**; average monthly student loan payments rose from $393 in 2016 to **$431 in 2025** (Federal Reserve Board of Governors, FHFA, and U.S. Department of Education) [26].
- 50% of all adults with debt delayed home purchase (20% delayed 5+ years). By age group: 70% of those aged 28-43 delayed purchase (23% for 5+ years), vs. only 28% of those aged 61-78 [26].
- A high debt-to-income (DTI) ratio reduces mortgage eligibility [26].
- "Student loan repayments are forcing millions of young families to delay purchasing their first home, as they cannot afford to save for a down payment or qualify for a mortgage while also paying off student debt." — Transforming Student Debt to Home Equity Act, H.R. 7368, 117th Congress [26].
- Student debt is a greater obstacle to younger generations, especially **Millennials (born 1981-1996)** [26].
- Programs: Maryland Smartbuy Loan Program, Ohio's Grants For Grads program [26].

**Marriage and family (SoFi, 2026):**
- ~1 in 5 recent graduates with loans report delaying marriage and children [27].

**Retirement savings and stock ownership:**
- Student debt influences job-acceptance decisions for **56% of public-sector and 62% of private-sector workers**; public-sector employees with student debt are **14% more likely to view retirement savings as inadequate** [27].
- Borrowers with >$35,000 in debt are **27% less likely to be homeowners** [27].
- Korankye (Economic Analysis Letters, 2023, using PSID 2011-2017): "The presence of student debt decreases the probability that married households will own stocks, but the amount of student debt does not show a statistically significant effect" — suggesting the incidence of student debt raises perceived liquidity constraints and debt burden [28].

**Retirement decisions (Butrica & Karamcheva, IZA DP No. 13182, April 2020, SCF 1989-2016, ages 55-70):**
- More indebted older adults are **more likely to work, less likely to be retired, and expect to work longer** than those with less debt [29].
- Household debt among older Americans has risen dramatically; share of debt held by adults age 60-69 increased 61% and 90% for age 70+ between 2003-2018 [29].
- Between 1989 and 2016, share of households age 55-70 with debt increased from 64% to 75%; mean debt more than doubled ($48,800 → $125,300); median debt more than quadrupled ($14,500 → $61,000) [29].
- Student loans increased most rapidly: share of households with student debt more than tripled from 3% to 10%; median amounts rose from $5,400 to $18,000 [29].
- Average debt-to-asset ratio increased from 12% to 26%; average debt-to-income ratio rose from 45% to 107% [29].
- Those with debt are **11.2 percentage points more likely to work** and **10.3 pp less likely to be retired**; doubling per-person debt increases work likelihood by 1.1 pp and reduces retirement likelihood by 1.0 pp [29].
- Having mortgage debt raises work probability by 5.8 pp; a $10,000 credit card debt increase raises work likelihood by 9.4 pp vs. only 0.3 pp for mortgages [29].
- Student loan debt has no statistically significant effect on retirement behavior on average, but **reduces benefit receipt and retirement among the lowest-wealth older adults**; credit card debt increases likelihood of receiving Social Security benefits by 4.5 pp [29].

**COVID-era hardship (TICAS Class of 2020 report):**
- In California, borrowers were nearly **4x more likely than non-borrowers to lose housing** (22% vs 6%), 3x more likely to have difficulty paying for dependent care (30% vs 10%), and 2x as likely to miss a mortgage/rent/utility payment (41% vs 19%) [45].

**For-profit vs. nonprofit default rates:**
- Students at for-profit colleges default at much higher rates (**30% within 12 years** vs 4% at public and 5% at nonprofit colleges) [45].

### IV. OPPORTUNITY COST — FOREGONE WAGES DURING FOUR YEARS OF STUDY

- **NY Fed (Abel & Deitz, "Is College Still Worth It?", April 16, 2025):** Opportunity costs (forgone wages, estimated at **~$150,000 in 2024** using median wages of high school graduates) have risen, pushing the **average total cost of a degree from ~$140,000 in the late 1990s to $180,000 in 2024** [24].
- NY Fed 2014 (Abel & Deitz, Current Issues Vol. 20 No. 3): The total cost of a bachelor's degree was about **$122,000 in 2013**, with **forgone wages constituting the vast majority** [22].
- EducationData.org: The initial investment for a typical bachelor's degree from a state school totals **$270,811** (including tuition of $107,190, indirect costs of attendance such as room and board, student loan interest, and lost potential income) [16].
- Considering student loan interest and lost potential income, investing in a bachelor's degree can ultimately cost **upwards of $500,000** [6].
- BLS/EducationData.org benchmark: median weekly income for high school graduates is $899 ($46,748/year) — the income students forgo while studying [6]. A 2025 BLS figure cited by UNC Charlotte: $946/week (~$49,200/year) for HS-only workers [17].
- The NY Fed notes that part of the reason college returns have remained high is that **wages for those without a college degree have also been falling**, keeping the college wage premium near an all-time high **while reducing the opportunity cost of going to school** [22].

### V. NET PRESENT VALUE AND ROI CALCULATIONS — BREAKEVEN, VARIATION BY MAJOR, INSTITUTION, RACE/GENDER

#### A. NY Fed internal rate of return (IRR) estimates

**2025 analysis (Abel & Deitz, April 16, 2025):**
- Using internal rate of return methodology with quantile regression to estimate the return for the **median** (rather than average) graduate, the return to college is estimated at **12.5% in 2024** — "a rate well above the threshold for a sound investment" [24].
- This return has held between **12-13% for the past three decades** [24].
- Direct out-of-pocket costs have actually fallen in recent years after inflation adjustment — average published tuition was ~$21,000/year in 2024, but after grant aid the **average net price over four years was ~$30,000** [24].
- The median college graduate with a bachelor's degree earns about **$80,000/year compared to $47,000 for the median high school graduate** — a premium of over $32,000 (about 68%), near its all-time high [24].
- The wage premium tends to grow over one's career [24].
- Caveats: estimates apply only to graduates (not dropouts); factoring dropout risk would reduce the return by roughly **1.5 percentage points**; calculations assume average costs over four years and median college wages [24].

**2014 analysis (Abel & Deitz, "Do the Benefits of College Still Outweigh the Costs?", Current Issues 20(3)):**
- Despite rising tuition and falling wages for college graduates, analysis of four decades of data (1970-2013) shows both bachelor's and associate's degrees yield returns of **about 15% over the past decade** [22].
- College graduates earn **56% more than high school graduates** (bachelor's) and 21% more (associate's) [22].
- Bachelor's degree holders earn about **$1 million more over their lifetimes** than high school graduates; associate's holders ~$325,000 more [22].
- Net tuition for a bachelor's degree was $6,550 in 2013 (vs. $14,750 sticker price); associate's net tuition was negative (fully subsidized) [22].
- Returns vary significantly by major: **Engineering (21%), Math and computers (18%), Health (18%), Business (17%), Communications (15%), Social sciences (15%), Sciences (14%), Architecture (14%), Liberal arts (12%), Agriculture (11%), Leisure and hospitality (11%), and Education (9%)** [22].
- Even chronically underemployed college graduates earn positive returns — ranging from **7% (education majors) to 17% (engineering majors)** — because employers pay a premium for college graduates even in non-college-level jobs [22].

**SSRN follow-up ("When College Might Not Be Worth It," Abel & Deitz):** "In our last post, we showed that the economic benefits of a college degree still far outweigh the costs for the typical graduate, with a healthy..." [23]. The companion piece examines whether college is worth it for at least a quarter of graduates [24].

**NY Fed Instagram (Sept 11, 2025, with Richard Deitz):** "Does college pay off for everyone? In recent research, our economists find that the typical college graduate earns a return that easily surpasses the benchmark for a sound investment. However, this is not the case for everyone" [25].

#### B. EducationData.org ROI analysis (updated May 2026)
- An average bachelor's degree has a **560.53% lifetime return on investment**, with a median lifetime return up to **1,040.14%** [16].
- In the first decade, an average bachelor's degree has a **negative return on investment (-16.54%)**; **it takes roughly 12 years in the workforce to regain the investment** for a typical bachelor's degree [16].
- Projected average starting salary for someone with a bachelor's degree in 2026: **$72,069**; projected median salary among working bachelor's degree holders aged 25-64: **$87,722** [16].
- Professional degrees offer the highest potential ROI at **2,249%** [16].
- Bachelor's holders earn an estimated **$25,356 (41.2%) more than associate's degree holders** [16].
- ROI by major — most cost-efficient: management information systems and statistics (**1,758.59%**), finance (**1,580.53%**), computer and information sciences (**1,561.07%**), electrical engineering (**1,479.98%**) [16].
- Degrees with **negative ROI**: psychology (**-122.78%**), family and consumer sciences (**-100.62%**), liberal arts and humanities (**-94.03%**), education (**-51.61%**) [16].
- Additional majors: agriculture 301%, architecture 598%, business 915%, accounting 1,065%, communications 435.80%, criminal justice 174.48%, engineering 761.99%, English 134.91%, health 570.79%, nursing 732.33%, mathematics 976.87%, history 105.06% [16].

#### C. Georgetown CEW — "A First Try at ROI: Ranking 4,500 Colleges" (Nov 19, 2019; updated 2022)
- Ranks 4,500+ public, private nonprofit, and private for-profit colleges by ROI using **net present value (NPV)** calculations based on expanded U.S. Department of Education College Scorecard data (net price, median debt, median earnings) [47][49].
- The **median NPV for all colleges is $723,000 in the long term (40 years after enrollment)**, but only **$107,000 in the short term (10 years after enrollment)** [47][49].
- **Community colleges and many certificate programs have the highest ROI in the short term (10 years)** — 26 of the 30 institutions with the best 10-year NPV primarily grant certificates or associate's degrees; certificates in nursing are particularly valuable short-term [47].
- **Colleges that primarily award bachelor's degrees have the highest ROI in the long term (40 years)**. Eight of the top 10 long-term NPV institutions are private nonprofits [47].
- Top institutions: Albany College of Pharmacy and Health Sciences ($2,722,000 NPV), St. Louis College of Pharmacy ($2,714,000), MIT ($2,273,000), Stanford ($2,068,000), Maine Maritime Academy, Babson College, Harvard, Georgetown, and the US Merchant Marine Academy. Six of the top 10 have NPVs of $2 million or more at the 40-year horizon [47].
- **Public colleges have higher ROI than private colleges in the short term** due to lower tuition and less debt; however, **private nonprofit colleges have higher long-term ROI than public universities ($838,000 vs. $765,000 in long-term net economic gains)** [47].
- Private college graduates earn a median of **$41,000 ten years after enrollment** vs. $33,000 for public institution graduates, though their median debt is $17,000 vs. $7,000 [47].
- The lowest long-term NPV institutions: theological institutions, beauty schools, arts colleges, and a tribal college (ranging from about $240,000 to $294,000 in NPV) [47].
- Distribution: 50th percentile of long-term NPV is $718,000-$723,000; 75th percentile $867,000-$877,000 (mostly bachelor's-granting); 25th percentile $566,000-$573,000 (mostly non-bachelor's-granting) [47].
- Methodology: earnings 10 years after first attending serve as a proxy for future earnings; average annual net price represents total investment cost; discount rate ~2% (US Treasury securities); assumes no earnings increases after 10 years (conservative); does NOT deduct opportunity costs of foregone earnings [47].
- The median debt for a bachelor's degree (~$9,800) is slightly less than twice the overall median and twice that of a certificate program [47].
- Companion report "ROI of Liberal Arts Colleges": the median ROI of liberal arts colleges is **nearly $200,000 higher than the median for all colleges**; the 40-year median ROI of liberal arts institutions is **$918,000**, close to four-year engineering and technology schools ($917,000) and four-year business and management schools ($913,000) [49].
- 2022 update added a new metric: the share of students at an institution earning more than workers with only a high school diploma 10 years after enrollment. **An average of 60% of college students across institutions earn more than a high school graduate after 10 years. However, at 1,233 postsecondary institutions (30%), more than half of their students earn less than a high school graduate 10 years after enrollment** [50].
- Interactive ROI Rankings platform allows comparison of 4,500+ institutions over 10, 20, 30, and 40-year timeframes, using net cost of attendance, post-graduation earnings, and debt [51].

#### D. Critical analysis of the Georgetown ROI methodology (collegeroi.org / Leon Shivamber)
- The 2022 report factors in cost of degree and time value of money (both absent in the earlier College Payoff report) [48].
- Five persistent methodological problems identified:
  1. **Inconsistent time periods**: shifted from ages 24-64 to ages 18-58 — stopping at 58 truncates peak-earnings years [48].
  2. **Flat costs assumption**: assumes tuition doesn't increase during enrollment, though college costs have outpaced inflation by 90-150% since 1990 [48].
  3. **Pre-tax earnings**: a high school graduate pays ~$400,000 in federal taxes over a lifetime vs. ~$600,000 for a college graduate — that $200,000 differential reduces the after-tax NPV advantage by roughly 20-25% [48].
  4. **Discount rate too low**: CEW used 2.5% (College Payoff) then 2% (2022); credible benchmarks: government funding rate 5.4%, Parent PLUS up to 9.08%, NY Fed 5%, SF Fed 6.67%, CBO 5.91% [48].
  5. **Benchmark problem (most consequential)**: CEW uses a synthetic $15,000/year figure (near federal minimum wage) as the high school baseline, giving a $397,000 NPV baseline — but CEW's own College Payoff report implies a $924,000 NPV high school baseline from its $1.6M lifetime earnings figure. **Applying the $924,000 benchmark to the 2022 rankings of 4,526 institutions shows only 873 (19%) produce NPV at or above the high school baseline — meaning 81% deliver a return below direct workforce entry** [48].
- The 2025 ROI update abandoned discounting entirely (0% rate), which maximizes the apparent value of college since graduate earnings are backloaded [48].
- The underlying College Scorecard earnings/cost data is real and genuinely useful for comparing schools; it is the aggregate rankings and headline NPV conclusions that are flawed [48].

#### E. Breakeven point
- **~12 years** to recoup the cost of a bachelor's degree (by age 34); by age 31 when considering net cost (cost minus scholarships/discounts) [5].
- College Board *Education Pays 2026*: the typical graduate recoups the cost of a degree **by their mid-30s** [19].
- EducationData.org: ROI is negative (-16.54%) in the first decade; positive around year 12 [16].
- UNC System: many graduates recover degree costs within ~10 years [17].

#### F. Variation by major — detailed

**Georgetown CEW, "The Major Payoff" (October 15, 2025):**
- Prime-age workers with a bachelor's degree earn **70% more at the median** than workers with a high school diploma alone, with unemployment 2.9% vs. 6.2% [35].
- Median earnings vary significantly by major: from **$58,000 in education and public service fields to $98,000 in STEM fields** [35].
- Within 65 STEM majors, median earnings range from **$64,000 (miscellaneous agriculture) to $146,000 (petroleum engineering)** [35].
- Pharmaceutical sciences majors earn a median of **$145K** vs. **$51K** for early childhood education majors [31][35].
- **14 of the 19 humanities and arts majors lead to median earnings above $65,000** [35].
- Report analyzes 152 majors for prime-age workers (ages 25-54) and 142 majors for early-career graduates (ages 22-26), tracking median earnings, graduate degree earnings premiums, and unemployment rates [35].
- Engineering, business, computers/statistics/math, health, and physical sciences majors have the highest median earnings [35].
- Persistent racial/ethnic and gender disparities: male, white, and Asian/Asian American workers are overrepresented in STEM; women are overrepresented in education, healthcare, and social science fields [35].

**College Board, Education Pays 2026 (April 14, 2026):**
- Earnings vary by major — from about **$44,000 for performing arts graduates to over $80,000 for mechanical engineering and computer science graduates** [19].

**AEFP Live Handbook:**
- The difference between top-earning majors (e.g., engineering, economics) and bottom-earning majors (e.g., fine arts) is roughly **$2 million** over a lifetime [18].

#### G. Variation by institution type
- Private nonprofit bachelor's degrees have higher 40-year ROI ($838,000) than public ($765,000); public colleges have higher short-term ROI [47].
- For-profit institutions have worse average outcomes and higher default rates [18][12][45].
- Community colleges and certificate programs have the highest short-term ROI [47].
- Lovenheim & Smith (September 2022, edworkingpapers): 3,757 degree-granting institutions in 2019-20; 66% four-year, 34% two-year. Two-year colleges serve more disadvantaged populations (59.4% Pell Grant recipients vs. 46.8% at four-year colleges). Private for-profit institutions have the highest rates of Pell Grant and underrepresented minority enrollment. More selective institutions serve fewer economically disadvantaged students, have higher expenditures per student, and higher graduation rates (**75.4% for more selective vs. 40.3% for inclusive institutions**) [38].
- "There is clear evidence that **more-selective and higher-resource educational environments lead to higher returns**" [38].
- "Lower-SES students tend to invest in less-selective and lower-resource colleges. These differences, combined with the evidence on returns, suggest that features of the U.S. postsecondary system may actually reduce intergenerational economic mobility" [38].
- NATI (June 9, 2025) highlights that "short-term, sub-baccalaureate credentials in technical fields can yield salaries comparable to or greater than some bachelor's degrees" [51].

#### H. Variation by race and gender
- Women who work full-time, full-year earn **25% less than men at similar education levels** [32].
- At the highest education level, **Black/African American and Hispanic/Latino individuals earn close to a million dollars less than their white and Asian/Asian American counterparts** over a lifetime [32].
- Lifetime earnings by gender at bachelor's level: **$3.3M (men) vs. $2.4M (women)** [34].
- Black, Latino, Native American/Alaskan Native, and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander workers consistently earn **10-38% less** than the highest-earning groups (White or Asian workers) at various education levels [34].
- Webber & Carruthers: returns differ by race ($1.38M white vs. $1.0M Black) and gender ($1.56M men vs. $0.99M women) [18].

### VI. THE COLLEGE WAGE PREMIUM — HOW IT HAS CHANGED OVER TIME (ESPECIALLY 2016–2026)

#### A. Minneapolis Fed (2025) — "What happened to the college wage premium?"
- The college wage premium (the gap in average wages between college-educated and high school-educated workers) rose dramatically from **39% in 1980 to 79% by 2000**, but has remained **flat since then**, even declining slightly after the Great Recession. In 2023, it was slightly lower than its 2000 value [20].
- While the wage premium has stagnated, **the cost of a four-year degree has risen 40% between 2000-2001 and 2022-2023**, reducing the financial return on college education [20].
- Research by Leila Bengali and Robert Valletta (San Francisco Fed): both supply and demand factors are at play, but the key explanation is **increased substitutability between college-educated and high school-educated workers** — firms have become more willing to substitute high school-educated workers for college graduates, reducing demand for the latter [20].
- "In the 21st century, the nature of technological change has not advantaged college-educated workers to the same degree as before, so firms are able to employ high school-educated workers to a greater extent" [20].
- "This pattern we're seeing, it's not something that emerged only in the last three or four years when AI came on the scene. So I would not interpret this as being attributable specifically to AI" [20].
- The share of college graduates in the workforce grew from **31% in 2000 to 45% in 2025**; online job postings requiring a college degree declined from **1.2 per non-degree posting in 2010 to 0.6 per non-degree posting in 2020** [20].
- Despite stagnation, the college wage premium remains high (**still ~76% higher wages for college graduates**) [20].

#### B. College Board, Education Pays 2026 (April 14, 2026)
- Among full-time working adults, **four-year college graduates earn about 60% more than high school graduates — a wage premium that has been stable for decades** [19].
- In 2025, unemployment among young adults ages 25-34 was **3.1% for college graduates versus 5.8%** for those without a degree [19].
- **Only 4% of college graduates live in poverty** compared to 13% of high school graduates [19].
- Quotes: "The data show that education remains a powerful driver of opportunity, but there are differences in outcomes. The question isn't just whether education pays—it's which pathways lead to the strongest outcomes." — Jessica Howell, vice president of research at the College Board [19]. "Education Pays 2026 highlights the strong economic and social benefits associated with postsecondary education... changing public views of higher education and rapid technological advances are reshaping the landscape." — Matea Pender, senior research scientist and lead author [19].

#### C. 2016–2026 assessment
- BLS weekly premium: $1,543 vs. $930 in 2024 (66% premium) [1]; UNC Charlotte cites $1,533 vs. $946 (roughly 62% premium) for 2026 [17].
- Abel & Deitz (2025): median college graduate earns ~$80,000 vs. $47,000 for HS — a ~68% premium, "near its all-time high" [24].
- Investopedia (Nov 7, 2025, citing Abel & Deitz): median college graduates earn about **70% more**; the wage premium has held steady between **12-13% for three decades**; the premium increased because **high school-only wages have shrunk more than 25% in real terms since the early 1970s**, while college graduate salaries rose only about 5% [37].
- San Francisco Fed (June 2025): premium at about **75%** [37].
- NYU analysis of 5.8 million Americans (2024): annualized returns of about **10% for women and 9% for men** [37].
- Quantumrun (2026): household income gap widened from 2:1 (2004) to 2.3:1 (2024) [1].
- On AI: Abel and Deitz were skeptical that AI is having widespread effects on recent graduates' employment, pointing instead to tech sector weakness beginning in 2022 and general cooling of labor demand [37].

### VII. COMPARISON WITH OTHER INVESTMENTS (STOCK MARKET, REAL ESTATE)

#### A. College degree vs. stocks and bonds
- **NY Fed (2025):** The 12.5% return to college compares favorably to **long-term stock market returns (~8%) and bonds (~4%)** [24][17].
- **NY Fed (2024 data, via WAICU, June 2025):** "According to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, the return on investment (ROI) for a college degree has been remarkable — between 12 percent and 13 percent over the past three decades, reaching 12.5 percent in 2024. This rate of return surpasses that of many traditional investment vehicles, including stocks and bonds" [21].
- **Forbes (March 12, 2024):** "A college degree still offers better returns than the stock market despite rising tuition costs, a new study has found" [36].
- **Investopedia (Nov 7, 2025):** College graduates can expect a **12.5% median annual return on investment** over a lifetime, outperforming traditional investments (**S&P 500 long-term real returns under 7%; bonds under 2% annually**) [37].
- Caveats: stock returns are volatile and require timing; the S&P 500's average annual return was about 9.6% from 1992-2011, but yearly returns ranged from +37.58% (1995) to -37.00% (2008); the compounded annualized return was about **7.8%** [39]. J.P. Morgan cites S&P 500 average annual return of **10.6% from 1980-2024** (as of June 30, 2025) [40].
- "College is still worth it, at least, for most people. Even though some recent graduates may be having difficulty finding a good job right now, they are in a much better position than similarly aged workers without a college degree, who tend to have higher unemployment and lower wages." — Jaison R. Abel and Richard Deitz [37].

#### B. Timing and graduation delays
- Taking **five years to graduate drops the median return to about 9%, and six years to 7%** [37]. For about a quarter of graduates, college doesn't pay off much financially [37].

#### C. Real estate comparison
- Real estate as an alternative is complicated by the fact that student debt itself **impedes homeownership** (1.8% lower homeownership per $1,000 of debt) [26].
- NY Fed June 2026 data (via Instagram post): nationwide home price growth of **1.1% year-over-year** [25] — well below the degree's ~12.5% IRR.

#### D. Opportunity-cost framing of the comparison
- The dominant "investment" in a degree is **foregone wages (~$150,000 in 2024)** rather than tuition [24]; if that capital were invested in equities instead, it could grow substantially — but the NY Fed IRR methodology already internalizes these costs and still finds 12.5% [24][22].
- A portfolio vs. index comparison is imperfect: personal returns diverge from index performance due to different holdings, systematic investing, volatility drag, and fees (Leelyn Smith) [39]. Index definitions: DJIA (30 blue-chip companies), S&P 500 (500 large U.S. companies), Nasdaq Composite (~4,500 stocks), Wilshire 5000, Russell 2000 (small-cap), MSCI ACWI (46 countries), Bloomberg Barclays U.S. Aggregate Bond Index [39].

---

### VIII. ADDITIONAL CONTEXT

#### A. Non-completion as the greatest risk
- Only about **60% of four-year college students graduate** [18].
- For "some college" no degree: median lifetime premium only $260,000; after taxes/discounting just $17,000; only 48% earn more than the median HS graduate [18].
- "Arguably, the worst position for an individual to be in financially is to have borrowed but failed to complete her degree" [18].
- Fall 2020 COVID enrollment impacts: overall -3%; community colleges -13% (Black -16%, Latina/o -15%, Indigenous -15%); recent HS graduates -6.9%; lowest persistence among first-year students since 2012; over a million students newly defaulted on federal loans in the 12 months preceding the pandemic [45].

#### B. Broader economic wellbeing (Fed SHED 2025)
- Financial well-being remained stable at **73% of adults "doing okay" financially or "living comfortably"**, slightly below the pre-pandemic plateau of 75% (2018-2020); declines for young adults, low-income families, and Black adults [30].
- 86% of adults with bachelor's degrees reported doing okay vs. **41% of those without a high school degree**; by race: Asian 82%, White 79%, Hispanic 62%, Black 60% [30].
- 49% of adults under 30 lived with a parent in 2025, up 12 percentage points since 2019 [30].
- 63% could cover a hypothetical $400 emergency expense; 35% of non-retirees said retirement savings were on track [30].
- 1 in 4 workers used generative AI at work; graduate degree holders were more than 4x more likely to use AI (43%) than those with HS or less (10%); 81% of AI users agreed it saves time [30].

#### C. Enrollment and degree-completion context
- Total postsecondary enrollment: 18.9 million in fall 2023 [8].
- 71% of adults ever attended postsecondary; 37% hold at least a bachelor's degree [12].
- High school students' expectations to pursue higher education declined to the lowest level in 20 years, falling by nearly half between 2002 and 2022 [50].
- 30 states saw drops in full-time undergraduate enrollment over the past decade [50].

URL: https://cew.georgetown.edu/resource/the-college-advantage-weathering-the-economic-storm-2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This report by the Georgetown University Center on Education and the Workforce (CEW), authored by Anthony P. Carnevale, Tamara Jayasundera, and Ban Cheah, analyzes how the Great Recession (which began in December 2007) affected workers of different education levels and demonstrates the clear "college advantage" during economic downturns. It is based on Current Population Survey (CPS) data from 2007-2012 and is accessible at cew.georgetown.edu/collegeadvantage.

KEY FINDINGS:
• The unemployment rate for all four-year college graduates was 4.5 percent (May 2012), while recent college graduates (ages 21-25) faced a rate of 6.8 percent—over 50 percent higher. Recent high school graduates faced unemployment near 24 percent.
• College graduate unemployment peaked at 6.3 percent during the recession, compared to 13.4 percent for high school graduates (peak in February 2010). New college graduate unemployment peaked at 11.1 percent in July 2011, while new high school graduate unemployment peaked at 30 percent in January 2010.
• Workers with high school diplomas or less lost about 5.6 million jobs during the recession and an additional 230,000 jobs in recovery (net -5,841,000). Workers with Associate's degrees or some college lost 1.75 million jobs but regained 1.6 million. Workers with Bachelor's degrees or better gained 187,000 jobs during the recession and 2,012,000 more during recovery—a net gain of 2,199,000 jobs.
• Nearly four out of every five jobs destroyed by the recession were held by workers with a high school diploma or less.
• The underemployment rate for four-year college graduates was 8.4 percent, versus 17.3 percent for high school graduates. One out of seven new college graduates was underemployed in May 2012, compared to nearly half of new high school graduates.
• College graduates still earn nearly twice as much as high school graduates, with the college earnings premium at 97 percent.

INDUSTRY IMPACTS:
• Even in blue-collar industries, better-educated workers fared better. In manufacturing, employment dropped 19 percent for those with a high school diploma or less but only 9 percent for those with Bachelor's degrees or better. In construction, employment dropped 24 percent for high school diploma holders versus 4 percent for college graduates.
• Manufacturing and construction accounted for nearly 5.2 million of the 7.2 million jobs lost; wholesale and retail trade added another 1 million in losses. Industries with high concentrations of college-educated workers (public administration, education, healthcare) held up relatively well, adding 1.5 million jobs.

GENDER IMPACTS:
• Men with Bachelor's degrees lost nearly 200,000 jobs in the recession, but gains by college-educated women more than offset those losses. Women with a high school diploma or less lost 2 million jobs, while men with high school diplomas or less lost 3.6 million.
• Two out of every three jobs lost by men were in construction and manufacturing. The recession prompted men to enroll in postsecondary education at faster rates than women, and men moved into fields traditionally dominated by women (such as nursing and healthcare) that are more "recession proof."
• Postsecondary enrollment grew by 7 percent in 2009 (after 1 percent growth in 2005) as workers sought shelter from the weak labor market, though growth slowed to 3 percent in 2010.

LONG-TERM TRENDS:
• Since 1989, employment growth has been driven entirely by workers with education beyond high school. The number of workers with a high school diploma as their highest attainment dropped by 14 percent from 1989 to 2012, while workers with some college or an Associate's degree increased 40 percent and workers with Bachelor's degrees or better nearly doubled.
• The shift toward more-educated workers stems from labor-saving technology (especially computing), automation of routine tasks, and globalization/offshoring of low-skilled jobs. Manufacturing shed 5.5 million jobs from 1980 to 2007 while healthcare and education added 11.6 million jobs.
• The report concludes that the recession "laid bare" the shortcomings of the American workforce, especially the lack of postsecondary education, leaving an urgent need to train workers for more skilled jobs.
</summary>

- There is a "scarring" effect: taking a non-college job can lead to skill stagnation and difficulty transitioning to college-level jobs.

- However, underemployed college graduates may benefit from jobs with higher "intrinsic quality" (nonmonetary amenities like respectful treatment, variety, skill development). --- SOURCE 3: The Far-Reaching Impact of Job Loss and Unemployment - PMC - NIH ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553243

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed academic article by Jennie E. Brand, published in the Annual Review of Sociology (February 11, 2015), titled "The Far-Reaching Impact of Job Loss and Unemployment." The article synthesizes research on the consequences of involuntary job displacement on workers' life trajectories.

**Key Topics and Findings:**

1. **Trends and Risk Factors**: Job displacement has become a common feature of the U.S. labor market, driven by technological change, offshoring, immigration, outsourcing, weakened labor unions, and economic downturns. High displacement levels marked the last four U.S. recessions, with the "Great Recession" (2007-2009) being the deepest since the Great Depression. Unemployment reached 9-10% in 2009-2011, roughly twice the pre-crisis rate. Risk factors include being male, black/Hispanic, less educated, blue-collar/manufacturing workers, and those with low job tenure, though risks increased for women, whites, and college-educated workers in the 1990s.

2. **Methodology**: The study of displacement is treated as a "natural experiment" because job loss is a relatively exogenous labor market shock, enabling stronger causal inference. However, selection bias remains a concern. Scholars found few differences across various causal estimators (regression, matching, difference-in-difference, fixed effects). Plant closure studies offer stronger internal validity but limited generalizability.

3. **Economic Effects**: Displaced workers face long-term earnings losses—an immediate 33% earnings loss and up to 15% loss six years after separation (Couch and Placzek 2010). Cumulative lifetime earnings loss is roughly 20%, with "wage scarring" lasting up to 20 years post-displacement. Reemployed workers more often find part-time work with lower job quality. Losses are cyclical: men displaced in mass layoffs when unemployment is below 6% lose 1.4 years of pre-displacement earnings, versus 2.8 years when unemployment exceeds 8% (Davis and von Wachter 2012). Older workers, those with high tenure, industry-changers, and the less-educated suffer greater losses. There is debate over whether layoffs (stigmatizing) versus plant closings produce different economic outcomes (Gibbons and Katz 1991 vs. Krashinsky 2002).

4. **Psychological Effects**: Displaced workers report 15-30% higher rates of depressive symptoms and anxiety compared to non-displaced workers, plus loss of psychosocial assets (self-esteem, life satisfaction, sense of control). Effects vary by demographic characteristics, work-role centrality, coping resources, and economic context. Reemployment mitigates but does not eliminate these effects, particularly for professionals/white-collar workers. A "social norm effect" means contexts of widespread unemployment lessen the social-psychological impact, though economic losses are larger during recessions.

5. **Physical Effects**: Job loss is linked to worse self-rated health, cardiovascular disease, increased hospitalization, higher use of disability benefits, increased suicide, and mortality. Gallo et al. found job loss doubled the risk of myocardial infarction and stroke among older workers. Sullivan and von Wachter (2009) found a 50-100% increase in mortality the year following displacement and a 10-15% increase over the next 20 years. Causal inferences remain contested due to selection bias, though plant closure studies corroborate findings.

6. **Family Effects**: Displaced workers face increased risk of family tension and disruption. Layoffs (but not plant closings) increase divorce risk (Charles and Stephens 2004). Parental displacement negatively affects children's self-esteem, educational attainment, grade repetition, dropout, and adult income. Paternal displacement has stronger effects on children than maternal among married couples, but displacement among single mothers also significantly harms children's outcomes.

**Conclusions**: While reemployment mitigates some negative effects of job loss, it does not eliminate them. Future research should attend more fully to how economic and social-psychological effects intersect and extend beyond displaced workers themselves.
</summary>

"Job loss is an involuntary disruptive life event with a far-reaching impact on workers' life trajectories... Research suggests that displacement is associated with subsequent unemployment, long-term earnings losses, and lower job quality; declines in psychological and physical well-being; loss of psychosocial assets; social withdrawal; family disruption; and lower levels of children's attainment and well-being."

--- SOURCE 4: Are Young College Graduates Losing Their Edge in the Job Market? ---
URL: https://www.clevelandfed.org/publications/economic-commentary/2025/ec-202514-are-young-college-graduates-losing-their-edge-in-the-job-market

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Economic Commentary from the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (EC 2025-14, published November 24, 2025) by Alexander Cline (Research Analyst) and Barış Kaymak (Economic and Policy Advisor) examines whether young college graduates are losing their job market edge. Using Current Population Survey (CPS) panel data spanning 1976–2025 for respondents aged 22–27, the authors find that the unemployment gap between young high school and college graduates has narrowed to its lowest level since the late 1970s—currently 2.5 percentage points (as of July 2025, near the March 2024 all-time low of 2.4 percentage points).

Key findings:
- The narrowing gap reflects two contrasting developments: young high school workers benefit from the historically tight postpandemic labor market, while young college workers face unemployment rates rarely seen outside recessions.
- The primary driver is a secular decline in the job-finding rate among young college graduates that began around 2000. College graduate job-finding rates trended upward from 1976 to 2000, then declined sharply.
- By around 2019, the job-finding rates of the two education groups converged, ending a long period of relatively easier job-finding prospects for college graduates.
- Historically (1976–2000), high school graduates had lower unemployment exit rates (41.2% vs. 47.0%) and higher entry rates (3.9% vs. 1.8%). This has reversed: high school graduates now exit unemployment faster than college graduates (41.5% vs. 37.1%), with nearly a 10 percentage point decline in college graduates' exit rate.
- Discouragement rates (leaving the labor force) show no differential trends between the groups, indicating the exit rate reversal is driven by job-finding, not discouragement.
- Entry rates into unemployment remain stable, with high school graduates' entry rates still above college graduates' rates, meaning college graduates retain advantages in job stability and compensation once hired.

The authors use two methods for decomposition: monthly employment-status transitions from CPS panel data, and Shimer's (2005) duration-based approach. The commentary contextualizes findings against concerns about AI automation of entry-level positions and persistent earnings effects of poor early-career outcomes (citing Kahn 2010; Oreopoulos, von Wachter, and Heisz 2012).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: How Has COVID-19 Changed the Job Outcomes for Recent Graduates? - Braven ---
URL: https://braven.org/2021/03/memo-3-how-has-covid-19-changed-the-job-search-and-outcomes-for-recent-graduates

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This memo (third in a series from Braven, a nonprofit) examines how COVID-19 changed job outcomes for recent college graduates, providing a data-driven analysis of pre-pandemic labor market conditions, COVID-19 impacts, coping strategies, and the challenges of starting a job remotely.

PRE-COVID-19 LABOR MARKET CONTEXT: Despite headlines calling 2020 "the best market in 50 years," data shows recent graduates' employment never fully recovered from the 2008-2009 Great Recession. Federal Reserve Bank of New York research found unemployment for recent college graduates was higher even a decade after the Great Recession than in the early 2000s or 2006-2007. Underemployment rates (~40% of recent graduates in jobs not requiring their degree) remained higher than early 2000s levels. Median earnings for recent graduates did not increase from 2000-2019 after inflation adjustment, and the bottom quarter earn less ($32,000) than 2000s graduates ($32,664). Underemployment has long-term effects: initially underemployed graduates are 5x more likely to remain underemployed after 5 years, and 75% of those still underemployed at 5 years remain so at 10 years. Nearly half of women graduates are underemployed vs. 37% of men. Positives pre-COVID included faster job growth for degree-requiring jobs and more protection from automation (62% of high-school-only workers in automation-susceptible jobs vs. 28% of bachelor's degree holders).

COVID-19 IMPACT ON OVERALL LABOR MARKET: 22M jobs were lost at pandemic start; six months later still 11.5M jobs deficit. Groups most likely to become unemployed: 45+, less than college degree, women, earning under $60K/year. Unemployment varied by race (Black workers 9.2%, Hispanic 8.6% in January 2021 vs. 5.7% White, 6.6% Asian). While overall unemployment recovered (6.3% January vs. 14.7% April), job growth stalled (only 49,000 jobs added January 2021 vs. 4.8 million June 2020). High-wage employment nearly fully recovered (0.5% below pre-pandemic), but middle and low-wage employment fell 6.7% and 27.6% respectively. High-wage job postings recovered more slowly than low-wage postings.

COVID-19 IMPACT ON RECENT GRADUATES: Recent graduates were hit especially hard. A July 2020 NACE survey found 7.8% of employers revoked or planned to revoke job offers to the class of 2020 (vs. 9.5% peak during Great Recession); 31% of employers delayed start dates. The pandemic's timing was especially damaging - fall campus hiring (finance, consulting, accounting) had closed, and spring recruiting roles (education, PR, creative industries) were hard hit. Graduate school application cycles had already ended. Entry-level applicants faced competition from laid-off workers with 1-2 years of experience. Historical reference: during the Great Recession, only 56% of 2010 graduates held at least one job by spring 2011, of which only 52% said it required their degree (a 27% "quality jobs" rate). A UK site found only 18% of graduates had jobs vs. typical 60% that time of year. For the class of 2021, employers expected to maintain hiring at 2020 levels, but NACE warned employers made the same projection for the class of 2009 before cutting college hiring by 22%.

COPING STRATEGIES: Students increasingly turned to the "gig economy" (willingness rose from 54% pre-COVID to 69%) and flocked to technology roles (software engineer, data analyst, data scientist applications increased). Technical degrees offer advantages in an increasingly digital world, and jobs increasingly require hybridized technical skills.

STARTING A JOB REMOTELY: New graduates face disadvantages learning company culture remotely, which traditionally happens through everyday peer interactions. A March 2020 Glassdoor survey found only 68% of 18-34-year-olds confident they could work efficiently. A Harvard Business Review survey found 38% of managers agreed remote workers performed worse, and 34% of workers said supervisors "expressed a lack of confidence in their work skills." Given that early-career interactions build workplace confidence, the remote environment provides a challenging starting point for graduates.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Frontiers | Review of the impacts of COVID-19 pandemic on the employment of college graduates in China and countermeasures to it ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2024.1390055/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a POLICY AND PRACTICE REVIEWS article published in Frontiers in Public Health on 07 June 2024 (Vol. 12, DOI: 10.3389/fpubh.2024.1390055), authored by Huicui Wang and Chun Wang from the Department of Student Affairs, Qingdao University, China. The study reviews the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on the employment of college graduates in China and the countermeasures taken in response.

METHODOLOGY: The study used diversified research methods including literature review, comparative analysis, and questionnaire surveys. It analyzed big data from the Zhaopin recruitment website regarding recruitment demand, job supply, employment market prosperity, and job-seeking channels. A tracking survey of Chinese college graduates was conducted annually from October to December (2016-2023), with sample sizes growing from 110,800 (2016) to 715,000 (2023), using multi-stage, hierarchical, equal-probability sampling with schools, subject categories, and majors as the three sampling levels. The Analytic Hierarchy Process was used for correlation analysis.

FIVE KEY IMPACTS OF COVID-19 ON COLLEGE GRADUATE EMPLOYMENT:
1. Recruitment demand reduced - Global economies except China showed negative growth in 2020 (US -3.5%, Japan -4.8%, Germany -5.0%, France -9.0%, Britain -10.0%). Global working hours fell by 5.2% in Q1 2020 and 18.2% in Q2. COVID-19 led to a 30% decline in U.S. labor demand. By May 2020, unemployment rose to 7.4% in Europe and 15% in the US. Tourism, aviation, and hotel industries (major recruiters of graduates) saw significant demand declines, though emerging industries like digital economy, online education, and telemedicine grew.
2. Employment competition rose - College graduates increased from 8.74 million (2020) to 11.79 million (2024, a record). Fewer students studied abroad due to lockdowns, and overseas-educated graduates returning to China increased 67.3% year-on-year in 2020, intensifying domestic competition.
3. Employment channels changed - Offline recruitment fairs shifted to "cloud recruitment" (online). Online recruitment hindered mutual understanding between employers and graduates and made it harder to assess communication and practical skills.
4. Psychological anxiety increased - Anxiety and depression were major global problems. Cross-country research (Poland, Russia, Germany and others) found anxiety at 30% and depression at 40.3%. In China, college student emotional responses included fear (87.7%), neurasthenia (44.8%), depression (37.4%), obsessive-compulsive anxiety (17.3%), and hypochondriasis (11.6%). Delayed graduations, lack of experimental materials, and lost personal instruction increased anxiety.
5. Employment structural contradiction intensified - The gap between graduate CIER index and national CIER index widened from 0.17 (Q1 2018) to 1.06 (Q3 2022). The ILO's "World Employment and Social Outlook: Trends 2024" predicted global unemployment rising from 5.1% (2023) to 5.2% (2024).

GOVERNMENT COUNTERMEASURES (7 measures): (1) Public institutions absorption - guiding graduates to army, grassroots units, expanding teacher recruitment and research assistant positions, attracting graduates to state-owned enterprises; (2) Private enterprise absorption - tax reductions, unemployment insurance refunds, employment subsidies, guaranteed loans; (3) Innovation and entrepreneurship to drive employment - incubation services, training, entrepreneurship loans; (4) Expanding further education enrollment - in 2020 postgraduate enrollment increased by 189,000 and associate-to-baccalaureate upgrades by 322,000; (5) Optimizing public services - 24.365 all-day online campus recruitment platform, simplified processes, 2-year retention of unemployed graduate status; (6) Providing employment subsidies - skills enhancement, job-seeking, and entrepreneurship subsidies, with targeted support for poor and disabled graduates; (7) Lowering employment threshold - reforming teacher certification so teachers could obtain certificates after inauguration.

COLLEGE/UNIVERSITY COUNTERMEASURES (5 measures): (1) Providing high-quality positions via large-scale online job fairs and multi-channel information release; (2) Improving employability through classroom teaching, daily management, and social practice; (3) Optimizing campus services through "Internet + services" smart employment system, keeping hukou/files for 2 years, providing interview rooms; (4) Strengthening psychological counseling to alleviate anxiety; (5) Strengthening employment guidance through courses, recruitment information, and encouraging graduates to consider private companies.

IMPLICATIONS: For government - increase public institution recruitment and schedule exams earlier, collaborate with leading enterprises, combine regional characteristics with innovation/entrepreneurship, anticipate employment pressure from expanded further education ("depreciation of academic qualifications"), strengthen subsidy supervision, innovate supply-demand matching mechanisms, reduce vocational qualification requirements. For colleges - the article's implications section was cut off in the provided content.

CONCLUSION: The employment promotion measures introduced by the Chinese government and colleges significantly promoted college graduate employment. The findings are significant for countries worldwide to cope with similar emergency events, alleviate employment pressure, and promote better and fuller employment of college graduates.
</summary>

This Fast Fact from the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES), published in the 2024 Condition of Education report, examines employment rates (employment-to-population ratios) of young adults aged 25 to 34 in the United States. Data are based on March reference periods, with 2019 data representing ~1 year before the coronavirus pandemic, 2020 at pandemic onset, 2021 and 2022 roughly 1-2 years into the pandemic, and 2023 close to when the federal COVID-19 public health emergency declaration ended (May 11, 2023). - Approximately 80% of 25- to 34-year-olds were employed.

Historical trends:
- From 2013 to 2019 (pre-pandemic), overall employment rose from 75% (2013) to 79% (2019).
- During the pandemic (2020-2023), employment was lowest in 2021 (76%).
- In 2023, employment rates at each education level were higher than in 2021 and not measurably different from 2019 levels. Example: for high school completers, rates were 74% in 2019, 68% in 2021, and 74% in 2023.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This research article, published in Demography (2015), examines differences in lifetime earnings by educational attainment in the United States. Using data from the Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP) matched to longitudinal tax earnings records from the Social Security Administration (SSA), the authors estimate 50-year work career effects of education on lifetime earnings for both men and women.

**Key findings:**

- **Gross lifetime earnings:** Men with a high school diploma earn approximately $1.54 million over a lifetime; those with a bachelor's degree earn $2.43 million; and those with a graduate degree earn $3.05 million. Accounting for key covariates reduces the estimated lifetime earnings return to college by approximately 30%.

- **Net present value at age 20 (4% discount rate):** The value of a bachelor's degree compared to high school drops to about $259,000 for men and $180,000 for women.

**Methodology:** The study uses a semi-synthetic cohort approach, combining four birth cohorts (1932-1939, 1942-1949, 1952-1959, 1962-1969) to estimate 50-year earnings from ages 20 to 69. The authors employ quantile regression at the median, controlling for race/ethnicity, marital status, number of children (for women), region of birth, and high school academic preparation.

**Key comparisons:** The study finds that purely synthetic cohort methods (using cross-sectional data) overstate the earnings gains associated with a bachelor's degree by 23% for men and 42% for women compared to the longitudinal administrative data approach. --- SOURCE 17: Educational Attainment and the Evolution of Cumulative ... ---
URL: https://www.bostonfed.org/-/media/Documents/Workingpapers/PDF/2026/WP2605.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Federal Reserve Bank of Boston Research Department working paper (No. 26-5, March 2026) by Pinghui Wu and Annie Liu examining how educational attainment shapes long-term cumulative earnings across 45 US birth cohorts (1933-1977). 

**Methodology:** The study uses a linked dataset combining the Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS-ASEC) with restricted-use Detailed Earnings Records (DER) from the Social Security Administration (SSA), covering 1978-2021 and 1.4 million workers. The primary outcome is 20-year cumulative earnings (log of summed annual wage income, inflation-adjusted using PCE), examined at two career stages: early-career (ages 25-44, cohorts born 1953-1977) and late-career (ages 45-64, cohorts born 1933-1957). Five education categories are analyzed: less than high school (LTHS), high school graduates, some college, bachelor's degree, and advanced degree.

**Key Findings:**
- Men with advanced degrees experienced the most robust earnings growth: +0.40 log points in late-career earnings (1933-1957 cohorts) and +0.28 log points in early-career earnings (1953-1977 cohorts). Bachelor's degree holders saw more modest growth (+0.20 and +0.23 log points), concentrated among cohorts born 1951-1965.
- Men with sub-baccalaureate education saw largely flat earnings trajectories. Men with LTHS born after 1965 experienced modest gains, likely due to exposure to higher minimum wages.
- Women at all education levels experienced broad-based robust earnings growth, with larger increases for those with bachelor's or advanced degrees. Late-career cumulative earnings rose 0.39-0.50 log points for degree holders and 0.25-0.37 log points for less educated women (1933-1957 cohorts).
- Extended work life was the primary growth margin for less educated men in the late-career stage, contributing 80+% of total earnings growth for men with a high school diploma versus only 15% for those with advanced degrees. This reflects changes in Social Security's normal retirement age (rising from 65 to 66.5) that created incentives for delayed retirement.
- Both men's college premium and advanced-degree premium expanded by more than 0.20 log points across the cohorts. Women's college premium grew steadily while their advanced-degree premium remained largely flat (modest gains only among 1965-1977 cohorts).
- Education premium growth across cohorts stems primarily from newer cohorts entering the labor market with larger wage gaps. After labor market entry, evolution of premiums is determined by life-cycle effects that are remarkably stable across cohorts.
- Point-in-time premiums measured at younger ages substantially underestimate long-term cumulative education premiums (e.g., early-career cumulative college premium of 0.61 log points for 1973-1977 female cohorts versus 0.36, 0.55, and 0.57 log points at ages 25, 35, and 45).
- Within-group earnings dispersion increased substantially among men born 1933-1957, particularly in the late-career stage, driving sharper cumulative inequality growth compared with women or younger cohorts.
- The pace of within-group dispersion changes across cohorts is largely determined at labor market entry and remains stable over the life cycle, indicating cohort effects actively drive cross-sectional inequality trends.

**Contributions:** This is the first comprehensive empirical analysis of long-term cumulative earnings by educational attainment across US birth cohorts, extending work by Guvenen et al. (2022), Tamborini et al. (2015), and others. The research demonstrates that conditions at labor market entry critically shape long-run inequality dynamics.
</summary>

This Urban Institute brief by Jason Cohn, published November 19, 2024, examines how college graduates' earnings change over 25 years after graduation, with implications for higher education accountability policy. Recent federal policies like the gainful employment rule link federal aid access to post-completion earnings, but proposals differ on when to measure earnings. The author analyzed average earnings trajectories for associate's, bachelor's, master's, and professional degrees using College Scorecard and American Community Survey data for the first 5 years post-graduation, then extending the ACS analysis for 20 additional years.

Key findings: (1) Earnings growth is typically high in the initial years after graduation, especially for bachelor's and professional degrees where real annual growth nears or exceeds 10 percent; (2) Earnings growth slows considerably between years 6 and 10, except for professional degree graduates whose earnings continue growing rapidly through the first 10 years; (3) Master's degree holders show the most consistent earnings growth, never exceeding 6 percent annually in any of the first 25 years. The author notes that accountability policy effects are sensitive to which measurement year is chosen, particularly for bachelor's and professional degrees, since professional degree earnings continue growing rapidly for a decade.

The study matters because measuring earnings too early may not capture a credential's true value, while waiting too long could allow poor-performing programs to operate with inadequate outcomes. Additionally, the growing use of income-driven repayment plans creates closer links between earnings trajectories and how quickly students repay debts.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This January 2026 College Transitions article examines whether trade school or a college degree pays more, concluding that neither path universally wins—financial outcomes depend on the specific occupation, debt load, and career length. It reframes the question from "trades vs. degrees" to "what does the specific job I want require, and what does each path cost?"

KEY DATA POINTS:
• Trade/Vocational pathway: 6 months–2 years training, $5,000–$20,000 total cost, $50,000–$75,000 median wage, ~3.5–4.5% unemployment
• Bachelor's pathway: 4 years (2–3 online), $40,000–$65,000 (online/nonprofit) up to $200,000+ (private residential), ~$78,000 median wage, ~2.3% unemployment, ~$900,000 lifetime earnings premium over HS diploma
• Top trade wages (BLS 2024): Elevator Installers $99,000, Nuclear Power Reactor Operators $107,800, Radiation Therapists $89,530, Electrical Power-Line Installers $82,340, Dental Hygienists $81,400, Electricians $61,590 (11% growth), HVAC $57,300 (9% growth)
• Highest bachelor's fields: Computer/IS Managers $169,510, Financial Managers $156,100, Software Developers $132,270, Civil Engineers $99,490; lower fields like General Studies/Liberal Arts pay $40,000–$55,000 at entry
• Field of study is the primary determinant of earnings, more than the credential type itself

COST & OPPORTUNITY COST:
Trade programs are substantially cheaper. Apprenticeships cost $0–$5,000 and pay apprentice wages from day one; DOL reports registered apprenticeship graduates earn average starting wages of $77,000 with minimal/no debt. Opportunity cost of four years in school is $90,000–$110,000 in foregone income. Online degrees reduce this by allowing full-time work during study.

LIFETIME EARNINGS: Trades outperform in the first 5–10 years (debt-free position enables compounding savings), while degrees pull ahead at the 10–15 year mark due to management/executive career ceiling potential.

AUTOMATION RISK: Field-based physical trades (electrical, plumbing, HVAC) have low automation risk; routine administrative/clerical roles have higher exposure; high-skill professional/STEM roles are relatively safe. The most vulnerable are routine, process-based, location-stable middle tasks.

CASE STUDY: Alex (business degree, $52,000 with $35,000 debt at 22) vs. Jordan (electrician, $61,000 debt-free with 4 years experience at 22). Jordan's net worth leads through the first decade; Alex may catch up by 35 through management tracks. A combined pathway (trade first, online degree later) often produces the strongest outcomes.

Bottom line: Trade school wins on speed and upfront cost; a bachelor's wins on long-term ceiling potential and is required for the highest-earning professional occupations. The best path aligns with a specific high-demand occupation with controlled debt.
</summary>

URL: https://www.erdc.wa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/publication_201507_stem_degree_earnings_premium.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Summary

This is a research paper published in July 2015 by the Washington State Education Research and Data Center (ERDC) within the Office of Financial Management, funded by a Workforce Data Quality Improvement (WDQI) grant from the U.S. Department of Labor. The paper estimates the earnings premium associated with STEM bachelor's degrees compared to non-STEM degrees, broken out by gender and race, for workers in Washington state.

**Methodology:** The study uses data from the ERDC P-20 Data Warehouse, covering students who graduated from Washington public high schools between 2005 and 2007 and earned a bachelor's degree from a Washington public university. The study explicitly corrects for selection bias using **propensity score matching (PSM)** — one of the first studies to do so. Propensity scores were estimated via logistic regression using high school GPA, free/reduced-price lunch participation, high school region, county unemployment rate, and Washington State Need Grant receipt. Earnings outcomes come from Washington state Unemployment Insurance (UI) wage records, adjusted to 2013 dollars. Workers were included only if they had earnings in all four quarters of a calendar year, and individuals pursuing post-baccalaureate education were excluded.

**Key Findings:**

**Overall Gender Gap (8th year after high school):**
- **Male STEM earnings premium: $18,300** over non-STEM males
- **Female STEM earnings premium: $2,800** over non-STEM females (a $15,600 gap)
- Males with STEM degrees earned median real annual earnings of **$59,700** vs. $41,400 for non-STEM males
- Females with STEM degrees earned **$41,000** vs. $38,200 for non-STEM females
- Female STEM earnings premium remained at or below zero through the first seven years after high school

**Race Breakdown (8th year after high school):**
- **Male STEM premium by race:** White +$16,300, Asian +$21,900, ANP +$18,100
- **Female STEM premium by race:** White +$1,400, Asian +$7,400, ANP -$5,200 (negative, likely due to small sample size)
- Male STEM earnings: White $60,500, Asian $58,900, ANP $52,900
- Female STEM earnings: Asian $46,900, White $40,000, ANP $29,500

**Major Choice Differences:**
- Females were roughly **half as likely** as males to choose a STEM major (15.6% of females vs. 31.8% of males in the sample)
- Female STEM majors concentrated in biological and environmental sciences (top 3 majors: cell/cellular and molecular biology 15.7%, biology 11.6%, biochemistry 7.1%)
- Male STEM majors more dispersed across engineering and computer science (top 3: mechanical engineering 8.1%, civil engineering 6.5%, cell/molecular biology 6.0%)

**Occupational Differences (from American Community Survey):**
- 20.9% of male workers with STEM degrees work as software developers; only 3.2% of females do
- The leading occupation for females with STEM degrees is **registered nurses (9.0%)**, which is not a STEM occupation
- Weighted average hourly wage for top-10 male STEM occupations: **$44.23** vs. **$28.12** for females (approximately $32,100 annual gap at full-time work)

**Conclusion:** The study demonstrates that STEM degrees have a substantially higher earnings payoff for males than females in Washington state. Possible explanations cited include gender-based discrimination, male-oriented culture in high-tech organizations, child-bearing/family responsibilities, and differing tastes and preferences. The authors note the gender sorting into STEM begins early in the educational pipeline and suggest a broader perspective on gender equality in STEM may be needed.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We find the STEM earnings premium (STEM median earnings – non-STEM median earnings) for males is $18,300 for the eighth year after high school graduation. In stark contrast, the female STEM earnings premium remains quite low through the first seven years after high school and rises to $2,800 in the eighth year."

--- SOURCE 14: No, we are not producing too many STEM graduates - Economic Innovation Group ---
URL: https://eig.org/stem-graduates

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This analysis article, published January 21, 2025, by the Economic Innovation Group (EIG) and originally appearing on the Agglomerations Substack, challenges claims that the U.S. is producing too many STEM graduates. The piece was written by Connor O'Brien and Ben Glasner in response to the H-1B visa social media debate, where critics cited Census Bureau data showing 72 percent of STEM graduates work in non-STEM occupations.

The authors argue that this statistic masks a more positive story. First, the data has classification problems—14 percent of STEM majors go into "STEM-related" jobs (like physicians and nurses, who are counted as leaving STEM only because there is no undergraduate medical education in the U.S.). Additionally, STEM graduates frequently take high-paying jobs in other fields that require their skills.

Key data points include: Among 13.7 million STEM majors in non-STEM jobs, 36 percent earn more than STEM majors in STEM jobs. While the median STEM major in a STEM job earned $110,000 in 2023, over 4.9 million STEM majors earned at least that much in non-STEM jobs (comparable to the 5.1 million STEM majors working in STEM jobs). Among engineering majors in non-STEM careers, 49 percent earn more than the median for all STEM occupations.

Controlling for degree level, age, and hours worked, having a STEM degree provides a 9 percent earnings boost in STEM occupations but a 23 percent earnings boost in non-STEM occupations—both statistically significant. The authors note that STEM is hardly unique in sending graduates to other fields (fewer than one-quarter of art graduates work in art occupations), and that within-field retention rates alone cannot distinguish between over-producing fields and those producing highly-coveted graduates.

The authors conclude that the data strongly supports the positive interpretation: students major in STEM in large part because such degrees yield significant financial returns across a wide range of jobs, making this "a success, not a failure." The code and data behind the analysis are available in a linked GitHub repository.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"On balance, the evidence is much stronger for the second, positive story." (referring to STEM skills being in high demand across the economy)

2. **Racial and Ethnic Disparities**: Only 37 percent of the 2 million bachelor's degree earners in 2021 were students of color.
