#### E. Default and delinquency — post-pandemic resurgence

**NY Fed Liberty Street Economics (May 13, 2025) — "Student Loan Delinquencies Are Back":**
- Student loan delinquency rate surged from below 1% to nearly **8%** after the on-ramp preventing negative credit reporting expired in October 2024 [15].
- **13.7% of student loan borrowers (nearly 6 million) were 90+ days past due or in default** in Q1 2025, comparable to the 14.4% rate in Q1 2020 [15].
- **Among borrowers required to make payments, nearly 1 in 4 (23.7%) were behind** [15].
- Highest delinquency rates concentrated in the South: Mississippi (44.6%), Alabama (34.1%), West Virginia (34.0%), Kentucky (33.6%), Oklahoma (33.6%), Arkansas (33.5%), Louisiana (31.8%). Lowest: Illinois (13.7%), Massachusetts (14.0%), Connecticut (14.5%), Vermont (14.7%), New Hampshire (14.8%) [15].
- Older borrowers are more affected: over 25% of those aged 40+ with a payment due are delinquent; average age of a delinquent borrower rose from 38.6 to 40.4 [15].
- 56.6% of newly delinquent borrowers already had subprime credit scores (<620). However, **2.4 million newly delinquent borrowers had scores above 620** and will face steep borrowing cost increases or credit denial. Over 2.2 million saw their credit scores drop more than 100 points; over 1 million saw drops of at least 150 points [15].
- The U.S. Department of Education, with the Treasury, began collection efforts in May 2025, including **wage garnishment and tax refund/Social Security payment seizure** [15].

**NY Fed Liberty Street Economics (May 12, 2026) — "Federal Student Loan Defaults Return":**
- Student loan payments were paused from March 2020 to September 2023, with a 12-month "on-ramp" (through October 2024). First delinquencies appeared on credit reports in 2025:Q1 [13].
- Approximately **1 million federal student loan borrowers defaulted in 2025:Q4**, and an additional **2.6 million defaulted in 2026:Q1** — totaling 3.6 million borrowers [13].
- **Over 17% of student loan borrowers have fallen at least 90 days past due at least once** [13].
- The average borrower entering default is nearly 40 years old (38.9 years, up from 36.4 pre-pandemic), with a notable shift toward older borrowers (50+). Most defaulters were NOT past due before the pandemic: nearly 30% were current, ~50% had no payment due, and only about 20% were past due [13].
- Defaults are concentrated in Southern states (Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, South Carolina) [13].
- Defaulted borrowers saw credit scores drop an **average of 91 points (from 567 to 476)** [13].
- Newly defaulted borrowers also tend to be behind on other debts: nearly 40% past due on auto loans, 56% on credit cards, and 20% on mortgages [13].
- The authors believe the largest wave of defaults has passed, though a second wave may emerge from the **7 million borrowers in the defunct SAVE repayment plan** who are yet to re-enter repayment [13].
- Spillover to broader credit markets is likely limited: defaulted/delinquent borrowers represent only 2% of the credit population and hold small shares of total debt balances (2.7% of auto loans, 2% of credit cards, 1% of mortgages) [13].

**SoFi (July 28, 2026):**
- ~9 million borrowers with $220 billion in loans in default (March 2026), more than 13% of federally managed portfolio [27].
- 15.9% of borrowers at least 60 days past due (returning to pre-pandemic levels; was 16.7% in August 2019, dropped to 2.3% during payment pause); 90+ day delinquency rate: 10.3% in Q1 2026 [27].
- ~20% of borrowers in active repayment (~3.5 million) at least 30 days delinquent [27].
- Federal loans enter default after **270 days** of missed payments; default can trigger wage garnishment, seizure of tax refunds, loss of federal aid eligibility [27].
- Highest delinquency in the South: Louisiana (22.6%), Mississippi (22.3%), Georgia (21.1%) [27].
- ~13 million borrowers on income-driven repayment (IDR) plans (~44% of those in repayment); 6.5+ million borrowers remained in SAVE plan forbearance at end of 2025 amid litigation; 44.6% on standard 10-year fixed payment plan; average borrower takes **~20 years to pay off loans** [27].
- New repayment assistance plan (RAP) launched **July 1, 2026**, replacing existing income-driven plans; borrowers with pre-date loans have until July 1, 2028 to choose between RAP, tiered standard plan, or IBR. Under RAP, remaining balance forgiven after 360 payments over at least 30 years (longer than previous 20-25 year timelines) [27].
- Forgiveness: $87.6 billion discharged across ~1.18 million borrowers through PSLF and related programs (avg ~$78,200 per PSLF borrower, through September 2025). Early in the program (2018-2020), **99.7% of PSLF applications were rejected**. Teacher Loan Forgiveness: $3.87 billion across 469,867 teachers (avg $8,497). Federal forgiveness applications have an 11.2% acceptance rate. Final PSLF rule taking effect July 1, 2026 narrows qualifying employers [27].
- Education Data Initiative: Only 3.3% of PSLF applications have been approved since inception, though $46.8 billion has been forgiven through PSLF; $197.3 million through Teacher Loan Forgiveness [11].
- COVID-19 impact: Federal loan interest was 0% from March 2020 to September 2023; 66% of federal debt remained in forbearance until September 2023; as of the report, 44% of federal borrowers are in repayment, 21% in forbearance [11].
- Loan servicer issues: 70% of complaints relate to mismanagement/deception; Navient was sued by CFPB in 2017 and is no longer contracted to service federal loans as of 2022; "Operation Game of Loans" pursued 36 enforcement actions against student debt relief companies, securing judgments worth over $131 million [11].

#### F. Federal Reserve Board SHED 2024 (published May 2025)
- 71% of adults have enrolled in postsecondary education; 37% hold a bachelor's degree or higher [12].
- Educational attainment varies significantly by parental education (**66%** of those with a college-educated parent earn a bachelor's vs. **25%** otherwise) and by race/ethnicity (Asian 67%, White 41%, Black 28%, Hispanic 21%) [12].
- 30% of all adults have taken out student loans for their own education; 17% still owe money (borrowers), 24% have fully repaid [12].
- The **median outstanding education debt is between $20,000-$24,999**; 28% of borrowers owe less than $10,000 [12].
- Borrowers who attended for-profit institutions are more likely to have debt and to be behind on payments (**65% with debt, 35% behind**) compared to public (38% with debt, 16% behind) and private non-profit (54% with debt, 15% behind) [12].
- As of October 2024, **57% of borrowers were required to make monthly payments** (up from 37% in 2022). **20% of borrowers were behind on payments or in collections** (up from 16% in 2023) [12].
- Borrowers with less education and lower incomes are more likely to be behind: 30% behind for those with some college/associate degree; 27% behind for those earning under $25,000 [12].
- Among all who ever borrowed: **59% have fully repaid their loans, 33% are current on payments, and 8% are behind** [12].

#### G. Impact on major life decisions

**Homeownership (EducationData.org, 2026):**
- **Homeownership among recent college graduates declines 1.8% for every $1,000 of student loan debt** [26].
- Average monthly mortgage payments rose from $1,318 in 2016 to **$2,005 in 2025**; average monthly student loan payments rose from $393 in 2016 to **$431 in 2025** (Federal Reserve Board of Governors, FHFA, and U.S. Department of Education) [26].
- 50% of all adults with debt delayed home purchase (20% delayed 5+ years). By age group: 70% of those aged 28-43 delayed purchase (23% for 5+ years), vs. only 28% of those aged 61-78 [26].
- A high debt-to-income (DTI) ratio reduces mortgage eligibility [26].
- "Student loan repayments are forcing millions of young families to delay purchasing their first home, as they cannot afford to save for a down payment or qualify for a mortgage while also paying off student debt." — Transforming Student Debt to Home Equity Act, H.R. 7368, 117th Congress [26].
- Student debt is a greater obstacle to younger generations, especially **Millennials (born 1981-1996)** [26].
- Programs: Maryland Smartbuy Loan Program, Ohio's Grants For Grads program [26].

**Marriage and family (SoFi, 2026):**
- ~1 in 5 recent graduates with loans report delaying marriage and children [27].

**Retirement savings and stock ownership:**
- Student debt influences job-acceptance decisions for **56% of public-sector and 62% of private-sector workers**; public-sector employees with student debt are **14% more likely to view retirement savings as inadequate** [27].
- Borrowers with >$35,000 in debt are **27% less likely to be homeowners** [27].
- Korankye (Economic Analysis Letters, 2023, using PSID 2011-2017): "The presence of student debt decreases the probability that married households will own stocks, but the amount of student debt does not show a statistically significant effect" — suggesting the incidence of student debt raises perceived liquidity constraints and debt burden [28].

**Retirement decisions (Butrica & Karamcheva, IZA DP No. 13182, April 2020, SCF 1989-2016, ages 55-70):**
- More indebted older adults are **more likely to work, less likely to be retired, and expect to work longer** than those with less debt [29].
- Household debt among older Americans has risen dramatically; share of debt held by adults age 60-69 increased 61% and 90% for age 70+ between 2003-2018 [29].
- Between 1989 and 2016, share of households age 55-70 with debt increased from 64% to 75%; mean debt more than doubled ($48,800 → $125,300); median debt more than quadrupled ($14,500 → $61,000) [29].
- Student loans increased most rapidly: share of households with student debt more than tripled from 3% to 10%; median amounts rose from $5,400 to $18,000 [29].
- Average debt-to-asset ratio increased from 12% to 26%; average debt-to-income ratio rose from 45% to 107% [29].
- Those with debt are **11.2 percentage points more likely to work** and **10.3 pp less likely to be retired**; doubling per-person debt increases work likelihood by 1.1 pp and reduces retirement likelihood by 1.0 pp [29].
- Having mortgage debt raises work probability by 5.8 pp; a $10,000 credit card debt increase raises work likelihood by 9.4 pp vs. only 0.3 pp for mortgages [29].
- Student loan debt has no statistically significant effect on retirement behavior on average, but **reduces benefit receipt and retirement among the lowest-wealth older adults**; credit card debt increases likelihood of receiving Social Security benefits by 4.5 pp [29].

**COVID-era hardship (TICAS Class of 2020 report):**
- In California, borrowers were nearly **4x more likely than non-borrowers to lose housing** (22% vs 6%), 3x more likely to have difficulty paying for dependent care (30% vs 10%), and 2x as likely to miss a mortgage/rent/utility payment (41% vs 19%) [45].

**For-profit vs. nonprofit default rates:**
- Students at for-profit colleges default at much higher rates (**30% within 12 years** vs 4% at public and 5% at nonprofit colleges) [45].

### IV. OPPORTUNITY COST — FOREGONE WAGES DURING FOUR YEARS OF STUDY

- **NY Fed (Abel & Deitz, "Is College Still Worth It?", April 16, 2025):** Opportunity costs (forgone wages, estimated at **~$150,000 in 2024** using median wages of high school graduates) have risen, pushing the **average total cost of a degree from ~$140,000 in the late 1990s to $180,000 in 2024** [24].
- NY Fed 2014 (Abel & Deitz, Current Issues Vol. 20 No. 3): The total cost of a bachelor's degree was about **$122,000 in 2013**, with **forgone wages constituting the vast majority** [22].
- EducationData.org: The initial investment for a typical bachelor's degree from a state school totals **$270,811** (including tuition of $107,190, indirect costs of attendance such as room and board, student loan interest, and lost potential income) [16].
- Considering student loan interest and lost potential income, investing in a bachelor's degree can ultimately cost **upwards of $500,000** [6].
- BLS/EducationData.org benchmark: median weekly income for high school graduates is $899 ($46,748/year) — the income students forgo while studying [6]. A 2025 BLS figure cited by UNC Charlotte: $946/week (~$49,200/year) for HS-only workers [17].
- The NY Fed notes that part of the reason college returns have remained high is that **wages for those without a college degree have also been falling**, keeping the college wage premium near an all-time high **while reducing the opportunity cost of going to school** [22].

### V. NET PRESENT VALUE AND ROI CALCULATIONS — BREAKEVEN, VARIATION BY MAJOR, INSTITUTION, RACE/GENDER

#### A. NY Fed internal rate of return (IRR) estimates

**2025 analysis (Abel & Deitz, April 16, 2025):**
- Using internal rate of return methodology with quantile regression to estimate the return for the **median** (rather than average) graduate, the return to college is estimated at **12.5% in 2024** — "a rate well above the threshold for a sound investment" [24].
- This return has held between **12-13% for the past three decades** [24].
- Direct out-of-pocket costs have actually fallen in recent years after inflation adjustment — average published tuition was ~$21,000/year in 2024, but after grant aid the **average net price over four years was ~$30,000** [24].
- The median college graduate with a bachelor's degree earns about **$80,000/year compared to $47,000 for the median high school graduate** — a premium of over $32,000 (about 68%), near its all-time high [24].
- The wage premium tends to grow over one's career [24].
- Caveats: estimates apply only to graduates (not dropouts); factoring dropout risk would reduce the return by roughly **1.5 percentage points**; calculations assume average costs over four years and median college wages [24].

**2014 analysis (Abel & Deitz, "Do the Benefits of College Still Outweigh the Costs?", Current Issues 20(3)):**
- Despite rising tuition and falling wages for college graduates, analysis of four decades of data (1970-2013) shows both bachelor's and associate's degrees yield returns of **about 15% over the past decade** [22].
- College graduates earn **56% more than high school graduates** (bachelor's) and 21% more (associate's) [22].
- Bachelor's degree holders earn about **$1 million more over their lifetimes** than high school graduates; associate's holders ~$325,000 more [22].
- Net tuition for a bachelor's degree was $6,550 in 2013 (vs. $14,750 sticker price); associate's net tuition was negative (fully subsidized) [22].
- Returns vary significantly by major: **Engineering (21%), Math and computers (18%), Health (18%), Business (17%), Communications (15%), Social sciences (15%), Sciences (14%), Architecture (14%), Liberal arts (12%), Agriculture (11%), Leisure and hospitality (11%), and Education (9%)** [22].
- Even chronically underemployed college graduates earn positive returns — ranging from **7% (education majors) to 17% (engineering majors)** — because employers pay a premium for college graduates even in non-college-level jobs [22].

**SSRN follow-up ("When College Might Not Be Worth It," Abel & Deitz):** "In our last post, we showed that the economic benefits of a college degree still far outweigh the costs for the typical graduate, with a healthy..." [23]. The companion piece examines whether college is worth it for at least a quarter of graduates [24].

**NY Fed Instagram (Sept 11, 2025, with Richard Deitz):** "Does college pay off for everyone? In recent research, our economists find that the typical college graduate earns a return that easily surpasses the benchmark for a sound investment. However, this is not the case for everyone" [25].

#### B. EducationData.org ROI analysis (updated May 2026)
- An average bachelor's degree has a **560.53% lifetime return on investment**, with a median lifetime return up to **1,040.14%** [16].
- In the first decade, an average bachelor's degree has a **negative return on investment (-16.54%)**; **it takes roughly 12 years in the workforce to regain the investment** for a typical bachelor's degree [16].
- Projected average starting salary for someone with a bachelor's degree in 2026: **$72,069**; projected median salary among working bachelor's degree holders aged 25-64: **$87,722** [16].
- Professional degrees offer the highest potential ROI at **2,249%** [16].
- Bachelor's holders earn an estimated **$25,356 (41.2%) more than associate's degree holders** [16].
- ROI by major — most cost-efficient: management information systems and statistics (**1,758.59%**), finance (**1,580.53%**), computer and information sciences (**1,561.07%**), electrical engineering (**1,479.98%**) [16].
- Degrees with **negative ROI**: psychology (**-122.78%**), family and consumer sciences (**-100.62%**), liberal arts and humanities (**-94.03%**), education (**-51.61%**) [16].
- Additional majors: agriculture 301%, architecture 598%, business 915%, accounting 1,065%, communications 435.80%, criminal justice 174.48%, engineering 761.99%, English 134.91%, health 570.79%, nursing 732.33%, mathematics 976.87%, history 105.06% [16].

#### C. Georgetown CEW — "A First Try at ROI: Ranking 4,500 Colleges" (Nov 19, 2019; updated 2022)
- Ranks 4,500+ public, private nonprofit, and private for-profit colleges by ROI using **net present value (NPV)** calculations based on expanded U.S. Department of Education College Scorecard data (net price, median debt, median earnings) [47][49].
- The **median NPV for all colleges is $723,000 in the long term (40 years after enrollment)**, but only **$107,000 in the short term (10 years after enrollment)** [47][49].
- **Community colleges and many certificate programs have the highest ROI in the short term (10 years)** — 26 of the 30 institutions with the best 10-year NPV primarily grant certificates or associate's degrees; certificates in nursing are particularly valuable short-term [47].
- **Colleges that primarily award bachelor's degrees have the highest ROI in the long term (40 years)**. Eight of the top 10 long-term NPV institutions are private nonprofits [47].
- Top institutions: Albany College of Pharmacy and Health Sciences ($2,722,000 NPV), St. Louis College of Pharmacy ($2,714,000), MIT ($2,273,000), Stanford ($2,068,000), Maine Maritime Academy, Babson College, Harvard, Georgetown, and the US Merchant Marine Academy. Six of the top 10 have NPVs of $2 million or more at the 40-year horizon [47].
- **Public colleges have higher ROI than private colleges in the short term** due to lower tuition and less debt; however, **private nonprofit colleges have higher long-term ROI than public universities ($838,000 vs. $765,000 in long-term net economic gains)** [47].
- Private college graduates earn a median of **$41,000 ten years after enrollment** vs. $33,000 for public institution graduates, though their median debt is $17,000 vs. $7,000 [47].
- The lowest long-term NPV institutions: theological institutions, beauty schools, arts colleges, and a tribal college (ranging from about $240,000 to $294,000 in NPV) [47].
- Distribution: 50th percentile of long-term NPV is $718,000-$723,000; 75th percentile $867,000-$877,000 (mostly bachelor's-granting); 25th percentile $566,000-$573,000 (mostly non-bachelor's-granting) [47].
- Methodology: earnings 10 years after first attending serve as a proxy for future earnings; average annual net price represents total investment cost; discount rate ~2% (US Treasury securities); assumes no earnings increases after 10 years (conservative); does NOT deduct opportunity costs of foregone earnings [47].
- The median debt for a bachelor's degree (~$9,800) is slightly less than twice the overall median and twice that of a certificate program [47].
- Companion report "ROI of Liberal Arts Colleges": the median ROI of liberal arts colleges is **nearly $200,000 higher than the median for all colleges**; the 40-year median ROI of liberal arts institutions is **$918,000**, close to four-year engineering and technology schools ($917,000) and four-year business and management schools ($913,000) [49].
- 2022 update added a new metric: the share of students at an institution earning more than workers with only a high school diploma 10 years after enrollment. **An average of 60% of college students across institutions earn more than a high school graduate after 10 years. However, at 1,233 postsecondary institutions (30%), more than half of their students earn less than a high school graduate 10 years after enrollment** [50].
- Interactive ROI Rankings platform allows comparison of 4,500+ institutions over 10, 20, 30, and 40-year timeframes, using net cost of attendance, post-graduation earnings, and debt [51].

#### D. Critical analysis of the Georgetown ROI methodology (collegeroi.org / Leon Shivamber)
- The 2022 report factors in cost of degree and time value of money (both absent in the earlier College Payoff report) [48].
- Five persistent methodological problems identified:
  1. **Inconsistent time periods**: shifted from ages 24-64 to ages 18-58 — stopping at 58 truncates peak-earnings years [48].
  2. **Flat costs assumption**: assumes tuition doesn't increase during enrollment, though college costs have outpaced inflation by 90-150% since 1990 [48].
  3. **Pre-tax earnings**: a high school graduate pays ~$400,000 in federal taxes over a lifetime vs. ~$600,000 for a college graduate — that $200,000 differential reduces the after-tax NPV advantage by roughly 20-25% [48].
  4. **Discount rate too low**: CEW used 2.5% (College Payoff) then 2% (2022); credible benchmarks: government funding rate 5.4%, Parent PLUS up to 9.08%, NY Fed 5%, SF Fed 6.67%, CBO 5.91% [48].
  5. **Benchmark problem (most consequential)**: CEW uses a synthetic $15,000/year figure (near federal minimum wage) as the high school baseline, giving a $397,000 NPV baseline — but CEW's own College Payoff report implies a $924,000 NPV high school baseline from its $1.6M lifetime earnings figure. **Applying the $924,000 benchmark to the 2022 rankings of 4,526 institutions shows only 873 (19%) produce NPV at or above the high school baseline — meaning 81% deliver a return below direct workforce entry** [48].
- The 2025 ROI update abandoned discounting entirely (0% rate), which maximizes the apparent value of college since graduate earnings are backloaded [48].
- The underlying College Scorecard earnings/cost data is real and genuinely useful for comparing schools; it is the aggregate rankings and headline NPV conclusions that are flawed [48].

#### E. Breakeven point
- **~12 years** to recoup the cost of a bachelor's degree (by age 34); by age 31 when considering net cost (cost minus scholarships/discounts) [5].
- College Board *Education Pays 2026*: the typical graduate recoups the cost of a degree **by their mid-30s** [19].
- EducationData.org: ROI is negative (-16.54%) in the first decade; positive around year 12 [16].
- UNC System: many graduates recover degree costs within ~10 years [17].

#### F. Variation by major — detailed

**Georgetown CEW, "The Major Payoff" (October 15, 2025):**
- Prime-age workers with a bachelor's degree earn **70% more at the median** than workers with a high school diploma alone, with unemployment 2.9% vs. 6.2% [35].
- Median earnings vary significantly by major: from **$58,000 in education and public service fields to $98,000 in STEM fields** [35].
- Within 65 STEM majors, median earnings range from **$64,000 (miscellaneous agriculture) to $146,000 (petroleum engineering)** [35].
- Pharmaceutical sciences majors earn a median of **$145K** vs. **$51K** for early childhood education majors [31][35].
- **14 of the 19 humanities and arts majors lead to median earnings above $65,000** [35].
- Report analyzes 152 majors for prime-age workers (ages 25-54) and 142 majors for early-career graduates (ages 22-26), tracking median earnings, graduate degree earnings premiums, and unemployment rates [35].
- Engineering, business, computers/statistics/math, health, and physical sciences majors have the highest median earnings [35].
- Persistent racial/ethnic and gender disparities: male, white, and Asian/Asian American workers are overrepresented in STEM; women are overrepresented in education, healthcare, and social science fields [35].

**College Board, Education Pays 2026 (April 14, 2026):**
- Earnings vary by major — from about **$44,000 for performing arts graduates to over $80,000 for mechanical engineering and computer science graduates** [19].

**AEFP Live Handbook:**
- The difference between top-earning majors (e.g., engineering, economics) and bottom-earning majors (e.g., fine arts) is roughly **$2 million** over a lifetime [18].

#### G. Variation by institution type
- Private nonprofit bachelor's degrees have higher 40-year ROI ($838,000) than public ($765,000); public colleges have higher short-term ROI [47].
- For-profit institutions have worse average outcomes and higher default rates [18][12][45].
- Community colleges and certificate programs have the highest short-term ROI [47].
- Lovenheim & Smith (September 2022, edworkingpapers): 3,757 degree-granting institutions in 2019-20; 66% four-year, 34% two-year. Two-year colleges serve more disadvantaged populations (59.4% Pell Grant recipients vs. 46.8% at four-year colleges). Private for-profit institutions have the highest rates of Pell Grant and underrepresented minority enrollment. More selective institutions serve fewer economically disadvantaged students, have higher expenditures per student, and higher graduation rates (**75.4% for more selective vs. 40.3% for inclusive institutions**) [38].
- "There is clear evidence that **more-selective and higher-resource educational environments lead to higher returns**" [38].
- "Lower-SES students tend to invest in less-selective and lower-resource colleges. These differences, combined with the evidence on returns, suggest that features of the U.S. postsecondary system may actually reduce intergenerational economic mobility" [38].
- NATI (June 9, 2025) highlights that "short-term, sub-baccalaureate credentials in technical fields can yield salaries comparable to or greater than some bachelor's degrees" [51].

#### H. Variation by race and gender
- Women who work full-time, full-year earn **25% less than men at similar education levels** [32].
- At the highest education level, **Black/African American and Hispanic/Latino individuals earn close to a million dollars less than their white and Asian/Asian American counterparts** over a lifetime [32].
- Lifetime earnings by gender at bachelor's level: **$3.3M (men) vs. $2.4M (women)** [34].
- Black, Latino, Native American/Alaskan Native, and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander workers consistently earn **10-38% less** than the highest-earning groups (White or Asian workers) at various education levels [34].
- Webber & Carruthers: returns differ by race ($1.38M white vs. $1.0M Black) and gender ($1.56M men vs. $0.99M women) [18].

### VI. THE COLLEGE WAGE PREMIUM — HOW IT HAS CHANGED OVER TIME (ESPECIALLY 2016–2026)

#### A. Minneapolis Fed (2025) — "What happened to the college wage premium?"
- The college wage premium (the gap in average wages between college-educated and high school-educated workers) rose dramatically from **39% in 1980 to 79% by 2000**, but has remained **flat since then**, even declining slightly after the Great Recession. In 2023, it was slightly lower than its 2000 value [20].
- While the wage premium has stagnated, **the cost of a four-year degree has risen 40% between 2000-2001 and 2022-2023**, reducing the financial return on college education [20].
- Research by Leila Bengali and Robert Valletta (San Francisco Fed): both supply and demand factors are at play, but the key explanation is **increased substitutability between college-educated and high school-educated workers** — firms have become more willing to substitute high school-educated workers for college graduates, reducing demand for the latter [20].
- "In the 21st century, the nature of technological change has not advantaged college-educated workers to the same degree as before, so firms are able to employ high school-educated workers to a greater extent" [20].
- "This pattern we're seeing, it's not something that emerged only in the last three or four years when AI came on the scene. So I would not interpret this as being attributable specifically to AI" [20].
- The share of college graduates in the workforce grew from **31% in 2000 to 45% in 2025**; online job postings requiring a college degree declined from **1.2 per non-degree posting in 2010 to 0.6 per non-degree posting in 2020** [20].
- Despite stagnation, the college wage premium remains high (**still ~76% higher wages for college graduates**) [20].

#### B. College Board, Education Pays 2026 (April 14, 2026)
- Among full-time working adults, **four-year college graduates earn about 60% more than high school graduates — a wage premium that has been stable for decades** [19].
- In 2025, unemployment among young adults ages 25-34 was **3.1% for college graduates versus 5.8%** for those without a degree [19].
- **Only 4% of college graduates live in poverty** compared to 13% of high school graduates [19].
- Quotes: "The data show that education remains a powerful driver of opportunity, but there are differences in outcomes. The question isn't just whether education pays—it's which pathways lead to the strongest outcomes." — Jessica Howell, vice president of research at the College Board [19]. "Education Pays 2026 highlights the strong economic and social benefits associated with postsecondary education... changing public views of higher education and rapid technological advances are reshaping the landscape." — Matea Pender, senior research scientist and lead author [19].

#### C. 2016–2026 assessment
- BLS weekly premium: $1,543 vs. $930 in 2024 (66% premium) [1]; UNC Charlotte cites $1,533 vs. $946 (roughly 62% premium) for 2026 [17].
- Abel & Deitz (2025): median college graduate earns ~$80,000 vs. $47,000 for HS — a ~68% premium, "near its all-time high" [24].
- Investopedia (Nov 7, 2025, citing Abel & Deitz): median college graduates earn about **70% more**; the wage premium has held steady between **12-13% for three decades**; the premium increased because **high school-only wages have shrunk more than 25% in real terms since the early 1970s**, while college graduate salaries rose only about 5% [37].
- San Francisco Fed (June 2025): premium at about **75%** [37].
- NYU analysis of 5.8 million Americans (2024): annualized returns of about **10% for women and 9% for men** [37].
- Quantumrun (2026): household income gap widened from 2:1 (2004) to 2.3:1 (2024) [1].
- On AI: Abel and Deitz were skeptical that AI is having widespread effects on recent graduates' employment, pointing instead to tech sector weakness beginning in 2022 and general cooling of labor demand [37].

### VII. COMPARISON WITH OTHER INVESTMENTS (STOCK MARKET, REAL ESTATE)

#### A. College degree vs. stocks and bonds
- **NY Fed (2025):** The 12.5% return to college compares favorably to **long-term stock market returns (~8%) and bonds (~4%)** [24][17].
- **NY Fed (2024 data, via WAICU, June 2025):** "According to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, the return on investment (ROI) for a college degree has been remarkable — between 12 percent and 13 percent over the past three decades, reaching 12.5 percent in 2024. This rate of return surpasses that of many traditional investment vehicles, including stocks and bonds" [21].
- **Forbes (March 12, 2024):** "A college degree still offers better returns than the stock market despite rising tuition costs, a new study has found" [36].
- **Investopedia (Nov 7, 2025):** College graduates can expect a **12.5% median annual return on investment** over a lifetime, outperforming traditional investments (**S&P 500 long-term real returns under 7%; bonds under 2% annually**) [37].
- Caveats: stock returns are volatile and require timing; the S&P 500's average annual return was about 9.6% from 1992-2011, but yearly returns ranged from +37.58% (1995) to -37.00% (2008); the compounded annualized return was about **7.8%** [39]. J.P. Morgan cites S&P 500 average annual return of **10.6% from 1980-2024** (as of June 30, 2025) [40].
- "College is still worth it, at least, for most people. Even though some recent graduates may be having difficulty finding a good job right now, they are in a much better position than similarly aged workers without a college degree, who tend to have higher unemployment and lower wages." — Jaison R. Abel and Richard Deitz [37].

#### B. Timing and graduation delays
- Taking **five years to graduate drops the median return to about 9%, and six years to 7%** [37]. For about a quarter of graduates, college doesn't pay off much financially [37].

#### C. Real estate comparison
- Real estate as an alternative is complicated by the fact that student debt itself **impedes homeownership** (1.8% lower homeownership per $1,000 of debt) [26].
- NY Fed June 2026 data (via Instagram post): nationwide home price growth of **1.1% year-over-year** [25] — well below the degree's ~12.5% IRR.

#### D. Opportunity-cost framing of the comparison
- The dominant "investment" in a degree is **foregone wages (~$150,000 in 2024)** rather than tuition [24]; if that capital were invested in equities instead, it could grow substantially — but the NY Fed IRR methodology already internalizes these costs and still finds 12.5% [24][22].
- A portfolio vs. index comparison is imperfect: personal returns diverge from index performance due to different holdings, systematic investing, volatility drag, and fees (Leelyn Smith) [39]. Index definitions: DJIA (30 blue-chip companies), S&P 500 (500 large U.S. companies), Nasdaq Composite (~4,500 stocks), Wilshire 5000, Russell 2000 (small-cap), MSCI ACWI (46 countries), Bloomberg Barclays U.S. Aggregate Bond Index [39].

### VIII. ADDITIONAL CONTEXT

#### A. Non-completion as the greatest risk
- Only about **60% of four-year college students graduate** [18].
- For "some college" no degree: median lifetime premium only $260,000; after taxes/discounting just $17,000; only 48% earn more than the median HS graduate [18].
- "Arguably, the worst position for an individual to be in financially is to have borrowed but failed to complete her degree" [18].
- Fall 2020 COVID enrollment impacts: overall -3%; community colleges -13% (Black -16%, Latina/o -15%, Indigenous -15%); recent HS graduates -6.9%; lowest persistence among first-year students since 2012; over a million students newly defaulted on federal loans in the 12 months preceding the pandemic [45].

#### B. Broader economic wellbeing (Fed SHED 2025)
- Financial well-being remained stable at **73% of adults "doing okay" financially or "living comfortably"**, slightly below the pre-pandemic plateau of 75% (2018-2020); declines for young adults, low-income families, and Black adults [30].
- 86% of adults with bachelor's degrees reported doing okay vs. **41% of those without a high school degree**; by race: Asian 82%, White 79%, Hispanic 62%, Black 60% [30].
- 49% of adults under 30 lived with a parent in 2025, up 12 percentage points since 2019 [30].
- 63% could cover a hypothetical $400 emergency expense; 35% of non-retirees said retirement savings were on track [30].
- 1 in 4 workers used generative AI at work; graduate degree holders were more than 4x more likely to use AI (43%) than those with HS or less (10%); 81% of AI users agreed it saves time [30].

#### C. Enrollment and degree-completion context
- Total postsecondary enrollment: 18.9 million in fall 2023 [8].
- 71% of adults ever attended postsecondary; 37% hold at least a bachelor's degree [12].
- High school students' expectations to pursue higher education declined to the lowest level in 20 years, falling by nearly half between 2002 and 2022 [50].
- 30 states saw drops in full-time undergraduate enrollment over the past decade [50].

# Career Stability and Mobility for Bachelor's Degree Holders vs. Non-Degree Holders in the United States

## List of Queries and Tool Calls Made

The following searches were conducted via the Tavily search API across three rounds:

**Round 1:**
1. "BLS unemployment rate bachelor's degree vs high school graduate 2016 2026"
2. "underemployment college graduates Federal Reserve Burning Glass Institute"
3. "degree creep jobs requiring degrees management positions Harvard Business School dismissed by degrees"
4. "earnings trajectory bachelor's degree vs non-degree career lifetime Georgetown CEW"

**Round 2:**
5. "layoff risk job loss rate by education level re-employment speed college degree"
6. "COVID-19 pandemic impact value college degree labor market college wage premium 2020 2021"
7. "coding bootcamp outcomes vs college degree apprenticeships return on investment earnings"
8. "age earnings profile college graduates lifetime earnings growth trajectory education level"

**Round 3:**
9. "registered apprenticeship outcomes earnings vs college degree trade school ROI United States"
10. "STARs skilled through alternative routes Opportunity@Work degree requirements hiring research"
11. "college wage premium by industry STEM degree value 2023 2024"

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

---

### 1. EMPLOYMENT RATES — UNEMPLOYMENT RATES FOR BACHELOR'S DEGREE HOLDERS VS. HIGH SCHOOL GRADUATES (BLS DATA, 2016–2026)

#### 1.1 April 2026 — BLS The Economics Daily ("Unemployment rate remains lower for people with more education")

- "In April 2026, the unemployment rate was 2.8 percent for people with a bachelor's degree and higher, compared with 3.2 percent for people with some college or an associate degree, 4.7 percent for high school graduates, and 6.4 percent for those without a high school diploma."
- "The unemployment rate was unchanged at 4.3 percent in April, and the number of unemployed people changed little at 7.4 million."
- "Unemployment rates for adults age 25 and older remained lower for people with more education."
- "Data for October 2025 were not collected due to the federal government shutdown." January 2026 estimates were revised to incorporate updated population controls.
- The data spans from April 2006 to April 2026, sourced from the Current Population Survey.
- A notable spike occurred during the COVID-19 pandemic (April 2020: 21.2% for those without a high school diploma, 8.4% for bachelor's degree holders).

#### 1.2 FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis) — Unemployment Rate, High School Graduates, No College, 25 Yrs. & over (Series LNS14027660)

- Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Population Survey (Household Survey), from the Employment Situation release.
- Key data points: **Jul 2026: 4.0%; Jun 2026: 4.2%; May 2026: 4.4%; Apr 2026: 4.7%; Mar 2026: 4.7%.**
- The data shows a declining trend from March to July 2026, dropping from 4.7% to 4.0%.
- Monthly, seasonally adjusted series; most recent update August 7, 2026; next release September 4, 2026.

#### 1.3 January 2025 — BLS The Economics Daily ("Unemployment 4.5 percent for high school grads with no college in January 2025")

- "In January 2025, the unemployment rate for people 25 years and older who were high school graduates with no college was 4.5 percent. Those with less than a high school diploma had an unemployment rate of 5.2 percent. The unemployment rate for people with some college or an associate degree was 3.5 percent. Those with a bachelor's degree or higher had the lowest unemployment rate, 2.3 percent."
- "A year earlier, in January 2024, unemployment rates were 4.3 percent for high school graduates and 2.1 percent for those with at least a bachelor's degree."
- "Since 2000, some of the lowest unemployment rates for high school graduates with no college were 3.3 percent (in March and April 2000 and July 2023); some of the lowest rates for people with bachelor's degrees or higher were 1.5 percent (in April, November and December 2000)."
- COVID-19 pandemic spike (April 2020): 21.2% for those without a high school diploma, 17.7% for high school graduates, 15.5% for some college, and 8.4% for bachelor's degree holders.
- The article includes a comprehensive monthly table of seasonally adjusted unemployment rates from January 2000 to January 2025.

#### 1.4 BLS Table A-4 — Employment status of the civilian population 25 years and over by educational attainment (June 2026)

**Not seasonally adjusted:**
- Less than a high school diploma: Labor force 8,516 (thousands); participation rate 44.2%; unemployment rate 4.7%
- High school graduates, no college: Labor force 36,683; participation rate 56.3%; unemployment rate 4.0%
- Some college or associate degree: Labor force 35,227; participation rate 61.0%; unemployment rate 3.6%
- Bachelor's degree and higher: Labor force 66,347; participation rate 71.1%; unemployment rate 2.8%

**Seasonally adjusted:**
- Less than high school: 5.5%; High school: 4.2%; Some college: 3.6%; Bachelor's+: 2.7%

- "The data shows a clear inverse relationship between educational attainment and unemployment rates, with higher education levels corresponding to lower unemployment and higher labor force participation rates."

#### 1.5 Wooclap blog ("Unemployment rate for college graduates: Key statistics [2025]")

- "2.5% — that's the unemployment rate for college graduates aged 25 and older in the United States today."
- Recent graduates aged 22-27 face 5.3% unemployment, more than double the rate for all college graduates and higher than the overall U.S. labor force rate of 4.0%.
- High school graduates: 4.2%; those without a diploma: 6.2%.
- Evolution over the past decade: graduate unemployment fell from 4.7% (post-2009) to 2.1% by 2018, spiked to 8% during COVID, recovered to 2.0% in 2023, then rose to 4.5% by 2025.
- "Only 27% of bachelor's degree holders work in jobs that closely match their major, with 40-45% of graduates reporting a complete mismatch between their field of study and their career."
- "Computer Science and Computer Engineering graduates face unexpectedly high unemployment at 6.1% and 7.5% respectively, challenging assumptions about STEM superiority in the job market."
- Female recent graduates experience 16.1% unemployment compared to 13.8% for males.
- "Only 13% of graduates are ready to start jobs immediately upon graduation, according to industry surveys, highlighting a critical skills mismatch between education and employer needs."
- Field of study variation ranges from 1.0% unemployment (Animal Sciences) to 7.5% (Computer Engineering).
- Regional disparities: rural graduates earn $42,400 vs $52,100 in metro areas.
- "Big Tech firms cut new graduate hiring by 25% in 2024."
- Globally: OECD nations average 86% employment for bachelor's holders; the EU maintains 82.3% graduate employment; high-performers like Australia (1.7% unemployment) and Japan (97.3% employment offer rate) achieve strong outcomes; India's graduate unemployment reached 28.7% in 2022.

#### 1.6 NCES Fast Facts (Employment rates of young adults, ages 25–34)

- "In 2023, some 80 percent of 25- to 34-year-olds were employed. The employment rate was higher for those with higher levels of educational attainment... highest for those with a bachelor's or higher degree (88 percent); and lowest for those who had not completed high school (60 percent)."
- "The overall employment rate was higher for 25- to 34-year-old males (85 percent) than for their female peers (76 percent) in 2023."
- "The gender gap was smallest for those with a bachelor's or higher degree (6 percentage points); and largest for those who had not completed high school (31 percentage points)."
- Female employment: highest among those with a bachelor's or higher (85%), lowest among those without high school completion (42%).
- "From 2013 to 2019 (i.e., prior to the coronavirus pandemic), overall employment for 25- to 34-year-olds increased from 75 percent in 2013 to 79 percent in 2019. During the pandemic—from 2020 through 2023—overall employment for 25- to 34-year-olds was lowest in 2021 (76 percent)."
- "At each level of educational attainment, the employment rates for 25- to 34-year-olds in 2023 were higher than the rates in 2021 and not measurably different from the rates in 2019, the year immediately before the pandemic." Example: for high school completers, rates were 74% in 2019, 68% in 2021, and 74% in 2023.

#### 1.7 College Board — Education Pays 2026 (newsroom release, April 14, 2026)

- Four-year college graduates earn about **60% more** than high school graduates — "a wage premium that has been stable for decades."
- "In 2025, unemployment among young adults ages 25–34 was 3.1% for college graduates versus 5.8% for those without a degree."
- "Only 4% of college graduates live in poverty compared to 13% of high school graduates."
- "The typical graduate recoups the cost of a degree by their mid-30s."
- Earnings vary by major — from about $44,000 for performing arts graduates to over $80,000 for mechanical engineering and computer science graduates.
- "Completion matters, informed choices matter"; college graduates report better health outcomes and higher civic engagement.
- Quotes: "A college degree is one of the largest investments most families make, and students and families are right to ask what they can expect in return," said Jessica Howell, vice president of research at the College Board. "The data show that education remains a powerful driver of opportunity, but there are differences in outcomes. The question isn't just whether education pays—it's which pathways lead to the strongest outcomes." "Education Pays 2026 highlights the strong economic and social benefits associated with postsecondary education," said Matea Pender, senior research scientist at the College Board and lead author. "At the same time, changing public views of higher education and rapid technological advances are reshaping the landscape."

#### 1.8 BLS Career Outlook — "Education pays, 2020" (2020 data, workers age 25+, full-time wage/salary workers)

**2020 median weekly earnings and unemployment rates by education:**
- Doctoral degree: $1,885/week; 2.5% unemployment
- Professional degree: $1,893; 3.1%
- Master's degree: $1,545; 4.1%
- Bachelor's degree: $1,305; 5.5%
- Associate degree: $938; 7.1%
- Some college, no degree: $877; 8.3%
- High school diploma, no college: $781; 9.0%
- Less than high school: $619; 11.7%

- "Unemployment rates were higher in 2020 than 2019 at all education levels due to pandemic job losses. Weekly earnings rose at all levels, though partly because lower-paid workers were more likely to lose jobs in 2020, pushing up earnings estimates."
- "Even in the best of economic times, data show that workers who have higher levels of education typically earn more and have lower rates of unemployment compared with workers who have less education. In the challenging economy created by the COVID-19 pandemic, the data tell a similar story."

---

### 2. UNDEREMPLOYMENT RATES

#### 2.1 Burning Glass Institute / Strada Education Foundation — "Talent Disrupted: College Graduates, Underemployment, and the Way Forward"

- "Today, only about half of bachelor's degree graduates secure employment in a college-level job within a year of graduation."
- "One of the biggest risks students face is that their degree will not provide access to a college-level job."
- "While a college education is still worth it for the typical graduate, it is not a guarantee: college students face an increasing degree of risk."
- The study tracked over 10 million career paths from the past decade (online career histories of tens of millions of graduates plus census microdata for millions more), examining underemployment rates, lost earnings, and associated factors over the first decade post-graduation.
- Key variables analyzed: degree field, student demographics (race/ethnicity and gender), institutional characteristics (selectivity, low-income student concentration, type), and internship participation.
- Authors: Andrew Hanson, Carlo Salerno, Matt Sigelman, Mels de Zeeuw, and Stephen Moret.
- Associated WSJ-published findings: "nearly half of recent college graduates are underemployed, working in jobs that do not require a degree"; the study "emphasizes the importance of a graduate's first job and the significant role internships play in securing college-level employment"; "many graduates remain in roles that underutilize their skills, fueling the debate over the rising costs of higher education."

#### 2.2 St. Louis Fed Open Vault (August 13, 2025, by Heather Hennerich, featuring St. Louis Fed economic policy advisor Oksana Leukhina)

- More than half of college graduates (52%) are underemployed (working jobs that don't typically require a college degree) a year after graduation, per a 2024 report from The Burning Glass Institute and Strada Institute.
- Underemployment is highly persistent: "Seventy-nine percent of those who began with a college-level job were still in one 10 years after graduation... As much as 52% of college graduates are underemployed upon initial labor market entry. They are likely to stay that way—even 10 years after graduation, 45% of college graduates are underemployed."
- Underemployment cuts into the "college premium": "A typical recent college grad who holds a job that requires a college degree earns about 88% more than a typical high school graduate who never went to college, but a recent underemployed graduate makes only 25% more."
- "If you're a college grad and you are underemployed, you're basically making the same money as a college dropout on average." — Oksana Leukhina
- There is a "scarring" effect: "Maybe you get it because you didn't have some of the required skills, but then you're not going to gain them if you're just staying in that kind of job. And your résumé is going to reflect your job history. It's going to be really hard to get out of that." — Oksana Leukhina
- Majors with highest underemployment: Criminal justice (67.2%), Performing arts (62.3%), Medical technicians (57.9%), Liberal arts (56.5%), Anthropology (55.9%).
- Majors with lowest underemployment: Nursing (9.7%), Education (16.0%), Elementary education (16.1%), Computer science (16.5%), Chemical engineering (16.5%).
- However, underemployed college graduates may benefit from jobs with higher "intrinsic quality" (nonmonetary amenities like respectful treatment, variety, skill development). Even low-wage college graduates tend to occupy higher-intrinsic-value occupations such as librarians, curators, social workers, artists, and writers.

#### 2.3 Federal Reserve Bank of New York — "The Labor Market for Recent College Graduates"

- Latest update (2026:Q2): "Labor market conditions remained challenging for recent college graduates through the second quarter of 2026. The unemployment rate stayed elevated at about 5.6 percent, and the underemployment rate edged up to 42 percent."
- Underemployment is defined as "a college graduate working in a job that typically does not require a college degree," determined using the U.S. Department of Labor's O*NET Education and Training Questionnaire.
- Underemployment figures are calculated as a percentage of those holding a bachelor's degree or higher (including graduate and professional degree holders).
- Early-career graduates are those aged 22 to 27; mid-career graduates are aged 35 to 45.
- Data span from 1990 to the present; national measures; new unemployment/underemployment data posted quarterly (typically February, May, August, November); wages and outcome data released annually (typically February).
- "Outcomes by major" data cover only the most recent year available from the American Community Survey.
- Analysis framework described in: "Underemployment in the Early Careers of College Graduates following the Great Recession" (NBER) and "Are Recent College Graduates Finding Good Jobs?" (2014, New York Fed's Current Issues in Economics and Finance).

#### 2.4 Federal Reserve Bank of New York — LinkedIn post (2025:Q3 data)

- "The underemployment rate for recent college graduates rose to 41.8 percent in 2025:Q3—its highest level since 2020," while their unemployment rate stood at 5.3%.
- "This marks a reversal from pre-pandemic trends when underemployment hovered around 34%."
- "College graduates now comprise a record 25% of total U.S. unemployment."
- Drivers: slower white-collar hiring and a mismatch between degrees in humanities/social sciences and available roles in tech and trades.
- Guy Berger, Ph.D.: "TL;DR: 2025 was a bad year for young college and high school grads in the labor market... but it was associate degree holders that got hammered the hardest." Unemployment for college grads ages 20-24 rose from 6.43% (2024) to 7.18% (2025); for associate degree holders ages 20-24, it rose from 4.37% to 5.50%.
- The National Association of Colleges and Employers reported that average starting salaries for bachelor's and doctoral degree graduates of the Class of 2024 rose noticeably, while master's-level salaries remained flat.
- Cleveland Fed (shared by Esther Landin): "For decades, college graduates have typically faced lower unemployment rates, found jobs faster, and experienced more stable employment... However, some of the long-standing job market advantages offered by having a college degree may be eroding."
- Bain & Company: "71% of US employers say they can't find the talent that they need, yet the youth unemployment rate was more than double the overall unemployment rate in July."

#### 2.5 Marketplace / Burning Glass Institute (August 6, 2025, by Melissa DiMarzio)

- "In society at large, managers have come to see a degree as a minimum ticket to ride," said Matt Sigelman, president of the Burning Glass Institute.
- According to the Federal Reserve Bank, in March 2025, the unemployment rate for college graduates aged 22–27 hit 5.8%, compared to the overall unemployment rate of 4.2% — "the largest disparity in over 30 years (excluding the pandemic spike in 2021)."
- "Since 2023, like 85% of the rise of the unemployment rate is concentrated in new market entrants," said Suzanne Kahn, vice president of Think Tank at the Roosevelt Institute. "And the rise in unemployment for college graduates has been like triple that of everybody else, which is just, I think, sort of unprecedented."
- Sigelman warned that 10 million new college graduates will enter the workforce over the next decade, but a study by the Burning Glass Institute found that 52% of graduates with only a bachelor's degree end up underemployed a year after graduation.
- Attribution of the phenomenon to degree inflation: "many jobs now require degrees not because the work is harder, but because more people have degrees."

#### 2.6 Braven memo (March 2021) — pre-COVID underemployment context

- Research by Burning Glass and Strada Institute shows that "those who are initially underemployed after graduation are 5x more likely to be underemployed after 5 years than those who were not initially underemployed. After 10 years, 75% of those still underemployed at the five-year mark remain underemployed."
- Underemployment rates (~40% of recent graduates in jobs not requiring their degree) remained higher than early 2000s levels even before COVID.
- Nearly half of women graduates are underemployed vs. 37% of men.
- "During the Great Recession, 56% of 2010 graduates held at least one job by spring 2011. Of those who did find work, only 52% said the job required their college degree. This would imply a 'quality jobs' rate of 27% 12 months after graduation."

---

### 3. JOB SECURITY — LAYOFF VULNERABILITY, JOB LOSS, AND RE-EMPLOYMENT SPEED

#### 3.1 Georgetown CEW — "The College Advantage: Weathering the Economic Storm" (Great Recession analysis; CPS data 2007–2012)

- "College has proved to be the best umbrella in this historic economic storm and the best preparation for the economy that is emerging in recovery."
- "Nearly four out of every five jobs destroyed by the recession were held by workers with a high school diploma or less."
- Workers with high school diplomas or less lost about 5.6 million jobs during the recession and an additional 230,000 jobs in recovery (net -5,841,000).
- Workers with Associate's degrees or some college lost 1.75 million jobs but regained 1.6 million.
- Workers with Bachelor's degrees or better gained 187,000 jobs during the recession and 2,012,000 more during recovery — a net gain of 2,199,000 jobs.
- Unemployment peaks: College graduate unemployment peaked at 6.3% during the recession, compared to 13.4% for high school graduates (peak in February 2010). New college graduate unemployment peaked at 11.1% in July 2011, while new high school graduate unemployment peaked at 30% in January 2010.
- May 2012 snapshot: 4.5% unemployment for all four-year college graduates; 6.8% for recent college graduates (ages 21-25); ~24% for recent high school graduates.
- Underemployment (May 2012): 8.4% for four-year college graduates vs. 17.3% for high school graduates. One out of seven new college graduates was underemployed vs. nearly half of new high school graduates.
- The college earnings premium stood at 97% (college graduates earn nearly twice as much as high school graduates).
- Industry impacts: In manufacturing, employment dropped 19% for those with a high school diploma or less but only 9% for those with Bachelor's degrees or better. In construction, employment dropped 24% for high school diploma holders versus 4% for college graduates.
- Manufacturing and construction accounted for nearly 5.2 million of the 7.2 million jobs lost; wholesale and retail trade added another 1 million in losses. Industries with high concentrations of college-educated workers (public administration, education, healthcare) held up relatively well, adding 1.5 million jobs.
- Gender impacts: Men with Bachelor's degrees lost nearly 200,000 jobs in the recession, but gains by college-educated women more than offset those losses. Women with a high school diploma or less lost 2 million jobs, while men with high school diplomas or less lost 3.6 million. Two out of every three jobs lost by men were in construction and manufacturing.
- Long-term structural trends: Since 1989, employment growth has been driven entirely by workers with education beyond high school. The number of workers with a high school diploma as their highest attainment dropped by 14% from 1989 to 2012, while workers with some college or an Associate's degree increased 40% and workers with Bachelor's degrees or better nearly doubled.
- Drivers: labor-saving technology (especially computing), automation of routine tasks, and globalization/offshoring of low-skilled jobs. Manufacturing shed 5.5 million jobs from 1980 to 2007 while healthcare and education added 11.6 million jobs.
- Postsecondary enrollment grew by 7% in 2009 (after 1% growth in 2005) as workers sought shelter from the weak labor market, though growth slowed to 3% in 2010.

#### 3.2 Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland — Economic Commentary EC 2025-14 (November 24, 2025), "Are Young College Graduates Losing Their Edge in the Job Market?" (Alexander Cline and Barış Kaymak)

- Using CPS panel data spanning 1976–2025 for respondents aged 22–27, the authors find "the unemployment gap between young high school and college graduates has narrowed to its lowest level since the late 1970s—currently 2.5 percentage points (as of July 2025, near the March 2024 all-time low of 2.4 percentage points)."
- "The narrowing gap reflects two contrasting developments: young high school workers benefit from the historically tight postpandemic labor market, while young college workers face unemployment rates rarely seen outside recessions."
- "The primary driver is a secular decline in the job-finding rate among young college graduates that began around 2000. College graduate job-finding rates trended upward from 1976 to 2000, then declined sharply."
- "By around 2019, the job-finding rates of the two education groups converged, ending a long period of relatively easier job-finding prospects for college graduates."
- Historically (1976–2000), high school graduates had lower unemployment exit rates (41.2% vs. 47.0%) and higher entry rates (3.9% vs. 1.8%). This has reversed: high school graduates now exit unemployment faster than college graduates (41.5% vs. 37.1%), with nearly a 10 percentage point decline in college graduates' exit rate.
- Discouragement rates (leaving the labor force) show no differential trends between the groups, indicating the exit-rate reversal is driven by job-finding, not discouragement.
- Entry rates into unemployment remain stable, with high school graduates' entry rates still above college graduates' rates, meaning college graduates retain advantages in job stability and compensation once hired.
- Methods: monthly employment-status transitions from CPS panel data, plus Shimer's (2005) duration-based approach. Context: AI automation of entry-level positions and persistent earnings effects of poor early-career outcomes (citing Kahn 2010; Oreopoulos, von Wachter, and Heisz 2012).
- Headline quote: "For decades, college graduates have typically faced lower unemployment rates, found jobs faster, and experienced more stable employment than high school graduates without college experience... However, some of the long-standing job market advantages offered by having a college degree may be eroding."

#### 3.3 Academic research — Brand, Jennie E., "The Far-Reaching Impact of Job Loss and Unemployment," Annual Review of Sociology (published online February 11, 2015)

- "Job loss is an involuntary disruptive life event with a far-reaching impact on workers' life trajectories... Research suggests that displacement is associated with subsequent unemployment, long-term earnings losses, and lower job quality; declines in psychological and physical well-being; loss of psychosocial assets; social withdrawal; family disruption; and lower levels of children's attainment and well-being."
- Displacement has become common due to technological change, offshoring, immigration, outsourcing, weakened labor unions, and economic downturns. The Great Recession (2007-2009) was the deepest since the Great Depression, with unemployment reaching 9-10% in 2009-2011 (roughly twice the pre-crisis rate).
- Risk factors for displacement: being male, black/Hispanic, less educated, blue-collar/manufacturing workers, and those with low job tenure — though risks increased for women, whites, and college-educated workers in the 1990s.
- Economic effects: Displaced workers face an immediate 33% earnings loss and up to 15% loss six years after separation (Couch and Placzek 2010). Cumulative lifetime earnings loss is roughly 20%, with "wage scarring" lasting up to 20 years post-displacement. Reemployed workers more often find part-time work with lower job quality.
- Losses are cyclical: men displaced in mass layoffs when unemployment is below 6% lose 1.4 years of pre-displacement earnings, versus 2.8 years when unemployment exceeds 8% (Davis and von Wachter 2012).
- Older workers, those with high tenure, industry-changers, and the less-educated suffer greater losses.
- Psychological effects: displaced workers report 15-30% higher rates of depressive symptoms and anxiety; loss of psychosocial assets (self-esteem, life satisfaction, sense of control). Reemployment mitigates but does not eliminate these effects, particularly for professionals/white-collar workers. A "social norm effect" means contexts of widespread unemployment lessen the social-psychological impact, though economic losses are larger during recessions.
- Physical effects: job loss is linked to worse self-rated health, cardiovascular disease, increased hospitalization, higher use of disability benefits, increased suicide, and mortality. Gallo et al. found job loss doubled the risk of myocardial infarction and stroke among older workers. Sullivan and von Wachter (2009) found a 50-100% increase in mortality the year following displacement and a 10-15% increase over the next 20 years.
- Family effects: Layoffs (but not plant closings) increase divorce risk (Charles and Stephens 2004). Parental displacement negatively affects children's self-esteem, educational attainment, grade repetition, dropout, and adult income.
- Methodology note: job loss is treated as a "natural experiment" enabling stronger causal inference; plant closure studies offer stronger internal validity but limited generalizability.

---

### 4. PROMOTION, CAREER ADVANCEMENT, AND "DEGREE CREEP"

#### 4.1 Harvard Business School — "Dismissed by Degrees" (October 25, 2017; HBS, Accenture, and Grads of Life)

- Analyzed 26 million job postings and surveyed 600 business and HR leaders to document "degree inflation" — requiring a four-year college degree for middle-skills jobs that previously did not require one.
- "Over 6 million middle-skills jobs in the U.S. are at risk of degree inflation."
- "In 2015, for example, 67 percent of production supervisor job postings asked for a college degree, while only 16 percent of people employed in that role had one—a 'degree gap' of 51 percent."
- Two-thirds of employers agree that requiring a bachelor's degree for a middle-skills job makes it harder to fill.
- Three in five employers reject qualified middle-skill candidates with relevant experience in favor of recent college graduates.
- Half of employers pay higher compensation to recent college graduates (11-30% more) than non-degree workers in the same job, yet degreed workers are more likely to leave.
- Employers generally perceive degreed and non-degreed workers as nearly equally productive.
- "Degree inflation is corrosive to U.S. competitiveness in two ways. It slams the door of opportunity in the face of Americans with the experience to do a job or the aptitude to grow into it. It simultaneously makes it harder for American companies to find and retain affordable talent," said Harvard Business School Professor of Management Practice Joseph B. Fuller.
- "While talent may be equally distributed, opportunity in this country is not," said Gerald Chertavian, CEO and Founder of Year Up and Principal of Grads of Life.
- Report recommendations: (1) identify middle-skills occupations prone to degree inflation, (2) explore alternative proxies to a college degree, (3) evaluate hidden costs of hiring degreed vs. non-degreed workers, and (4) invest in strategies to attract and retain workers with the right competencies rather than depending on credentials alone.
- Grads of Life describes the phenomenon as one that "not only harms U.S. businesses, it closes off critical career pathways and excludes millions of Americans from securing gainful employment." Full report title: "Dismissed by Degrees: How degree inflation is undermining U.S. competitiveness and hurting America's middle class."

#### 4.2 Harvard Business School — follow-up study on skills-based hiring (Institute for Business in Global Society; Joseph Fuller)

- Examined more than 11,000 job postings at U.S. firms from 2014 to 2023.
- While many major companies (including Apple, Walmart, GM, and Target) and over 20 state governments have eliminated degree requirements, hiring of non-degree candidates increased by only 3.5 percentage points overall. When accounting for the small number of jobs where requirements were actually dropped, the increase falls to less than a percentage point — "fewer than 1 in 700 new hires benefited from these reforms."
- Almost all changes occurred in just 37% of companies examined.
- At companies successfully implementing skills-based hiring, non-degree hires showed 10 percentage points higher retention rates and saw average salary increases of 25% when hired into roles that previously required degrees.
- "We found measurable but pretty modest changes, and that some companies have done better than others," said Joseph Fuller. "But overall, removing the barrier that a post-secondary degree poses to hiring more broadly will take a lot of doing."
- "When viewed from the vantage point of job postings, skills-based hiring seems to be a juggernaut," the study said. "However, a deeper analysis of actual hiring patterns suggests a wide gap between intent and impact. Simply dropping stated requirements seldom opens jobs to those who don't have a college degree."
- "Changing your hiring policy is, at best, the end of the beginning," Fuller said. "Or maybe it's just a plain old beginning if you are aiming to accomplish, frankly, something more than virtue washing."
- "Stripping out the artificial constraints of gratuitous requirements both eases recruitment burdens in a tight labor market and substantially increases worker retention – all while creating substantial opportunity and mobility for workers."
- Recommendations: (1) train hiring managers to evaluate candidates based on skills and experience; (2) give managers confidence to take perceived risks on non-degree candidates; (3) support non-traditional hires after onboarding; (4) recognize that cultural change takes time.

#### 4.3 Harvard Business School — "The Emerging Degree Reset" (white paper; Joseph B. Fuller and colleagues)

- Examines the emerging trend of employers dropping bachelor's degree requirements in many middle-skill and even some higher-skill roles, reversing the long-term "degree inflation" trend dating back to the Great Recession.
- "Some 46% of middle-skill and 31% of high-skill occupations experienced material degree resets between 2017 and 2019."
- "Only 27% of the changing occupations could be considered 'cyclical resets,' or short-term responses to the pandemic. The majority (63%) appear to be 'structural resets' that began before the pandemic, representing a measured and potentially permanent shift in hiring practices."
- "When employers drop degrees, they become more specific about skills in job postings, spelling out the soft skills that may have been assumed to come with a college education, such as writing, communication, and being detail-oriented."
- "Based on these trends, we project that an additional 1.4 million jobs could open to workers without college degrees over the next five years."
- The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the shift, but the reset began before the crisis.

#### 4.4 Opportunity@Work — STARs and the "paper ceiling"

- STARs = "Skilled Through Alternative Routes": working adults who have a high school diploma but do not have a bachelor's degree.
- Over 70 million American workers (approximately 50% of all U.S. workers) are STARs.
- "Over the past 20 years, STARs have been denied access to almost 7.5 million middle- and high-wage jobs that were once open to them" (the "paper ceiling").
- "The wage gap between STARs and workers with bachelor's degrees has doubled over the last 40 years, with STARs' wages actually declining since 1976."
- "It takes STARs more than 30 years of work experience to earn what a college graduate earns on day 1 of their career."
- STARs are segmented into: 2.8 million "Shining STARs" (work in high-wage jobs despite barriers); 31.9 million "Rising STARs" (low- and middle-wage jobs but have skills for higher-wage categories); 41.4 million "Forming STARs" (low- and middle-wage jobs with limited pathways). (The Learn & Work Ecosystem Library cites slightly different figures: 4 million Shining, 32 million Rising, 35 million Forming, based on the "Reach for the STARs" report.)
- By demographic: 61% of Veteran workers are STARs; 66% of workers in rural areas; 50% of women workers; 51% of White workers, 62% of Black workers, 54% of Hispanic workers, 28% of AAPI workers, and 70% of Native American workers.
- Research shows millions of STARs have demonstrated skills for jobs that would pay at least 50% higher than their current job.
- Wikipedia summary: STARs comprised approximately 70 million U.S. workers as of 2021; the term was first defined in a 2020 NBER research paper by Peter Q. Blair. The majority of American workers (approximately 64% as of 2020) do not have a four-year bachelor's degree, including 68% of Black workers and 79% of Hispanic workers. Research from December 2020 indicates that 30 million STARs have the skills to earn 70% more than their current wages. However, 60% of STARs who changed jobs over the past decade transitioned to new positions with the same or lower wages.
- Press release findings ("State of the Paper Ceiling"): Between 2000-2020, nearly 7.5 million jobs previously available to STARs became inaccessible as over 70% of new roles added to the labor market required degrees. STARs have regained nearly 10% of those middle- and high-wage jobs (more than 750,000 jobs since 2020), with potential to access 10 million more roles by 2030 if skills-first hiring becomes the norm. 38% of employers now recognize the Tear the Paper Ceiling campaign (up 43% since 2022), with 83% of those employers more likely to hire skilled workers without bachelor's degrees. 15% of STARs now identify with the term, with 72% feeling confident applying for degree-requiring jobs when they have relevant skills. The Tear the Paper Ceiling Coalition and STARs Public Sector Hub have collectively opened over 500,000 middle- and high-wage jobs to STARs since 2022. Quote from CEO Byron Auguste: "This report shows what is possible when awareness and behavior change together: job postings are measurably more open to STARs than in the early 2000s. Skills-first hiring isn't a theory—it's starting to work where and when it is fully embraced."
- Tear the Paper Ceiling site: skills content for nearly 900 U.S. occupations analyzed; "Over the last 30 years, the wage gap between STARs and bachelor's degree holders has doubled; adjusted for inflation, STARs now earn less on average than in 1976. A 2022 study found it takes STARs more than 30 years on the job to earn what college graduates earn on day one."
- Learn & Work Ecosystem Library: Stellarworx launched 2021 (talent matching platform powered by SkyHive AI), growing employer enrollment from 67 to 150 employers between 2021 and 2023 (124% increase), decommissioned October 2024 in anticipation of STARSight Connect (launched 2025). Tear the Paper Ceiling campaign launched Fall 2022 with the Ad Council and Ogilvy; Accenture, Chevron, and Google signed pledges. Opportunity@Work received a $20 million grant from Yield Giving (MacKenzie Scott's philanthropy) in July 2024.
