### 4. Social Mobility — Does College Act as an Equalizer?

**Chetty / Equality of Opportunity Project Findings**

- Brookings Institution (Reeves and Krause, January 11, 2018), "Raj Chetty in 14 charts": (1) Chances of moving from bottom to top income quintile are lower in the U.S. than in other nations like Canada. (2) There is a strong relationship between parents' incomes and their children's adult incomes—inequality is strongly inherited. (3) Relative intergenerational mobility rates in the U.S. have been flat for decades. (4) Absolute mobility has sharply declined—most Americans born in 1940 ended up better off than their parents, but only half of those born in 1980 did. (5) Place matters significantly for mobility, with cities in the Deep South and Midwest having more sluggish mobility. (6) Children who move from low-mobility to high-mobility areas do better, especially if they move early. (7) Housing vouchers that help families move to higher-opportunity areas significantly boost children's later earnings if moves occur before age 13. (8) There is a gender gap—boys growing up in low-opportunity places feel effects more strongly than girls. (9) Childhood poverty damages outcomes for boys more than girls. (10) Experienced kindergarten teachers boost earnings by $1,104 on average. (11) **College education acts as a leveler, reducing the correlation between parents' income and children's adult incomes.** (12) **However, college attendance is strongly related to household income, making higher education a "great stratifier" in practice.** (13) Inventors are much more likely to have been raised in affluent families. (14) Poverty takes nearly 10 years off men's lifespan from age 40. Conclusion: "The bad news is that there are very high, structural barriers to social mobility in the U.S. The good news is that these barriers are not insurmountable, and can be lowered through the sustained application of good policies." [50]

- Raj Chetty lecture (Dartmouth, May 8, 2023; also Berkeley Hitchcock Lectures, October 25–26, 2023; and YouTube "Can Data Rebuild the American Dream?"): Children's chances of earning more than their parents have fallen from 90% to 50% over the past half century in America (92% of children born in 1940 earned more than their parents; today only about 50% do). "Economic connectedness"—the fraction of high-income friends that low-income people have, measured via Facebook data of 72 million people—"turns out to be the single strongest predictor of upward economic mobility that we or anybody else has identified." Three policy approaches: (1) reducing segregation by helping families move to higher-opportunity areas through better housing voucher design; (2) place-based investment in struggling communities; (3) improving access to higher education, noting that few colleges both enroll many low-income students and offer strong earnings outcomes. [51][52][53]

**Mobility Report Cards — The Role of Colleges**

- Chetty, Friedman, Saez, Turner, and Yagan, "Mobility Report Cards: The Role of Colleges in Intergenerational Mobility" (NBER Working Paper No. 23618; administrative data on over 30 million college students from 1999–2013): (1) Children from the top 1% of the income distribution are 77 times more likely to attend an Ivy League college than those from the bottom income quintile. (2) Children from low- and high-income families have similar earnings outcomes conditional on the college they attend, indicating that low-income students are not mismatched at selective colleges. (3) Rates of bottom-to-top quintile mobility are highest at certain mid-tier public universities, such as the City University of New York and California State colleges; rates of upper-tail (bottom quintile to top 1%) mobility are highest at elite colleges, such as Ivy League universities. (4) The fraction of students from low-income families did not change substantially between 2000–2011 at elite private colleges but fell sharply at colleges with the highest rates of bottom-to-top-quintile mobility. The study is descriptive and does not identify causal effects. [54][55]

- NBER Digest summary of the same paper: "The degree of income segregation across colleges is comparable to the degree of income segregation across neighborhoods in the average American city." Case study: At Columbia, 5% of students came from the bottom quintile and 61% of those reached the top quintile (3.1% mobility rate). At SUNY Stony Brook, 16.4% came from the lowest quintile and 51% reached the top quintile (8.4% mobility rate). For reaching the top 1% of earnings, Columbia far outperformed: 15% of bottom-quintile students reached the top 1% versus only 2% at Stony Brook. Mean instructional expenditure at Ivy-plus colleges is $54,000 per student versus $8,000 at colleges ranked in the top 10% by mobility rate. [56]

**Low-Income / First-Generation Student Outcomes**

- Pell Institute, "Moving Beyond Access – College Success for Low-Income, First-Generation Students" (Dr. Jennifer Engle with Dr. Vincent Tinto): Examines how the combined impact of being both low-income and first-generation correlates with a range of factors that lower the students' chances of successfully earning a college degree. Students who are both low-income and the first in their families to attend college face the greatest risk of failure in post-secondary education. Using U.S. Department of Education data, the report covers how these students participate in higher education (persistence and degree attainment rates), barriers they face, strategies colleges can pursue, and recommendations for institutional and government actions. [57][58]

- American Sociological Association Footnotes (Kristen A. Renn, Vol. 50, Issue 2), "Low-Income, First-Generation College Students": As of 2015–2016, 56 percent of all undergraduates were first-generation (neither parent held a bachelor's degree); about half of first-generation students are also from low-income families. **Only 11 percent of low-income, first-generation students—compared to 55 percent of continuing-generation students—had earned a bachelor's degree within six years of enrolling.** Median adjusted household income: $99,600 for first-generation degree holders vs. $135,800 for second-generation degree holders. Median household wealth: $152,000 for first-generation vs. $244,500 for continuing-generation households. 66 percent of first-generation graduates incurred education debt vs. 56 percent of peers. The article frames higher education as both "an engine of social mobility and a machine of social reproduction." Chetty's "mobility report cards" show highest mobility rates at less selective public institutions with many low-income students and good graduate outcomes. The #RealCollege movement emphasizes that most LIFG students attend community colleges and public comprehensives. [59]

- Pell Institute Research Briefs: High school students' aspirations to earn a bachelor's degree have fallen to their lowest point in two decades. In 2022, only 44% of students expected to complete a four-year degree, down from 72% in 2002—a 28-point decline. Among first-generation students, expectations fell even more steeply, from 60% in 2002 to 33% in 2022. Among students with at least one parent holding a bachelor's degree, expectations fell from 83% to 53%. The share of students reporting they "did not know" their expected education level nearly tripled, from 10% in 2002 to 27% in 2022. Data drawn from NCES Secondary Longitudinal Studies Program (Education Longitudinal Study of 2002, High School Longitudinal Study of 2009, and High School and Beyond Study of 2022). [60]

- Pell Institute blog, "Centering First-Generation Voices: Lessons from TRIO Students" (April 26, 2025): Highlights how higher education transforms the lives of first-generation students through economic stability, career advancement, and personal growth. Student-identified solutions: removing financial barriers, expanding academic and career support (paid internships, mentorship), creating supportive identity-based communities, and increasing faculty/staff diversity. [61]

- NBER Working Paper No. 33921 (Barr and Castleman, June 2025), "Increasing Degree Attainment Among Low-Income Students": RCT of the Bottom Line (BL) college advising program (Boston, Worcester, NYC, Chicago; 2,422 students from classes of 2015 and 2016). Students randomly offered intensive advising were 7.6 percentage points more likely to earn a bachelor's degree within five years of high school (a 16% increase relative to the control group mean of 47.1%). For the first cohort, students were 9.6 percentage points more likely to earn a bachelor's degree within six years. Effects were largest among students with "suboptimal" baseline college preferences. Shifts in college quality account for roughly 70% of the advising effect. BL advising increases bachelor's degree attainment by over two percentage points per $1,000 spent—more cost-effective than most rigorously-evaluated financial aid programs (less than 0.5–1.0 percentage points per $1,000). Context: only 1 in 10 low-income students obtain a bachelor's degree by age 25, versus half of those from high-income families; the average public high school counselor has roughly 300 students on their caseload and spends less than 19% of time on college counseling. [62]

**Elite Colleges and Upward Mobility (International Evidence)**

- NBER Working Paper No. 22900 (Seth D. Zimmerman), "Elite Colleges and Upward Mobility to Top Income Positions" (Chilean data): The 1.8% of college students admitted to elite business programs account for 41% of leadership positions, 39% of top 0.1% incomes, and 45% of top 0.01% incomes. Admission raises leadership positions by 44% and probability of attaining top 0.1% income by 51% overall, but gains accrue only to male applicants from high-tuition private high schools (54% increase in leadership, 69% in top incomes); effects for women and other male students are indistinguishable from zero. Peer ties formed between similar-background classmates appear to drive the effects. Elite medical programs show large returns for women and low-SES men, contrasting sharply with business programs. [63]

- NBER Working Paper No. 31737, "Elite Colleges as Engines of Upward Mobility: Evidence from Colombia's Ser Pilo Paga" (SPP program, ~40,000 students 2014–2018): SPP increased immediate college enrollment by 28.7 p.p. (69.5%), likelihood of attending a high-quality college by 43.7 p.p. (241%), and bachelor's degree attainment from HQ colleges by 32.3 p.p. (330%). Nine years post-high school, monthly earnings were ~18 log points higher—among the largest effects in the literature—with greater likelihood of being in the top 25% and top 1% of the earnings distribution. The policy eliminated the SES gap in B.A. attainment, college quality, skills, and returns to ability among equally-achieving students. No adverse impacts on aid-ineligible students. Marginal value of public funds estimated at 5.2 (test-score cutoff) and 3.4 (poverty cutoff). [64]

### 5. Networking and Social Capital — Alumni Networks, Peer Effects, and Professional Connections

**The Value of Alumni Networks**

- Christensen Institute report (Freeland Fisher and Price, February 2021), "Alumni Networks Reimagined": Only 9% of college graduates reported their alumni network was helpful or very helpful in the job market (Strada-Gallup Alumni Survey)—the "9% problem." The report identifies four roles alumni can play: (1) mentors for student success and persistence; (2) sources of career advice and referrals; (3) providers of experiential learning and client projects; and (4) staff for program delivery. Key innovations include Firsthand, Mentor Collective, PeopleGrove, Parker Dewey (micro-internships), Riipen, and programs like COOP, Basta, and Climb Hire. Colby College's "Pay It Northward" generated 700+ opportunities for the Class of 2020 during the pandemic, achieving a 90% job placement rate. **"Access to relationships had the single greatest effect on graduates' belief that their education was 'worth the cost'" (Gallup-Purdue Index Study, 2015).** "Advancement offices are money-makers... Offices focused on job placement, on the other hand, get sub-$100,000 budgets and are often relegated to a distant corner of campus." (Troy Williams, University Ventures). Institutions focus on mining alumni financial capital but fail to activate their social capital. In an outcomes-based postsecondary market focused on employment and ROI, students' access to networks will likely matter more. [65][66]

- Blackbaud blog (February 18, 2026), "Part 1: Closing the Social Capital Gap in Higher Ed" (Ryan Stoner, co-founder of Mentor Spaces): Social capital (relationships, networks, and informal guidance) is as influential as academic preparation for persistence, employment, and economic mobility. Economists Raj Chetty and colleagues at Opportunity Insights have demonstrated that cross-class connections are among the strongest predictors of upward mobility. A majority of college students report graduating without a functional professional network. Effective mentorship programs share four evidence-based characteristics: intentional structure, consistency, belonging-centered design, and guided agency. Alumni mentors report stronger emotional connections to their alma mater; mentorship often reactivates previously disengaged alumni. "Financial aid removes barriers to access—but without intentional access to networks and guidance, many scholarship recipients still lack the social capital needed to fully leverage their education." [67]

- Gallup Alumni Survey (formerly Gallup-Purdue Index): 50% of all alumni "strongly agree" their university education was worth the cost. **College graduates are almost 2X more likely to be engaged at work if they had a mentor who encouraged them to pursue their goals and dreams. Graduates are 1.4 times more likely to be thriving in five key elements of well-being if a professor cared about them as a person.** Gallup benchmarks against a nationally representative study of 95,000 college graduates. [68]

- Related Gallup findings: Only 9% of graduates find their online alumni network helpful in the job market, and only 31% "strongly agree" their university education was worth the cost (per 360alumni summary of Gallup report). Gallup-Purdue Index found that alumni who had caring professors, encouraging mentors, and meaningful internships were more likely to report stronger workplace engagement and well-being. Purdue survey found 79% of alumni working full-time for an employer, compared to 67% of public college graduates. [69][70][71][72]

- Princeton Review, "How to Leverage Your College Alumni Network": Alumni networks offer students a friendly introduction to networking, built on the shared connection of attending the same school. "In the end, networking comes down to building relationships, and you have something major in common: You both said 'yes' to the same school." Alumni can provide advice on career paths, entry-level jobs, and how college experiences prepared them for success. [73]

- Maria Gallo (Trinity College Dublin), "Global Alumni Networks and Social Class" (*Policy and Practice: A Development Education Review*, Spring 2025; 60 interviews across Czechia, Germany, Sweden, the UK, Denmark, and Ireland): Global alumni networks function as epistemic communities or "thought collectives," creating a new definition of social class for scholarship returnees to global South communities. Unlike traditional alumni networks focused on nostalgia and philanthropy, government-led networks motivate alumni toward voluntary civic action addressing the SDGs. Case studies: Germany's AlumniPortal Deutschland (oldest network, est. 2008, 120,000+ alumni), Sweden's Swedish Institute Alumni, Denmark's Danida Alumni Network, Czechia Alumni, the UK's Alumni UK, and Ireland's Kader Asmal Alumni. The 2024 research reveals a shift: networks increasingly offer career support and professional development, recognizing that supporting social class mobility enables alumni to become better advocates. "Global alumni networks create a cascade effect: offering lifelong support to alumni contributes to social class mobility, thus leading to the building of 'thinking communities' of active global alumni citizens." [74]

### 6. Life Satisfaction and Happiness — Subjective Well-Being and Education

- MSU Denver RED (spring 2024): Despite declining confidence in higher education (Gallup poll: 36% in 2023, down from 48% in 2018), evidence shows college graduates tend to be happier, healthier, and more prosperous. Aaron Richmond, Ph.D., MSU Denver psychology professor: "What we do see with education is you have fewer chronic worries, lower rates of depression and suicide and lower neuroticism." The 30–40 age range shows the strongest correlation between education and life satisfaction. Cynthia Erickson, Ph.D.: "What makes a difference is people feel like they have a professor who cares about them or who has engaged in some sort of project outside of class. Those people report higher levels of well-being in the workplace after they leave college." Student loan debt over $40,000 negatively impacts thriving. [75]

- Andersson (*Socius*, 2018, American Sociological Association), "Against All Odds or by Dint of Privilege? Happiness and Life Satisfaction Returns to College in the US" (General Social Survey 1972–2014): For women, happiness and life satisfaction gains from college are highest for those from disadvantaged backgrounds (resource substitution pattern), strongest for older women and earlier cohorts. For men, life satisfaction gains from college are highest for those from privileged backgrounds (cumulative disadvantage pattern), especially for younger men and recent cohorts; men showed no significant heterogeneity for happiness returns. Overall, college degree attainment was positively associated with subjective well-being for all groups. The author argues women face more limited opportunities, making college more pivotal for their well-being, especially when coming from disadvantaged families. For men, college may amplify existing advantages, particularly in recent decades with rising inequality. [76]

- Meta-analysis (*Frontiers in Psychology*, 2025; PMC), "The impact of education on subjective well-being: a meta-analysis based on 59 empirical studies" (185 effect sizes, 2012–2023): Educational level (r=0.709) and higher education participation (r=0.522) strongly influenced SWB, while lifelong learning engagement showed a moderate but significant positive association (r=0.406). The relationship was moderated by rural-urban factors and publication year. Conclusion: "Education should be emphasized continuously, and education equity ought to be improved further so that both rural and urban residents gain high levels of SWB in the future." [77]

- BMC Psychology (Volume 14, article 45, 2026), "Enhancing happiness and life satisfaction in university students: analysis with a machine learning approach" (China Family Panel Studies, 816 participants 2022 wave, 724 external validation 2020): Among university students, 15.9% reported low happiness and 28.9% reported low LS. Random Forest achieved best performance for happiness prediction (AUC = 0.831 test set, 0.741 external validation); XGBoost performed best for LS (AUC = 0.730 and 0.748). SHAP analysis revealed **interpersonal relationships were the strongest predictor of happiness, while future confidence was the top predictor of LS.** Shared predictors across both outcomes included future confidence, interpersonal relationships, depressive symptoms, and the relationship with mother. [78]

- Replicability-Index (Ulrich Schimmack, April 2025), "Subjective Indicators of Well-Being: Life Satisfaction": Life satisfaction is a subjective indicator in the normative sense—it allows individuals to evaluate their lives based on their own criteria. In contrast, positive affect (PA) and negative affect (NA) are rooted in hedonistic theories where well-being is defined by affective experience. "SWB is not a well-defined theoretical construct." The article recommends studying PA, NA, and LS separately rather than collapsing them into a composite score. "Life satisfaction is a valid indicator of happiness only under the assumption that happiness cannot be objectively defined and that people can generate meaningful, personal theories of well-being." [79]

### 7. Marriage and Family Outcomes — Education, Marriage Stability, Divorce, and Family Formation

**Divorce Gap by Education**

- BLS Monthly Labor Review (Aughinbaugh, Robles, and Sun; NLSY79 cohort born 1957–1964, tracked ages 15 to 46 through 2010): About 85% of the cohort married by age 46 (86.8% overall); among those who married, almost 30% married more than once. Approximately 42–44% of first marriages ended in divorce by age 46. **The "divorce gap" between college graduates and less-educated groups grew larger than in earlier cohorts. Over half of marriages of those who did not complete high school ended in divorce vs. approximately 30% for college graduates.** College-educated men and women married at older ages (26.5 average at first marriage for those with bachelor's+ vs. 22.7 for those with less than high school). Among the NLSY79 cohort, divorce among college graduates fell to 29.7% from 34.8% in earlier cohorts, while overall divorce rose to 44.8% from 40.8%. Men with bachelor's degrees were about 11 percentage points more likely to marry by 46 than men without high school diplomas; the gap for women was only ~4 percentage points. For men, college graduates' probability of divorce was ~25 percentage points lower than high school-only graduates; the difference was roughly half as large for women. About a quarter of college-educated men divorced vs. 35% of college-educated women. Marriage rates declined across cohorts: 93.1% of the 1940–1945 cohort married vs. 89.5% of 1950–1955 cohort vs. 86.8% of NLSY79 cohort. [80]

- Pew Research Center (Wendy Wang, December 4, 2015), "The link between a college education and a lasting marriage" (National Center for Health Statistics / National Survey of Family Growth, 2006–2010 data): About half of first marriages in the U.S. are likely to survive at least 20 years. **College-educated women have a 78% chance of a first marriage lasting at least 20 years, compared to only 40% for women with a high school education or less.** College-educated adults are more likely to be married overall: 65% of those with a bachelor's degree or more were married (2014, ages 25+), versus 53% of less-educated adults. College-educated men: 65% of men with bachelor's degrees could expect their first marriage to last 20+ years, versus 50% of men with a high school diploma or less. Possible reasons: college-educated adults marry later in life and are more financially secure. By race/ethnicity: Asian women have the highest chance of long-term marriage (nearly 70%), followed by about half of Hispanic and white women, and 37% for black women. Among men, Hispanics have the highest likelihood (62%), compared with 54% of white men and 53% of black men. [81]

- Kim McErlean (*Demographic Research*, 2021; NSFG 2006–2019 female data, first marriages of 6,356 women): **Overall marital dissolution and divorce rates are declining over time; however, this downward trend is driven entirely by those with higher education. Those with the least education are seeing rising marital dissolution rates, even when controlling for correlated risk factors.** The 5-year marital dissolution rate gap between the most and least educated grew from 12% (2000–2004 cohort) to 23% (2010–2014 cohort). The divorce rate gap (11%) is much smaller than the dissolution gap (23%), showing the least educated are more likely to informally separate rather than formally divorce. By the 2010–2014 cohort, college-educated women had a 70% lower dissolution risk than those without a high school degree. [82]

- Isen and Stevenson (NBER Working Paper No. 15725, February 2010), "Trends in Marriage, Divorce and Fertility": Historically, women with more education were the least likely to marry, but this marriage gap has eroded as the returns to marriage have changed. College-educated women now are about as likely to marry as those without a degree; college-educated black women are now the most likely to marry among blacks. The age of first marriage has risen for all, but especially for college-educated women: among white women with a college degree, ever-married rates at age 25 fell from 74% in 1970 to 36% in 2007 (vs. 90% in 1970 and 52% in 2007 for high school graduates). **"Both men and women with a college degree have been consistently less likely to divorce and have also experienced a larger decline in divorce probabilities in the last few decades."** Among college graduates marrying in the 1970s, 37% of female and 34% of male marriages ended in divorce within 20 years; rates for the 1980s cohort fell back to 1960s levels. College-educated women marry later, have fewer children, are less likely to view marriage as "financial security," are happier in their marriages and with their family life, and are not only the least likely to divorce, but have had the biggest decrease in divorce since the 1970s. Remarriage rates have fallen for all groups. Fertility declines with education; the delay in fertility is concentrated almost exclusively among college-educated women. [83]

- The Center for Divorce Education (2019 U.S. Census Bureau data): Divorce rates by education level: Bachelor's degree or higher: 25.9%; Associate's degree: 30.1%; Some college: 36.3%; High school diploma: 38.8%; Less than high school diploma: 45.3%. Nearly 78 percent of college-educated women married for the first time between 2006 and 2010 can expect their marriages to last at least two decades, and marriages of college-educated couples last longer than they did 30 years ago. Three factors influencing the relationship: (1) Economic stability; (2) Access to support networks; (3) Cognitive skills (communication, decision-making, conflict-resolution). [84]

### 8. The Counterargument — The Case Against College

**Declining Confidence in Higher Education**

- Gallup (July 8, 2024), "U.S. Confidence in Higher Education Now Closely Divided": Americans are split into roughly equal thirds: 36% have "a great deal or quite a lot" of confidence, 32% have "some," and 32% have "little or no" confidence in higher education. This reflects a sharp decline from 2015, when 57% had high confidence and only 10% had little or none. **Party divisions:** Republicans' confidence changed most dramatically—in 2015, 56% of Republicans had high confidence and 11% had little/none; today, 20% are confident and 50% have little or none. Independents fell from 48% to 35% confidence, and Democrats from 68% to 56%. Reasons for lack of confidence: 41% cite colleges pushing political agendas/"too liberal"/indoctrination; 37% say colleges don't teach relevant skills or degrees don't lead to jobs; 28% cite cost concerns and student debt. A majority of Republicans lacking confidence (53%) cite political agendas, while Democrats primarily cite cost. **68% say higher education is headed in the wrong direction** (31% right direction), including 81% of those with "some" confidence and 30% of those with high confidence. Americans are significantly more confident in two-year colleges than four-year colleges. (Gallup telephone survey June 3–23, 2024, 1,005 adults, ±4 percentage points; web survey of 2,000+ Gallup Panel members, conducted with the Lumina Foundation.) [85]

**Pew Research Center: "Is College Worth It?" (May 2024)**

- Based on Census Bureau Current Population Survey, Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances, and a Pew survey of 5,203 U.S. adults (Nov. 27–Dec. 3, 2023): After decades of falling wages, young workers (25–34) without a bachelor's degree have seen earnings increase over the past 10 years, wealth has risen, and fewer live in poverty. However, outcomes also improved for college graduates, so the earnings gap between the two groups has NOT narrowed. **A narrow majority (54% in 2023) of workers ages 25–34 do not have a four-year college degree.** **Only 22% of U.S. adults say the cost of college is worth it even if someone has to take out loans.** Even among four-year college graduates, only about a third (32%) agree—though they are more likely than non-graduates to say this. 58% of four-year college graduates (vs. only 26% of those without a degree) say their education was extremely or very useful in providing skills/knowledge for a well-paying job. Republicans are more likely than Democrats to question the importance of college for getting a well-paying job. About 4 in 10 Americans say a college degree is not too or not at all important to get a well-paying job. [86]

**Student Debt Crisis**

- Federal Reserve Board, "Report on the Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2023" (May 2024, SHED data): 70% of adults ever enrolled in education after high school; just over half received at least a certificate/technical degree, and 37% received at least a bachelor's degree. Educational attainment varies by demographics: Asian adults (90% enrolled, 67% bachelor's) vs. Hispanic adults (58% enrolled, 21% bachelor's). Adults with college-graduate parents were far more likely to earn a bachelor's degree (66% vs. 25%). More than half of adults who ever enrolled beyond high school said lifetime financial benefits exceeded costs; one in five said costs were higher. Those who completed at least an associate degree were far more likely to see net benefits (68% of bachelor's holders vs. 43% with associate degree vs. 28% without degree completion). Perceptions of value were lower among those with student loans (44% saw net benefits) vs. those who paid off or never had debt (68%). Value varied by institution type: 64% public, 66% private not-for-profit, but only 38% for-profit attendees saw net benefits. 45% of attendees would complete more education in hindsight; only 10% would complete less or not attend. 39% of those with for-profit bachelor's degrees would attend a different school. **30% of all adults took out student loans (18% still owe, 24% repaid fully). Median outstanding education debt was between $20,000 and $24,999; 28% of borrowers owed less than $10,000.** Debt incidence by institution: 40% public, 57% private not-for-profit, 63% private for-profit attendees had debt. 5% of all adults had loans for a child's or grandchild's education (median $15,000–$19,999). Black borrowers were more likely than White or Hispanic borrowers to carry higher debt balances. Following the payment restart (October 2023): 65% of borrowers were required to make payments; 16% of borrowers were behind or in collections. Borrowers with less education or lower income were more likely to be behind: 22% of associate degree holders vs. 7% of bachelor's holders; 24% of those earning under $25,000 vs. 7% earning $100,000+. Hispanic (27%) and Black (23%) borrowers had higher rates of being behind than White (10%) and Asian (13%) borrowers. 27% of for-profit institution borrowers were behind vs. 13% public and 11% private not-for-profit. Among those who EVER borrowed: 57% had completely paid off loans (up 7 percentage points). [87]

- The Pew Charitable Trusts (December 2024), "The Student Loan Default Divide: Racial Inequities Play a Role": **Half (50%) of Black and 40% of Hispanic or Latino borrowers have had a loan default compared with less than a third (29%) of White borrowers.** Of borrowers who have ever defaulted, around three-quarters of Black (74%) and Hispanic or Latino (75%) borrowers reported doing so more than once (redefault), compared with 56% of White borrowers. 70% of Black borrowers reported 2019 annual household income under $50,000; 83% of Black borrowers were first-generation students and 45% did not complete the degree for which they borrowed. Consequences of default: Treasury offsets (tax refund and Social Security seizure), wage garnishment (up to 15% of income), collection fees (up to ~24% of principal and interest), credit notation for seven years, ineligibility for financial aid and repayment plans, and potential loss of professional licenses. The top three reasons for default and redefault: having other higher-priority debts (72%), feeling overwhelmed (71–74%), and having unaffordable payments (68–67%). [88]

- A 2024 Money Magazine/Pew Research Center poll (Facebook post): 86% of U.S. workers with student loans believe their college degree was not worth the financial burden; only 22% of Americans believe college is worth it if it requires taking out loans. [89]

**The "BA Trap" and Underemployment**

- FREOPP (Foundation for Research on Equal Opportunity), "How Unnecessary College Degree Requirements Hurt the Working Class": Degree requirements increased by 60% since 2007, even after controlling for changes in job types (Blair & Deming study). In 1990, just 9% of secretaries had college degrees; the proportion has nearly quadrupled to 33% today. Workers without bachelor's degrees face a "paper ceiling"—employment penalties at every career stage (Blair, Debroy, and Heck NBER study). **Four in ten recent college graduates are underemployed, earning just $37,330/year vs. $47,470 for graduates in appropriate jobs.** Bachelor's degree holders among middle-class workers (earning $40,000–$60,000) rose from 26% in 1980 to 38% today. The share of Americans 25+ with a four-year degree rose from 21% in 1990 to 38% by 2022. Harvard Business School's 2017 report "Dismissed by Degrees" found 67% of production supervisor job postings requested degrees though only 16% of current workers had one. Top occupations driving degree inflation: managers and administrators (over 1 million excess degrees), registered nurses (738,754 excess degrees), computer software developers, salespersons, and secretaries. Case studies: Secretaries' salaries rose only 23% since 1990 yet education requirements quadrupled; registered nurses present the strongest case for degree requirements (BSN share rose from 46% to 73%, salaries rose 43%, and studies link BSN-educated nurses to better patient outcomes); promotion to management is significantly harder without a degree (during the Great Recession, degree-holders were more than twice as likely to be promoted). Policy recommendations include employers removing degree requirements, states removing degree requirements from public-sector jobs (ten states—Alaska, Colorado, Maryland, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Utah, Virginia—have announced skills-based hiring efforts; Maryland saw a 34% increase in applications from non-degree holders), and repealing laws mandating unnecessary degree requirements. [90]

- College Flight Path (2026 data): College graduates earn a median of roughly $80,000 annually vs. $47,000 for high school graduates (Federal Reserve Bank of New York data). The 2026 job market is the most competitive since the pandemic: unemployment for college grads ages 22–27 reached 5.3% in March 2026; **underemployment is 41.5%**; nursing has the lowest underemployment at 12.8%. Average student loan debt is $39,375. Students overestimate expected salaries by ~$24,000 (expecting $80,000 vs. actual $56,153). AI impacts ROI: 47% of students have considered switching majors due to AI; AI-exposed occupations saw 16% relative employment decline for early-career workers (2022–2025). [91]

**The Rise of Skill-Based Hiring / Degree Reset**

- Burning Glass Institute, "The Emerging Degree Reset" (Matt Sigelman): Employers are resetting degree requirements in a wide range of roles, dropping the requirement for a bachelor's degree in many middle-skill and even some higher-skill roles. This reverses a trend toward degree inflation in job postings going back to the Great Recession. Based on current trends, the research projects that **an additional 1.4 million jobs could open to workers without college degrees over the next five years**, potentially opening opportunities for the two-thirds of Americans without a college education. While the Covid-19 pandemic accelerated this process, the reset began before the crisis and is likely to continue after it. [92]

- Lightcast (February 2022, summarizing the Burning Glass report based on over 51 million job postings): Between 2017 and 2019, close to 46% of middle-skill and 37% of high-skill occupations experienced a reset in their education requirements. Postings now list hard (technical) and soft (social) skills in place of bachelor's degrees ("downcredentialing"). Only 27% of the postings that dropped requirements were "cyclical" (direct responses to Covid), while 63% of affected jobs were adjusted between 2017 and 2019. **"Jobs do not require four-year college degrees... Employers do."** By requiring a bachelor's degree, employers immediately disqualify the 64% of working-age Americans who do not have one. IBM announced in 2021 that it had removed the degree requirement for over half of its US job postings. The White House announced a skills-based hiring approach in June 2020 and January 2021. [93]

- CNBC (April 25, 2022): The tech industry faces severe labor gaps, with more than 450,000 open cybersecurity jobs. In February 2022, there were 11.27 million job openings versus 6.27 million unemployed people—a record 5 million more openings than available workers. Examples: Only 26% of Accenture's software quality-assurance engineer postings and 29% of IBM's postings required a degree; 50% of IBM's U.S. job openings do not require a four-year degree. In January 2021, the White House limited the use of educational requirements for federal IT positions, noting that focusing on degrees "excludes capable candidates and undermines labor market efficiencies." Accenture's apprenticeship program (launched 2016) has hired 1,200 people, 80% without a four-year degree, and now aims to fill 20% of U.S. entry-level roles. Bank of America no longer requires degrees for most entry-level jobs; its Pathways program exceeded its goal of hiring 10,000 people from low- and moderate-income neighborhoods by 2023 two years early, and committed to another 10,000 by 2025. Dell Technologies expanded recruitment to community colleges, associate degrees, apprenticeships, and certificate programs. [94]

- Stand Together (originally Forbes BrandVoice): Fewer than 40% of Americans hold a bachelor's degree, yet most jobs still require one, causing employers to miss out on more than 70 million qualified U.S. workers without degrees. Between 2017–2019, 46% of middle-skill and 31% of high-skill occupations saw declines in degree requirements (2022 Harvard Business School and Burning Glass Institute study). An Indeed survey found 59% of employers would consider dropping degree requirements. In June 2020, President Trump signed an executive order directing the federal government to de-emphasize degrees. In March 2022, Maryland Gov. Larry Hogan made Maryland the first state to eliminate degree requirements for most government jobs, resulting in a 41% increase in non-degree hires from May–August 2022. New Jersey, Virginia, and Utah (98% of state jobs) also dropped degree requirements. Bank of America, Dell, Delta Airlines, IBM (29% of IT jobs), and Accenture (43% of IT jobs) reduced degree requirements. Benefits cited include reduced turnover costs (non-degree workers stay 34% longer in jobs), higher loyalty and satisfaction, and more agile workforces. The 2022 HBS/Burning Glass report estimates dropping degree conditions could open 1.4 million jobs to workers without degrees over five years. [95]

**FREOPP Return on Investment Research**

- FREOPP, "Is College Worth It? A Comprehensive Return on Investment Analysis" (Preston Cooper; ~30,000 bachelor's degree programs at 1,775 colleges): For students who graduate on time, the median bachelor's degree has a net ROI of $306,000, but variation is enormous. After accounting for the risk of dropping out or taking longer than four years, median ROI drops to $129,000, and **28% of programs have negative ROI. When adjusted for the full underlying cost of education, 37% of programs have negative ROI.** Four in five engineering programs have ROI above $500,000, but only 1% of psychology programs do; 69% of engineering programs deliver $1 million+ lifetime payoff; 85% of computer science programs exceed $500,000. The best program in the country is computer science at Caltech (ROI over $4.4 million), followed by finance at Penn's Wharton School ($4.35 million). Over 100 programs at colleges with acceptance rates below 20% have negative ROI, including Harvard's ethnic and gender studies major (negative $47,000) and Penn's film program (negative $140,000). The median bachelor's degree produces earnings of ~$39,000 at age 25, $65,000 at age 35, and just over $71,000 at age 45. College graduates earn 67% more than high school graduates overall. **Choice of major is more important than choice of institution, explaining nearly half the variation in ROI.** A majority of psychology programs (58%) are negative-ROI after completion adjustment; the median psychology student waits 23 years before ROI turns positive. Every year in college costs students around $24,000 in foregone earnings. A quarter to a third of four-year college students never graduate, and dropouts typically lose over $100,000. For-profit colleges have poor completion outcomes (19% on-time graduation vs. 41% at public and 57% at private nonprofits), leading to 55% of their programs having negative ROI. [96]

- FREOPP, "Does College Pay Off? A Comprehensive Return on Investment Analysis" (53,000 degree and certificate programs): **31 percent of students are enrolled in programs with negative ROI (~23% of bachelor's, 43% of associate, and ~43% of master's degree programs).** Median bachelor's degree ROI: $160,000; median subbaccalaureate program: just $18,000. Highest-paying majors: engineering ($949,000 median ROI), computer science ($652,000), nursing ($619,000), economics ($549,000). Low/negative ROI majors include fine arts, English, education, and psychology. **Undergraduate technical trade certificates have stronger ROI ($313,000 median) than the median bachelor's degree.** Graduate ROI is mixed: law ($470,000 median), medicine, and dentistry often exceed $1 million; but half of master's programs have no ROI, and the MBA has a median ROI of just $101,000 with 39% negative. Princeton's computer engineering program has the highest ROI at $7.1 million; USC's drama program is negative $540,000. **About 29% ($122 billion of $418 billion) of federal Pell Grant and loan funding between 2018–2022 went to negative-ROI programs.** Median graduate earnings at age 27: ~$52,000 vs. counterfactual $37,000 (39% wage premium, vs. the 68% raw premium). "The more important question is when college is worth it." [97]

- FREOPP College ROI Tool (oaprep.com): FREOPP calculated ROI for approximately 53,000 degree and certificate programs. 23% of bachelor's degree programs have a negative ROI; 6% have expected ROI greater than $1 million; the median bachelor's program has an estimated ROI of approximately $160,000. Engineering, computer science, nursing, and economics have particularly strong returns. Technical-trade certificate programs can have a higher payoff than a typical bachelor's degree. [98]

- FREOPP ROI in Higher Education hub: Bachelor's degree programs have a median ROI of $160,000; associate degree and certificate programs show variable ROI by field (two-year liberal arts degrees have no ROI, while technical trade certificates outperform the typical bachelor's degree); nearly half of master's degree programs leave students financially worse off, but professional degrees in law, medicine, and dentistry are highly lucrative; roughly a third of federal Pell Grant and student loan funding goes to programs that do not provide students with a positive ROI. [99]

### Additional Contextual Findings

- Pew Research Center, "Public Opinion Polling Basics" (Scott Keeter): Polls provide an equal voice to everyone in the population regardless of wealth, age, education, or race. A cautionary example: an opt-in poll found 20% of adults under 30 agreed "the Holocaust is a myth," while Pew's probability-based panel found only 3%. National polls in 2020 overstated Joe Biden's margin over Trump by 3.9 percentage points on average (largest error since 1980); accuracy improved in 2022. Response rates have declined dramatically; people with higher education and income are more likely to participate in surveys. [33]

- Scholarships.com (community service scholarships page): Volunteer service has seen a huge resurgence among young people after declining with the COVID-19 pandemic. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, between 2022–2023, more than 28% of Americans age 16 and over participated in formal volunteer service. [27]

- Wayne State University Volunteer Hub: Connects students to volunteer opportunities on campus and in the Detroit community; reports service hours to the student's Involvement Record; partners with SHARE Detroit, a community engagement platform. [100]

args.research_topic: Financial Return on Investment (ROI) of a Bachelor's Degree in the United States — Comprehensive research on the financial dimension of whether a college degree is worth it. This should cover: (1) Lifetime earnings premium — how much more do bachelor's degree holders earn vs. high school graduates over a career? Use data from the Federal Reserve, Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), Georgetown University Center on Education and the Workforce, and the Social Security Administration. (2) Tuition and fee costs — average cost of a 4-year degree at public and private institutions, including recent trends (2016-2026). Use data from the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) and College Board. (3) Student debt statistics — average debt at graduation, default rates, and the impact on major life decisions (homeownership, marriage, retirement savings). Use data from the Federal Reserve, New York Fed Consumer Credit Panel, and Department of Education. (4) Opportunity cost — foregone wages during 4 years of study. (5) Net present value and ROI calculations — what is the financial breakeven point? How does ROI vary by major, institution type, and race/gender? (6) The college wage premium — how has it changed over time, especially from 2016-2026? (7) Comparisons with other investments (stock market, real estate) as alternative uses of tuition money. Cite specific reports, academic papers, and government data sources with dates and publication details.

Career Stability and Mobility for Bachelor's Degree Holders vs. Non-Degree Holders in the United States — Comprehensive research on career outcomes. This should cover: (1) Employment rates — unemployment rates for bachelor's degree holders vs. high school graduates, using BLS data 2016-2026. (2) Underemployment rates — how many college graduates work in jobs that don't require a degree? Use data from the Federal Reserve, St. Louis Fed, and Burning Glass Institute. (3) Job security — how does degree attainment affect likelihood of job loss, layoff vulnerability, and re-employment speed? (4) Promotion and career advancement opportunities — degree requirements for management positions, the "degree creep" phenomenon where jobs that didn't used to require degrees now do. (5) Earnings growth over a career — how does the earnings trajectory differ between degree holders and non-degree holders? (6) Industry variation — which fields/industries have the strongest degree premium? (7) The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the value of degrees in the labor market. (8) The rise of alternatives — coding bootcamps, trade schools, apprenticeships, and their relative career outcomes. Use data from BLS, Georgetown CEW, Burning Glass Institute, Harvard Business School's "Dismissed by Degrees" report, and academic research on credentialing.

Broader Personal and Societal Benefits of a College Education in the United States — Comprehensive research covering non-financial dimensions. This should cover: (1) Health outcomes — correlation between education level and life expectancy, health behaviors, health insurance coverage, and chronic disease rates. Use CDC, NIH, and academic research. (2) Civic engagement — voting rates, volunteerism, charitable giving, and community involvement among college graduates vs. non-graduates. Use data from the Pew Research Center, CIRCLE, and the Corporation for National and Community Service. (3) Intergenerational benefits — how parental education affects children's educational attainment, health, and income. (4) Social mobility — does college act as an equalizer for disadvantaged students? Use data from the Equality of Opportunity Project (Raj Chetty et al.), Pell Institute, and the National Bureau of Economic Research. (5) Networking and social capital — the value of alumni networks, peer effects, and professional connections. (6) Life satisfaction and happiness — research on subjective well-being and education levels. (7) Marriage and family outcomes — correlation between education and marriage stability, divorce rates, and family formation. (8) The counterargument — the case against college: the student debt crisis, the "BA trap" of low-paying jobs requiring degrees, the rise of skill-based hiring, and the growing skepticism about the value of college. Use data from Pew, Gallup, the Federal Reserve, the Foundation for Research on Equal Opportunity (FREOPP), and academic research.

messages.content:
# Financial Return on Investment (ROI) of a Bachelor's Degree in the United States — Research Findings

## List of Queries and Tool Calls Made

**Round 1 — Core statistics (earnings, tuition, debt, wage premium):**
1. "lifetime earnings premium bachelor's degree vs high school graduate 2024 2025 Federal Reserve BLS Georgetown University"
2. "average cost of 4-year degree public private college 2024 2025 NCES College Board tuition trends"
3. "average student debt at graduation 2024 2025 Federal Reserve New York Fed default rates"
4. "college wage premium over time 2016-2026 bachelor's degree ROI"

**Round 2 — ROI studies, debt impact on life decisions, Georgetown payoff, investment comparisons:**
5. "Federal Reserve Bank New York Abel Deitz college degree benefits costs ROI 17 percent 2024"
6. "student loan debt impact homeownership marriage retirement savings Federal Reserve Bank New York research"
7. "Georgetown University College Payoff 2021 lifetime earnings by major bachelor's degree"
8. "college degree investment vs stock market S&P 500 return comparison tuition alternative investment"

**Round 3 — NCES data, TICAS debt at graduation, Georgetown ROI by institution:**
9. "NCES average tuition fees public private 4-year 2016 2026 price of attending college Digest of Education Statistics"
10. "TICAS average debt at graduation bachelor's degree class of 2024 student debt report"
11. "Georgetown CEW A First Try at ROI breakeven college investment by institution type 2019"

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### I. LIFETIME EARNINGS PREMIUM — BACHELOR'S vs. HIGH SCHOOL GRADUATES

#### A. 2024 BLS and Census data (reported via Quantumrun, 2026)
- Professional degree holders earn the most at **$2,363/week**, compared to $738 for those without a high school diploma and $930 for high school graduates [1].
- Bachelor's degree holders earn **$1,543/week — a 66% premium over high school graduates** ($930/week) [1].
- Annualized income ranges from $38,376 (no diploma) to $122,876 (professional degree) [1].
- Households headed by someone with a bachelor's degree or higher had a **median income of $132,700 in 2024**, versus **$58,410** for those with only a high school diploma. The income gap has widened from 2:1 in 2004 to **2.3:1 in 2024** [1].
- Unemployment rates (2024 BLS): range from 1.2% (doctoral degree) to 6.2% (no high school diploma). Bachelor's degree holders had a **2.5% unemployment rate** [1].
- Lifetime earnings (Georgetown CEW): range from $1.6 million (high school diploma) to $4.7 million (professional degree). A bachelor's degree yields **$2.8 million, a 75% premium over high school** [1].
- The earnings–education relationship holds even at early career stages; field of study and occupation matter considerably alongside credential level [1].

#### B. Social Security Administration research summary (Tamborini, Kim & Sakamoto, 2015, Demography 52: 1383–1407)
- Men with bachelor's degrees earn approximately **$900,000 more in median lifetime earnings** than high school graduates; women earn **$630,000 more** [2].
- Men with graduate degrees earn $1.5 million more; women with graduate degrees earn $1.1 million more [2].
- After controlling for socio-demographic variables, the differences are reduced but still substantial: men with bachelor's degrees earn **$655,000 more**, and women earn **$450,000 more** than high school graduates [2].
- Using a 4% annual real discount rate, the **net present lifetime value at age 20** of a bachelor's degree relative to a high school diploma is **$260,000 for men and $180,000 for women**; for graduate degrees, $400,000 for men and $310,000 for women [2].
- Data source: 2004 Survey of Income and Program Participation matched to Social Security Administration longitudinal records [2].

#### C. Full academic paper (PMC version of the same study)
- Gross lifetime earnings — Men: high school diploma ~**$1.54 million**; bachelor's degree **$2.43 million**; graduate degree **$3.05 million**. Women: **$811,000**, **$1.44 million**, **$1.87 million** respectively [3].
- Net lifetime earnings (after controlling for covariates): the gap between HSG and BA decreases from **$896,000 to $655,000 for men** and from **$630,000 to $445,000 for women**. Accounting for key covariates reduces the estimated lifetime earnings return to college by approximately **30%** [3].
- Net present value at age 20 (4% discount rate): **~$259,000 for men and $180,000 for women** [3].
- Methodology: semi-synthetic cohort approach combining four birth cohorts (1932-1939, 1942-1949, 1952-1959, 1962-1969) to estimate 50-year earnings from ages 20 to 69, using quantile regression at the median, controlling for race/ethnicity, marital status, number of children (women), region of birth, and high school academic preparation [3].
- Purely synthetic cohort methods (cross-sectional data) **overstate the earnings gains associated with a bachelor's degree by 23% for men and 42% for women** compared to longitudinal administrative data [3].
- Authors' conclusion: "Our results confirm the persistent positive effects of higher education on earnings over different stages of the work career and over a lifetime, but also reveal notably smaller net effects on lifetime earnings compared with previously reported estimates" [3].

#### D. Association of Public and Land-grant Universities (APLU)
- College graduates are **half as likely to be unemployed** as peers whose highest degree is a high school diploma [4].
- Typical earnings for bachelor's degree holders are **$40,500 (86%) higher** than those whose highest degree is a high school diploma [4].
- **87% of bachelor's degree holders report financial wellbeing**, 20 percentage points higher than any other education level [4].
- **Median lifetime earnings are $1.2 million higher** for bachelor's degree holders [4].
- In 2023, median income for recent graduates (ages 22–27) reached **$60,000/year** for bachelor's degree holders vs. **$36,000** for high school graduates [4].
- Jobless rate for bachelor's degree holders is less than 3%; poverty incidence is **3.5 times lower** than for high school graduates [4].
- **Over the past decade, all net job growth has gone to workers with bachelor's or graduate degrees** [4].
- Bachelor's degree holders are **47% more likely to have employer-provided health insurance**, with employers contributing 74% more toward coverage [4].
- Studies suggest those who attended some college live **seven years longer** than peers with no postsecondary education [4].
- Two-thirds of bachelor's degrees in the U.S. are awarded by public universities [4].

#### E. Utah System of Higher Education (January 10, 2017; based on College Board "Education Pays 2016")
- College graduates with a full-time job earn **67% more** than high school graduates working full-time [5].
- By age 64, those with a bachelor's degree earn, on average, **50% more** than high school graduates [5].
- The unemployment rate for 25- to 34-year-olds with a bachelor's degree was **2.6% (2016)**, more than five percentage points below the rate for those with just a high school education [5].
- **99% of jobs filled since December 2007 have gone to workers with at least some college education** (Georgetown University) [5].
- In Utah, 3 out of 4 college graduates are employed within 12 months of graduation; Utah's 2015-16 graduates were estimated to provide $48 million in increased tax revenues annually; bachelor's degree recipients paid an estimated **91% more in taxes** than those with a high school diploma [5].
- Higher educational attainment provides greater insulation from economic downturns (Great Recession unemployment data) [5].

#### F. UNC Charlotte (2026, citing BLS and UNC System data)
- Workers with a bachelor's degree earn about **$1,533 per week** on average, compared with **$946 per week** for workers with only a high school diploma (BLS) [17].
- Economists at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York estimate that the **average return on a college degree is around 12.5%**, a level they consider a strong long-term investment [17].
- Across the UNC System, a 2023 ROI analysis (with the Burning Glass Institute) found graduates see a **median lifetime return on investment of about $500,000** after accounting for tuition costs; 94% of undergraduate programs produce positive financial returns; graduates earn ~$1.2 million over their lifetimes on average; many recover degree costs within ~10 years [17].
- UNC System enrollment increased 3.4% for 2025-26 [17].
- "The biggest financial risk in college isn't always picking the wrong major. **It's not finishing the degree at all**" [17].

#### G. AEFP Live Handbook (Webber & Carruthers, updated July 2026)
- The median college graduate in 2023 can expect to earn **$1.3 million more than the median high-school graduate** over a lifetime. After accounting for taxes, costs, and discounting, the net benefit is roughly **$243,000** [18].
- Quasi-experimental causal estimates consistently show returns of **8–18% per year of schooling** [18].
- Approximately **26% of college graduates are predicted to earn less than the median high-school graduate** [18].
- Returns differ by race (**$1.38M for white graduates vs. $1.0M for Black graduates**) and gender (**$1.56M for men vs. $0.99M for women**) [18].
- The choice of major matters more than the choice of institution [18].
- Only about **60% of four-year college students graduate**. For those with "some college" but no degree, the median lifetime premium is only **$260,000** (vs. $1.3M for graduates); after taxes and discounting it's just **$17,000**. Only 48% of "some college" individuals earn more than the median high-school graduate [18].
- 37% of bachelor's degree holders pursue graduate degrees [18].
- "The single greatest risk-factor for college not 'paying off' is failure to graduate" [18].

#### H. Minneapolis Fed (2025)
- Lifetime earnings for bachelor's degree holders average **$2.8 million** versus **$1.6 million** for high school graduates [20].

---

### II. TUITION AND FEE COSTS — AVERAGE COST OF A 4-YEAR DEGREE (INCLUDING 2016–2026 TRENDS)

#### A. College Board, Trends in College Pricing 2025 (2025-26 academic year)
**Published (sticker) tuition and fees:**
- Public four-year in-state: **$11,950** (+$340, 2.9% increase) [8]
- Public four-year out-of-state: **$31,880** (+$1,060, 3.4% increase) [8]
- Public two-year in-district: **$4,150** (+$110, 2.7% increase) [8]
- Private nonprofit four-year: **$45,000** (+$1,750, 4.0% increase) [8]

**Price variation by location:**
- Public two-year in-district tuition ranges from $1,440 (California) to $8,900 (Vermont) [8]
- Public four-year in-state tuition ranges from $6,360 (Florida) to $18,090 (Vermont) [8]

**Net prices (after grant aid):**
- First-time students at public two-year colleges have had enough grant aid to cover tuition and fees since 2009-10 [8]
- Net tuition at public four-year institutions **peaked at $4,450 (2012-13) and declined to an estimated $2,300 (2025-26)**, in 2025 dollars [8]
- Net tuition at private nonprofit four-year institutions declined from $19,810 (2006-07) to an estimated **$16,910 (2025-26)**, in 2025 dollars [8]

**Family income:** Between 1994 and 2024, average income rose 58% for the top quintile of families, but only 33% for the lowest quintile (adjusted for inflation) [8].

**Institutional finances:** State and local funding per student in 2023-24 was **$11,680** (national average), ranging from $5,510 (NH) to over $20,000 (CT, HI, IL, AK) [8].

**Enrollment:** Total postsecondary enrollment rebounded to **18.9 million in fall 2023** (+455,000, 2% growth) after three years of Covid-era declines. Public two-year enrollment fell 8.6% between fall 2019 and fall 2023 overall, but grew 4.3% between fall 2022 and fall 2023 [8].

#### B. NCES Digest of Education Statistics, Table 330.20 (2023 edition, prepared January 2024; AY 2021-22 and 2022-23)
**2022-23 national figures:**
- Public 4-year institutions: **$22,389 total charges** ($9,750 tuition and required fees, $7,167 room, $5,472 board) [41]
- Private 4-year institutions: **$49,654 total** ($35,248 tuition and fees) [41]
- Public 2-year institutions: **$3,598 in-state tuition/fees**; $8,565 out-of-state [41]

**State examples:**
- Highest public 4-year total charges: Vermont ($30,887) and Connecticut ($30,046) [41]
- Lowest public 4-year totals: Wyoming ($15,244) and Utah ($16,030); DC is an outlier at $6,152 (no room/board data) [41]
- California had the lowest public 2-year in-state tuition/fees at $1,286 [41]
- Private 4-year totals ranged widely, with Massachusetts highest at $71,563 total ($53,789 tuition) [41]

#### C. EducationData.org — Average Cost of College (2022-23 academic year)
- The average total cost of college (including tuition, fees, books, supplies, and living expenses) is **$38,270 per student per year** [6].
- The average cost of college has more than doubled in the 21st century; the **compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of tuition is 4.04%** [6].
- In-state students at public 4-year institutions living on campus spent **$27,146 annually** (tuition: $9,750) [6].
- Out-of-state tuition at public 4-year institutions averages **$28,386** [6].
- Private nonprofit university students living on campus paid **$58,628 annually** ($38,421 for tuition and fees) [6].
- Community college in-district tuition averages **$3,598** [6].
- Considering student loan interest and lost potential income, **investing in a bachelor's degree can ultimately cost upwards of $500,000** [6].
- The median weekly income for high school graduates is $899 ($46,748/year), representing lost income potential while studying [6].
- Student borrowers pay an average of **$2,636 in interest each year** and spend roughly **20 years paying off loans** [6].
- In 1963 the annual tuition at a 4-year public college was $243 (equivalent to $2,489 in 2024 dollars). From 1963 to 2022, tuition increased at a **CAGR of 2.34% after adjusting for inflation**. Between 2012-13 and 2022-23, tuition increased **25.6%** at all 4-year colleges [6].
- Most expensive states for public university tuition: Vermont ($17,600), New Hampshire ($17,019), Pennsylvania ($16,217). Least expensive: Florida ($4,540), Wyoming ($5,100), District of Columbia ($6,152) [6].

#### D. College Shortcuts — Tuition Costs Comparison 2025 (2024-25 academic year)
- In-state students at public four-year institutions pay an average of **$11,610 in tuition and fees** (total budget $29,910) [7].
- Out-of-state students at public four-years average **$30,780** (total budget $49,080) [7].
- Public two-year college students pay **$4,050** (total budget $20,570) [7].
- Private nonprofit four-year students pay **$43,350** (total budget $62,990) [7].

#### H. BestColleges — Cost of College Every Year Since the 1960s (NCES data)
- One year's college tuition and fees cost just over **$4,939 in 1963**, rising to roughly **$14,690 by 2022** (2022-23 constant dollars) — tuition has more than tripled, or increased by over 125% (~2.3 times) [43].
- The average total cost of a year of college (including room and board, books, and supplies) rose from about $12,130 in 1963 to just under $28,000 in 2022 — more than doubled, an increase of 128% [43].
- Between 2000 and 2022, average tuition and fees rose by 60%, from $9,204 to $14,688 per year. Between 2010 and 2022, tuition rose by 13%, from $12,979 to $14,688 [43].
- Room and board almost doubled between 1963 and 2022, increasing 81% from $7,187 to $12,986. From 2000 to 2022, room and board rose about 39% while tuition rose 60% [43].
- The period 1973-1980 was one of the only periods when average tuition and fees decreased. Tuition rose again by 1981-82 and continued rising nearly every year since. The only other exception was between 2020 and 2022, when tuition and fees dropped by about 6% [43].
- Between 2000 and 2022, tuition increased most at private nonprofit two-year institutions (+68%). Four-year public colleges saw the steepest price hikes from 2000-2022, jumping from roughly $13,000 to just over $20,000 annually (39% increase) [43].
- Between 1963 and 2022, average cost of attendance increased most at private institutions (180%, or 2.79x); four-year institutions increased ~147%, two-year institutions increased 63%, and public institutions rose 130% [43].
- From 2012-2022, average total cost rose 5%, from $26,209 to $27,673. Public school costs rose from $19,458 to $20,401 (~5%); private college costs rose from $44,668 to $49,320 (~10%) [43].
- College tuition became more expensive than room and board for the first time in 1999 [43].
- Over the last decade, total cost of attendance increased 8% at four-year schools for students living on campus versus 2% for students living off campus [43].

### III. STUDENT DEBT STATISTICS

#### A. Aggregate debt totals (Education Data Initiative, updated July 16, 2026; NY Fed; SoFi)
- Total student loan debt: **$1.863 trillion**; federal debt **$1.724 trillion (91.1%)**; private debt 9.13% [11].
- **42.6 million federal borrowers** [11].
- Average federal balance: **$40,467**; total average balance (including private): **$43,521** [11].
- SoFi reports average debt of **$39,547** per borrower; student loan debt is the **third-largest category of U.S. household debt** (behind mortgages and auto loans) [27].
- Debt grew from $1.02 trillion in 2015 to $1.83 trillion in 2025 (~80% increase over the decade) [27].
- Trends: After declining in 2023-24 (first YoY declines in over a decade), debt resumed growth in 2025. In 2026 Q1, total debt increased $57.2 billion YoY. Federal debt grew $31.3 billion in H1 2026. Quarterly YoY growth averaged 3.63% in H1 2026. Private loan debt totaled $166.4 billion in 2026 Q1 [11].
- Most borrowers pay between **$200 and $299 per month** [27].

#### B. NY Fed Consumer Credit Panel / Equifax (Mangrum & Wang, 2025 Student Loan Update, 2024Q4)
- **Total student loan borrowers: 43.1 million** as of 2024Q4, down from a peak of ~44.5 million in 2017-2018 [14].
- **Total outstanding balances: $1.612 trillion** in 2024Q4, up from $1.507 trillion in 2019Q4 [14].
- Distribution: largest share of borrowers (26.1%) have balances between $10,000-$25,000; ~2.3% have balances over $200,000 [14].
- Age: borrowers under 30 declined from 15.9M (2019) to 14.0M (2024); borrowers aged 30-39 increased from 12.0M to 12.7M. Balances are highest among 30-39 year olds ($530.8B) [14].
- Payment status (affected by Fresh Start program beginning late 2022): defaulted borrowers dropped dramatically from **4.5M (2019) to just 189,000 (2024)**; borrowers 90+ days delinquent fell from 2.0M (2019) to 252,000 (2024). The majority of borrowers now have "current, balance same or higher" status (27.2M) [14].
- Median credit score for all borrowers rose from **662 (2019) to 684 (2024)** [14].
- Median balance rose from $17,532 (2019) to **$19,124 (2024)**; average balance rose from $34,280 to **$37,390** [14].
- State data (2024Q4): California has the most borrowers (3.95M) and highest total balance ($156B), followed by Texas (3.9M, $133.2B), Florida (2.7M, $108.1B), and New York (2.5M, $100.3B). DC has the highest average balance ($59,990) and median balance ($27,540) [14].

- By degree type (SoFi, NPSAS-based): associate $23,854; bachelor's **$29,490 (public)** / **$33,689 (private nonprofit)**; master's $81,870 average / $95,381 private nonprofit; MBA $76,996; doctoral $77,331; professional degrees: medical school $235,788, law $167,399, professional-doctorate (private nonprofit) $281,817 [27].

Lowest — Utah ($18,344, 39%), New Mexico ($20,868, 45%), California ($21,125, 46%), Nevada ($21,357, 46%), Washington ($23,993, 47%) [46].

Prestigious institutions: Stanford ($24,337, 16% in debt), Yale ($14,884, 14%), UChicago ($26,560, 13%), Caltech ($16,950, 28%).
